<meta>This page begins the preface of a medical-philosophical treatise. The author, Angelo Poliziano, addresses Niccolò Leoniceno regarding his critique of Avicenna and Pliny the Elder.</meta>

# ANGELO POLIZIANO
## TO NICCOLÒ LEONICENO
### GREETINGS.

<margin>
More danger from the doctor than the disease.
</margin>

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'D' showing a landscape with a castle tower and a figure in the foreground.</image-desc>
Those lectures of yours, Niccolò, in which you refute the ignorance of Avicenna <note>Avicenna (Ibn Sina) was a Persian physician whose "Canon of Medicine" was the standard medieval textbook, though Renaissance humanists like Leoniceno began to challenge his translations and interpretations</note> and teach the younger physicians in what great darkness of things they are involved, I do not know whether they have brought me more pleasure or pain. For I have rejoiced wonderfully that those matters, upon which the life and health of men depend, have been brought into the light by that man above all whom I have always valued most highly for his talent and learning. And yet, I have grieved in turn for the sake of the human race, because it allows this dismal ignorance to rage against itself for so long with impunity, and sometimes purchases the hope of life at a price from those very sources whence the most certain death proceeds. For who does not see that there is more danger from the doctor than from the disease, since one illness is treated in place of another, and the wrong remedies are applied for the wrong conditions? 

But if that ancient age had produced you, Niccolò—the age in which rewards were rendered according to merit—you would not have lacked even the honors of the gods; unless, perhaps, we believe it is a greater thing to snatch one or two people from death, as Aesculapius <note>The Greek god of medicine and healing</note> did, than to rescue all men alike from the very danger of death, as you yourself are doing. Therefore, I beseech you, continue on the path you have begun: namely, so that by this one labor you may both produce immortal glory for yourself and provide life and health to all those who have truly been "sickly mortals" <note>original: "mortalibus ægris," a Virgilian poetic phrase for humanity</note> until now. 

However, as to the fact that you also refute our Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, author of the "Natural History"</note>, as if he had mistaken the rock-rose <note>original: "cisthon"</note> for ivy, in this matter—to speak freely and as a friend—I disagree with you entirely. Nor shall I fear to boldly undertake the defense of that man who deserved so excellently of life and letters, especially against you—that is, against an eminent philosopher, to whom nothing ought to be more ancient <note>meaning "more important" or "more venerable"</note> than the truth itself. For those [arguments] are from your scho—

<summary>Angelo Poliziano writes to the scholar Niccolò Leoniceno, praising his critique of medieval medical ignorance (specifically Avicenna) while politely defending the Roman author Pliny the Elder against Leoniceno's botanical corrections.</summary>
<keywords>Angelo Poliziano, Niccolò Leoniceno, Avicenna, Pliny the Elder, medical humanism, history of medicine, Aesculapius, botanical errors</keywords>

--- Page 7 ---
<meta>This page continues the scholarly correspondence between Angelo Poliziano and Niccolò Leoniceno regarding botanical nomenclature in classical texts.</meta>

# ANGELO POLIZIANO TO NICCOLÒ LEONICENO

Socrates is a friend, but truth is a greater friend; and while both are dear, more honor must be given to the truth. <note>A variation of the famous Aristotelian maxim "Amicus Plato, sed magis amica veritas."</note> You claim, then, that Pliny—just like Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the Persian physician whose medical texts were central to Medieval and Renaissance learning.</note>—does not distinguish the *cisthos* <note>The Rock-rose (Cistus).</note> from the *hedera* <note>Ivy (Hedera).</note>; if this were so, it would be a grave error, since the rock-rose differs greatly from ivy in shape, color, and medicinal properties. You add that this is more surprising in Pliny than in Avicenna, because Pliny, being skilled in the Greek language, ought to have known how to separate *cisthos* from *cissos* (which is ivy). You bring forward an argument as to why he does not separate one from the other: because in Book 16, Chapter 34 of his *Natural History*, he divides ivy into male and female, and says the flower of both is similar to the wild rose. Then, in Book 24, he also divides that *cisthos* (under which the *hypocisthis* <note>A parasitic plant that grows on the roots of the rock-rose.</note> grows) into male and female, attributing a rose-colored flower to the male and a white flower to the female. Finally, you note that he even claims to have mentioned this *cisthos* among the ivies. Therefore, you seem to conclude thus: Since Pliny teaches in Book 24 that he made mention of the *cisthos* among the ivies, yet the word itself is nowhere cited previously among the ivies, it is an easy conjecture that the *cisthos* was included by him under the name of "ivy"—especially since he divides ivy into male and female just as he does the *cisthos*, and describes a flower among the ivies. Now that I have set forth your view, I shall explain my opposing opinion. I deny that mention of the *cisthos* was made by Pliny anywhere among the ivies, except in Book 24, where he clearly distinguished it from ivy. For as to what you take as Pliny's testimony—that he spoke elsewhere of the *cisthos* among the ivies—I do not concede this at all. For to me, where he says this (namely in Book 24), he seems to be discussing the *cisthos* only up to that specific clause, which in his text reads:

<margin>,,</margin> Under these especially grows the *hypocisthis*. But immediately after
<margin>,,</margin> that, there is a punctuation mark, and the words begin anew thus: That
<margin>,,</margin> which we mentioned among the ivies, called *cissos erithranos* <note>original: "cissos erithranos" — likely a corruption of the Greek 'cissos erythranos' or red-berried ivy.</note> by those same people...

<summary>Angelo Poliziano debates Niccolò Leoniceno on whether Pliny the Elder confused the rock-rose (cistus) with ivy (hedera), arguing that a misreading of Pliny's text has led to a botanical misunderstanding.</summary>
<keywords>Angelo Poliziano, Niccolò Leoniceno, Pliny the Elder, Avicenna, botany, rock-rose, ivy, philology, Natural History</keywords>

--- Page 8 ---
<meta>This page continues Angelo Poliziano’s philological analysis of botanical terms in Pliny the Elder’s "Natural History," specifically focusing on the distinction between ivy and the rock-rose.</meta>

# THE WORKS OF ANGELO POLIZIANO
<note>Poliziano (1454–1494) was a leading Italian humanist scholar known for his rigorous correction of classical texts.</note>

...is like ivy. Given your own elegance in literature, I do not fear that you will fail to recognize the figure of speech, such as that found in Ovid:
> The letter which you read comes from the abducted Briseis. <note>original: "Quam legis à rapta Briseide litera venit." From Ovid's Heroides 3.1. Poliziano is discussing a grammatical construction where "quam" (which) refers to a noun following it.</note> And again:
> That health which she herself will lack unless you give it, 
> the Cretan girl sends to the Amazonian hero. <note>original: "Quam nisi tu dederis, caritura est ipsa salutem, Mittit amazonio cressa puella viro." From Ovid's Heroides 4.1-2 (Phaedra to Hippolytus).</note>

But if you prefer to refer that "which" to what precedes it, you would be forced to refer it to the *hypocisthis* <term>hypocisthis: a parasitic plant (Cytinus hypocistis) that grows on the roots of the rock-rose</term>, for this stands earlier in the text, rather than to the *cisthos* <term>cisthos: the rock-rose (Cistus)</term>. Yet he [Pliny] is entirely silent regarding the *hypocisthis* earlier—that is, in Book 16 among the ivies—even though he speaks there of the *erithranos* <note>A type of ivy mentioned by Pliny.</note>. Furthermore, he never mentions *cisthos* anywhere else among the ivies, nor does the distinction between male and female seem as specific to *cisthos* as it is to nearly all trees and shrubs—a fact which Pliny himself does not hide. What of the fact that the flower is also described differently? In ivy, the flower of the male and female is the same color, but in *cisthos* they are clearly of different colors. 

As for his comparison of the ivy-like flower to the wild rose, I think he is suggesting not so much the color, but rather the downy fuzz <note>original: "lanuginem"</note> such as is found inside roses; this is why Theophrastus <note>Ancient Greek philosopher and the "father of botany."</note> called the ivy flower *chuoedes* <note>original: "χυοώδη" (chuoōdē), meaning downy or woolly.</note>. Therefore, I believe it is sufficiently clear that there is nothing forcing us to admit that Pliny, in Book 16, included the *cisthos* among the ivies. However, in Book 24, he did link *cisthos* to ivy, just as he did with *chamaecissos* <term>chamaecissos: ground-ivy</term>—not because he believed *cisthos* and ivy were the same thing, but because the Greeks call it by a "neighboring name" (for those are his words). 

Lest anyone be deceived by the similarity of the name, he applied a distinction most carefully in the very place where the occasion for confusion arose. Not content with that, he also added properties of the *cisthos* that are entirely different from ivy. For nowhere previously did he describe ivy as being larger than thyme, or having leaves like basil, or finally, having a white flower. Therefore, who can now doubt that we must rule in favor of Pliny? Not even a suspicion of that error should touch him. I confess I wonder in passing how it came into your mind...

<summary>Poliziano uses grammatical analysis and botanical evidence from Ovid, Pliny, and Theophrastus to argue that the rock-rose (cisthos) should not be confused with ivy (hedera), despite their similar Greek names.</summary>
<keywords>Angelo Poliziano, Pliny the Elder, botany, philology, ivy, rock-rose, Ovid, Theophrastus, Latin grammar, plant classification</keywords>

--- Page 9 ---
<meta>This page continues a scholarly correspondence regarding the botanical and philological accuracy of Pliny the Elder, specifically addressing the origins of plant names.</meta>

# LETTER TO NICCOLÒ LEONICENO

...it would be a mistake to consider the plant *ledon*—or if you prefer, *lada*, from which *ladanum* <note>A sticky resin obtained from Cistus shrubs, used in ancient medicine and perfumes</note> is named—to be a purely Latin word. It is as if Dioscorides <note>Pedanius Dioscorides, a Greek physician and botanist of the 1st century AD</note> and other ancient Greeks did not use both *leda* and *ladanum* everywhere as native and vernacular terms. 

These are the points I had to raise to you, my dear Niccolò, in defense of Pliny. Whether they are true or false I do not know, but they seem likely enough to me. If these arguments are approved by a man as learned as yourself, I shall truly rejoice that a Latin author is not in the same state of risk as the barbarians <note>A reference to non-classical or medieval scholars whose Latinity was considered inferior by Renaissance humanists</note>. If not, I await your response to these modest thoughts of mine. Indeed, since Pliny’s authority is held in the highest regard among the most educated men,

->his reputation should either not have been challenged at all,<-
->or it should have been shaken somewhat more forcefully<-
->than you certainly seem to have done so far.<-
->Farewell. At Florence, the 3rd day<-
->of January, in the year<-
->1491.<-

<summary>In this concluding portion of a letter, the author defends Pliny the Elder's botanical terminology against Niccolò Leoniceno, arguing that certain plant names have legitimate Greek origins rather than being Latin errors.</summary>
<keywords>Niccolò Leoniceno, Pliny the Elder, botany, philology, Dioscorides, ladanum, Renaissance humanism, Florence</keywords>

# INDEX OF NOTABLE THINGS

<meta>catchword: Hermolaus</meta>

Epiglossis <note>A term likely referring to the uvula or a specific part of the tongue; literally "upon the tongue"</note> **137.**
The error of Pliny regarding *teramnos* and *ateramnos* <note>original: "teramno & ateramno"; these are Greek terms for legumes that either cook easily or remain hard</note> **102.**

<meta>This page marks the beginning of the main text, following the alphabetical index. It transitions from the reference list of medicinal terms to the formal preface of Nicolaus Leonicenus’s work. # NICCOLO LEO-
## NICENO’S TREATISE ON THE ERRORS
### of Gaius Pliny, an otherwise most learned man,
### and of many others in the field of medicine,
### addressed to Angelo Poliziano.

<margin>The judgment of the barbarians <note>original: "barbarorum"; Leoniceno uses this term to refer to medieval Arabic and Scholastic authors whom the Humanists believed had corrupted classical knowledge</note> concerning those devoted to the study of eloquence.</margin>
<margin>Giovanni Pico</margin>
<margin>Lorenzo de' Medici.</margin>

<image-desc>A large historiated woodcut initial 'G' depicting a seated scholar in a cap and robes, holding a book, within a square frame decorated with foliage.</image-desc> I rejoice greatly, Angelo <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494), a leading Italian humanist scholar and poet</note>, most learned man, that my effort in refuting the ignorance of the "barbarians" who wrote on medicine is approved by you, a man who can never be praised enough. For I do not hold that opinion of you which perhaps many do—those who are of the "heresy" <note>original: "haeresi"; used here in the sense of a mistaken school of thought</note> that an eloquent man cannot judge other disciplines; as if a mastery of them must necessarily be lacking in one who has been steeped in the study of fine letters and more refined humanity <term>humanitas; the "humanities," encompassing grammar, rhetoric, history, poetry, and moral philosophy</term>. I know your most piercing intellect; I have known your fervent study since childhood, no less toward the teachings of philosophy than toward the mastery of oratory and poetry. In all of these you have made such progress that your illustrious homeland, Florence, employs you as a teacher of all the liberal arts.

Nor is it truly a wonder that you are one of the very few who, in our age, have joined eloquence with wisdom, since in the study of that same wisdom you have as a leader and companion a man of divine genius, our Giovanni Pico della Mirandola <note>A famous Renaissance philosopher known for his "Oration on the Dignity of Man"</note>, with whom you spend days and nights in the meditation of every kind of learning. Furthermore, every aid for the noble practice of philosophy is supplied to you by the favor and grace of Lorenzo de' Medici <note>Lorenzo "the Magnificent," the de facto ruler of Florence and a massive patron of the arts and sciences</note>, the greatest patron of studies in this age. By sending messengers throughout the entire world, he seeks out books in every branch of knowledge with the greatest effort, sparing no expense, so that you and other distinguished talents might strive toward the study of the fine arts—

<summary>This page serves as the formal opening of Nicolaus Leonicenus's influential critique of Pliny the Elder’s botanical and medical accuracy. It features a dedication to the scholar Angelo Poliziano and praises the intellectual circle of Florence, including Giovanni Pico della Mirandola and their patron Lorenzo de' Medici.</summary>

<keywords>Niccolo Leoniceno, Pliny the Elder, medical errors, Angelo Poliziano, Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, Lorenzo de' Medici, Humanism, Florence, Renaissance medicine, barbarians</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the dedicatory letter to Angelo Poliziano. Leoniceno moves from praising Poliziano’s intellect to defending his own critical method, specifically why he dares to correct the esteemed Roman author Pliny the Elder.</meta>

# NICOLAUS LEONICENUS
<meta>catchword: to prove</meta>

<margin>A famous saying of Lorenzo de' Medici.</margin>
...provides the most abundant tools for those striving. I have heard from your own account that a famous saying came from the mouth of Lorenzo <note>Lorenzo de' Medici (1449–1492), the "Magnificent" ruler of Florence and a great patron of the arts and sciences</note>: that he wished you and our friend Pico <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494), a brilliant philosopher and close associate of Poliziano and Lorenzo</note> would provide him with such great incentives for buying books that, his funds finally failing, he would be forced to pawn his entire household furniture. Since, therefore, all the goods of both mind and fortune are most abundant in you, there is no reason why—with Angelo Poliziano speaking on my behalf against the "barbarians" <note>original: "barbaros"; Leoniceno refers to medieval Arab and Scholastic authors whose translations of Greek science he considered corrupt</note>—I should henceforth fear anyone who might take up their defense. 

However, while you judged that I rightly rebuked these "barbarians," you do not approve of the fact that I have placed Pliny—who deserved so well of life and letters—into the same "game of chance" <note>original: "aleam"; a metaphor for being put at risk or under scrutiny</note> as those Barbarians. You argue that his authority among the most skilled is so great that I either ought not to have challenged it at all, or if I thought it had to be overturned, it should have been done by me more forcefully than I seem to have done so far. 

If perhaps by these words you—who can speak to me of all things as a friend—silently accuse me of rashness and impudence for seeking to rebuke a man of such great reputation through a kind of slander, I have an excuse already prepared from your own letter. For you admit the truth of what is frequently read in our schools: "Plato is a friend, but truth is a greater friend" <note>original: "Amicus Plato, amica ueritas"; a traditional maxim emphasizing that intellectual honesty must outweigh personal loyalty to a teacher or authority</note>; but when both are friends, it is a pious duty to prefer truth in honor. 

Since, therefore, I felt that Pliny, no less than the others, was deceived in his description of ivy by the similarity of the name of another plant, which among the Greeks 
<margin>Cisthos. Cissos.</margin> 
is called *cisthos* <note>Rock-rose (Cistus)</note>; and because ivy is called *cissos* by the Greeks, he mixed up their characteristics not without error. I did not want, as much as was in my power, to allow truth itself to lie in obscurity. 

As for your opinion that this error should have been pointed out by me more forcefully and clearly: know that it was not then my intention to destroy Pliny’s authority. For when I was dictating those words, my chief struggle was with the "barbarians," and therefore when the discussion turned to ivy, the nature of which was not sufficiently known to Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the Persian physician whose "Canon of Medicine" was the standard medical textbook in Europe at the time</note>...

# ON HERBS AND SHRUBS.

...I was striving to prove, in passing, and as if in a brief overview, I also mentioned Pliny while naming others. I did not say, however, that he had erred together with Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian physician whose "Canon of Medicine" was the standard textbook in Europe for centuries</note> and the rest, but rather that he seemed to be involved in the same error as the others. See how much more modestly I then spoke of Pliny than of the others, whom I asserted did not merely seem to deviate in the same error, but clearly wandered astray. But if it had been my intention then, or were so even now, to bring Pliny’s errors to light, I could have then, and could also now, fill an entire volume about them. Nevertheless, I decided that a few out of many should be revealed in this place, so that you may understand that I was not led by a rash judgment, but by the most certain reasons to believe that Pliny erred in the description of ivy <note>original: "hederæ"</note>, just as he did in many other matters pertaining to medicine.

<margin>Dioscorides.</margin>
Indeed, let this first be agreed upon between me and you: that among the Greeks, as well as the Latins, and even the Barbarians <note>Leoniceno refers here to medieval Arabic authors and the "scholastic" thinkers who followed them</note>, **DIOSCORIDES** <note>Pedanius Dioscorides (c. 40–90 AD), a Greek physician whose "De Materia Medica" is the foundational text of botany</note> is the supreme and primary author to whom trust should be given in the descriptions of herbs and shrubs. For Pliny himself seems to have followed him no less than Theophrastus <note>The "Father of Botany" and successor to Aristotle</note> in this regard, such that anyone who knows both languages, Greek and Latin, may recognize entire sentences of Dioscorides translated by Pliny almost word for word.
<margin>Pliny borrowed many things from Dioscorides.</margin>
Furthermore, **GALEN** <note>Claudius Galenus (129–c. 216 AD), the most influential physician of the Roman Empire</note>—a man preeminent both in all the liberal arts and especially in the discipline of medicine—confesses in his book *On Simple Medicines* <note>original: "de simplicibus medicaminibus"; "simples" were medicines made from a single natural ingredient</note> that he refrained from describing the appearances of herbs because Dioscorides had already satisfied this study abundantly. Nor did Serapio the Arab <note>Probably Serapio the Younger, a 12th-century author whose work on medicinal plants was popular but, according to Humanists like Leoniceno, full of mistranslations of Greek sources</note>, when he set out to describe herbs, indicate them by any other characteristics than those of Dioscorides. Although he himself, by not correctly imitating Dioscorides in all things, filled his books with innumerable errors—which, unless I hoped they would eventually be brought to light through the study and diligence of an illustrious...

...of the prelate Hermolao Barbaro <note>Hermolao Barbaro (1454–1493), an influential Venetian scholar and diplomat who attempted to "cleanse" Pliny's texts of medieval corruptions</note>, Patriarch of Aquileia, a man most skilled in all disciplines, I would certainly record [the errors] more willingly than I am about to recite these of Pliny at present. This is both because it gives me more pleasure to act against "barbarians" <note>Leoniceno uses "barbarians" to refer to medieval Arabic and scholastic authors who did not use original Greek sources</note> than against Latins, and because a greater danger threatens the human race from the ignorance of Serapion <note>Serapion the Younger (12th century), an influential author of a book on "Simple Medicines"</note> than from Pliny. 

<margin>Serapion.</margin>
Indeed, in our age, almost all physicians follow Serapion in the knowledge of simple medicines <note>Natural ingredients used as drugs, as opposed to "compounds"</note>, while they judge that Pliny should not even be read, because they believe he should be held in the rank of grammarians or orators, rather than among philosophers or physicians. 

I, however, though I do not deny that Pliny cultivated the study of all branches of learning, believe that many things about which he wrote in his books on *Natural History* were not sufficiently understood or investigated by him. From this, it followed that since he was not writing what he himself knew, but rather what he had collected from various writings by different authors, he often seems to have reported different things as being the same, and the same things as being different. 

I hope that I will easily prove this matter to you—a most learned man—if, setting aside bias for a little while, you are willing to weigh and examine these errors we are about to note in Pliny more diligently, not as Pliny’s advocate, but rather as a judge. I do not wish, however, to bring to the examination of reason those things treated by Pliny that pertain to astronomy or the remaining parts of philosophy in this place; for more things would occur to me to be censured than would suit my present purpose. 

Among those, however, there is one, perhaps the greatest, which he did not hesitate to set down in writing in the second book of his volume on *Natural History*: that the moon is larger than the earth. Nevertheless, Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the preeminent astronomer of antiquity</note> and many other distinguished astronomers have proved by mathematical reasons—than which none can be firmer—that the moon is much smaller than the earth. This can also be easily shown from those things which Pliny himself wrote in that same place. For if the shadow of the earth...

<meta>This page continues Leoniceno’s critique of Pliny the Elder’s scientific accuracy. Here, he concludes a technical astronomical argument regarding the size of the moon and the nature of eclipses before transitioning to his primary subject: the identification of medicinal plants.</meta>

### ->ON HERBS AND SHRUBS.<-

a 3

<note>original: "ræ"</note> [shadow] of the earth, falling into which the moon is darkened, is either equal to or exceeds the size of the moon; otherwise, the moon could not be entirely hidden by the darkness of that shadow. <margin>The moon is smaller than the earth.</margin> Moreover, that same shadow cast by the earth—since the sun (against which the earth places itself to cast a shadow) exceeds the size of the earth—must necessarily be thinned out into a peak and take the shape of a cone or an inverted spinning top. <note>Leoniceno is describing the conical shape of the earth's shadow during a lunar eclipse. If the sun is larger than the earth, the shadow must eventually taper to a point.</note> Pliny himself confirms this in the same place. By this reasoning, it is gathered that the diameter of the width of the shadow darkening the moon is much smaller than the diameter of the earth. Now, if the width of the shadow is less than the width of the earth, and that same width of the shadow either equals or even exceeds the width of the moon, it follows necessarily that the moon is smaller than the earth.

As for the argument Pliny offers for his assertion—namely, that it would be impossible for the whole sun to be taken away from the earth by the intervention of the moon <note>A solar eclipse.</note> if the earth were larger than the moon—it is so weak that anyone who has even sampled the principles of astronomy or optics <note>original: "perſpectiuas", referring to the science of how objects appear to the eye based on distance and angle.</note> could easily refute it. For when the sun eclipses, it is not taken away from the whole earth through the intervention of the moon; rather, due to the variety of locations on the earth, in some places it fails totally, in others only in part, and in some places it does not fail at all. Nothing prevents it from failing totally for certain lands even though the moon is smaller than the earth, since the principles of optics prove that unequal bodies—such as the sun and the moon—can appear equal because of their unequal distances from the earth. Thus it happens that, since the moon presents itself to us as being as large as the sun appears because of its proximity (while the sun is much farther away from us), it is not surprising that the sun is sometimes totally removed from human sight in some curve of the earth by the moon's intervention.

But let us leave aside these matters pertaining to mathematics and come to those things from which our discussion took its beginning: let us deal with herbs, shrubs, and other earthly things adapted for the use of medicine. Let us see whether Pliny, in all these things, agrees with Dioscorides, Galen, and Paul <note>Paul of Aegina (c. 625–690 AD), a Byzantine Greek physician whose medical encyclopedia was a standard reference.</note>, and other excellent physicians, and with the [truth] itself...

## OF NICCOLÒ LEONICENO ##

...whether experience, the mistress of all things, agrees; or whether, as it is commonly said, even the great Homer sometimes nods <note>A reference to the Roman poet Horace’s famous line "quandoque bonus dormitat Homerus," suggesting that even the greatest authors make mistakes.</note>.

And let us begin first with those instances in which a similarity of name—as in the case of the **cistus** and the **cissus** <note>original: "cistho & cisso." The *cistus* is the rockrose, while *cissus* is the Greek name for ivy.</note>—provided Pliny with the occasion for error. Indeed, it pleases me that I am writing to you, whom I know to have been as diligent in the books of our physicians as you have been in those of the orators and philosophers. This will allow me to be more brief, since it will not be necessary to write out every saying of **Dioscorides**, **Galen**, or **Paul** <note>Paul of Aegina, a 7th-century Byzantine physician.</note> to prove what I assert; you, or anyone else of a learning similar to that of **Angelo Poliziano** <note>A renowned Renaissance humanist and friend of Leoniceno, to whom this work is addressed.</note>, will very easily be able to find these in their proper places among those authors whose testimony I shall cite. For it should be enough for me, lest I be wordy, to have revealed both the author and the order of the volume where one ought to look, if anyone should wish to read the words themselves.

**Dioscorides**, **Galen**, and **Paul** write that many herbs and shrubs have leaves similar to **horehound** <note>original: "marrubio." In Greek, this is *prassion*.</note>. All of these, Pliny records as having leaves similar not to *prassion* (that is, horehound), but to *prasson* (that is, a leek). <margin>Orminos.</margin> Thus, in his twenty-second book, he said that **Orminos** <note>Likely Clary Sage (*Salvia horminum*).</note> has a seed similar to cumin, but the rest is like a leek. So too with **balloten**, which by another name he calls **black horehound** <note>original: "marrubium nigrum."</note> from the similarity of its leaves; yet in Book 27, Pliny wrote that it is called "black leek" by the Greeks under another name, and that it consists of leaves even larger than those of a leek. <margin>Stachys.</margin> Similarly, in Book 24, he noted that **stachys** has a similarity to a leek, though with longer and more numerous leaves. 

In Book 27, while treating the types of **leuce**, **leucoleuce**, and other herbs, the same Pliny—deceived by the similarity of the name and the form of the word—also numbered **leucographis** <note>Literally "white writing."</note> among them. <margin>Leucographis</margin> Without a doubt, he seems to have thought that *leucographis* was an herb, even though **Dioscorides**, **Galen**, and **Paul** testify that it is a type of stone, which is called by another name, **moroxus** <note>A type of stone, possibly French chalk or a variety of soapstone, used anciently in medicine and for marking.</note>. And lest anyone should perhaps object on Pliny’s behalf that there is also an herb which is designated by the same name as the stone, Pliny ascribed the very same powers and properties to *leucographis* [as an herb]...

<summary>Leoniceno identifies a recurring error in Pliny the Elder's work: the confusion of plants with similar-sounding names, specifically mistaking "horehound" (prassion) for "leek" (prasson) and a "stone" (leucographis) for an "herb."</summary>

### ON HERBS AND SHRUBS. 7 ###

...which **Dioscorides**, **Galen**, and **Paul** <note>Paul of Aegina.</note> likewise recorded under a stone of the same name. Furthermore, **Pliny** writes concerning <term>leucographis</term> <note>original: "leucographide"; literally "white-writer," a substance used in ancient medicine, sometimes classified as a stone and sometimes as an herb.</note> that he had not found it described by any authors, even though **Dioscorides** sufficiently identified both what it is and its nature in his fifth book on simple medicines.

<margin>Mountain Germander</margin> On account of a similar proximity of names, **Pliny** took <term>polium</term> <note>Mountain germander (*Teucrium polium*).</note> for <term>tripolium</term> <note>Sea aster (*Aster tripolium*).</note>, and <margin>Sea Aster</margin> conversely took <term>tripolium</term> for <term>polium</term>. For in his twenty-first book, he describes two kinds of mountain germander, just as **Dioscorides** does: one of the field and the other of the forest, both with leaves similar to the white hair of an old man. But the "miracle" that he attributes to the mountain germander—that its leaves appear white in the morning, purple at midday, and blue at sunset—is actually written by **Dioscorides** regarding the flower of the sea aster. Indeed, mountain germander and sea aster differ greatly from one another, not only in the variety of places where each grows, but also in their shape, color, and even their properties. For mountain germander of both kinds grows partly in fields and partly in the mountains; however, sea aster grows only in maritime places where the sea waves strike. Mountain germander has, as we said, leaves like the white hair of an old man—which is where it gets its name among the Greeks <note>The Greek word "polios" means "gray" or "whitish."</note>—while sea aster consists of leaves like <term>isatis</term> <note>Woad (*Isatis tinctoria*), a plant used for blue dye.</note>, just as **Dioscorides** writes of both, and **Pliny** himself confirms in his twenty-sixth book. 

<margin>A passage of Pliny is corrected</margin> For what is read in **Pliny** regarding the sea aster—"with a sufficiently thick leaf, a flower a palm high"—is an error of the manuscript; <margin>,,</margin> for it ought to be read this way: "Sea aster grows on maritime rocks <margin>,,</margin> where the wave strikes, neither in the sea nor on the ground, <margin>,,</margin> with a leaf thicker than woad, a stem a palm high, divided <margin>,,</margin> at the tip." For **Pliny** translated almost all these things word-for-word <margin>,,</margin> from **Dioscorides**. But regarding what the same **Pliny** later adds—that this herb seems to some to be the same as mountain germander—I marvel that he chose to follow and imitate the error of those people rather than wanting to disprove and reject it, especially since he assigned the "miracle" read about the sea aster's flower to the leaves of the mountain germander. Yet this would be a small danger to life if he had not also, in turn, ascribed the medicinal powers of mountain germander to the sea aster; for he writes that the root of sea aster is given to those with liver disease...

...boiled in grain; which remedy of sea aster <note>original: "tripolij"</note> is read in no physician of greater authority. However, **Galen**, in the eighth book of his work *On Simple Medicines*, is the authority that mountain germander <note>original: "Polium"</note> helps not only the liver, but clearly all the defects of the internal organs.

<margin>Heraclium. We call it the "little root," according to **Hermolaus Barbarus**.</margin>
**Dioscorides** writes in his fourth book that a certain type of poppy, called <term>heraclium</term> <note>likely a species of wild poppy, possibly *Papaver hybridum*</note> by some, has a thin leaf similar to <term>struthio</term>—that is, the herb so named <note>Saponaria or Soapwort</note>. But because *struthion* among the Greeks also signifies a sparrow, **Pliny**, deceived by the ambiguity of the name, referred this similarity to the bird rather than to the herb. For he writes of heraclium in his twentieth book: "There is another heraclium in the wild, with leaves that, if you look from afar, represent the appearance of sparrows." But one who cannot find the truth from the thing itself might think it significantly more probable that a herb has leaves very similar to another herb rather than to birds.

<margin>Empetrum</margin>
Where <term>empetrum</term> <note>literally "on the rock"; refers to various rock-growing plants like crowberry or sea-samphire</note> grows, and what powers it has in drawing out bile and phlegm, **Pliny** writes in book twenty-seven in the same manner as **Dioscorides**; however, he joins other powers to it, saying that it induces urine and breaks stones, which are recorded by no other author regarding this *empetrum*. On the contrary, **Galen** testifies in his sixth book that *empetrum*, which is also called <term>prassoides</term> <note>leek-like</note>, is useful only for purgings. But the effects that **Pliny** had read in the other *empetrum*—which is also called <term>sarxiphages</term> <note>original: "Sarxiphages"; literally "flesh-eater," a Greek term for plants that break down stones, later becoming "Saxifrage"</note>—handed down by Greek authors and especially **Dioscorides**, he ascribed to this *empetrum* (which is distinct from the *sarxiphages* and has a purgative power), having been deceived by the ambiguity of the name.

<margin>Betony</margin>
**Pliny** depicts <term>betonica</term> <note>Wood betony (*Stachys officinalis*)</note>—called so by the Romans and <term>cestrum</term> by the Greeks—as having the leaf of <term>lapatium</term> <note>Dock or Sorrel</note>. However, **Dioscorides**, whose observation is more reliable, describes it with the leaf of an Oak. Yet, the same **Dioscorides** records that another betony—which is called <term>britanica</term> by another name—has the leaves of dock, so that it is likely **Pliny** depicted one in place of the other.

# ON HERBS AND SHRUBS #

<margin>Parthenium</margin>
<margin>Dog-fennel</margin>
**Pliny** writes in his twenty-first book that <term>Parthenium</term> <note>original: "Parthenium"; here referring to plants like feverfew or pellitory-of-the-wall</note> is called <term>perdicium</term> <note>partridge-herb</note> and <term>muralium</term> <note>wall-herb</note> by **Celsus**. He then attributes the same powers to this *Parthenium* (the one called "wall-herb") that **Dioscorides** assigns to a different *Parthenium*, which is called <term>chamemelon</term> <note>chamomile</note> by another name, because its leaves and flowers differ very little from the herb chamomile. Some of the more recent physicians call this chamomile-like *Parthenium* herb <term>cotula</term> <note>dog-fennel or mayweed</note>. However, this *Parthenium* is not the one called *perdicium* and *muralium* by **Celsus**; rather, it is a different one which the Greeks call <term>helxine</term>, and which is also simultaneously named *perdicium* and *Parthenium*. Among the Latins, it is called <term>parietaria</term> <note>pellitory-of-the-wall</note> or *muralium*, because it grows everywhere on walls. In our own age, the common people, having removed one letter, call it *paritaria* instead of *parietaria*. This same herb—whether it be called *muralium* or *parietaria*—is counted by **Celsus** in the third book of his *On Medicine* among those things that have the power to suppress and cool at the same time. Indeed, this specific faculty is attributed by almost all medical authorities to that *Parthenium* which is called *perdicium* and *parietaria*, but not to the other one which is also called *chamemelon*. For these are the words of **Dioscorides** regarding that plant: 

> The leaves have a cooling and astringent faculty. 

Neither **Paulus** <note>Paul of Aegina</note> nor **Galen** have handed down anything different concerning it. **Pliny** himself likewise confirms in his twenty-second book that the same plant is named both *Parthenium* and *perdicium*.

<margin>The root of Cyclamen</margin>
Similarity—not only of names, but sometimes of the things themselves—also deceived **Pliny**. For he seems to have believed that the root of <term>cyclamen</term> <note>sowbread</note>, which is called "earth-turnip" <note>original: "rapum terrae"</note> because of its roundness, was the root of the <term>round aristolochia</term> <note>round birthwort</note>, which also received its name from the roundness of its root. For in his twenty-fifth book, in the place where he distinguishes four types of *aristolochia*, he writes that the root of the one called "round" is named "poison of the earth" <note>original: "uenenum terrae"</note> by the fishermen of Campania; and that when it is crushed and mixed with lime and scattered in the sea, the fish immediately fly to it with wonderful

# NICOLAUS LEONICENUS #

...[by] desire, and that they immediately floated up dead. This same thing, as I have learned from most respected men, is done in our own age by those same fishermen—not with the root of <term>round birthwort</term> <note>original: *aristolochia rotunda*</note>, but rather with the root of <term>cyclamen</term> <note>original: *cyclaminus*</note>, for the sake of enticing and killing the fish. **Pliny** himself also attributes these same effects not to round birthwort, but to the root of a certain cyclamen in his twenty-fifth book. Either, therefore, it must be admitted that there are two roots which produce the same effects—though it is neither found written by any author that one of them is the root of the round birthwort, nor is it proven by experience—or it must be said that the cyclamen, which has a round root, is a fourth kind of birthwort. Nothing could be said that is more contrary to the nature of things. 

<margin>The origin of Birthwort.</margin> For indeed, the name <term>Aristolochia</term> <note>Birthwort</note> among the Greeks, as **Dioscorides** and **Pliny** himself testify, comes from the fact that it is "best for those in childbirth" <note>From the Greek *aristos* (best) and *lochia* (childbirth or delivery)</note>. Yet the root of the cyclamen is so hostile to pregnant women that if a pregnant woman should even step over it, she may suffer a miscarriage, as **Dioscorides** and several other distinguished physicians have reported, and **Pliny** himself also confirms.

Although there are many herbs that turn with the sun, 
<margin>Heliotrope</margin> **Dioscorides** nonetheless identifies two kinds of <term>heliotrope</term> <note>literally "sun-turner"</note>: one with leaves like basil and a white-reddish curved flower that looks like a scorpion's tail—which is why it is called <term>scorpiuros</term> <note>scorpion-tail</note> among the Greeks. The other, with similar leaves, grows near marshes. **Pliny**, however, in his twenty-second book, while also describing two kinds of heliotrope, seems to include in them that species of <term>endive</term> <note>original: *intibi*</note> which is called <term>cichorium</term> <note>chicory</note> by physicians using the Greek name. For 

> >> he writes thus in that same book concerning the heliotrope: "We have often spoken of the miracle of the heliotrope, which turns itself with the sun even on a cloudy day, so great is its love for that star; at night, as if with longing, it closes its blue flower. Its kinds are two: the <term>three-seeded</term> <note>original: *tricoccum*</note> and the <term>sun-turner</term> <note>original: *heliostrophium*</note>; the latter is taller, though neither exceeds a height of half a foot. The seed is collected in a small pod during the harvest. It grows only in rich soil, and especially in cultivated ground; the three-seeded kind grows everywhere. If you boil..."

# ON HERBS AND SHRUBS #

b 2

<meta>catchword: Pliny</meta>

» [it is] found to be pleasing in foods. What other kind of <term>heliotrope</term> <note>original: *heliotropium*; a plant that turns toward the sun</note> could there be, whose flower is blue and which grows only in rich and cultivated soil, and which, if cooked, is pleasing in foods, other than that species of <term>Intibum</term> <note>original: *Intibum*; likely endive or chicory</note> which we have already mentioned? Nevertheless, **Dioscorides**, when he treated <term>seris</term> <note>a Greek name for chicory-like plants</note>, thought it necessary to identify it as a single species of that same *seris*, and he assigned to it properties far different from the powers of heliotrope. Therefore, one must wonder how **Pliny**, in this passage where he seems to describe *Intibum*, can nonetheless assign to it the same powers and potencies that **Dioscorides** handed down regarding both kinds of heliotrope. This wonder is increased even more by the fact that the same **Pliny** had noted the remedies of the *Intiba*—and especially of that which is called <term>cichorium</term> <note>chicory</note> by the Greeks, whose blue flower turns with the sun—in a previous book (specifically Book 21), in its proper place; these remedies differ greatly from those handed down regarding both types of heliotrope.

<margin>Cinquefoil</margin>
By a similar error, **Pliny** took <term>pentaphyllon</term> <note>original: *pentaphyllon*; Greek for "five-leaf," known today as Cinquefoil</note> and the plant that bears <term>fraga</term> <note>strawberries</note> to be the same thing. He judged that the characteristics and powers of *pentaphyllon* should be ascribed to that same plant alongside the name *pentaphyllon*. For in Book 25, he reported this concerning the plant:
» <term>Pentaphyllon</term> is unknown to no one, since it is also commended for producing <term>fraga</term> <note>strawberries</note>.
I would think, however, that in such a well-known matter, this is an error of the manuscript rather than of **Pliny**, and that <term>trifolium</term> <note>original: *trifolium*; "three-leaf"</note> ought to be read instead of *pentaphyllon*. For that plant which is commended for producing strawberries, and which is unknown to no one, does not consist of five leaves, but of three—unless **Pliny** were to subjoin other Greek names afterward and offer other indicators which are not proper to any plant other than *pentaphyllon*.

<margin>Adarches</margin>
**Pliny** counts <term>Adarches</term> <note>a medicinal substance found on reeds</note> among the species of reeds in Book 16, where he writes:
» There is also [a substance] growing in Italy by the name of <term>adarcha</term>; it is a marshy substance found only on the bark under the very head [of the reed], and is most useful for the teeth.
But **Dioscorides**, **Galen**, and **Paulus** <note>Paulus Aegineta, a 7th-century medical writer</note> wrote that *Adarches* is not a species of reed, but rather a certain salty encrustation adhering to reeds in dried-out marshes.

# NICOLAUS LEONICENUS #

<margin>Lemnian earth.</margin>
**Pliny**, in his thirty-fifth book, counts **Lemnian red ochre** <note>original: *lemniam rubricam*; a reddish earth or clay used as a pigment and medicine</note> among the various natural colors. He notes that the ancients gave it the "palm" <note>the prize of highest honor</note> among all other types of red earth. Furthermore, he records that this substance—which was much celebrated by the ancients along with the island where it is produced—was not usually sold unless it was sealed; for this reason, it was given the name <term>sphragis</term> <note>from the Greek *sphragis*, meaning a "seal" or "signet"</note> among the Greeks. He also testifies that <term>minium</term> <note>a red pigment, often cinnabar or red lead</note> was coated and adulterated with this earth, and that it is an excellent substance for use in medicine. Indeed, he attributes all the same powers to this Lemnian red ochre that the ancient physicians ascribed to **sealed earth** <note>original: *terra sigillata*; medicinal clay tablets stamped with an official seal, used as an antidote to poison and for treating wounds</note>. It appears, therefore, that **Pliny** believed Lemnian red ochre and Lemnian *sphragis*—or sealed earth—were one and the same thing.

However, **Galen**—who was a most diligent investigator of both other substances used in medicine and especially of this sealed earth—was a man who (as he writes of himself) sailed on long journeys to the island of **Lemnos** for no other reason than to observe the Lemnian *sphragis* with his own eyes: to see how it was produced and what its nature was. In his book *On Theriac, Addressed to Piso*, he shows most clearly that Lemnian red ochre is one thing, and Lemnian *sphragis* is another. For in that same book, he writes the following concerning the Lemnian *sphragis*, or sealed earth:

> It is better not to call it red ochre, but rather earth; for there is a certain red ochre produced on the island of Lemnos which we use for other purposes, different from those for which sealed earth is applied.

In the ninth book of his work *On Simple Medicines*, the same **Galen** distinguishes **Lemnian earth** into three types. The first is that which was called "sacred," which no one except the priestess of **Diana** <note>the Roman name for the Greek goddess Artemis; her priestesses on Lemnos traditionally collected and sealed the earth</note> was permitted to touch; it was also impressed with the seal of that same goddess, and for <margin>The Lemnian seal.</margin> that reason it was called the **Lemnian seal** <note>original: *lemnium sigillum*</note>. The second type is that which is truly red ochre, which woodworkers and carpenters used <note>likely as a chalk or pigment for marking lines</note>. The third is that which has cleansing properties, and for that reason, its primary use was among <term>fullers</term> <note>workers who cleaned and processed wool and cloth</note>. Therefore, if in a matter which **Galen** investigated so curiously, one ought to believe him more than **Pliny**, then **Pliny** was not correct in what [he wrote]...

<summary>Leonicenus highlights an error by Pliny the Elder regarding "Lemnian earth," noting that while Pliny confused red ochre with medicinal sealed earth, the physician Galen personally visited Lemnos to distinguish three distinct types of the substance.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Nicolaus Leonicenus’s scholarly critique of Pliny the Elder’s *Natural History*. ### ON HERBS AND SHRUBS ###

Since **sealed earth** <note>original: *terra sigillata*; a medicinal clay stamped with an official seal</note> had been described by the ancient physicians, he [Pliny] believed that the **Lemnian red ochre**—which is categorized among pigments and was not so famous that it was sold only when sealed, nor does it share the same medicinal uses as the Lemnian seal—should be added to the same category. All these points prove that **Pliny** was occasionally deceived by the similarity of the substance itself, but more often by the similarity of the name, leading him to believe that things which are entirely distinct were actually the same.

<margin>
ivy (*cissus*).
rockrose (*cisthus*).
</margin>
Now, regarding **cissus** <note>from the Greek *kissos*, meaning ivy</note> and **cisthus** <note>the rockrose, a shrub of the genus *Cistus*</note>: although I had intended to respond to the arguments you raised in defense of **Pliny** through a private letter rather than a book—since I have no desire for public academic disputes with a man who is a dear friend, whom I cherish and respect—this passage nevertheless demands that I demonstrate, with even more evidence than I provided in my lectures, that **Pliny** could not tell them apart. In his seventeenth book, when describing every kind of **ivy** <note>original: *hedera*</note>, **Pliny** first divides them into male and female. He claims the flower of both resembles a **wild rose**, with the male flower tending toward purple. By this, he meant it to be understood that the female flower is whiter. However, this distinction between male and female—along with the similarity of the flower's shape and the difference in its color—is clearly described in relation to the **rockrose** (*cisthus*), and not the ivy, by **Theophrastus**, **Dioscorides**, or any other author of significant authority. It is highly probable, therefore, that **Pliny**, deceived by the similarity of the names, attributed what is recorded about the two types of rockrose to the ivy. 

Furthermore, in his twelfth book, while discussing **ladanum** <note>a sticky resin, also called labdanum, used in perfumes and medicine</note> and explaining how it is combed from the beards of he-goats, **Pliny** wrote the following: <insert>“But when the flower of the **ivy** <note>original: *hedera*</note> is grazed upon during the morning pastures while Cyprus is dewy; then, after the mist is dispersed by the sun, it [the resin] sticks to the damp hair as dust, and thus the ladanum is combed off.”</insert> Could it be shown any more clearly that **Pliny** mistook **cissus** (that is, ivy) for **cisthus**? For who besides **Pliny**—who substituted ivy for the rockrose—ever reported that this fatty substance comes from the *lada* herb (also called *cisthus*)...

<meta>This page continues Leonicenus’s argument that Pliny the Elder confused two similarly named plants: the rockrose (cisthos) and ivy (cissos). The previous page established that Pliny incorrectly attributed the characteristics of the rockrose's flower to the ivy.</meta>

# NICOLAUS LEONICENUS #

it is called **labdanum** <note>original: *ladanum*; a sticky resin used in perfumes and medicine</note>, and it is said to adhere to the beards of goats grazing on **ivy** <note>original: *hedera*</note> or the flower of ivy. However, regarding this **rockrose** <note>original: *cistho*</note> or **lada**—a name which, as the word *ladanum* itself indicates, is derived from that very plant—**Dioscorides**, **Galen**, **Paulus** <note>Paul of Aegina, a 7th-century Byzantine physician</note>, and whoever else has written on the origin of labdanum, have reported with one voice that it comes from the rockrose, not from **cissos** <note>Greek: *kissos*</note>, which is ivy. Indeed, **Pliny** himself writes in the same passage:
» "There are those in Cyprus who call the herb from which it is made *lada*; for they call the product *ladanum*."
And later, in Book 24, he wrote about this same herb and labdanum no differently than the men mentioned above; for these are his words:
» "The herb from which labdanum is made in Cyprus is called *ledon*, and it adheres to the beards of goats."
Therefore, it is the **cisthos**, **lada**, or **ledon**—and not the **cissos**, that is, ivy—to whose flower goats graze and cause the labdanum to stick to their beards. Pliny himself clearly confirms this in this passage, namely in Book 24, although in Book 12 he seemed to have doubted whether it was ivy or the *lada* from which labdanum was made in Cyprus. I would believe the origin of this doubt arose from the fact that he had read in various authors that labdanum was collected sometimes from the *cisthos* and sometimes from the *lada*, not realizing that both names indicate the same herb.

Yet the very method that **Pliny** suggests—the way in which labdanum sticks to the beards of goats—easily shows that the shrub or herb upon which that oily substance sits is low-growing and spreads itself across the ground, not lifting itself from the earth by climbing trees as ivy does. For he writes:
» "Then, when the mist is dispersed by the sun, it adheres to the damp hair [of the goats] in the form of dust."
The beards of goats grazing on ivy (which, as some prefer, is called *hedera* because it seeks out high places <note>a folk etymology linking *hedera* to *edita*, meaning "high things"</note>) would not become damp from mist turning to dust when the sun disperses it, unless they were grazing not on *cissos* (ivy), but rather on **chamaecissos** <note>literally "ground-ivy," a low-creeping plant</note>. And yet, how could this even happen on the Island of **Cyprus**, where, if we believe that most serious author **Theophrastus**, not even ivy grows? For the Island of Cyprus is toward Asia...

<summary>Leonicenus argues that Pliny the Elder made a botanical error by confusing ivy with the rockrose (Cistus) as the source of labdanum resin. He points out that the collection method—goats picking up resin on their beards—requires a low-growing plant, whereas ivy is a climber.</summary>

belonging [to that region], as all cosmographers <note>Scholars who described the world’s geography and nature.</note> agree; nor does Pliny himself disagree, for he even asserts that **ivy** <note>original: *hedera*</note> was planted in Asia by **Harpalus** <note>The treasurer of Alexander the Great who attempted to cultivate Greek plants in Babylon.</note> in vain. Whether it actually flourished in that same region of the world <note>original: *coeli tractu*; literally "tract of the sky," referring to climate or latitude.</note> during his own time, he did not dare to assert, writing only this: "Ivy is now said to be born in Asia." From this, it appears clearer than light that Pliny fell into the same error as **Avicenna** <note>The famous Persian physician Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037).</note>, when, in his book on simple medicines, he indicated that the herb from which **labdanum** <note>original: *ladanum*; a sticky resin.</note> is made was a species of ivy. <margin>,</margin> "under these especially is born **hypocistis**." <note>A parasitic plant (*Cytinus hypocistis*) that grows on the roots of rockroses.</note> From this he seems to suggest that while hypocistis is born especially under these types of rockrose, it is also born sometimes under ivies, though not as frequently. For Pliny had not said anything about other types of rockrose in that place or elsewhere, so that the word "especially" could be referred to a comparison with them rather than with ivies.

I can therefore conclude this: in Pliny's work, ivy is divided into male and female; the flower of both is described by the same author as being similar to a wild rose; on the island of Cyprus, when the ivy flower is grazed upon, labdanum sticks to the beards of goats; it is also indicated that hypocistis sometimes grows under ivies. However, all these things are written about ivies by no author except Pliny, nor are they proven by the senses or experience. Rather, they are clearly handed down regarding two types of rockrose, and are known to be so by actual use. These, therefore, are the most evident arguments that Pliny wandered off into the same error as the others, who did not know how to distinguish *cisthos* <note>The Greek name for the rockrose.</note> from *cissos* <note>The Greek name for ivy.</note>, that is, from ivy. And indeed, I believe the author of the book entitled *Cornucopia* <note>Niccolò Perotti (1429–1480), an Italian humanist scholar.</note>—a man, it appears, not lacking in diligence in the investigation of herbs, nor entirely unskilled in them—was moved by these reasons
<margin>Perottus.</margin> when, in treating of ivies, he wrote that *cisthos* is counted by some among the types of ivy. For this is so manifest in Pliny that no doubt can be had about it...

# OF NICOLAUS LEONICENUS #

be concluded. But since the proverb says, "if the blind lead the blind, both fall into a pit," that same man—otherwise most learned in Greek literature <note>Leonicenus likely refers to his contemporary, the scholar Hermolaus Barbarus, with whom he frequently sparred over classical interpretations.</note>—thought that the **rockrose** <note>original: *cisthon*</note> was a small shrub different from the **lada** <note>A specific variety of rockrose, *Cistus ladanifer*.</note>; he believed that "cisthos" came from the former and **ladanum** <note>A sticky resin used in medicine and incense.</note> (that is, the fatty substance that settles on the leaves) from the latter. Yet **Dioscorides**, **Galen**, and **Paul** <note>Paul of Aegina, a 7th-century Byzantine physician.</note> all testify that the rockrose and the *lada* (or *ledon*) are the same plant, and it is from this plant that the scent called ladanum takes its name.

Indeed, Pliny does not seem to have erred in this matter alone—taking entirely different things to be the same, as we showed above—but also because he thought the same things were different due to a variety of names. Furthermore, even regarding those plants called by the same name, he described them so differently in various places that anyone might rightly judge that he considered them to be distinct species, even if they were actually the same.

<margin>**Woad** <note>original: *Glastum*</note></margin> Pliny writes in Book 22 that clothes are dyed with the juice of a plant similar to **plantain** <note>original: *plantago*; a common flat-leafed herb.</note> called **woad** <note>original: *glastum*</note>, and that this is the name for the herb among the Gauls. In our own age, with only a few letters changed, it is called **woad** <note>original: *guadum*; likely referring to the Italian *guado*.</note>. Yet it is well-established that this same herb is called **isatis** <note>original: *isatidem*</note> by the Greeks. For Dioscorides writes that dyers of wool use the juice of the *isatis*, and that the herb has a leaf similar to the plantain, and is called *gluta* or *glastum* by the Romans. However, in Book 20, Pliny makes *isatis* a third kind of **wild-growing lettuce** <note>original: *lactucæ*</note>, and in a fourth place <note>original: *quarto*; referring to a different section or book.</note> he says that wool dyers use a plant similar to **wild dock** <note>original: *lapatio syluestri*; a broad-leafed weed.</note>. That Pliny easily indicates in that same passage that this plant is also called *isatis* by the Greeks is clear, because he attributes the same effects to this fourth kind that Dioscorides assigns to *isatis*. Therefore, since Pliny added no warning in that place that this plant called *isatis* by the Greeks was the same one he had taught was called *glastum* by the Gauls in Book 22, it appears he was truly ignorant of which herb the Greeks meant by the name *isatis*. Otherwise, he would have written that it possessed the same powers in his fourth kind of wild lettuce as he had previously...

<summary>Leonicenus identifies a major error in Pliny’s natural history: failing to realize that the Gallic "glastum" (woad) and the Greek "isatis" are the same plant, leading to redundant and contradictory descriptions. He also critiques contemporary scholars for following these ancient errors blindly.</summary>

### ON HERBS AND SHRUBS ###

...in the case of **woad** <note>original: *isatis*</note>, just as he had done with the **woad-dye** <note>original: *glastum*</note>, Dioscorides would have assigned to it the leaves of a plantain.

<margin>**Soapwort** <note>original: *Struthion*</note></margin>
What of the fact that—unless there is a corruption in the manuscript—that which is called *isatis* by the Greeks is said to be called **little-root** <note>original: *radicula*</note> by the Romans? Furthermore, in Book 19 of that same Pliny, it is written to consist of olive leaves, yet later in Book 24, he suggests that this same *radicula* is not *isatis*, but rather **soapwort** <note>original: *struthion*</note> by those same Greeks, and that its branches are prepared for the use of dyers. What, then, shall be this confusion of names and of the things themselves? If the same herb is read in Pliny sometimes by the name of *glastum*, sometimes *radicula*, sometimes *isatis*, and sometimes *struthion*? And if it is described now with the leaf of an olive, now a plantain, and now indeed a **dock** <note>original: *lapatium*; a common perennial herb</note>?

<margin>**Pietro Barozzi** <note>1441–1507; the Bishop of Padua and a respected humanist scholar known for his interest in science.</note></margin>
It is not without reason, therefore, that the venerable prelate Pietro Barozzi, Bishop of Padua—who is as eminent in the discipline of all the liberal arts as he is no less than the physicians themselves in this branch of medicine—judges that the knowledge of herbs in our times is almost impossible. This is because their ancient names are unknown to us. Indeed, we possess no evidence handed down by the ancients so manifest that just as many opposing points might not lead one toward a contrary opinion. Whether this difficulty of teaching or learning the science of herbs originates from the fact that at various

<margin>**The knowledge of herbs is most difficult.**</margin>
seasons of the year, herbs change their appearance with their age, or because it is not as easy for a human to describe their colors and shapes as it is for nature to paint and form them. From this arises that disagreement among authors in identifying these plants, and from this comes that ambiguity of names, so that nearly the greater part of physicians do not know what the ancient authors intended to signify by the terms **soapwort** <note>original: *struthion*, which the Arabs call *condisi*</note>, **eupatory** <note>original: *eupatorium*</note>, **greater centaury** <note>original: *centaurea maior*</note>, **chickweed** <note>original: *alsine*</note>, or **butcher's broom** <note>original: *oxymyrsine*</note>. Those who indeed believe that they know are involved in even greater error. For since our age has [drifted] from Hippocrates, Dioscorides, Galen, and all ancient medicine toward certain talkative...

For it would not be excessively difficult to learn, if not everything, at least most of those things which are so common that they are sometimes used not only for medicine but for other purposes as well, just as we are about to point out concerning **butcher’s broom** <note>original: *oximirsine*; Ruscus aculeatus</note> and **burdock** <note>original: *aretio*, likely a variant of *arction*</note>. Since these and other similar names are very different from the ones we use today to signify the same things, it frequently happens that when these same names are read in the books of the ancients, they are thought to be either foreign medicines or things far removed from common use. Yet, there is no one who does not have them in their own garden or who does not use them very frequently—though not without danger, when someone uses them differently than the ancient authors of medicine established. Indeed, we cannot even guess what they thought about such things if the names commonly used by them are unknown. Then, truly, the greatest error occurs (as we have said) when someone thinks they know what is indicated by a certain name from the ancients, when in fact that thing is included by those same ancients under a different naming convention. This happens with **eupatory** <note>original: *eupatorio*; usually hemp-agrimony or agrimony</note>, **greater centaury**, **argemony** <note>original: *argemonio*; a type of poppy</note>, and many other plants; in place of these, plants different from those the ancients designated by those names are daily accepted by the physicians of our age. However, it was not so much Pliny who provided the occasion for these errors as the **Arab authors** <note>The "Arabs" refers to the great Islamic physicians like Avicenna and Mesue, whose Latin-translated works dominated European medicine for centuries.</note>, who themselves passed down different accounts of the same thing.

### ON HERBS AND SHRUBS.

Simon was ignorant of what the Greeks meant by **isatis** <note>original: *isatis*; woad (Isatis tinctoria), a plant used to produce blue dye</note> and what the Arabs meant by **Nil** <note>original: *Nil*; an Arabic term usually referring to indigo dye or the indigo plant</note>. Though in this latter case, Simon should be forgiven, for the Arabs themselves are not consistent regarding the same **Nil**, as we have proved from the writings of **Serapion**. **Avicenna** also, although he aimed to describe the powers and properties of plants rather than indicate their physical forms, nevertheless brings about a deserved suspicion that he too stumbled and was of two minds regarding what **isatis** was, since he writes about the same **isatis** in three places under the word **Nil**. For under the letter **N**, he writes the same things about **Nil** as **Dioscorides** does about **isatis**; for he divides it in the same way into cultivated and wild, and attributes almost the same powers and properties to the herb **Nil** that Dioscorides gives to **isatis**. But then again, the same **Avicenna** writes the following under the letter **G**:

> ” **Guasmein** <note>original: *Guaasmeín*; a Latinization of the Arabic *wasma*, meaning woad</note> is the leaf of **Nil**.

And he adds several other things that he had declared about the same leaf under the letter **N**. He adds only one thing: that it dyes the hair. In these matters, **Avicenna** does not differ much from himself or from **Dioscorides**, and is to be blamed only for writing about the same thing under different letters to no purpose. But under the same letter **G**, he seems to deviate greatly from **Dioscorides** and from the truth itself; for regarding the **grain of Nil** <note>original: *grano Nil*</note>, he writes:

> ” The **grain of Nil** 
> ” is **Indian safflower** <note>original: *cartamum indum*; likely Carthamus tinctorius, often used as a cheaper red/yellow dye</note>.

Then he adds many properties which have nothing to do with **isatis**, for which the same **Avicenna** had cited **Nil** or **nigel** <note>original: *nigel*; another variant for the plant yielding indigo</note> under the letter **N**. **Mesue** <note>Mesue the Younger, a name attached to influential 12th-century pharmaceutical texts</note> also, noticing this error, says when writing about **safflower** <note>original: *cartamo*</note> that some have falsely thought safflower to be the **grain of Nil**. Nor is there any less of a muddle <note>original: *colluuio*; literally a "wash-pot" or "cesspool," used here to mean a confusion of terms</note> in the works of the author of the **Pandects** <note>Matthaeus Sylvaticus, author of the *Pandectae Medicinae*, a massive medical dictionary</note> regarding these same things and names. ### ON HERBS AND SHRUBS.

The chief authority for this confusion, it seems to me, was **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina, the 11th-century Persian "Prince of Physicians"</note>. While he describes various compositions of *theriac* <note>a famous ancient "universal" antidote containing dozens of ingredients</note>, he sometimes calls the *troches* <note>medicinal lozenges; original: *trociscos*</note> mixed into that same theriac "troches of vipers," and at other times "troches of tirus." Yet these same troches in which vipers are placed are called "theriac troches" by the Greeks for no other reason than that *theria* <note>Greek: *thēria*, meaning "wild beasts" or "venomous creatures"</note>—that is, vipers, which belong to the genus of wild animals—are added to them. Nevertheless, as I have said, this conviction persists among our modern doctors that the *tirus* is a different serpent from the viper. Because they believe it is found only in Egypt, they think that the best theriac is brought to us from nowhere else but Memphis.

**Gentile [da Foligno]** <note>a famous 14th-century Italian physician and commentator</note>, an authority of the highest standing in our own age, also shares this view. In his expositions on the fifth book of **Avicenna**, he judges that the vipers from which **Avicenna** teaches the troches are made are not the same kind of serpent about which **Nicander** <note>a 2nd-century BC Greek poet and physician</note> wrote. **Nicander** wrote on this subject in a most elegant Greek poem, which we have translated into the English tongue <note>original: "into the Latin tongue"</note> as best we could:

> The savage viper bites off her husband's head
> With a deadly tooth; but the offspring, born of his seed,
> Tear the mother's vitals as they seek the light:
> Thus they avenge the father's death at their very birth.

Regarding this passage, these are the words of **Gentile**:
> It appears that "viper" is used as a general term for common serpents, not for those specific ones that cut off the head of the male during mating, which leads the children to tear the mother open to avenge him <note>original: *matris vindictam*, literally "vengeance of the mother," though contextually implying vengeance for the father against the mother</note>.

However, **Galen** <note>the most influential physician of the Roman Empire</note> teaches in his book *On Theriac, to Piso* that it is precisely this kind of serpent described by **Nicander**, and not "common serpents" as **Gentile** believes, that must be mixed into the theriac. ,, ...fit for destruction. For they say that the female receives the seed of the male with an open mouth, and once it is received, she bites off his head; such is the deadly embrace of vipers. Now, although these things are not written by **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (980–1037), the influential Persian physician whose "Canon of Medicine" was a standard textbook in Europe</note> concerning vipers, he nevertheless sets forth many other details about them which **Galen** <note>the most famous physician of the Roman Empire, whose works formed the basis of Western medicine for centuries</note> also relates in that book we mentioned, *On Theriac*, addressed to Piso, regarding *echidnae*—that is, vipers. <meta>This page continues Niccolò Leoniceno’s detailed investigation into the botanical errors found in the "Canon of Medicine" by Avicenna and its medieval commentators. # NICCOLÒ LEONICENO

...some think it is *matricaria* <note>feverfew</note>, and others *cotula* <note>mayweed or stinking chamomile</note>, as Gentilis <note>Gentile da Foligno (d. 1348), an influential Italian physician and commentator on Avicenna</note> testifies. However, whatever "white alacoen" <note>A corrupted transliteration of an Arabic plant name</note> may be, it is certain that *amaracus* <note>marjoram</note>—for which one reads *emeruche* in Avicenna—signifies none of those things which various authors explain regarding "white alacoen." For *amaracus* is a fragrant herb, which is called by another name, *sampsycus*, or is very similar to that same *sampsycus*. Indeed, Dioscorides <note>The primary Greek authority on botany</note> testifies in his third book that *sampsycus* is called *amaracus* by another name by the people of Cyzicus and Sicily; many others, among whose number is Pliny, confirm the same.

In the same Avicenna, in the first description of the Theriac <note>A famous ancient "universal antidote" and panacea, often containing dozens of ingredients including viper flesh</note>, one reads *sceae montanae* <note>A corrupted Latin rendering of an Arabic term</note>; Gentilis explains this as being either *sticados* <note>French lavender, *Lavandula stoechas*</note> or *absinthium* <note>wormwood</note>. But it cannot signify *sticados* in this passage, for that is placed above under its own proper name. Nor can it be wormwood, since no mention is made of wormwood in the Theriac of Andromachus <note>Andromachus the Elder, physician to Nero and creator of the most famous Theriac recipe</note> by any author. Furthermore, in the first composition of this same Theriac that Avicenna writes, one reads 
<margin>Scordion <note>Water germander</note>.</margin>
*scordion*; however, in the second description, *allium sylvestre* <note>wild garlic</note> is written in place of that same *scordion*. 

From this, a most widespread error has spread: because *scorodon* <note>original: "scorodon"</note> signifies garlic among the Greeks, they take wild garlic for *scordion*, not only in the Theriac but in many other compositions. But *scorodon agrion* <note>original: "scorodon agrion"</note>—that is, wild garlic—is one thing, and the herb *scordion* is another. As Dioscorides writes in his third book, *scordion* consists of leaves like those of the *trisago* <note>germander</note>, and it is a primary remedy against poisons and the bites of serpents. For this reason, it is mixed into the Theriac and many other antidotes, and not without cause. Regarding this same herb, Galen writes the following opinion in his work *On the Theriac, to Pamphilianus*, and in his book *On Antidotes*: 

"The best *scordion* is brought from Crete, although that found among other nations is not to be rejected. It has been written concerning it by the weightiest authorities of medicine that when it happened that the bodies of those who had fallen in battle lay unburied for a long time, whichever bodies happened by chance to lie upon *scordion* were found to be much less <note>The text likely continues to say "decayed" or "putrified" on the following page.</note>"

...the remaining parts felt the putrefaction, and especially those parts of the whole body which the touch of the herb itself protected. Likewise, Galen <note>A Greek physician whose work formed the basis of Western medicine for centuries</note> himself, in the ninth book of his work *On Simple Medicines* <note>original: "de simplicibus medicaminibus"</note>, testifies that this herb is particularly commended among others that resist putrefaction. 

But if, as Galen writes in his book *On Theriac to Pamphilianus* <note>original: "de theriaca ad Pamphilianum"</note>, the flaw of a single adulterated drug can corrupt the entire composition of the Theriac <note>A famous ancient "universal antidote" containing dozens of ingredients</note>, how can we hope that the same mixture is being perfectly prepared today, when the majority of the simple medicines joined within it are unknown? Unless, perhaps, we believe the Arabs or Egyptians of today are more learned than Avicenna <note>A Persian polymath and author of the "Canon of Medicine"</note> ever was—among whom it is well established that all study of philosophy and medicine was abolished long ago by the command of their leader, Muhammad, as the story goes. <note>Leoniceno reflects a common 15th-century European view that Islamic scientific progress had been halted by religious restrictions.</note> It is rather less surprising, since neither among us nor among them is there a certain knowledge of this antidote, that the Theriac in our times does not provide those effects which the ancient physicians promised of it. But lest the lengthiness of my writing cause weariness in the readers, let us return to the subject from which we digressed—that is, to Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, author of "Natural History"</note> himself.

<margin>Cudweed.</margin>

He further testifies to its excellent effect in binding the bowels when taken in dry wine. However, Dioscorides <note>The primary Greek authority on botany</note>, in his third book, writes not that it is called *clematides* by the Greeks, but rather that *gnaphalium* <note>cudweed, from the Greek word for a "lock of wool" due to its fuzzy texture</note> is called *centunculus* by the Romans.
