He <note>Pliny the Elder, a Roman author of a massive encyclopedia of natural history</note> diligently and accurately described all species of clematis <note>A genus of climbing plants</note>, yet he does not suggest that any of them were called by this name by the Greeks in the way he describes: a plant with beaked leaves resembling the hood of a traveling cloak <note>original: "penularum"</note> lying in the fields.

The same Pliny, in that same Book 24 and in the same place where he names the *centunculus* <note>possibly cudweed</note>, also counts the *lagine* among the clematis plants—which he called *lasine* in Book 22.

<margin>Lasine.</margin> Regarding the *lasine*, he writes the following in Book 22:
> It is beneficial for those suffering from consumption <note>original: "phtisim," referring to tuberculosis</note>. 

But in Book 24, he says of the *lagine*: 
> It helps those with consumption when taken with honey. 

Likewise, regarding the *lasine*: 
> It produces an abundance of milk in women. 

Similarly, regarding the *lagine*: 
> It produces an abundance of milk. 

Also regarding the *lasine*: 
> Smeared on the heads of infants, it nourishes the hair and makes the skin of the head more resilient. 

Likewise, regarding the *lagine*: 
> And smeared on infants, it feeds the hair. 

He testifies that both of them, both *lasine* and *lagine*, are pleasing in foods and stimulate sexual desire.

The similarity of these names and their almost identical effects could serve as proof that one should read either *lasine* or *lagine* in both books, and that Pliny pointlessly repeated the same plant under these different names. Furthermore, Pliny writes that this same *lagine* is called *echiten* by some, as well as "slender scammony" <note>original: "tenue scamoniū"</note>. This statement leads me to suspect that *lagine* and *echiten* might be written instead of *elxine* and *eusine*, perhaps through an error in the manuscript. Indeed, no plant is recognized that can more truly be called "slender scammony" than the one the Greeks call by other names: *elxine*, *eusine*, and even *cissampelon* <note>Greek for "ivy-vine"</note>. All of these possess the characteristics of scammony <note>A plant known for its potent laxative properties</note>. 

Indeed, in his fourth book, Dioscorides <note>A Greek physician and the father of pharmacognosy</note> writes that *elxine* has leaves similar to ivy. Yet, in the same book, the same Dioscorides writes that scammony likewise has leaves like ivy and *elxine*. The *elxine* also bears a white flower, chalice-shaped <note>original: "calathi figura"</note>, and it drips with much milk-like sap, and it moves the bowels just like scammony. <margin>Bindweed</margin>

From all this, it is concluded that what we said is true: Avicenna fell into a greater error than Pliny. Yet Dioscorides, Galen, and Paul [of Aegina] wrote about only one *arction* called *prosopite* <note>original: "prosopite"</note>, that is, "the mask-plant." That this is the same *arction*, or the same *personatia*, which Pliny describes in both the first and second place, is most clearly shown by Pliny's own words; for regarding the first, he writes: "Some call *arction* 'personatia,' no leaf is wider than its own, and it bears large burrs <note>original: "lappas"</note>." 

<margin>Burdock.</margin>
Here, without a doubt, Pliny refers to that plant which our people call both <term>bardana</term> <note>Burdock (*Arctium lappa*), famous for its large leaves and sticky burrs</note> and the "greater burr." The ancients called it *personatia* because they used its massive leaves to make masks <note>The Latin *persona* means mask; the broad leaves were used by actors or children to cover their faces</note>. For the same reason, Dioscorides, Galen, and Paul called this same plant *prosopite* <note>original: "prosopiten," from the Greek *prosopon* for face/mask</note>—that is, the "mask-plant"—and recorded that it consists of leaves like the gourd, though darker and hairier.

Pliny, in Book 15, describes the <term>chamaedaphne</term> <note>original: "Chamædaphnẽ," literally "ground-laurel," usually identified as the Butcher's Broom or Alexandrian Laurel</note> thus: "There is also the wild *chamaedaphne* shrub, and the Alexandrian, which some call *idaea*, some *hypoglotton* <note>original: "hypoglotton," meaning "under-tongue"</note>, others *daphne*, others *carpophylon*, and others *hypelaten*. Ida and around Heraclea of Pontus, but only in mountainous areas." ...[it is clear] that Pliny provides different descriptions for the same plant. For the first description is found in the entry for Alexandrian laurel <note>original: "daphne alexandrina"</note>, but not in the dwarf laurel <note>original: "chamædaphne"</note> as handed down by Dioscorides in Book IV. <margin>Sharp-myrtle (Oxymirsine).</margin>
This same Pliny, after describing the cultivated myrtle <note>original: "myrtam satiuam"</note> in Book XXIII and assigning its powers and properties, later adds the properties of wild myrtle, which is called <term>oxymirsine</term> <note>Literally "sharp myrtle," usually identified as Butcher’s Broom (*Ruscus aculeatus*)</note> by the Greeks. He did this to such an extent that he seems to have thought that *oxymirsine* (also called wild myrtle) differs from cultivated myrtle only by the distinction of being wild versus cultivated, just like many other types of herbs, shrubs, and small trees.

<margin>Butcher’s Broom (Ruscus).</margin>
For that reason, he often mentions <term>ruscus</term> <note>Butcher’s Broom</note>—which is called *oxymirsine* and wild myrtle by the Greeks—in separate places as if it were a different thing from *oxymirsine*, even though he attributes no other powers to *ruscus* than those he gives to *oxymirsine*. However, in the same Book XXIII, Pliny cites Castor <note>Castor of Rhodes, an ancient botanist cited by Pliny</note>, who correctly believed that the plant the Greeks call *oxymirsine* is the same as the Latin *ruscus*—commonly called <term>bruscus</term> by physicians—from which country brooms were made in Pliny's time, just as they are today. But besides Castor, Dioscorides also testifies in his fourth book that *oxymirsine*, or wild myrtle, is called *ruscus* by the Romans. To tell the truth, however, Pliny’s error in doubting whether *oxymirsine* was *ruscus* or another shrub differing from cultivated myrtle only as a wild variety, was less significant than the error of Serapio the Arab <note>An influential 9th-century Persian physician whose botanical works were central to Medieval medicine</note>. Serapio asserted that *oxymirsine* is a tree bearing the fruit called 

<margin>Cubebs.</margin>
<term>cubeb</term> <note>original: "Cubebe"; a pungent berry related to black pepper (*Piper cubeba*)</note> by the Arabs. He relied on a rather frivolous reasoning, since neither Galen regarding *oxymirsine* (wild myrtle), nor Dioscorides regarding <term>carpesium</term> <note>An aromatic plant often confused with cubebs in the Middle Ages</note>—that is, cubebs, for so the Arabs interpret *carpesion*—[wrote] anything in their [books] on simple [medicines]...

# NICCOLÒ LEONICENO

...had recorded in their book on medicines. However, <margin>Carpesium</margin> carpesium is a far different thing from oxymyrsine. Anyone who knows both fruits—namely, <term>cubebs</term> <note>The pungent berries of *Piper cubeba*</note> and the red berries produced by <term>oxymyrsine</term> <note>Also known as Butcher's Broom (*Ruscus aculeatus*)</note> (or *ruscus*) which resemble cherries—will easily judge how much Serapion <note>Serapion the Younger, a 12th-century Arabic medical writer</note> was deceived by his own conjecture. 

Nor is Serapion only mistaken in thinking that cubebs are the fruit of oxymyrsine, which Dioscorides wrote about; he is also mistaken because he believes carpesium—which Galen mentions, but Dioscorides does not—is the same as cubebs. For carpesium and oxymyrsine are not the same plant. Furthermore, although the Arabs (including Avicenna) take cubebs in place of carpesium, Galen indicates that carpesium meant something else to the Greeks than those small grains which the Arabs call cubebs. In his book *On Theriac, to Piso* <note>original: "de theriaca ad Pisonem"</note>, Galen writes that carpesium consists of certain thin, aromatic stalks similar in taste to <term>phu</term> <note>The ancient Greek name for Valerian</note>—that is, the fragrant root of a certain herb that some believe to be what is commonly called <term>valeriana</term> (valerian). However, not everything Dioscorides writes about *phu* matches the characteristics of valerian.

In Avicenna, however, who attributes almost everything Galen said about carpesium to cubebs, there is another error. For while Galen writes, as we said, that carpesium has powers similar to *phu* but consists of a more subtle substance, in the Latin translations of Avicenna this is read not of *phu*, but of <term>Rubea</term> <note>Madder (*Rubia tinctorum*), a plant used for red dye and medicine</note>. For these are the words of Avicenna himself, identifying cubebs as carpesium:

> "The power of Cubebs is indeed similar to madder <note>original: "rubeæ"</note>; however, it is of a more subtle substance."

<margin>Aera.</margin> Dioscorides writes in Book II that the grain the Greeks call <term>aera</term> is the same as what our people call <margin>Lolium.</margin> <term>lolium</term> <note>Darnel or "tares" (*Lolium temulentum*), a weed often found in wheat fields</note>. Furthermore, the effects of this same *aera* recorded by Aristotle in his book *On Sleep and Waking* and by Pliny in Book XVIII—namely, that it most clearly causes a heaviness of the head and dizziness—prove this identification. Pliny, however, in the same book and chapter, describes *aera* and *lolium* separately, as if *lolium* differed from *aera*...

# NICCOLÒ LEONICENO

### ON HERBS AND SHRUBS

...names them separately <note>The text likely begins with "separatim," referring to Pliny naming plants as distinct species that may be identical</note>. For if he thought that <term>lolium</term> <note>darnel or cockle, a common weed in grain fields</note> and <term>æra</term> <note>The Greek term for darnel</note> were the same, it is strange that—just as with many other crops and their defects where Latin names were available, such as <term>grain</term> <note>original: "frumentum"</note>, <term>barley</term> <note>original: "ordeum"</note>, and <term>oats</term> <note>original: "auena"</note>—he did not think he should use Greek terms, yet he did not follow that same rule for lolium, especially since it is a name so commonly used by everyone. 

However, a similar error regarding oats is also read in the same book and chapter. For when he explains the defects of crops at the beginning, he writes that barley degenerates into oats. A little further down, the same Pliny reports that barley is killed by <term>festuca</term> <note>A straw-like weed or fescue</note>, which is named <term>ægilops</term> <note>A type of wild oat</note>. But if we believe Dioscorides <note>A 1st-century Greek physician and botanist</note>, what is called *ægilops* by the Greeks is named *oats* by the Latins. 

Galen <note>An influential Roman-era Greek physician</note> also, in the first book of his work *On Foodstuffs*, testifies that when the cultivation of <term>wheat</term> <note>original: "tritico"</note> and barley turns out poorly, the former frequently turns into *æra* and the latter into *ægilops*. This is the strongest evidence that *æra* is the same thing as lolium, and *ægilops* is the same as oats.

<margin>French nard.</margin>
What Pliny calls French <term>nard</term>, Dioscorides calls Celtic nard, as is very clearly indicated by what is reported about Celtic and French nard by both authors. Dioscorides writes in his first book that this same Celtic nard grows in the Alps of Liguria and is called <term>saliunca</term> by the inhabitants. 

<margin>Saliunca.</margin>
Pliny, however, treats French nard and saliunca in separate sections as if they were different things. Nevertheless, in Book 21, he admits that <term>saliunca</term> is a fragrant herb which is most pleasant if placed among clothes; he also testifies that it grows in the Alps and records its use in medicine as being not much different from Celtic nard.

<margin>Sion herb.</margin>
The same Pliny writes in Book 22 that <term>Sion</term> <note>Water parsnip (*Sium latifolium*)</note> grows in water and has leaves like those of <term>apium</term> <note>Celery or wild parsley</note> but broader, and he assigns other properties and powers to it which Dioscorides also records in his second book. Later, in Book 28, Pliny writes almost the same things about <term>silao</term>: 

<margin>Silaus.</margin>
<term>Silaus</term> <note>Likely pepper-saxifrage (*Silaum silaus*)</note> grows in gravelly and perennial streams, [at a height of] a cubit...

He also notes how Pliny mistakenly categorizes French nard and saliunca as different plants despite their identical descriptions in other classical sources.</summary>

# NICCOLÒ LEONICENO

...such a plant, due to its similarity to celery <note>original: "apij"; likely referring to water-parsley or water-parsnip</note>, is cooked like a vegetable with great benefit to the bladder. Both descriptions undoubtedly apply to that herb, similar to celery, growing in water, which some falsely call *senectionem* <note>groundsel</note>, while others commonly call it *crissones* <note>watercress</note>. However, it seems Pliny wanted to indicate one thing by the name <term>sij</term> <note>Sium, or water-parsnip</note> and another by the name <term>silai</term>; or, if *sion* should be read instead of *silai*, he would have described the same herb in two places to no purpose.

<margin>Cinnabar.</margin>
What of the fact that Pliny sometimes seems to follow a common opinion? For in Book 34, he writes that **Cinnabar**—whose color in paintings properly renders the appearance of blood—is the blood of a dragon crushed by the weight of dying elephants, mixed with the blood of both animals. He confirms that this "cinnabar" is useful for antidotes and medicines. 

Indeed, he rightly rebukes the doctors of his own time who used <term>minium</term> <note>Today known as red lead, but historically confused with mercury-based cinnabar</note> instead of this cinnabar, simply because it too was called cinnabar. For this cinnabar, which is also called minium, is a poison, since <term>quicksilver</term> <note>mercury; original: "argentum uiuum"</note> is made from it—just as, conversely, artificial cinnabar is made from quicksilver, which we commonly call *cenabrium*. 

Nor am I unaware that many doctors even in our own time fall into the same error. When they find "cinnabar" written in their <term>Recipes</term> <note>original: "Receptis"; the formal written instructions for compounding medicines</note>, they are deceived by the similarity of the name and use *cenabrium*, which is proven to be a poison. 

Therefore, just as I advise that this cinnabar should be avoided in medical use, I also do not suggest seeking the gore of dragons and elephants from India. I consider it a fable that the cinnabar used for painting and medicine is prepared from the mixed blood of two animals. I am easily moved by the authority of that most serious witness, **Dioscorides** <note>A Greek physician whose "De Materia Medica" was the primary botanical authority for 1,500 years</note>, who in the fifth book of his work—where he treats metals—asserts that some people, deceived by the similarity of color, falsely thought cinnabar was dragon’s blood. Indeed, the conviction of the ancients regarding this same name still persists; for even today, that mineral substance which Dioscorides and Galen call **cinnabar** <note>original: "cinnabarim"; a bright red mineral consisting of mercury sulfide</note> is commonly called **dragon's blood** <note>original: "sanguis draconis"</note>. Although almost all doctors in our age, following the error of Serapion and Avicenna <note>Medieval Islamic physicians whose works were foundational in European medicine</note>, judge that kind of dragon's blood which is in use to be the juice of a certain herb, 

<margin>Ironwort.</margin>
which is called **sideritis** <note>original: "sideritis"; often called ironwort, it was believed to heal wounds made by iron weapons</note> by the Greeks. But Dioscorides wrote most fully concerning the herb sideritis and all its kinds. However, he taught that from none of its species is such a juice squeezed out that doctors and painters alike might use for their respective work. Yet we find this dual use in both painting and medicine in that which they call pure dragon's blood; and regarding cinnabar, both Dioscorides and Pliny testify to the same, which most moved me to think that the cinnabar written about by Pliny and the ancient Greek authors is the same thing as what we commonly call 

<margin>Dragon's blood.</margin>
**dragon's blood**. For this also yields a color most similar to blood, and it is rare and difficult to find, nor is it less expensive than it is read to have been among the ancients, when it is sold pure and unadulterated. For that which is displayed for sale everywhere in the apothecaries' shops is adulterated, though we accept it as genuine for use in medicine: just as we accept a certain cheap and common earth in place of **Lemnian earth** <note>A famous medicinal clay from the island of Lemnos</note>, which, as we said above, the ancient doctors called the **Lemnian seal** <note>original: "lemnium sigillum"; so named because the clay was shaped into tablets and stamped with a seal to guarantee its authenticity</note>. But in this neglect of all things, even those pertaining to life, there is surely room for pardon if one thing is carelessly taken for another—provided that ignorance does not rush headlong into poison. This occurs, as we said regarding cinnabar, for which artificial **minium** <note>red lead, which is highly toxic</note> is often received, which we have shown to be a poison. ### THE WRITINGS OF NICCOLÒ LEONICENO

However, this error is not one that results in the destruction of life. In place of the **argemony** herb <note>original: "argemonio"; likely the prickly poppy or a type of windflower</note>, which **Dioscorides** <note>A 1st-century Greek physician and botanist</note> writes in his second book has a leaf similar to the **wild poppy**, a similarly red flower, and a round root dripping with plenty of saffron-colored sap: they use another shrub which, although it differs greatly from the true argemony in both appearance and medicinal power, is nevertheless proven to be useful in many diseases. In place of **agrimony** <note>original: "eupatorio"; named after Mithridates Eupator</note>, the discovery of King Eupator, a common herb is taken that grows everywhere in ditches; although its true nature is unknown to most, it is nonetheless certain that it is not a poison. In place of the **white thorn** <note>original: "Spina alba"</note> which the **Arabs** call ***bedaguard*** <note>from the Persian "bad-award," referring to a type of thistle or the mossy gall found on roses</note>, since this is unknown to physicians, they use the **wild rose sponge** <note>original: "spongiola rosæ syluestris"; a mossy gall caused by a wasp, also called a robin's pincushion</note> which grows on thorns: for even if this differs greatly in medical use from the white thorn, this substitution is not fatal.

Let us pardon these and other errors, even though they are worthy of reproach, since they do not bring about manifest death. We grant this to those whose interest it should have been to investigate these matters—so necessary for the use of medicine—more diligently and subtly than many other things of no importance to life; provided that they do not admit the seed of **hemlock** <note>original: "cicuta"</note>, which everyone knows to be a poison, in place of the seed of **wild rue**. A single accent should not be of such great importance, 
<margin>Armel.</margin>
<margin>Wild rue.</margin>
yet when ***Armel*** is written among the **Arabs** with an aspiration <note>i.e., pronounced or written with an 'H' as 'Harmel'</note> it signifies **hemlock**; when written without the aspiration, it signifies **wild rue**. Thus, sometimes human life is endangered by such a tiny mark. Indeed, I have quite often warned the craftsmen <note>the apothecaries or pharmacists</note> who prepare pills from **hermodactyls** <note>original: "hermodactylis"; a plant often used to treat gout, likely Colchicum</note> and "foul pills" <note>original: "fœtidas"; likely referring to *Pilulae foetidae*, a recipe containing strong-smelling resins like asafoetida</note> about this error, nor do I cease to warn them daily, although more trust is placed in long-standing custom than in me. 

But if they would listen to me, they would not add to **lapis lazuli pills** that stone which painters everywhere use. **MONTAGNANA**, 
<margin>Lapis lazuli.</margin>

I believe one must guard against the counterfeit just as much as against a poison like minium <note>original: "minium"; red lead</note>, which we pointed out is commonly called cinnabar. And for that reason, nothing is read among the Greek authors concerning this stone regarding its effectiveness in purging black bile, or that it produces the other effects **Mesue** <note>Yuhanna ibn Masawayh, a 9th-century Persian physician whose works were foundational to Western pharmacy</note> writes about—
<margin>**Armenian stone.**</margin>
effects which I believe could more truly be affirmed of the **Armenian stone** <note>original: "lapis armenus"; a blue copper mineral, likely azurite, used as a pigment and purgative</note>. For even Mesue himself, although he distinguishes **lapis lazuli** <note>a deep-blue metamorphic rock</note> from the Armenian stone, nonetheless did not record very different powers and properties in either. **Serapio** <note>likely Serapion the Younger, an influential Arabic medical author</note>, however, when he describes lapis lazuli and explains its powers, reports nothing other than what is passed down by the Greeks concerning the Armenian stone, nor does he later mention the Armenian stone in any other place. This is certainly no weak argument that Serapio thought it was the same stone, called "Armenian" from the soil in which it is born, and "lazuli" from its sky-blue color, which the **Arabs** call *lazul*. **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina, the famous Persian polymath</note>, although he writes separately about *azul*—that is, lapis lazuli—and about the Armenian stone among other stones, nevertheless, almost everything he reports about lapis lazuli is written by Greek authors, especially **Dioscorides** and **Galen**, regarding the Armenian stone. For these are Avicenna's words regarding lapis lazuli:

> Its power is like the power of that to which gold adheres <note>referring to substances used in soldering gold</note>. Dioscorides, in his fifth book concerning the Armenian stone, says: "It does the same things as **chrysocolla**" <note>literally "gold-glue"; in this context, a green or blue copper mineral like malachite or azurite</note>. Avicenna, on *azul* or lapis lazuli, says: "It possesses a rooting-out power, a putrefying power, and its cleansing ability comes with sharpness and a little astringency." **Galen** and **Paulus** <note>Paul of Aegina, a 7th-century Byzantine physician</note> say almost the same about the Armenian stone: "It has cleansing powers with sharpness, and a certain small capacity for binding <note>astringency</note>."

Avicenna likewise says of lapis lazuli: "It makes the hairs of the eyelids good, and is the ultimate remedy, as it is said, because of the property within it; and it is said that it is because it evacuates the bad humors <note>the four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—believed to control health</note> that prevent hair from growing well." Galen writes in almost the same vein concerning the Armenian stone...

..[will bene]fit <note>This continues the sentence from the previous page: "I believe it will benefit..."</note>: Since, therefore, it is endowed with such a nature, it is mixed into medicines for the eyes. They also grind it separately and reduce it into a kind of powder, using it dry to increase the hair of the eyelids <note>original: "pilos palpebrarũ"</note> when some of them fall out due to the sharpness of the humors <note>The "humors" were the four vital fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—thought to control health in ancient and medieval medicine.</note>, and others do not grow or receive nourishment. For once the sharpness of these humors has been consumed, the eyelid is restored to its natural state. From these accounts, which are so similar and almost identical—those of **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina, the 11th-century Persian "Prince of Physicians"</note> as well as **Dioscorides** <note>A 1st-century Greek physician and author of *De Materia Medica*</note> and **Galen** <note>The most influential Greek physician of the Roman Empire</note> regarding lapis lazuli and Armenian stone—it can appear to anyone that Avicenna, just like **Serapio** <note>An influential Arabic pharmacological writer</note>, designates Armenian stone by the name "lapis lazuli."

Indeed, Serapio is more to be praised in this matter than Avicenna. This is because once he had identified the Armenian stone under the name of lapis lazuli, he decided that nothing more needed to be written separately about the Armenian stone as if it were a thing different from lapis lazuli—an error which Avicenna is proven to have committed. But if Avicenna adds a few things regarding lapis lazuli, such as that it possesses a "rooting out" <note>original: "eradicatiuam"; having the power to pull out or destroy from the root</note> and "decaying" <note>original: "putrefactiuam"</note> power—which are not written about Armenian stone by the Greeks, but rather about another metal-like substance which the same Greeks call *cyaneus* <note>original: "cyaneus"; from the Greek *kyanos*, likely referring to a deep blue mineral or artificial pigment like blue frit</note>—it is surely no wonder that Avicenna, as in many other cases, has mixed together the properties of different things in this stone as well.

From this, it happens that he seems to be inconsistent with himself and to write things that are mutually contradictory regarding this same stone. For if it has a rooting-out power, as he writes of it, how does it nourish or produce hair by a property within it, when it ought to uproot them by that same "eradicative" power? Furthermore, if it also causes decay <note>original: "putrefactiuus"</note>, since those things which have the power of causing decay are numbered among poisons <note>original: "uenena"</note> by the most learned physicians, and especially by Galen, by what logic could pills made from it be taken without danger to life? For this is what I meant when I indicated that no small danger looms from the use of lapis lazuli. For I judge it to be the same...

### ON HERBS AND SHRUBS.

...which **Dioscorides** <note>A 1st-century Greek physician</note> and **Galen** <note>The most influential physician of the Roman Empire</note> identify under the name of *cyaneum* <note>original: "cyanei"; likely referring to a deep blue mineral or pigment like ultramarine or a copper-based blue</note>, and which the same Dioscorides in Book V testifies has the power of destroying and causing putrefaction. Therefore, none of the Greek authors taught that *cyaneum* should be swallowed in pills for the sake of purging **black bile** <term>atra bilis: one of the four "humors" in ancient medicine, believed to cause melancholy if in excess</term>, in the same way they did for Armenian stone. 

Nor am I unaware that there are some substances which, when taken by themselves, are deadly poisons, yet when mixed with other things are rendered healthful. But someone might ask: what use or reason discovered this property in lapis lazuli? Unless, perhaps, we wish to place our trust in this matter in the Arabic authors, who likely did not know how to distinguish lapis lazuli from Armenian stone, since they note the powers and properties of one in the description of the other. 

Indeed, **Serapio** <note>A 9th-century Arabic pharmacological writer</note> himself is not entirely free of this error. For although he writes only about lapis lazuli—by which name he intended Armenian stone to be understood—the words of Galen that Serapio attributes to lapis lazuli were actually written by Galen regarding Armenian stone. At the end, however, he adds from the opinion of a certain **Alchanzi** <note>Likely referring to Al-Kindi or another medieval Arabic authority</note> that lapis lazuli has a scorching and putrefying power, and therefore removes warts. 

This power, however, as we have said, does not belong to Armenian stone, but rather to another medicine, which is called *cyaneum* by the Greeks and *coeruleum* <note>original: "coeruleum"; the Latin term for sky-blue or dark blue pigments</note> by the Latins. Nor indeed is it surprising that **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina, the 11th-century Persian "Prince of Physicians"</note> hesitated over what Armenian stone was (which is unknown even to the physicians of our age), since he was so uncertain and doubtful regarding **hemlock** <note>original: "cicuta"; a highly toxic plant</note>, a herb so common. In that case, he reported it to consist sometimes of cucumber leaves, sometimes of **mandrake** <note>A plant with a root often shaped like a human, used as an anesthetic and associated with magic</note>, according to the various opinions of different authors; and he calls it now *succara*, now *alpharas*, and sometimes **black henbane** <note>original: "hyoscyamũ nigrũ"; a toxic plant used in small doses as a sedative</note>. 

For in Book II of his work *On Simple Medicines*, he describes hemlock under the name *succara*; indeed, he attributes the same effects to *succara* that Dioscorides attributes to hemlock. In the fourth book, however, where he deals with poisons, he calls hemlock not *succara* but *alphaphars*, and thinks it is *napellus* <term>napellum: a name for Aconite or "monkshood," a lethal poison</term>, or a poison...

...which kills man, but does not kill thrushes. And afterwards he adds the same cause for this fact which **Galen** <note>The most famous physician of the Roman Empire, 2nd century AD</note> brings forward—not regarding monkshood <note>original: "napello"</note> and thrushes, but rather regarding hemlock and starlings. These indeed are the words of Galen in the third book of *On Simple Medicines*:

<margin>Hemlock.</margin>
> Hemlock indeed kills man because of the width of the passages and the abundance of heat, and because of the great power the arteries have in drawing it in; while its strength is still potent, it reaches the heart. It does not kill starlings, however, for the opposite reasons.

The same Galen writes to the same effect in the second book of *On Foods*, and the third book of *On Temperaments*, concerning hemlock and starlings, but not concerning monkshood and thrushes, as is commonly repeated by almost all physicians. These doctors, relying solely on the authority of **Avicenna** <note>The 11th-century Persian "Prince of Physicians" whose Canon of Medicine was a standard university text</note>, constantly affirm that which they have found through no actual experience. For who would know whether thrushes feed on monkshood without harm, since what monkshood actually is does not even appear certain from Avicenna himself? The symptoms which are recorded by Avicenna in one who has swallowed monkshood are the same as those written by **Dioscorides** and **Paulus** <note>Paulus Aegineta, a 7th-century Byzantine physician</note> regarding those who have drunk *toxicon*. 

<margin>Arrow poison.</margin>
Now, *toxicon* <note>original: "toxicon"; the root of the word "toxic"</note> is a certain kind of poison with which arrows were dipped by the ancients: for this is its name among the Greeks, because missiles, which they call *toxeumata*, were especially treated with this substance. But Avicenna himself, a little further down, names this same kind of poison with a corrupted word, writing *tussom* instead of *toxicon*, and he confesses that he knows neither its nature nor its name. Nevertheless, he hands down the same effects for it based on the opinions of others as Dioscorides and Paulus note in *toxicon*, and which Avicenna had written a little above regarding monkshood. 

Moreover, what is read in the author of the *Pandects* <note>Likely referring to the "Pandectae Medicinae" of Matteo Silvatico, a 14th-century botanical encyclopedia</note> and believed by almost all physicians—that monkshood is a species of aconite—cannot be affirmed from Avicenna's opinion. 

<margin>Monkshood.</margin>
<margin>Aconite.</margin>
For aconite is twofold, according to Galen: one which kills wolves, and is therefore called *lycoctonos* <note>original: "lycoctonos"; from the Greek for "wolf-slayer"</note> among the Greeks; the other which kills panthers...

Regarding these two types of monkshood <note>original: "aconiti"</note>, **Avicenna** followed the same **Galen**, but treated them separately from the common monkshood <note>original: "napello"</note> under the name **wolf-strangler** <note>original: "strangulatoris adib"; *adib* is the Arabic word for wolf</note> and **leopard-strangler**. But if Avicenna is proven to have been ignorant of plants that are no less harmful than they are healing, what help can we hope for from that man's teaching, whether in avoiding poisons or in selecting remedies? And yet, professors of all arts seem to undertake and promise these two things: namely, the knowledge of both good and evil within their own art.

The same Avicenna—to return to the point from which we digressed—calls the same **hemlock** <note>original: "cicutā"</note> by the name **black henbane** <note>original: "hyoscyamum nigrum"</note> in the same fourth book, where he deals with poisons. For whatever symptoms are described by Avicenna in one who has swallowed black henbane, and the remedies against that same poison, are no different from those which **Dioscorides** <note>The primary Greek authority on botany and pharmacy, 1st century AD</note> and **Paulus** <note>Paul of Aegina, a 7th-century Byzantine physician</note> noted regarding hemlock. Nor does the same Avicenna seem any less uncertain regarding the other herb, which we suggested should be accepted in place of hemlock in the **pills of hermodactyls** <note>original: "pillulis ex hermodactylis"; *hermodactylus* literally means "fingers of Hermes," a plant used for joint pain</note>. He places its gum among the poisons, and describes symptoms and remedies for those who have swallowed this gum that match what Dioscorides and Paulus noted—not for the gum of **wild or mountain rue** <note>original: "ruta syluestris"</note> (for it is nowhere read that any species of wild rue has such a gum that is poisonous), but rather for a certain poison called **ixia** <note>original: "ixia sa"; likely referring to the poisonous sap of the chameleon thistle</note>, which **Nicander** <note>A 2nd-century BC Greek poet and physician</note> also mentions in his *Theriaca* <note>A famous poem on venomous animals and their cures</note>. Avicenna also, in the same fourth book where he teaches the cure for the bite of a viper, writes that wild rue is not **harmel** <note>original: "harmel"; the Arabic name for wild rue, *Peganum harmala*</note>, as many believe, despite the fact that Dioscorides, Galen, and Paulus all testify that a certain type of wild rue is called *moly besasa* and *harmalum*. This is because, as those same authors report, it has the power of cutting through and dispersing thick and sticky...

# NICCOLÒ LEONICENO

...these **humors** <note>In ancient medicine, the four fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—which had to be balanced for health</note> in joint pains, for which pills made from **hermodactyls** <note>A plant likely related to the autumn crocus (*Colchicum autumnale*), traditionally used to treat gout</note> are effective, since such pains arise largely from a defect of those humors. I would consider these more useful to apply than **hemlock** <note>original: "cicutā"</note>, which by its coldness might increase the disease rather than remove it. **Galen** <note>The most influential Greek physician of the Roman Empire (c. 129–216 AD)</note> indeed, in the first book of *On Simple Medicines*, testifies that the seed of hemlock is the coldest of all others. Yet in the fifth book of the same work, although he approves of some violently cold substances for the sake of dulling the senses when unbearable pains torture the patient, he nevertheless condemns the use of hemlock entirely, as it is harmful not only due to its coldness but also its excessive moisture.

But I do not know how it happened that, while one medical error after another suggested itself for correction, our discourse has tumbled down from **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder, author of the *Natural History*</note> to **Avicenna** <note>The Latinized name of Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the Persian polymath whose *Canon of Medicine* dominated European universities</note>. If I wished to wander at length in explaining the errors of this author, there would be no end to this work, since all his books on medicine—and especially the second, in which he treats of **simple medicines** <note>original: "simplicibus medicaminibus"; individual medicinal ingredients, mostly plants, as opposed to "compounds" or mixtures</note> about which we have spoken so far—teem with innumerable errors. I am not unaware of those I pass over, but I omit them for the sake of brevity; for I have destined another labor for a different volume, in which the errors of Avicenna alone will be fully addressed. Therefore, let it suffice for the present to have noted these things in Pliny, and also in passing in others who have written incorrectly about the same matters, at least in my opinion. I thought these things should be written to you, **Angelo** <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494), the brilliant Italian humanist and poet to whom Leoniceno dedicated this work</note>, most learned man, and submitted to your most grave and significant judgment. If they are approved by you, a man of most penetrating learning, I shall indeed rejoice, having your patronage against the envy of detractors—an envy which I have no doubt will arise against me, especially now that this volume is published and dedicated to your name. But if, regarding these matters pertaining to Pliny, you feel far differently than I do, and judge that I rather than Pliny am in error, I will not rejoice less...

...[Polizia]nus, and that **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder, author of the *Natural History*</note> is defended by you, and that I am corrected and amended by a man who is most dear to me. For since we are dealing here not with the weight of words, but with matters upon which human health and life depend, it would truly be impious and inhumane to wish to defend my own errors—just as you might defend those of others—so strenuously and obstinately against the truth. But to speak of myself: I have written all these things which I have included in the present volume with a mind free from all contention and looking only toward the truth. A significant argument for this could be that, just as I have written against Pliny, I have likewise felt it necessary to challenge **Serapion** <note>Likely Serapion the Younger, an influential 12th or 13th-century Arabic author on medicinal plants</note> and **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina, the Persian physician whose *Canon of Medicine* was a standard university textbook</note>, as well as many others who were occupied in writing about **simple medicines** <note>original: "simplicibus medicaminibus"; medicines made from a single natural ingredient, usually a plant</note> on the same subject matter as Pliny. In those instances where they seemed to me to dissent from **Dioscorides** <note>A 1st-century Greek physician and author of *De Materia Medica*</note>, **Galen** <note>The most famous Greek physician of antiquity, whose theories dominated Western medicine for over a thousand years</note>, and **Paul** <note>Paul of Aegina, a 7th-century Byzantine physician</note>, and even from **Nature** herself, the parent of all things, I have spoken out so that I might consult the common safety of mankind. Whether I have performed this duty rightly or wrongly for the time being will be your responsibility, and the duty of others who are able to judge such matters: to pronounce judgment without any personal bias, looking not so much at the authority of the writers as at the truth itself.

->Farewell.<-

# THE EPISTLE OF NICCOLÒ LEONICENO
## TO HERMOLAO BARBARO,
### PATRIARCH OF AQUILEIA.
<note>Hermolao Barbaro (1454–1493) was a Venetian scholar and diplomat. As the "Patriarch of Aquileia," he held a high ecclesiastical and political office, but he was most famous in the Renaissance for his "Castigationes Plinianae," a work that corrected thousands of errors in the text of Pliny the Elder.</note>

<image-desc>An ornamental woodcut initial 'V' depicting a scholar seated at a desk in a study, working on a manuscript.</image-desc>
It could scarcely be expressed, most learned Hermolao (and let this preface of yours be granted to me in this place, since, as I hear many say wittily and skillfully, more people now know Hermolao as the man of letters than as the candidate <note>original: "candidatum"; a play on words referring to the white toga worn by Roman office-seekers, suggesting Barbaro's fame as a scholar eclipsed his political career</note>), how much joy and pleasure I received from the publication of your most erudite work, the *Plinian Corrections*. This is not only because the books of **Pliny’s** *Natural History*—which were previously held to be so full of errors and, as it were, dead, that if Pliny himself had come back to life and inspected them in their formerly corrupted state, he would have utterly denied they were his—may now be confessed as restored to light and in a certain way reborn through your study and diligence. It is also because a manifold harvest, gathered from various volumes in both the **Greek** and **Latin** languages, is contained within that same work alongside the corrections of Pliny. Certainly, no one should be displeased by the thousands of wounds inflicted upon Pliny by printers or scribes <note>original: "librarijs"; refers to the copyists who introduced errors into manuscripts before the age of printing</note>; for while you strove to heal those wounds, they provided you the opportunity to write so many things worthy of remembrance. I know for certain that there will be many who will seek not so much the true reading of Pliny’s text, but rather your own excellent learning displayed in that book.

Indeed, what delighted me most of all in that work was the very thing that most people might have suspected would be troublesome to me: that a defense of Pliny was undertaken in passing in certain places where I had noted errors in that author. For I am not the kind of man who wishes my writings to be read without contradiction. For as it is written at the end of the book published regarding the errors of **Pliny** and other physicians...

it is written <note>Referring to Leoniceno's own previously published work, *De Erroribus in Medicina* (On Errors in Medicine), 1492</note>, that I would be joyful if someone were to take up the defense of **Pliny** and demonstrate that I, rather than so great a man, had erred. I wished for this to be understood as a suggestion made not so much to **Angelo Poliziano**, to whom that same book was dedicated, but plainly to all the learned men in all of Italy. 

But because the same **Angelo Poliziano**—a man otherwise most occupied in interpreting the books of poets, orators, and philosophers—has until now deferred doing so, either because he judged that the defense of **Pliny** should be postponed for his other more serious studies, or because he thought that the refutation of my little book should be pardoned for the sake of our old friendship, I was grieving that this task had been neglected by many others who are truly and honestly learned. 

Instead, I saw this duty of protecting **Pliny** seized upon by certain men who, in their whole lives, had handled nothing less than those very matters concerning which I had a disagreement with **Pliny**. Indeed, so that they might even know what those matters were, they were secretly scouting them out from me through my own disciples. For what could they themselves do, since they had never applied themselves to the study of medicine, nor had they ever read the authorities of the **Greek** physicians, whom I had cited to confirm my own opinions? Or, if they were only now beginning to read them, since they were ignorant of **Greek** letters, they could not understand even a single word unless they were taught by others the very things they were shamelessly going to publish under their own names. And, lest they should seem to have contributed nothing of their own, they would fight on **Pliny’s** behalf with quarrels and insults. 

Since, therefore, I was truly grieving not a little that I had a dispute with men who were not only unskilled, but also insolent and abusive, at last either chance or reason brought forth such a defender as **Pliny** deserved: you, specifically, **Hermolao**. You are held to be so great in every kind of learning that you alone in our age represent that famous **Marcus Varro**, who was once considered the most learned of the **Latins** and **Greeks**. <note>Marcus Terentius Varro (116–27 BCE) was an ancient Roman scholar often called "the most learned of the Romans." Comparing Barbaro to Varro is the highest possible academic compliment in the Renaissance.</note>

...they heard: that a stone from a great siege engine had been hurled, and no one could hope that walls which were not overturned by such a machine could ever be demolished by mere slings. > The East and West winds rush forth, and the South wind,
> thick with tempests, and they roll vast waves to the stars, <note>Leoniceno is quoting Virgil’s *Aeneid* (1.85-86) to describe the "storm" of scholarly criticism.</note>

yet against the onset of so many winds and barking waves, it remains stable and unshaken. I decided to stand firm and, the greater the force that attacked me, the more boldly I would fight for the truth. Regarding the second kind of *parthenium* <note>Likely Feverfew or Pellitory-of-the-wall.</note>, which **Celsus** had named as different from the one **Pliny** thought was the same, you felt exactly as I did. You judged along with me that **Dioscorides** did not think that *saliunca* <note>Wild Nard.</note> was different from **Celtic nard**; although you judged that more credit should be given to **Pliny**, who held the contrary opinion. Concerning the poppy, the "Hercules plant," and the plant similar to *struthio* <note>Soapwort (*Saponaria officinalis*).</note>—and not "sparrows" <note>A famous philological error: the Greek word *strouthos* can mean "sparrow," but the medicinal plant is *struthion*. It suggests that their thinking is so perfectly aligned that they have become indistinguishable from one another.</note> This is not because you borrowed from me, or I from you, but because there is such a consensus of our minds. Indeed, several very learned men who were present were quite amazed when we were conversing with one another about **medicinal simples** <note>Term: <term>Simples</term> (individual medicinal plants or minerals used as ingredients).</note> in the palace of the most illustrious Duke **Ercole** <note>original: "Herculis"; Ercole I d'Este, Duke of Ferrara and a noted patron of the arts and sciences.</note> at **Ferrara**. They marvelled that before I had even opened my mouth to speak, you had anticipated my thoughts; and likewise, that from a single word you uttered, I had guessed what you intended to say next.

But if we happened to disagree on those things pertaining to **Pliny**—which are certainly few in number and of no great importance to life—it is surely less to be wondered at, especially in this subject matter, where no knowledge among physicians is considered more uncertain or inconsistent. Add to this that you have treated Pliny—whom you made as if your own adopted son by bringing him into a new light—with a fatherly spirit, being indulgent of his many errors, touching upon them lightly, and attributing almost all of them to the scribes or the printers. I, who was more of a stranger, acted perhaps more severely than was proper against a man who was, in my judgment, most excellent and well-deserving of the human race. However, since it is human to slip, to be deceived, and to err, I suspected that he had sometimes held a path straying from the truth. And therefore, when dealing with matters in which human health and life are contained—since in no other area is there such great danger as there is in this kind of <margin>The ignorance of physicians is a deadly matter.</margin> **ignorance**—I did not want the truth to lie in obscurity. And for that reason, [I wrote] the book...

<meta>Catchword: I (Ego)</meta>

I decided that my thoughts on the errors of **Pliny** <note>Gaius Plinius Secundus, or Pliny the Elder, the Roman author of the massive *Natural History*.</note> and other physicians should be published. Nor can you hold this against me as a fault, as many of my rivals have maliciously cast it as a crime to stir up hatred against me, calling me a rash and impudent man for daring to contradict so great an authority in the Latin language. For there is a most noble sentiment written by you in the thirty-second book of your *Corrections of Pliny* <note>original: "Plinianarum castigationum"; Barbaro’s own massive work of philological corrections to Pliny’s text.</note>, which could support my cause more than any other: 

> To suppress any thought of this kind is not to spare the ancients, but to grudge posterity. <note>original: "Cogitationem aliquam huiusmodi supprimere, non esse parcere ueteribus, sed inuidere posteris."</note>

It was, if I am not mistaken, your own thought that **Pliny**, not correctly imitating **Theophrastus** <note>The "Father of Botany," a Greek successor to Aristotle.</note>, wrote in the aforementioned book that **cinnabar** <term>minium</term> <note>A bright red mineral (mercury sulfide or red lead) used both as a pigment and in ancient medicine.</note> is found in Spain <note>original: "Hispanijs"</note>, but that it is hard and sandy; whereas Theophrastus was speaking not of Spain, but of the other **Iberia** <note>The ancient kingdom of Iberia in the Caucasus, roughly modern-day Georgia.</note> which is adjacent to the **Albanians** <note>Referring to Caucasian Albania, not the modern Balkan nation.</note>. If you, in matters that might perhaps be judged by some to be of minor concern, decided that even your beloved Pliny should not be spared, should I—who profess the art of healing—remain silent about the errors of an otherwise most learned man when I notice Pliny nodding off <note>A reference to the Roman poet Horace’s famous line that "even the great Homer sometimes nods," meaning that even the greatest authors can make mistakes.</note> in matters pertaining to human health? 

Though you will perhaps say: "Who ordered you to keep this silence?" For I did not forbid you from noting what Pliny wrote incorrectly, since I myself not only corrected the errors of copyists or manuscript flaws, but also revealed several of the author’s own hallucinations; yet I did not want to allow things that were very truly said by Pliny to be attributed to him as errors. If I must speak for myself before you, not as if before a censor regarding my character, but rather before a judge regarding my learning, I see that my case will be somewhat more difficult, because it is necessary for me to dissent from you, a man most learned and endowed with the highest dignity. Yet you ought to bear this with a more patient mind, since you were born and educated in that renowned city of **Venice**, in which there is no Caesar, no perpetual Dictator, from whose judgment it is not permitted to appeal.

Indeed, I believe that the more a person excels in wealth and honors, the more they ought to show themselves as an equal in a literary contest, lest they seem to want to extort by force what should be obtained through reason. **Nicholas V** <note>Pope Nicholas V (1397–1455), a famous humanist and founder of the Vatican Library.</note>, the Supreme Pontiff and likewise an exceptional patron of letters during his papacy, always granted this liberty to a certain theologian who was his close friend, whom he used to invite to debate on theology: that he should respond to him not as the Roman Pontiff, but as **Master Thomas of Sarzana** <note>The birth name of Nicholas V before he ascended to the papacy.</note>—for this had been his name before he rose to the height of the Pontificate—without any reverence or fear of his most sacred power. Did you not also, O Patriarch of Aquileia <note>Hermolao Barbaro, the recipient of this letter, was appointed Patriarch of Aquileia in 1491.</note>, at the end of your work, urge all learned men to pronounce their judgment freely on your writings? If you have granted to everyone the power of criticizing you or your works, how much more justly could I use that same power in defending my own? Therefore, so that I may now deal with you by that right which you have permitted both to others and especially to me (who was previously noted by you), the individual chapters of your defense of **Pliny** <note>Gaius Plinius Secundus, or Pliny the Elder.</note> will be brought forward in the same order and in almost the same words in which they were written by you; and it shall be submitted to the judgment of the learned whether they sufficiently vindicate Pliny from his errors.

### ON CISTUS AND IVY.

Does it not seem to you that Pliny was rightly rebuked in Book XII, he who named the **cistus** herb <note>original: "cisthon"; the Rockrose plant.</note>, from which **ladanum** <term>ladanum</term> <note>A sticky resin obtained from Cistus shrubs, used in ancient medicine and perfumery.</note> is made, as "ivy"? This was because, as you say, **Paul of Aegina** <note>A 7th-century Byzantine Greek physician.</note> also calls this cistus *cisson* <note>original: "cisson"</note>, that is, ivy, and **Dioscorides** <note>A 1st-century Greek physician and botanist.</note> records that the same is called *cissarion* <note>original: "cissarion"</note>, that is, little ivy? If I may say so with a preface of apology, most learned Hermolao, I have nowhere found in Paul or Dioscorides that the herb from which ladanum is prepared—which is the subject of our present dispute—is called *cisson*, that is, ivy, or *cissarion*, that is, little ivy...

[...ought] to be named, but rather *cisthos* <note>The Rockrose (*Cistus*).</note>, or *ledon*, or *ladon*: for these are the words of **Paul** <note>Paulus Aegineta, a 7th-century Byzantine Greek physician.</note> in the fourth volume of his book on medicine, in the section where he treats simple medicines: <note>original Greek: λάδανον ἀπὸ τοῦ κισσοῦ τοῦ λάδανον λεγομένου γίνεται</note> "Ladanum comes from the *cissos* <note>Here referring to a type of rockrose, though the Greek word usually means ivy.</note> which is called *ladanum*," that is, ladanum is named from the *cisthos* <note>rockrose</note> *ladon*. In this way **Galen** <note>The most influential physician of the Roman Empire (2nd century AD).</note> also testifies that the medicine called ladanum is made from the *cisthos*, and not from the *cissos* <note>ivy</note>. Nor did **Aëtius** <note>Aëtius of Amida, a 6th-century Greek medical writer.</note>—a physician who lived somewhat later than these men, yet nonetheless a figure of no small authority among the Greeks—use any other name for this same herb than *cisthos*. However, these two most noble physicians <note>Likely referring to Galen and Paul or Aëtius.</note> called another plant not far different from this one, under which **hypocistis** <note>A parasitic plant (*Cytinus hypocistis*) that grows on the roots of rockroses.</note> grows, not *cissaron*, but *cistharum*.

**Dioscorides** <note>The primary Greek authority on herbal medicine (1st century AD).</note>, however, writes that the other kind of *cisthos*, under which *hypocistis* grows, is named both *cistharum* and *cissaron* by some. But the other kind, from which ladanum is made, he says is called only *ledon* by some, not *cissaron*. From this it follows that the name *cissari*—which you <note>Hermolao Barbaro.</note> believe can be correctly called *hederula* <note>Little ivy.</note> in Latin—does not belong to the herb from which ladanum is generated, but rather to that one under which *hypocistis* grows, even by the testimony of Dioscorides. Moreover, if this ladanum-bearing herb were to be called by a name different from *cissos* or *hedera* <note>ivy</note>, it would be pronounced *kisos* <note>original: κίσος</note> rather than *kissos* <note>original: κισσὸς</note>, for the sake of creating a difference between it and ivy, at least in its accentuation. Therefore, the diminutive word formed from *kissos* <note>original: ἀπὸ τοῦ κισσοῦ</note> would not signify "little ivy," but a herb of its own specific genus—a conclusion that must also be reached regarding the other plant under which *hypocistis* grows.

Furthermore, **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder, author of the *Natural History*.</note> himself insinuated that *cisthos* did not share the same name as ivy, but was only assigned a "neighboring" <note>Similar or related.</note> name. Now, this neighboring name would be either *kisos* or *kissos*, from which the diminutive *kissaron* is derived, just as *kissaron* comes from *kissos*. But even if I were to grant you that this very plant is called *cissarion* by the Greeks (formed as a diminutive from *kissos*), I do not think it can be correctly named *hederula* <note>little ivy</note> by the Latins; for it does not follow that if *kissos* or *cissarion* signify many things among the Greeks, the plan... <note>The text cuts off here at the end of the page; the catchword is "tam," anticipating the word "plantam" (plant).</note>

In this error indeed, as in many others, was the author of the **Pandectae** <note>Matthaeus Silvaticus (c. 1280–1342), author of the *Pandectae Medicinae*, a massive medical dictionary.</note>, who, wishing (I believe) to protect **Avicenna** <note>The famous Persian physician Ibn Sina (11th century).</note> as well as **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder, author of the 1st-century *Natural History*.</note>—both of whom confounded the two medicines—accepted the name of ivy even somewhat more broadly than the others. <margin>Apion, a type of radish.</margin>

...and it signifies the mastic tree, and that type of onion which is called *skilla* <note>The sea onion (*Urginea maritima*), used in medicine.</note> by the Greeks and *scilla* by the Latins; however, in our usage, the word "mastic" <note>Latin: *lentiscus*</note> designates nothing other than the tree itself. Do you not criticize **Theodore Gaza** <note>A 15th-century Greek scholar and translator who was a central figure in the revival of learning; he translated Aristotle and Theophrastus into Latin.</note> in this work of yours on the corrections of **Pliny**—even though you admit that you set him before yourself as a model to be imitated above all others in your edition of **Themistius**? You carp at him because, being too eager to expand the Latin language, he translated that genus of wild radish which the Greeks call *apios* or *ischas* as "pear" <note>Latin: *pirum*</note> in Latin. He did this because *apios* among the Greeks also signifies a pear. For what else were you trying to imply, if not that the word for "pear" among the Latins does not have a double meaning as the word *apios* <note>original: "τοῦ ἀπίου"</note> does among the Greeks?

For my part, I will not hesitate to defend Theodore Gaza on this point. I believe he correctly translated *apios* as "pear," even when referring to the wild radish, because that type of radish seems to have received such a name among the Greeks precisely because its shape represents the image of a pear. Therefore, because of this same similarity, it might also be conveniently called a "pear" by our own people. Indeed, even the Greeks or the peasants—who have learned through experience the use of this same radish which both **Theophrastus** and **Dioscorides** <note>Pedanius Dioscorides (c. 40–90 AD), a Greek physician and the author of *De materia medica*, the primary botanical manual of the era.</note> reported—are now commonly accustomed to calling it *chamæpidium*, which means "ground-pear." They know by experience that its upper part induces vomiting, while the lower part moves the bowels.

However, there are many other instances where I judge that the same Theodore Gaza used Latin terms less correctly for the Greek ones. For this very type of radish of which we spoke—since it is read as not only *apios* but also *ischas* <note>Greek for "dried fig."</note> in some Greek manuscripts of Theophrastus—Theodore translated that name as *carica* <note>A specific type of dried fig from Caria in Asia Minor.</note>. But although it is read this way in Theophrastus (whose volumes on plants are largely corrupted), and although you did not correct that word in Pliny, Dioscorides—whose book is considered among the Greeks to be somewhat more accurate than that of Theophrastus—names this same medicine not *ischada*, but rather *ischiada*...

...called it a medicine. Even if it were also called *ischas* <note>original: "ischas"; a Greek term usually referring to a dried fig, but here used for a plant with a similar shape</note>, as is written in the works of **Theophrastus** and **Pliny**, the word for a dried fig <note>original: "caricae"</note> in our language still could not signify any species of radish, as a radish bears no resemblance to a dried fig. By the same reasoning I brought forward a little earlier regarding ivy, I would dare to confirm that, by a similar and indeed somewhat greater error, **Theodore Gaza** named "greater centaury" <term>Gall of the Earth</term> <note>Latin: *fel terrae*; a name usually reserved for the very bitter Lesser Centaury</note>. For since Theophrastus writes in Book IX of *On Plants* that the root of centaury
<margin>Greater Centaury.</margin>
can be preserved for ten years, he undoubtedly means the **greater centaury**, whose root—rather than its leaves—is used in medicine; conversely, in the **lesser centaury**, the leaves are used rather than the root. Not noticing this difference between the two types of centaury—perhaps because he had not read in **Dioscorides**, **Galen**, or even **Pliny** that the root of the lesser centaury is useless and therefore there is no necessity to preserve it—Theodore Gaza interpreted that passage of Theophrastus in this way:
> There is a general difference among all roots in that
> some last for more time and others for less: for the root of hellebore remains useful even for three hundred years; the **apple of the earth** <note>original: "malum terrae"; likely referring to sowbread or cyclamen</note> lasts for five or six; the **white chameleon plant** <note>original: "uernilago"</note> for forty; and the **gall of the earth** <note>referring here to centaury</note> for twelve. This latter root is quite fatty and thick.

Now, indeed, the error of Theodore Gaza appears manifest here. While Theophrastus was writing that the root of the greater centaury is fat and thick—just as Dioscorides and Pliny also wrote—they reported that the root of the lesser centaury is thin and of no use in medicine. Gaza, however, thought that what Theophrastus wrote referred to the lesser variety, which did not fit that plant at all; and for that reason, he called the centaury "gall of the earth." Certainly, the **lesser centaury** is more appropriately distinguished by that name because of its extraordinary bitterness; the **greater centaury**, however, is so far from being able to be called "gall of the earth" that it would be much more correctly called <term>Honey of the Earth</term> <note>Latin: *mel terrae*</note>. For its root is recorded by Dioscorides as being somewhat sweet, and those who know the plant have confirmed this to be true through experience. I certainly know that it is used by almost all doctors...

->### THE WORKS OF NICCOLÒ LEONICENO<-

...you say are unknown in our time. The **Conciliator** <note>Referring to Pietro d’Abano (1257–1315), a famous physician and philosopher known as "the Conciliator" for his work attempting to reconcile Greek and Arabic medicine.</note> also testifies in his *hundredth distinction* <note>original: "differentia centena"; a reference to d'Abano's *Conciliator Differentiarum*</note> that the **greater centaury** was unknown in his own age, although I believe he must have seen it a thousand times and frequently employed it in medical practice; this is exactly what happens very often to the physicians of our own time. 

But how can it be, someone will ask, that either the **Conciliator** or physicians after him were ignorant of a medicine whose use they once knew? For undoubtedly these things seem contradictory. But if I may speak in the manner of the sophists <note>Here, Leoniceno uses "sophists" to mean those who use clever logic or paradoxes.</note>, I would dare to say this: that the **greater centaury** is indeed known by physicians, and yet the **greater centaury** is not known by those same men—just as they recognize **eupatorium**, and yet do not recognize **eupatorium**. 

<margin>Certain things are known to physicians through use, but are unknown by their names.</margin>

In this matter, they are surely less to be excused than regarding the **greater centaury**. For although this plant is not only a foreign growth but is also a sprout of Italian soil, it does not grow in many places in Italy. Yet **eupatorium** grows everywhere: in meadows, in gardens, in thickets, on the plains, and in the mountains; unless we shut our eyes, it meets our gaze almost everywhere. 

Indeed, its appearance is so described by **Dioscorides** <note>A Greek physician and botanist of the 1st century AD.</note> and **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder, author of the *Natural History*.</note> that it seems almost to be placed before one's eyes. What sorts of herbs these are, and by what name they are commonly called by our people, I have decided to keep hidden on purpose. I do this so that I do not seem to want to snatch away your own most anticipated treatise on such matters—a charge which some, as I hear, have leveled against me in their writings, seeking to sow discord between you and me. 

I return to **Theodore** <note>Theodore Gaza, the humanist scholar whose translations Leoniceno is critiquing.</note>, who translated *thrialis* <note>original: "thrialidem"; likely a species of mullein or similar plant</note> as **burnet** <note>original: "bibinellam"; likely Pimpinella or Salad Burnet</note> and *scolopendrium* as **hart's tongue** <note>original: "lingua ceruina"; the Hart's Tongue Fern</note>. He was moved, no doubt, by the same zeal for enriching our language—a goal certainly not to be disapproved of, provided that the proper nature and property of the things themselves be preserved. 

For I shall remain silent about the **hart's tongue**, which is not the *scolopendrium* of the Greeks, but rather another plant they call *hemionites* <term>Mule's fern</term> <note>original: "hemionites"; likely *Asplenium hemionitis*.</note>. This plant is very close to the other in its medicinal powers, but differs greatly in its shape—although you, in your *corrections* <note>Likely referring to the "Castigationes Plinianae" of Hermolao Barbaro.</note>, wrote that both were so similar that it is difficult to distinguish...

->### ON HERBS AND SHRUBS<-

...to distinguish. Even if I say nothing of that [previous plant], at least because of the similarity of properties it has with **scolopendrium** <note>Spleenwort or Hart's-tongue fern</note>, **thrialis** <note>A plant whose leaves were used for lamp wicks</note> is entirely different from the one we commonly call **bibinella** <note>Pimpinella or Burnet</note>. For it is instead another plant which the Greeks call both *phlomum* <note>original: "phlomum"; Mullein</note> and *thrialis* <note>original: "thrialida"</note>—that is, *elychnium* <note>original: "elychnium"; meaning "wick-plant"</note>—because they use it for wicks in lamps. The Latins call it **verbascum**, and certain more recent authors call it "bearded yew" <note>original: "taxum barbatum"</note>.

<margin>The Milos tree.</margin>
With a similar error, **Theodore [Gaza]** <note>Theodore Gaza (c. 1398–1475), a leading humanist scholar who translated Greek scientific texts into Latin.</note> called the **milos tree** "yew" <note>original: "taxon"</note> in Latin, even though the yew tree is not called *milos* by the Greeks, but *smilax*. Concerning this *smilax*, **Theophrastus** <note>Theophrastus (c. 371–287 BC), Aristotle's successor and author of "Enquiry into Plants."</note> treated it as a distinct tree, separate from the *milos*. In that passage, Theodore even kept the Greek name—that is, he said *smilax*—where he could have translated it as "yew"; yet where it was necessary to write *milos*, perhaps because the Latin language has no name for this tree, he himself named it "yew." Theodore is more to be forgiven for this error, however, because our own **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder (23–79 AD), whose "Natural History" was the standard encyclopedia of the Middle Ages.</note>, deceived by a similar proximity, placed the *milos* tree among the species of *melia*—that is, the **ash tree**—in Book XVI. This is easy to notice if one carefully examines what Theophrastus wrote about the *milos* tree in Book III and what Pliny wrote about the various species of ash. See how many knots are tangled by Theodore (sometimes translating Theophrastus poorly) and by Pliny, which, unless you—the most learned of the learned—untie them, seem to me truly unsolvable.

<margin>Ground-laurel.</margin>
The same Theodore translates *chamaedaphne* <note>original: "chamædaphnem"; literally "ground-laurel"</note> as **periwinkle** <note>original: "vincam pervincam"</note> in his Theophrastus, even though *chamaedaphne* is another plant whose description in **Dioscorides** <note>Pedanius Dioscorides (c. 40–90 AD), whose "De Materia Medica" was the primary pharmacological text for 1,500 years.</note> is very different from the periwinkle. Indeed, for those contemplating the nature and appearance of the periwinkle more accurately, it will be seen as that which is designated by both Dioscorides and Pliny by the names **clematis**, **daphnoides**, and **polygonoides**.

Wherefore, since the hinge of our entire controversy turns on this, allow me to examine this passage more diligently with your kind permission, since it was not unbecoming for you to descend to reading and judging these trifles of ours. Until now we have disputed only about the name: whether it is permitted to call both kinds of rock-rose—namely, both the one that bears ladanum and the other under which **hypocistis** <note>original: "hipocistis"; a parasitic plant that grows on the roots of the rock-rose.</note> grows—"ivy" in Latin. <meta>This page continues Niccolò Leoniceno’s argument regarding the botanical errors of Theodore Gaza and Pliny the Elder. ### ON HERBS AND SHRUBS.
<i>

<note>The text begins mid-sentence, continuing an analogy from the previous page.</note> [ce]lestial <note>original: "caelestem"</note> things correctly into male and female, nor granted that both sexes possess the nature of barking; by that same reasoning, I believe, **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder, author of "Natural History."</note> neither rightly divides **ivy** <note>original: "hedera".</note> by the differences of male and female, nor correctly assigns to both a rose-like flower. This is because these traits are attributed to the **rock-rose** <note>original: "cistho"; the *Cistus* shrub.</note>, but not to the **ivy** <note>original: "cisso"; from the Greek *kissos*.</note>, by **Theophrastus** <note>The "father of botany" (c. 371–287 BC).</note> and **Dioscorides** <note>Greek physician and author of "De Materia Medica."</note>, and even by Pliny himself in Book 24. For even if I set aside that division of ivies into male and female placed by the same Pliny in Book 16—which perhaps someone might contend is common to absolutely all herbs, shrubs, under-shrubs, and trees—who has ever seen a rose-like flower on ivy?

Should the authority of Pliny, or of **Theodore** <note>Theodore Gaza (c. 1398–1475), the translator Leoniceno is critiquing.</note> interpreting Theophrastus, be of such great value that we ought to believe them rather than our own eyes? Indeed, the great philosopher **Aristotle** <margin>The judgment of the senses is most certain.</margin> valued the judgment of the senses so highly that he thought it vain to seek a logical reason when sensory evidence is present. **Galen** <note>The most influential physician of the Roman Empire.</note>, the prince of all physicians, thinks that those people should be considered insane who, when they can obtain proof from the senses, believe they must seek it from logical demonstrations. **Avicenna** <note>The Persian "Prince of Physicians" (c. 980–1037).</note>, an interpreter of the same Galen (as he himself admits), judged that those who refuse to believe their senses should be burned with fire or flogged, so that by feeling pain they might perceive that the judgments of the senses are true. 

And indeed, these most learned men have judged rightly: for why did nature grant us eyes and the craftsmanship of the other senses, unless so that we could rely on our own resources to look forward to and investigate the truth? We certainly ought not to abandon ourselves so far that, always following the footsteps of others, we decide nothing for ourselves. For this would truly be to see with others' eyes, to hear with others' ears, to smell with others' nostrils, to taste with another's intelligence, and to establish that we are nothing other than stones, if we were to commit everything to the assertions of others and think nothing should be discussed by ourselves. <meta>This page continues Niccolò Leoniceno’s discussion on the methodology of botanical classification. # NICCOLÒ LEONICENO

<meta>catchword: ipso</meta>

**Galen**, a man who was almost as much a philosopher as he was a physician, explained in the preface of his **Art of Healing** <note>original: "artis curatiuæ"; specifically his work *Ad Glauconem de Methodo Medendi*.</note> addressed to Glaucon the highest and most important principles of **scientific division** <term>Scientific division: The logical process of categorizing a subject into groups (genera) and subgroups (species).</term>. These principles, drawn from the treasures of **Platonic** teaching, dictate that one must begin from the first and highest categories, then cut these into other genera, species, or differences, and divide these again in the same manner until we finally arrive at those species which no longer admit further division.

Let us see, however, whether **Theophrastus** himself, the very master of such divisions, observed this rule and norm of classification. For if we believe **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder, the Roman author of the *Natural History*.</note> and **Theodore** <note>Theodore Gaza, a 15th-century scholar whose translations of Greek science into Latin were highly influential but often criticized by Leoniceno.</note> as they interpret the opinion of Theophrastus in Book VI, that first distinction of **ivies** <note>original: "hederarum"</note> into two primary categories—namely, male and female—was entirely omitted by Theophrastus in Book III. Yet that was the very place where he had established the plan to divide all the genera and species of ivy down to the most specific levels through their own individual differences. Instead, if we follow the translator Theodore, it is placed in Book VI, where there was no suitable opportunity to discuss ivies. Since this seemed **absurd** to Pliny, in Book XVI (where he had proposed to treat all kinds of ivy), he judged that he should begin with that very division of male and female. He believed it was a great error to mention it elsewhere rather than in the primary discussion regarding ivies.

Indeed, no one would dare to suggest that these differences of male and female were neglected by Theophrastus as if they were useless in the book where he had specifically set out to write accurately about ivies. This is because the same author affirms in the first book of his volume on plants that these same differences, wherever they can be found, ought to be the first ones adopted—either as the sole or the most important distinctions—among the genus of **wild plants** <note>original: "syluestrium plantarum"</note>, of which it is well known that ivy is one. 

Just as all the kinds or species of ivy are contained under one common **genus** <term>Genus: A broad category of related organisms.</term> called "ivy," so too the genus of ivy is referred back to another higher genus called the **shrub** <note>original: "frutex"</note>, and which from...

by **Theophrastus** himself, who distinguishes all plants into four genera: trees, shrubs, **sub-shrubs** <term>Sub-shrub (suffrutex): A plant that is woody at the base but has herbaceous (green, non-woody) stems above, like lavender or thyme.</term>, and herbs, a nature distinct from the other three. For these words are written by him at the beginning of that same book: "We have already spoken of trees; now let us teach concerning sub-shrubs and herbs." It follows: "And if any other types are included in these, we ought to note those as well, such as **grains** <note>original: "fruges"; referring to cereal crops.</note>: for these too desire to be counted among the herbs. Finally, Theophrastus, proceeding in the order he promised, speaks thus of the **sub-shrubs** <note>The Latin text here says "fruticibus," but the context of the argument suggests the sub-shrub category.</note>: "There are indeed very many kinds of them distinguished by the greatest differences: *cisthos* <note>original: "cifthos"; the rock-rose (Cistus).
