For all these, and the reed-like plants in general, you would assign to the nature of sub-shrubs. Indeed, the types and distinctions are held by each of these indicators, some being more evident, others more hidden. For of *cisthos* (or according to the Translator, **ivy**), there are two kinds: namely male and female, since one has a larger, harder, and more oily leaf, and a flower inclining toward purple; yet in both, the flowers are very close to **wild roses**, though smaller and without scent." should be ascribed to him, who could doubt that in this very place of the sixth book, he intended to make no mention of **ivy** <note>original: "hedera"</note>, which he had assigned to the genus of **shrubs** <term>Shrub (frutex): A woody plant smaller than a tree, usually with several stems arising from the base.</term> in the earlier books? Concerning which, moreover, he had abundantly asserted his position in Book III in the treatment of trees and shrubs. Nor indeed should anyone be deceived by the fact that because these Latin words, **shrub** <note>original: "frutex"</note> and **sub-shrub** <note>original: "suffrutex"</note>, differ by only one syllable, they might think there is also a minimal difference in the things themselves; for these same genera among the Greeks are diverse both in name and in nature: for the Greeks call the one *thamnon* <note>original: θάμνον; a shrub.</note> and the other *phruganon* <note>original: φρύγανον; a sub-shrub.</note>. Therefore, unless we wish to believe that **Theophrastus** <note>A student of Aristotle and the "father of botany."</note>—that most excellent philosopher, who wrote books on the natures of things, and also on dialectic, and the method and doctrine of division, more elegantly and copiously than his teacher **Aristotle** in the judgment of many—erred so childishly as to place ivy sometimes in the genus of shrubs and sometimes in the genus of sub-shrubs; so that in the discussion of ivies he had made in Book III, he would neglect the precepts of his own teaching, and—in the manner of a fool, as **Plato** says—passing over the first two genera at once, he would in a sense tear the parts asunder, so as to place ivy sometimes in the genus of shrubs and sometimes in the genus of sub-shrubs <note>The Latin text here repeats this phrase, a common printing error known as dittography.</note>, writing things conflicting and contrary to himself, by asserting that the flower of the ivy is now downy and now leafy; so that, finally, he would affirm those things which are entirely contrary to the senses in that history [of plants], in which he admits that most things are judged more by sight than by reason. 

We ought rather to think this: that **Theodore Gaza**, along with **Pliny**, who had perhaps found *cissos* <note>original: "cissum"; the Greek word for ivy.</note> written instead of *cisthos* <note>original: "cistho"; the Greek word for rock-rose.</note> in the sixth book of Theophrastus, were deceived by the change of a single small letter, and therefore they attributed to ivy those things which Theophrastus had handed down concerning a sub-shrub very different from ivy. > "For there is a slanted reed, not growing to a great height, but spreading itself near the ground in the manner of a shrub, very sweet to animals when tender; there is also the **marshy adarce** growing in Italy, useful for teeth under its very foliage, because its power is the same as mustard."

It implies that adarce is of the genus of reeds, just as the slanted reed is called *elegia* <note>A type of reed used for pipes or flutes.</note> by some. For that word "thicker" <note>original: "pleniore"</note>, if it stands thus, expresses the same sentiment he had set down above in Book XVI—namely, that adarce found under the foliage is more effective for the teeth. Or, we can make two words out of one and read it thus: "**clearly for the mouth** on the bark, growing under the foliage itself" <note>original: "cortice planè ori"; Leoniceno is suggesting a pun or textual emendation where "pleniore" (thicker) is actually "plane ori" (clearly for the mouth).</note>. It is as if he wished to suggest that it grows for the benefit of the mouth, of which the teeth are no small part. This would likewise agree marvelously with what he had testified in Book XVI regarding the use of this medicine for the teeth. This also supports our opinion: that Pliny nowhere says adarce is a salt-crust, unless...

# NICCOLÒ LEONICENO

...he showed in book 32, where he named it **calamachne** <note>A Greek term for a type of reed growth; literally "reed-froth."</note>: although by a fault of the manuscript that word has been corrupted into *calamochnum*. Nor indeed does he mention at all in this last book that he had written anything in the previous books about the same adarce—just as in book 20, when he was speaking about it, he thought it necessary to testify that he himself had touched it among the woods. For all these things prove most clearly that Pliny, in various places, held various opinions about adarce, which he sometimes signifies as a species of reed, and sometimes as the **salt-crust** clinging to reeds.

### ON DARNEL AND GOAT-GRASS.

<margin>
Pliny imitated **Theophrastus** <note>A Greek successor to Aristotle, often called the "father of botany."</note> in his agricultural writings.
</margin>
In the matter of **darnel** <note>original: "aera"; likely *Lolium temulentum*.</note> and **goat-grass** <note>original: "aegilope"; a weed often found in grain fields.</note>, I do not know whether Pliny is more to be blamed for deciding to use Greek names in matters so common—for which Latin names were not lacking—or rather because he affirmed things about those same herbs (identified by their Greek names) which our senses have discovered to be false. Indeed, you respond on Pliny's behalf regarding **darnel** in this way: that since the Greeks reported that **darnel** <note>original: "lolium"</note> strangles **wheat** <note>original: "triticum"</note> by binding itself around it, and this had not been particularly observed in Italy, he thought it safer to use the Greek word rather than the Latin one, calling it *aera* and not *lolium*. I would praise Pliny's plan—he who sought to hide the lies of the Greeks (if there were any who might have wished to lie so remarkably as to write that darnel kills wheat by binding itself around it, a thing observed neither in Greece nor in Italy) under the obscurity of a Greek word—if the word *aera* were not so common in the language of those same Greeks that its meaning is hidden from no one who has tasted even a little of Greek literature. However, so that we may free the Greek authors (truly most learned men who wrote about plants, and among others **Theophrastus**, whom Pliny especially imitates when writing on agriculture) from the suspicion of such a great error, here...

<meta>This page continues Niccolò Leoniceno’s critique of Pliny the Elder’s botanical accuracy. Leoniceno is specifically arguing that Pliny misinterpreted the Greek author Theophrastus regarding how certain weeds, such as darnel and goat-grass, affect crops.</meta>

# ON HERBS AND SHRUBS.

...[Theophrastus] never wrote about **darnel** <note>original: "aera" or "lolium"</note> that it kills wheat by binding around it, but only by taking away its nourishment, since it grows alongside the wheat. For these are the words of the same Theophrastus in the third book of *On the Causes of Plants*:

> “Indeed, the plant called **broomrape** <note>original: "orobanche"; a parasitic plant</note> kills bitter-vetch by its embrace and its pressure, and **flax-strangler** <note>original: "linodorum"</note> likewise destroys fenugreek by growing right onto its root; and others bring disaster to others, such as those which come forth together with individual crops, like **darnel** <note>original: "lolium"</note> and oats with wheat and barley, and **burdock** <note>original: "lappa"</note> with lentils, and others with others. All of these, however, kill for this reason: because they take away the food.”

From these words of Theophrastus—the meaning of which Pliny strove to express for the most part in book 18, where he deals with the defects of crops—the origin of Pliny’s error regarding *aera* and *aegilops* is easily shown. For because a little before he had mentioned Theophrastus’s account of **broomrape** <note>original: "orobanche"</note>, which strangles bitter-vetch with its embrace—for from that it gets its name among the Greeks <note>The name comes from *orobos* (vetch) and *anchein* (to strangle). Leoniceno is highlighting that Pliny misapplied this specific behavior to other weeds.</note>—he [Pliny] thought that the method of killing was the same for *aera* and *aegilops* (one of which **Theodorus** <note>Theodorus Gaza (c. 1398–1475), a Greek scholar whose Latin translations of Aristotle and Theophrastus were standard in the Renaissance.</note> translated as darnel and the other as oats). And so, after making mention of broomrape, which kills bitter-vetch by binding around it, Pliny later added that darnel kills wheat in a similar way, and **goat-grass** <note>original: "aegilops"</note> (which he calls *festuca*) kills barley. However, Theophrastus—whom, as can be seen, Pliny strove to imitate as much as possible when writing about these same things—teaches that although all the plants he discusses in that passage kill neighboring herbs for that general reason (that they take away the food), they do this in various ways. For **broomrape** indeed kills because it embraces and squeezes the bitter-vetch; **flax-strangler** <note>original: "linodorum"</note> because it grows onto the root of fenugreek; but **darnel** <note>original: "lolium"</note> and oats because they come forth with the wheat and barley—just like **cleavers** <note>original: "aparine"</note> (which I do not know if Theodorus correctly translates as **burdock** <note>original: "lappa"</note>) grows with lentils. Truly, anyone who knows these three plants would not doubt in the least that none of them have a nature for binding or wrapping around...

### ON GOAT-GRASS. <note>original: "De Aegilope"; Aegilops is a genus of grass often called goat-grass, which was historically confused with wild oats.</note>

You offer the reason why Pliny said **goat-grass** <note>original: "aegilops"</note> instead of **oats** <note>original: "avena"</note> in the same place: that since the Greeks distinguished two types of oats, namely **brome** <note>original: "bromus"</note> and **goat-grass**, and yet no one in Italy would have rendered this distinction, for this reason Pliny, in Book 18, when he had placed oats among the defects of grain, a little later discusses **fescue** <note>original: "festuca"</note>, which is called **goat-grass**. You claim he did this not because he did not know that this was a certain kind of oat—as you say some people mockingly claim, meaning me, of course, whom you give to be easily recognized by those who have read my booklet, even if you do not name me openly—but because he knew the other variety was celebrated by the name **brome**. These things you say on behalf of Pliny. 

I, however, in order to reject the charge of mockery with which you have marked me before you—whose character I would prefer to be approved rather than my learning—state that I have nowhere criticized Pliny through false accusation for not knowing that **goat-grass** was a certain kind of oat. Rather, I moved against him only for the reason that in the same chapter he chose to use sometimes the Greek and sometimes the Latin word for the same kind of oat. For as to what Pliny writes in Book 18—that **oats** are a defect of grain and that barley degenerates into them—this same thing Theophrastus in Book 6 of *On Plants* and Galen in Book 2 of *On Foodstuffs* also testify regarding **goat-grass**. 

Moreover, as to what Pliny says a little later—that barley is killed by **goat-grass**—Theophrastus himself attributes this in Book 5 of *On the Causes of Plants* to goat-grass, though in a different way than Pliny does. Pliny also, at some point, named the other variety either **brome** or **oats**, if not in the same chapter, then at least in the book. Thus, it seems an inexplicable reason why Pliny produces now a Greek and now a Latin name for the same kinds, such as **brome** brought from the East in Book 18...

# ON HERBS AND SHRUBS.

In Chapter 10, Pliny reports this, but in Chapter 7 of the same book, he had previously interpreted the same **brome** <note>original: "bromum"; a type of wild grass or wild oat</note> as **oats** <note>original: "auenam"</note>. There he writes: "Wheat has many coats, barley is most naked, as is **spelt-grits** <note>original: "alica"; a preparation of emmer wheat</note>, but especially **oats** <note>original: "auena"</note>. Its stalk is taller than that of wheat, as it is with barley; its **awn** <note>original: "arista"; the needle-like bristles on the ear of grain</note> is more biting than that of barley." Nearly all of these details are from the eighth book of **Theophrastus** <note>A 4th-century BCE Greek philosopher known as the 'Father of Botany'</note>, although many parts are corruptly translated. For these are the words of Theophrastus writing on the same matters:

> At the same time, the one [wheat] is in many husks, while the other [barley] is naked—or rather, it is most "naked-seeded." But **einkorn** <note>original: "τίφη" (tiphe)</note> and **emmer** <note>original: "ὀλύρα" (olyra)</note> and all such are many-layered, and most of all, so to speak, is **brome** <note>original: "βρόμος" (bromos); wild oats</note>. Furthermore, the stalk [of oats] is taller than that of wheat and barley, and wheat has the ear separated from the leaf; and the chaff of wheat is sweeter than that of barley.

This is how **Theodorus** <note>Theodore Gaza (c. 1398–1475), a Greek scholar whose Latin translations of Aristotle and Theophrastus were standard in the Renaissance</note> interprets it:

> In addition to these, wheat is covered with many tunics; barley remains naked, for it lacks a covering most of all. **Einkorn** <note>original: "Tipha"</note> also and **winter wheat** <note>original: "siligo"</note>, and everything of this kind, are enclosed in a manifold leaf; but most of all, so to speak, nature has covered the **oats** <note>original: "auenã"</note>. Indeed, the stalk is taller in wheat than in barley, the spike emerges more separated from the leaves, and the chaff from wheat is also much sweeter than that from barley.

If anyone compares the words of Pliny placed above with those we have added from the eighth book of Theophrastus, I do not think he will doubt that Pliny—just as he wrote that wheat has many tunics while barley is most naked in imitation of Theophrastus—so too in other matters, following Theophrastus, intended to say that **brome** is "many-layered" <note>original: "πολύλοβον" (polylobon)</note>, which is to say "most covered" oats, as Theodorus interprets it. But why he wrote that it was "most naked" (which is the contrary sense), I could no more provide a reason than I could for why the same Pliny said that **goat-grass** <note>original: "ægilopen"</note> kills barley by binding itself around it. No species of oats is recognized that does this, just as there is no species of **darnel** <note>original: "lolij"</note> that does so. This destroys your other defense regarding **tares** <note>original: "æra"; the Greek name for darnel</note>—namely, that Pliny said "tares" and not "darnel" because he seemingly meant a species of darnel rather than darnel itself. For it is equally unknown where on earth such a species of darnel might arise that kills wheat by binding itself around it. But why Pliny, in these so obvious...

# NICCOLÒ LEONICENO

This error is defended so laboriously by you, especially since you know that in this very passage—where Pliny distorted the nature of **darnel** <note>original: "æræ"; a common weed in grain fields</note> and **goat-grass** <note>original: "ægilopis"</note>—he was so prone to hallucination that he took the terms **teramnum** and **ateramnum** to be harmful herbs. In reality, these two words signify the "easy-cooking" <note>original: "coctile"</note> and "difficult-cooking" <note>original: "incoctile"</note> qualities of legumes in many places in the works of **Theophrastus** <note>A Greek philosopher and the successor to Aristotle, known for his foundational botanical texts</note>. Pliny believed that one of these, namely *ateramnos*, kills the bean in rich soil around Philippi <note>An ancient city in Macedonia</note>, while *teramnos* does so in thin soil when a certain wind blows. Since you do not know how else to excuse such a gross error by Pliny, you suspect the passage has been shortened due to a flaw in the manuscript. You even say in Book 9, Chapter 16, that you wonder why Pliny names the same fish sometimes in Greek and sometimes in Latin; you do not deny that Pliny often does this in other matters as well, such as with herbs, without testifying whether they are the same or different. If Pliny admitted this same kind of error in other things, why could he not also have admitted it in the case of darnel and **rye-grass** <note>original: "lolio"</note>, or goat-grass and **oats** <note>original: "auena"</note>? Or, if Pliny did not err in this, why did he give you occasion to wonder about him in other similar instances?

### ON WOAD AND ISATIS.

If, in Book 20, where it is written concerning **isatis** <note>original: "ifatide"; a plant used for blue dye, also known as woad</note> among the wild-growing lettuces, one reads **woad** <note>original: "glastum"</note> instead of "wild" <note>original: "fyluatico"</note>—as you think that word should be corrected—we who have accused Pliny of negligence in this passage will not be so much refuted as Pliny’s own text will be somewhat violated. This is because the transition from "wild" to "woad" is a long leap. Therefore, either nothing should be changed (as you assert appears in the handwritten manuscripts), or if "woad" is to be substituted for the word "wild" (however violently it may be intruded), you have judged that Pliny was rightly criticized by us, unless this correction were applied. Yet, how much more correctly would this entire passage in Pliny be emended if it were read: "There is another kind which the Greeks call *isatis*." ### ON HERBS AND SHRUBS

...is accepted, we are not a little surprised that this has escaped your own critical judgment. The third kind is a genus growing in the woods, which they call **wild woad** <note>original: "syluestrem isatim"; woad was a plant used primarily for blue dye</note>. For here you have carefully noted from the handwritten manuscripts that unless it is read in this way, the passage would remain defective. Therefore, there will be a second genus, which grows spontaneously in the fields like a lettuce, called not woad but simply **woad** <note>original: "isatis"</note>; the third kind, which is produced in the woods, is **wild woad**. However, the fourth kind, which wool-dyers use, is not "forest woad"—for that is a distinction belonging to the second kind—but rather ought to be called **cultivated woad** <note>original: "satiua"</note>. This fourth kind differs from the second because the former is sown, while the latter grows spontaneously in the fields.

If, therefore, **woad** <note>original: "glastum"; a Celtic name for the plant Romans called "vitrum"</note> is in no way inserted into the text (as seems more reasonable), then no doubt will remain that Pliny fell into his usual error. He designated the same plant under various names in places far apart in his work, as if they were two different things instead of one. With equal carelessness, he described **orach** <note>original: "atriplicem"; a leafy vegetable similar to spinach</note>—both the garden variety and the wild-growing kind—sometimes by its Latin name and sometimes by its Greek name, as if they were different herbs.

<margin>Orach</margin>
As a result of this confusion, he even sometimes attributed contrary effects to each. Regarding **orach**, when he discussed it and its properties in his second book, he passed down on the authority of **Pythagoras** <note>The famous Greek philosopher, to whom many dietary and botanical theories were attributed in antiquity</note> that it causes **the royal disease** <note>original: "morbos regios"; a historical term for jaundice, so called because it was supposedly treated with expensive remedies fit for royalty</note> and paleness. Yet soon after, in Book 27, writing about the same plant under the name **golden-vegetable** <note>original: "chrysolachani"</note>, he wrote that there were some who taught that if it were tied onto those suffering from the "royal disease" so that it could be seen, it would heal that malady. This same healing effect—if the seed is drunk with **honey-water** <note>original: "melicrato"</note>—is testified to by the most authoritative author **Dioscorides** <note>A Greek physician and botanist whose "De Materia Medica" was the standard medicinal text for centuries</note> and many other physicians. 

However, we refrain from proving to you that this is the same herb called **atriplex** by the Romans and **chrysolachanon** by the Greeks, lest in doing so we be subjected to the Greek proverb: **"The sow teaches Minerva"** <note>original: "Sus Mineruam"; a proverb used when a fool tries to instruct an expert (Minerva being the goddess of wisdom)</note>. For it is different for others, who have dared...

## ON PERSONATIA AND PERSOLATA.

<margin>Placidius the grammarian.</margin>
I thought Pliny should be noted in my own little book because in Book 25, in the same chapter, he described **burdock** <note>original: "personatiam"</note> twice; he named it **arctium** <note>original: "arctíum"</note> in both places, just as the Greeks do. However, he suggested that in Latin it is called **personatia** in one place and **persolata** in the other, as I see it pleases you to say. You say that this distinction of names, though known to Pliny, was not perceived by certain people for the reason (as I think) that in Book 25, in the other place where mention of *arctium* is made, I thought *personatia* should be written instead of *persolata*. But since you also admit that the word *persolata* is derived from *persola*—which name among the Latins, according to **Placidius the grammarian** <note>a 5th-century scholar who wrote a glossary of terms used by the playwright Plautus</note> who wrote on Plautine names, signifies a **mask** <note>original: "personam"</note>—then whether you read *personatia* or *persolata* in that other passage, Pliny is no more exempt from error. He depicted the same herb twice, now under the name of *personatia*, now under that of *persolata*, and even within the same chapter. 

But perhaps you did not wish to defend Pliny so much as you wished to accuse me, on the grounds that I had not seen the works of Placidius the grammarian. Truly, in a man who devotes himself to nothing less than the study of words <note>Leoniceno is a physician; he ironically suggests that as a man of science, he prioritizes "things" over "words"</note>, I do not think such a crime is very unpardonable, but can be washed away and purged by a single drop of water. ### ON VIPER’S BUGLOSS AND ALCIBIUM.

We would not criticize Pliny for writing in Book 27 that he had not found a description of what **alcibios** <note>a plant named after Alcibiades, who was said to have used it to cure a snakebite</note> was among the ancient authors, if Pliny himself had not already described that same **alcibium** in Book 25 under the name **viper’s bugloss** <note>original: "echios"</note> in the exact same manner as Dioscorides <note>A Greek physician and the primary authority on herbal medicine in the ancient world</note>. It appears that Pliny thought **viper’s bugloss** <note>original: "echis"</note> was different from **alcibium**; however, I have proved in my little book that they do not differ. This is because Pliny himself and other authors recorded the same medicinal effects for both. These other authors did not treat them separately, as Pliny did, but testified that the plant is called **viper's bugloss** <note>original: "echio"</note> or by another name, **alcibiadium** <note>original: "alcibiadium"</note>. 

While it seems to you <note>Addressing Hermolaus Barbarus</note> that the plant called *echios* or *alcibiadium* is distinct from the one Nicander <note>A 2nd-century BC Greek poet and physician</note> calls *echis* or *alcibium*, I must confess that I do not recognize such a distinction in Nicander’s work. I have explored this sufficiently to be certain that in the books of Dioscorides or Paul <note>Paul of Aegina, a 7th-century Byzantine physician</note>, no such difference in names—and much less in the plants themselves—is found. Indeed, when they discuss **viper’s bugloss** and **alcibiadium**, they assign them no other powers than those which Nicander gives to *echis* and *alcibium*. To be more precise, it makes no difference whether the same herb is called *echis*, *echios*, *alcibium*, or *alcibiadium* by various authors. Just as those who call it *alcubiacum* rather than *alcibiadium* clearly understand it to be the exact same thing, not something different.

...that discussion with you, a most learned man, concerning such matters has been profitable. Indeed, that authority of **Theophrastus** <note>a Greek philosopher and the "father of botany"</note> which you brought forward has made me far more confident in confirming those things I wrote long ago, rather than moving me to recant—unless "to recant" is taken to mean repeating the same song once more. The reasoning for that correction was this: Pliny himself, in that same Book 24, testifies that the same herb is called not only **lagine**, but also **echite**, and **thin scammony** <note>original: "tenue scamoniũ"; scammony is a purgative resin from a vine</note> by some. But I would not recognize any plant <margin>Thin scammony.</margin> that could properly be called **thin scammony**, except for that which **Dioscorides** <note>the most influential Greek physician and botanist of antiquity</note> depicted under the names **elxine**, **euxine**, and <margin>Cissampelos.</margin> **cissampelos** <note>original: "cissampeli"; likely a species of bindweed or ivy-like vine</note>, all with leaves similar to ivy, which he found winding itself around other things. Because of this nature, just as Dioscorides calls it **cissampelos**, so Pliny <margin>Bindweed.</margin> elsewhere calls it **bindweed** <note>original: "conuoluolum"</note>.

But regarding what I previously only suspected, I now have certain knowledge from **Theophrastus**; in whose manuscript—which you know is even more corrupt than Pliny’s—I think it should be written **elxine** or **eusine** instead of **iasion**, just as I think it should be written in Pliny instead of **lagine** or **lasine**. For concerning **lasine**, Pliny writes thus in Book 21: "The **lasine** has one leaf, but so folded that although it is one, it seems to be many." But **Theophrastus**, from whom Pliny (as is reasonable) received his information, records the same things about the flower of the **iasion** in Book 1 of his *History of Plants* that Pliny reports about the flower of the **lasine**, in these words:

> Some emerge with one leaf, yet showing the appearance of many, such as the flower in the **iasion**.

Do these descriptions not wonderfully suit the flower of that herb which the Greeks call **elxine** and **cissampelos**, and which Pliny (as I said) calls **bindweed** <note>original: "conuoluolum"</note> elsewhere? For this flower is, as Pliny says, a **rough draft of nature learning how to make lilies** <note>original: "rudimentũ naturæ lilia facere condiscentis"</note>: and although it has only one leaf, it is nonetheless distinguished by certain incisions, as it were, so that it appears divided into five parts.

### ON THE LEMNIAN SEAL.

In this, I think, he was guarding against the confusion which Pliny seems to have made, by placing Lemnian earth among the red-chalks and types of colors in Book 35 <note>The Latin text says "libro v &", likely a truncated reference to Book 35 (XXXV) of Pliny's *Natural History*, which deals with pigments and earths</note>.

# THE NEW WORK OF NICCOLÒ LEONICENO OF VICENZA ON THE ERRORS OF PLINY, AND
## of many other physicians, addressed to the distinguished physician Francesco Totto of Lucca.

<image-desc>A large ornamental woodcut initial 'E' decorated with leafy vines and floral motifs.</image-desc>
**E**very day, you have urged me in almost every letter to respond to you regarding certain errors of Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder (23–79 AD), author of the *Natural History*, a massive encyclopedia that was a standard reference for Renaissance scientists</note> that I noted some time ago. A certain physician, a friend common to both of us, argued that these errors should not be blamed on the author himself, but rather on the newly printed editions or perhaps on the handwritten manuscripts. He based this on the authority of another, older manuscript which he showed you in Venice. Your letters indicated to me that not only you, but also that same physician—a defender of Pliny—especially desired my response on these matters. Indeed, I have delayed until this day to satisfy both your request and his desire, because I did not willingly allow myself to be called back to that old game. For to tell the truth, it seems to me like a kind of game to dispute the errors of Pliny, when there are many other errors in the books of physicians who are highly esteemed in our own age—errors from which human life is in much greater danger. <margin>Why Pliny should be read.</margin> For there are very few who read Pliny for medical treatments; many more read him for his vocabulary and his divine eloquence—which cannot be denied. Therefore, I believe physicians should labor more concerning those authors whose authority can actually harm the lives of people in our century, rather than concerning Pliny, who is considered by many to be in the rank of historians and orators rather than physicians or philosophers. You, who have read many of my formal medical opinions <note>original: "consilia"; these were written medical advice or case studies provided by prominent doctors to patients or other practitioners</note> in which I look after the health of the sick, know that when I come to simple medicines <term>simples: medicinal plants or minerals used on their own, rather than as part of a complex mixture</term>, I reveal how many errors were made by Gentilis, Bartholomeo, Montagnana <note>Gentile da Foligno (d. 1348), Bartolomeo da Santa Sofia (d. 1389), and Bartolomeo Montagnana (d. 1460) were all influential medieval and early Renaissance medical authorities whose reliance on Arabic sources Leoniceno often criticized</note>, and other more recent authors.

<summary>Niccolò Leoniceno addresses Francesco Totto, explaining that while critics defend Pliny the Elder’s errors as mere copying mistakes, Leoniceno is more concerned with the dangerous botanical and medical errors found in the works of more recent medieval authorities.</summary>

...claimed, in which they do not doubt that Pliny erred, along with Hermolao Barbaro <note>original: "Hermolao Barbaro"; a famous Venetian scholar (1454–1493) who claimed to have corrected 5,000 errors in Pliny’s work</note>. It is the same regarding wheat: according to a very ancient manuscript and the eighth book of Theophrastus <note>The "Father of Botany" (c. 371–c. 287 BC)</note>, one should not read "*aera*" but rather "weed" <note>original: "herba"</note>; for the sprouted weed strangles the wheat. Concerning this, in the same book where mention is made of the Nile in Egypt, he says: "Nor does the earth itself produce the weeds that kill the wheat." Likewise: "Weeding occurs when the crop is in joint <note>a stage of cereal growth where the stem forms nodes</note> and the useless weeds are torn out." Regarding the bean, he says: "It does not require weeding, because it overcomes the weeds." Also: "Drought restrains weeds; for the weed kills the wheat by binding around it and its roots." In this regard, in equally faulty manuscripts, it is read as follows: "*Aera* sometimes grows in lean soil." Where mention was made above of the *ateramnus* <note>a Greek term for legumes that are difficult to boil or cook</note>, one should read not "*aera*" but "those" <note>original: "ea"</note>. But after these matters are finished, the author soon begins concerning *aera* thus: "The grain of *aera* is very small." 

This is the defense of Pliny regarding *aera*, in which Pliny's "patron" <note>Pandolfo Collenuccio, who wrote a defense of Pliny against Leoniceno’s criticisms</note> was so pleased with himself that, in the manner of a rooster leaping away from a fight, he somehow applauds himself, and exults and glories before his fellow citizens with these words which he immediately added: "**With this single defense, we have silenced the untimely clamor of many, and we have returned your citizen [Pliny] cleared of great slander, so that henceforth others may learn to read and discuss such a great author more diligently.**" 

These last words we shall hurl back at Pliny's patron himself, and we shall advise the man that, if he intends to defend such a great author, he should examine the words of both that author and the others he brings into his defense more diligently. He should better investigate what is being charged against him by his adversaries, lest by defending something other than that of which he is accused, he appears to betray the cause he represents. Indeed, with this very fault, Pliny's patron, in this first defense undertaken on behalf of Pliny regarding *aera*...

# OF NICCOLÒ LEONICENO

*...uccio* <note>The text continues from the previous page, completing the name of Pandolfo Collenuccio</note>, it clearly appears that he struggled. For it was never attributed to Pliny as an error that he described darnel <note>original: "æram"; the Greek term *aira*, usually referring to the weed *Lolium temulentum*</note> and rye-grass <note>original: "lolium"; the Latin term for the same or a similar plant</note> separately, since even among the masters of logic it is not considered an error if two or even more descriptions of the same thing are provided. Rather, what we noted in Pliny’s work was that in the same book, and in the very same chapter where he described darnel, he also named rye-grass, as if he did not know that darnel and rye-grass were the same thing.

For if he thought they were the same, why—as we have objected—did he not follow his own practice? In the case of other crops and their defects which had their own names in the Latin language, he did not think he should use Greek terms; why did he not observe the same rule for rye-grass, by calling it "rye-grass" <note>original: "lolium"</note> instead of "darnel" <note>original: "æram"</note>? 

But Pliny’s patron will argue that Pliny does not write "darnel" but "the weed" <note>original: "herbam"</note> kills the wheat by binding around it; the patron strives to demonstrate this from several other passages from both Theophrastus <note>An ancient Greek philosopher and the "father of botany"</note> and Pliny himself. But he labors in vain, since even Pliny’s patron himself—both in his own preface and in the very book of Pliny that he edited and corrected—confesses that Pliny describes darnel and not "the weed" in Book 18, Chapter 17. Likewise, he later says in Book 22 that the same Pliny recounts only the remedies and powers of rye-grass. 

But what kind of distribution is this, that rye-grass is described by Pliny under the Greek name *aera*, but the medicinal effects of the same grain are recounted under the Latin name? Did Pliny begrudge the knowledge of rye-grass to Romans who were ignorant of the Greek language? Did he wish to teach them only its remedies and powers? This would be in vain if the plant or the grain itself were unknown. 

Furthermore, it is not even true that Pliny teaches only the medical effects of rye-grass <note>original: "lolij"</note> and not those of darnel <note>original: "æræ"</note>. Indeed, if not in Book 22, then certainly elsewhere—specifically in Book 29—Pliny mentions "darnel flour" <note>original: "ærinea farina"; flour made from darnel</note> for medicinal use. He ought to have called this "rye-grass flour" in Latin if he were only recounting the remedies and powers of rye-grass, as Pliny’s patron claims. Therefore, let the patron learn, if he wishes to defend Pliny in every respect, to read through the whole of Pliny more diligently. For how would it help Pliny once...

Yet, he did not dare to publish such an absurd correction of Pliny’s manuscript—which he had praised to you privately—either in his own preface or in his edited version of Pliny’s text. For he could have been asked where he himself had ever learned from experience, or where he had read in a doctor or philosopher of serious authority, that a grain of ivy, just like darnel <note>original: "æræ"</note>, causes dizziness of the head when baked in bread. 

But since he has avoided the pitfalls of this question as much as he could, we shall tire him with other questions. We ask: what is that herb which kills the wheat by binding itself around it? What name does it have among Greek or Latin authors, or at least among the common people? We have said that the plant called *aera* in Greek by Pliny—though not without error, as the common manuscript writing holds—is called *lolium* <note>rye-grass or darnel</note> in Latin. 

Consider other plants: *orobanche* <note>original: "orobanche"; broomrape, literally "vetch-strangler"</note> which kills vetch, *aegilope* <note>original: "ægilope"; a type of wild grass</note> which kills barley, and the herb called *pelecinos* <note>original: "pelecinos"; hatchet vetch</note> in Greek (also called *securina*), which kills lentils in a similar way—that is, by binding around them. All of these had their own names among both the Greeks and the Latins. Did the "pest of wheat" alone remain nameless <note>original: "ἀνώνυμος" (anōnymos)</note>, even though it ought to be more famous insofar as wheat is more sought after than all other crops and therefore requires more defense against injury? If anyone dared to ascribe this lack of vocabulary to our own Latin language, they certainly would not attribute it to the Greeks. For the Greeks were able to say *pyranche* <note>original: "πυράγχην" (pyranche); literally "wheat-strangler"</note>, just as they say *orobanche*, if they had no other name for the herb that kills wheat by binding itself around...

...of killing, by which broomrape <note>original: "ὀροβάγχη" (orobanche); a parasitic plant</note> kills vetch. Add to this that Pliny is accustomed to indicate specific herbs to us by some resemblance if they lack a name, provided they have some remarkable power. For example, in the same Book 19, Chapter 17, he says a white herb similar to panic grass <note>original: "panico"; a type of millet</note> grows, occupying the fields and even deadly to cattle. Or, if he is ignorant not only of the name but even of a resemblance, he at least testifies that their name is unknown to men; as in the book and chapter already cited, he says the plague of starlings or sparrows is driven away from millet and panic grass by an herb whose name is unknown. He would also have done this regarding the herb that kills wheat by binding itself around it, if "weed" <note>original: "herba"; Collenuccio argued the text should read "herba" instead of "aera"</note> were written in this passage instead of "darnel" <note>original: "æra"</note>, as Pliny’s patron wishes. 

Furthermore, the examples that Pliny’s patron brings forward—where either Theophrastus or Pliny speak of herbs harmful to crops—are partly false or poorly understood, and partly have no relevance to the present passage. First, Theophrastus is wrongly cited regarding Book 8 of *On Plants* <note>Theophrastus’s *Historia Plantarum*</note>; for nowhere in that book are those words read which Pliny’s patron adduces: "because the sprouted herb strangles the wheat." 

If there are indeed any passages that seem to have such a meaning, they have no bearing on the present dispute, in which the question is whether there is any herb that kills wheat by binding itself around it <note>Leoniceno is distinguishing between parasitic "binding" plants and general "choking" due to overgrowth</note>. Indeed, Theophrastus writes these words in Book 8 of *On Plants*: 

> "For rains are at times otherwise harmful, and they often 
> spoil the seeds; but if not that, they certainly stir up 
> such a luxuriance of weeds <note>original: "herbæ"</note> that the crops are 
> strangled and lose all nourishment." 

These words, however, do not mean what Pliny’s patron contends—that crops are strangled by certain herbs wrapping themselves around them. Rather, the sense is that crops, by sometimes growing too much into stalks and leaves, are strangled by their own luxuriance <note>original: "luxuria"; refers to rank, excessive vegetative growth at the expense of the grain</note> and are deprived of nourishment. Virgil also mentions this defect of crops in the *Georgics*: 

-> The land grazes down the luxuriance of the corn while still in the blade. <-

But even Pliny himself, in Book 18, Chapter 17, writes concerning this same flaw in this manner:
> Among the flaws of the crops is also **luxuriance**, when they fall over <note>original: "procumbunt"; referring to "lodging," where grain stalks collapse under their own weight</note> due to their excessive fertility.

Theophrastus also testifies in Book 5 of *The Causes of Plants* <note>Theophrastus’s *De causis plantarum*</note> that not only crops but even certain trees are "strangled" by this flaw, where he writes as follows:
> There is perhaps also some kind of tree in which corruption occurs naturally and spontaneously, not through any external cause but while it is in a state of vigorous growth, as in the **pine**, when its roots are changed into **torch-wood** <note>original: "tædam"; highly resinous wood used for torches</note>. For this happens from an excess of nutrition: and since the trees are unable to transmit nourishment through the torch-wood, they die. This seems very close to what happens to animals that become excessively thick and fat: for since they cannot draw in air, nor use their breath in any way because of their obesity and density, they are strangled. For this reason, farmers not ineptly use this term for the pine: for they say the pine is "strangled" by obesity and fatness, since all things require some breath, or a loosening, or a freedom of the passages. Therefore, I would consider corruptions of this kind to be natural rather than accidental.

These are the words of Theophrastus. From his words, it appears that plants are "strangled" for two reasons: Either because other plants wrap themselves around them—in the way that they write **vetch** <note>original: "ervum"</note> is strangled by **broomrape** <note>original: "orobanche"</note>, and in nearly the same way **lentils** by **cleavers** <note>original: "aparine"; also known as goosegrass</note>, as both Theophrastus in Book 8 of *On Plants* and Galen in Book 1 of *On Foods* record—or not by an external injury, but by their own luxuriance and obesity, as Theophrastus testifies concerning sown crops in the cited book, and concerning trees in Book 5 of *The Causes*. 

Therefore, Pliny’s patron <note>Pandolfo Collenuccio, who defended Pliny’s accuracy</note> ought to have followed the advice he gives to other physicians in his preface: he should have either cited Theophrastus’s words more faithfully or examined them more diligently. # NICCOLÒ LEONICENO

...it kills the roots, except in this passage which we are discussing, where he himself does not amend the text but corrupts it by changing **darnel** <note>original: "aeram"; likely referring to *Lolium temulentum*</note> into **herb**. Other words of Pliny, which Pliny’s patron <note>Pandolfo Collenuccio</note> adduces from various passages concerning useless herbs killing wheat, or concerning the **weeding** <note>original: "runcatione"; the manual pulling of weeds</note> of the crop or the bean, pertain nothing to the present dispute. For in this, the question is not whether there are some useless herbs that kill grain and legumes—for their removal, weeding becomes necessary; indeed, who so ignorant of rural matters would doubt this? It is not, I say, this that is being asked, but rather that: whether there is some **special herb** which kills wheat by specifically binding itself around it.

As Theophrastus writes in Book 8 of *On Plants* <note>Theophrastus’s *Enquiry into Plants*</note>: even if there are certain herbs considered common flaws of all fruits, those which nevertheless prevail more among some are considered their own specific flaws. For example: **broomrape** <note>original: "orobanche"</note> of vetch, **cleavers** <note>original: "aparine"</note> of lentils. Regarding these flaws, which are specific to certain plants, a little above the words already touched upon, the same Theophrastus had written in this manner:

> You will find no genus that is entirely apt to pass into another except **einkorn** <note>original: "tiphen"; a primitive wheat</note> and seed, as I proposed during the first disputes; likewise, **darnel** <note>original: "lolium"</note> is born from corrupted wheat and barley; or if that is less likely, it is certainly beyond doubt that it is accustomed to grow among wheat, as even that **Pontic wheat**, nicknamed "the black," and the **seed of bulbs**, and those things which are accustomed to grow among other seeds. For **oats** <note>original: "auena"</note> also seem to come out more in barley, and in lentils the **wild vetch** <note>original: "aracus"</note>, a rough and hard thing, while in **yellow-vetch** <note>original: "aphacis"</note> there is the **hatchet-plant** <note>original: "securina"</note>, which is similar to a hatchet.

All these things are from Theophrastus, as interpreted by Theodore Gaza <note>A 15th-century Greek scholar and translator of Aristotle and Theophrastus</note>, which translator indeed converted **darnel** <note>original: "aeram"</note> as **rye-grass** <note>original: "lolium"</note>. Concerning which, the same Theophrastus says no one doubts it is accustomed to grow among wheat: although Pliny’s patron seems to assert that **darnel** is not a specific flaw of wheat, but rather just a weed. The same Theodore called **goat-grass** <note>original: "ægilopen"</note> **oats** in Latin, which is so specific...

<page-num>100</page-num>

...describes: Otherwise, neither **darnel** <note>original: "aera," the Greek term for darnel or tares</note>—that is, **tares**—nor **goat-grass**—that is, **wild oats**—nor the **hatchet-vetch** <note>original: "herba securina," likely *Securigera securidaca*</note> could kill lentils by wrapping themselves around them, unless a straight-stemmed plant could become a stem-clasping one. To this idea, both our own senses and nature, the parent of all things, are opposed; for nature has separated those plants that wind themselves around others from the straight plants around which they wind, not only by species, but also by genus. Therefore, Pliny, Theophrastus, and Galen have correctly and harmoniously described the peculiar defects of crops. However, Pliny has poorly—and discordantly from those same authors—recounted the method by which most of these weeds destroy the crops, and he asserted this even more in his later conclusion when he added these words:

> And all these indeed kill by their embrace. 

<margin>Pliny sometimes perverts Theophrastus.</margin>
More truly, and more in imitation of Theophrastus—whom Pliny seems to want to emulate everywhere when writing on the natures of plants, even though he perverts many of that same author’s meanings—he should have written thus: "And all these indeed kill for this reason, because they take away the **nutrients** <note>original: "pabulum," meaning the "food" or sustenance the plant draws from its environment</note>." For Theophrastus uses such words in the fifth book of *On the Causes of Plants*, where he discusses the specific pests that kill sown crops, writing as follows:

> Deaths also happen from other plants that are specific to them, as is evident in smaller plants: for that which is called **broomrape** <note>original: "orobanche," a parasitic plant</note> kills the **bitter vetch** <note>original: "ervum"</note> by its embrace and its squeezing; and **linoderum** <note>original: "linoderum," a parasitic weed often associated with flax</note> destroys **fenugreek** immediately by growing onto its root. And others bring destruction to others, such as those which come forth at the same time as individual crops—like **darnel** and **oats** with wheat and barley, and **cleavers** <note>original: "aparine"</note> with lentils, and others with others. Yet all of them kill for this reason: because they take away the nutrients, both what the earth provides and what comes from the sun and air. And the reason for them is manifest, because they clearly have a power of killing; for the words immediately written below manifest such a meaning: "Oil, however, and pitch, and fat; for these also have the power of killing," and so forth.

From these words of Theophrastus, it can easily be clear to anyone that **darnel**—that is, **tares**—and **goat-grass**—that is, **wild oats**—for such...

<page-num>101</page-num>

the words found in the Greek manuscript have this meaning: that one [weed] has the power to kill **wheat** <note>original: "triticum"</note>, and the other to kill **barley** <note>original: "hordeum"</note>, not by wrapping themselves around the plant, but by stealing its **nutrients** <note>original: "pabulum," literally "fodder" or food</note>. For even **broomrape** <note>original: "orobanche," a parasitic plant that grows on the roots of others</note> and **cleavers** <note>original: "aparine," also known as bedstraw, which has tiny hooks to climb other plants</note>, which have this nature of wrapping themselves around things, do not escape this common principle: they also kill by removing nutrients—both what the earth provides and what comes from the sun and the air. This is what **Theophrastus** <note>A student of Aristotle and the "father of botany"</note> seems to have wanted to suggest in this passage, by associating cleavers not with broomrape, as he does in his eighth book, but with **darnel** and **oats**. And yet, for those considering it more carefully, he had indicated the same thing in that eighth book, writing thus about broomrape and cleavers:

> **Some things also emerge that are clearly common to several plants; but because they are more powerful among some, they are considered specific to them. For example: broomrape of bitter vetch, and cleavers of lentils; because the former overcomes the bitter vetch most of all due to its weakness, while the latter most especially grows together among lentils.**

It is as if **Theophrastus** wants to say that even if broomrape overcomes **bitter vetch** <note>original: "ervuum"</note> most powerfully by its embrace and compression because of the vetch's weakness, it nevertheless also kills it by stealing its nutrients. **Cleavers**, however, kills the **lentil** most powerfully by taking its nutrients, since the weed itself thrives on the abundant nourishment found among lentils. For this is the meaning of the word <term>συμφυῆ</term> <note>original: "symphye," meaning "growing together" or "naturally joined"</note>, which Theophrastus uses here, and for which the translator rendered as "most especially grows together." However, in this passage (to excuse ourselves—that is, to free ourselves from the suspicion of the same fault of "false allegation" of Theophrastus for which we accused **Pliny’s** protector, especially among those who have read Theophrastus in Latin rather than Greek), I judged that these same readers should be warned: where **Theodore** <note>Theodore Gaza, a prominent 15th-century translator of Greek scientific texts into Latin</note> in his translation 

<margin>Pliny’s authority imposed upon Theodore.</margin>

of Theophrastus translates *aparine* as **burdock** <note>original: "lappa"</note>, he followed the error of **Pliny**. Pliny quite often in his books, where Theophrastus names *aparine*, calls it "lappa" in Latin, though he says he prefers to use the Greek word *aparine*, which Pliny nevertheless uses in various places.

Nor is Pliny proven to have erred because of this, for we can defend him with the authority of **Galen** <note>The most influential physician of the Roman Empire</note>, who, among the bad herbs growing in lentils, names hatchet-vetch no less than vetch.

<meta>This page follows Leoniceno’s argument that Pliny the Elder and his later defenders misunderstood the Greek terms "teramon" and "ateramon." On the previous page, Leoniceno challenged the idea that "ateramnum" was a specific weed, preparing to prove through the works of Theophrastus that these words actually describe the cooking quality of legumes.</meta>

-># NICOLAUS LEONICENUS<-

The terms "easy-to-cook" <note>original: *teramon*</note> and "difficult-to-cook" <note>original: *ateramon*</note> are used only for legumes, although it is not unreasonable to think that something similar or <gloss>the</gloss> same happens with grains; however, because the use is not the same, it is not as apparent. Even among legumes, these terms are not used equally for all, but are said mostly of beans and lentils—either because these are most naturally affected by such conditions, or because they are seen more often due to their frequent use. It happens quite widely: for there are many places that bear easy-to-cook crops, and others again that bear difficult-to-cook ones. For the most part, thin soils produce easy-to-cook crops. The state of the air also causes such a variation, and the proof is that the same fields, worked in the same way, sometimes produce easy-to-cook crops; however, near Philippi <note>An ancient city in Macedonia</note>, if the bean is being winnowed and is caught by the local wind, though it was easy-to-cook, it becomes difficult-to-cook.

This is, as Theodore <note>Theodore Gaza (c. 1398–1475), a Greek humanist and translator who translated Theophrastus into Latin</note> translated it: "Cookable" <note>original: *coctibile*</note> and "uncookable" <note>original: *incoctibile*</note> are terms usually used only for legumes, yet you might think not without reason that the same or something very close occurs in grains. But since the use is not the same, it can neither be perceived nor felt equally in all legumes; it is noticed chiefly in the bean and the lentil, either because these are born to be affected in a greater measure, or because they appear more often due to more frequent use. It happens quite broadly: for there are very many places that always bear cookable crops, and others that bear uncookable ones, but almost everywhere thin soils render crops more cookable. The condition of the sky can undoubtedly bring about a change of this sort; as proof, the same spots sometimes yield cookable, other times uncookable crops. When the bean is winnowed at Philippi, if it is blown upon by the local breeze, it becomes uncookable. These are the words of Theophrastus in Greek, and in Latin according to the translation of Theodore Gaza, a man most learned in both Greek and Latin literature.

From all of this, the error of Pliny is manifested clearer than the light of day. He reported the effect on the bean as "ateramnon"—that is, uncookable—near Philippi, arriving from the local wind upon that same bean. However, Pliny himself recorded this in a sense far different from that of Theophrastus or Theophrastus's translator, by wrongly imitating this entire passage of Theophrastus. Around Philippi, Pliny names "ateramnon" as a **herb** in rich soil by which the bean is killed, and "teramnon" as one in thin soil. For I believe it should be written thus according to Theophrastus, who mentions "teramnon" and "ateramnon" in Book VIII, although in another [place] than...

-># NICOLAUS LEONICENUS<-

> ...nature has covered the oat, so to speak. Moreover, the stalk is taller in wheat than in barley, and the ear emerges more distinctly from the leaves; the chaff is also much more pleasant from wheat than from barley.

Pliny, in his Eighteenth Book, Chapter Seven, as one may gather, wishing to interpret this passage of Theophrastus concerning *bromos* <note>original: *bromon*; the Greek name for oats</note>—for not only does Theodore <note>Theodore Gaza (c. 1398–1475), a scholar whose Latin translations of Theophrastus were standard in the Renaissance</note> interpret this word as "oat" <note>original: *auenam*</note> in this passage, but Pliny does as well—stated that it was "mostly naked." However, Theophrastus described it as *pollylobon* <note>Greek: "many-lobed" or "well-covered"</note>, which, as the same Theodore translated it, means "mostly covered." Common sense also supports this fact, since one may observe that the oat is covered by many tunics <note>A botanical term for the protective layers or husks of a grain</note>, as Theophrastus writes, and is not naked, as Pliny incorrectly reported by misinterpreting Theophrastus. And lest anyone suspect me of criticizing Pliny out of spite, I will set down the words of the same author from the book and chapter cited above; they are as follows:

> Wheat has many layers <note>original: *tunicæ*</note>, while barley and *alica* <note>original: *alica*; a type of emmer wheat or the grits made from it</note> are mostly naked, but especially the oat. The stalk is taller in wheat than in barley, and the beard <note>original: *arista*; the needle-like bristles on an ear of grain</note> is more biting in barley.

Who cannot see that Pliny intended to say the same things as Theophrastus when speaking of almost the same matters, except where he went astray regarding the oat? For Pliny’s words, "wheat has many layers," correspond to those of Theophrastus, "wheat is covered by many tunics." Likewise, "barley is mostly naked" is what Theophrastus says: "barley mostly lacks a covering." "The stalk is taller in wheat than in barley, and the beard is more biting in barley": Pliny's words carry the same meaning as the words of Theophrastus, "the stalk is taller in wheat than in barley, and the chaff is more pleasant from wheat than from barley." But the remaining points—namely, that *alica* (which Pliny seems to have substituted for *tipha* <note>A species of einkorn or spelt</note> or *siligo* <note>A fine white winter wheat</note>) is naked, and especially the oat—these are the errors of Pliny. According to both Theophrastus and physical observation, he ought to have said they are enclosed in multiple leaves, or "mostly covered." But if I may wander outside the Eighteenth Book, is not Pliny also proven to have erred in Book Thirty-Two regarding *aegilops* <note>A type of wild grass or weed often found in grain fields</note>?

This serves as a primary example of Leoniceno’s larger project to correct classical scientific errors using philology and direct observation.</summary>

These are Pliny's two errors regarding *bromos* <note>Greek name for oats</note> and *aegilops*, the two species of oats.

> And the herb of the same name, which grows in barley, heals *aegilopas* <note>original: "ægilopas". Here Pliny refers to an eye ulcer (aegilops) being treated by the herb of the same name.</note>. It has a leaf like wheat; its crushed seed is mixed with flour and applied, or its juice is expressed from the stalks and very large leaves after the ear has been removed, and it is worked into medicinal cakes with three-month flour.

But if Pliny’s defender wishes to stubbornly contend that *aegilops* is not the oat, nor a species of oat, let him show for himself what herb *aegilops* is. We, however, show it to be the oat, both from Dioscorides <note>A 1st-century Greek physician and botanist</note> and from Pliny himself, who describes it in the same manner as Dioscorides and records the same medicinal use. Moreover, in this very place—namely Chapter XI of Book XXV—he testifies that it grows in barley, just as he previously testified in Book XVIII, Chapter XVII, that barley degenerates into oats. We can demonstrate this by authorities, and furthermore by the authority of Theodore Gaza <note>A prominent Greek scholar and translator of the Renaissance</note>, a man born in Greece and no less learned in Latin than in...

I say, if one of two things must be taken away from Pliny, I would rather strip him of his knowledge of Greek letters than assign him an ignorance of things born from the earth—especially things so commonly known. Nor do I think this would be a great disgrace for Pliny if Greek erudition were taken from him, since much greater ornaments of Latin literature would remain for him. In these, he so surpassed all other authors of the Latin language that if the Muses had wished to speak in the Roman tongue, I do not think they would have spoken in the manner of Plautus <note>Titus Maccius Plautus was a Roman playwright. Ancient critics famously said that if the Muses spoke Latin, they would use his language.</note>, as some believe, but rather would have spoken in the manner of Pliny. 

<margin>Pliny's Eloquence.</margin>

But I wish he had possessed as much wisdom in his heart as he had eloquence in his native tongue. I do not indeed disapprove that learned men judge Pliny’s style to be divine and think it should be primarily imitated; rather, I praise it, and I plainly admit that those who do not have a taste for it are themselves lacking in taste. But in turn, I think those people are in another kind of folly who attribute such divinity to Pliny that it cannot enter their minds that Pliny could have wandered astray in any part of his work—whether he speaks of the appearance and nature of herbs, the circumference of the land and sea, or the magnitude of the stars. 

Recently, a certain friend in Ferrara <note>Ferrara was a major center of Renaissance learning where Leoniceno taught for many years.</note> warned me that, having happened to enter a boys' school, he heard the schoolmaster shouting loudly against me in defense of Pliny and a certain shyster lawyer <note>original: "leguleo," a derogatory term for a petty or unlearned lawyer.</note> who acted as Pliny's patron, pronouncing judgments on the sun and the moon. Then I said to my friend: "And what was that schoolmaster teaching his boys about the sun and the moon? That the sun is of the masculine gender and the moon of the feminine?" For I did not think a schoolmaster would have dared to "rise above his sandal" <note>original: "supra calceum ascendere." This is a reference to the Greek painter Apelles, who told a cobbler criticizing his work, "A shoemaker should not judge above the shoe." It means one should not speak on matters outside their expertise.</note>. 

"Not that," my friend replied, "but something greater. For he was trying to prove that Pliny held the same view as other mathematicians regarding the moon: namely, that it is smaller than the earth. This is based on where Pliny writes in the second book of his *Natural History*: 'The whole sun could not be taken away from the lands by the moon coming between them if the earth were larger...'" <note>Pliny is discussing solar eclipses here. The logic involves the relative sizes of the Earth, Sun, and Moon and how shadows are cast.</note>

I thought that one should read not <gloss>except</gloss> <note>original Greek: *plēn*</note>, but rather <gloss>before</gloss> <note>original Greek: *prin*</note>, lest if the word of exception is retained, a most obvious lie be present: that all animals bitten by a rabid dog go mad and die, *except* for man; whereas both man and the rest of the animals go mad and die from the bite of a rabid dog. Nor does he fear, as I said, to violate nature—which willed the bite of a rabid dog to be as harmful to man as to other animals—so that he may keep the decrees of his own art uncorrupted. 

But I shall address this man—bound to me by an old friendship, although as I finally discovered, it was a feigned one; since, though often praised by me before great men by whose help he passed his life, he does not return the same grateful proclamations, but rather ungrateful insults—I shall, I say, address this man, whether a true or a false friend, thus: "I ask you, my friend: if one of the two must be taken away from Aristotle—either the teaching of philosophy or his mastery of Greek grammar—which would you think should be removed? You, perhaps favoring your own profession, would rather judge Aristotle to be a bad philosopher so that you may prove him a good grammarian. You indeed act like a Greek grammarian."

**solecism** <note>A "solecism" is a grammatical mistake or intentional deviation from standard rules.</note> occurs when one conjunction is put in place of another; just as Porphyry <note>Porphyry of Tyros (c. 234–305 AD), a Neoplatonic philosopher and commentator on Aristotle.</note> admits that Aristotle clearly used "and" <note>original Greek: *kai*</note> instead of "or" <note>original Greek: *ē*</note>. <margin>Laurentius Valla</margin>
Laurentius Valla <note>Lorenzo Valla (c. 1407–1457), a famous Italian humanist and philologist known for proving the "Donation of Constantine" was a forgery.</note>, due to the scarcity of Latin books which plagued his age, believed many phrases were inconsistent with pure Latinity which, in our own age, are frequently found in Latin authors that have since been brought to light. But what need is there to contend with a Greek grammarian—especially an old friend—in such a laborious dispute? For we can both easily return to a state of favor and be called back into one harmony, by making Aristotle a good philosopher and a "not bad" grammarian. We do this by reading his first words in the place we are debating as follows: *all bitten things suffer before man* <note>original Greek: λυπῶσιν ἅπαντα τὰ δηχθέντα πρὶν ἄνθρωπος</note>, so that "suffers" <note>original Greek: λυπῇ (*lypē*)</note> is understood, or *before man* <note>original Greek: πρὶν ἄνθρωπον (*prin anthrōpon*)</note>, by understanding "to suffer" <note>original Greek: λυπᾶν (*lypan*)</note>. For he will not deny that the adverb "before" <note>original Greek: πρὶν (*prin*)</note> is joined with the indicative as well as with the infinitive, unless he wishes to deny the rules of his own art. This is also true in the second clause: *this disease destroys both the madness and whatever has been bitten by a rabid animal before man* <note>original Greek: ἀναιρεῖ τὸ νόσημα τοῦτο τὰς τε λύπας καὶ ὅτι ἂν δηχθῆ ὑπὸ λυπώσης πρὶν τὸν ἄνθρωπον</note>, by understanding "destroys" <note>original Greek: ἀναιρεῖ (*anairei*)</note>. 

However, I would more strongly approve of the accusative case in the first clause and the understanding of an infinitive verb, both because the construction is more common and because there is a great similarity between the Greek letters *eta* (η) and *upsilon* (υ), and therefore a slip from one to the other is easier <note>Leoniceno is suggesting a "paleographical" argument: that a scribe misread a letter, changing the meaning of the word.</note>. But, setting aside the rather thick-headed subtleties of the grammarians—whether Latin or Greek—let us now return to the physician who acts as Pliny's patron <note>Likely referring to a contemporary scholar who defended Pliny the Elder against Leoniceno's criticisms.</note>. Regarding him, I cannot wonder enough that a physician and philosopher, learned not only in my judgment but also in that of others, has allowed himself to be dragged into the "heresy" of the grammarians: the belief that Pliny is free from all error, even in those matters which pertain partly to the disciplines of the philosophers and partly to those of the physicians. For among other things in which he writes in his preface that Hermolaus <note>Hermolaus Barbarus (1454–1493), a scholar who published thousands of corrections to Pliny’s *Natural History*.</note> unjustly accused Pliny, he also seems to [accuse] Hermolaus...

-># ON HERBS AND SHRUBS.<-

...to note Hermolaus' <note>Hermolaus Barbarus (1454–1493) was an Italian scholar who famously sought to correct thousands of errors in Pliny’s Natural History.</note> error regarding the size of the sun, moon, and earth. But why he <note>Referring to the "defender of Pliny" mentioned below, likely Pandolfo Collenuccio.</note> should disagree with Hermolaus in these matters—who agrees with me against Pliny—I do not understand, since Pliny's defender has not yet revealed his own opinion in favor of Pliny against me and Hermolaus in this part, just as in many others. 

As for us, regarding this passage, we will openly pronounce what we think: that Hermolaus correctly established, along with Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the influential Greco-Egyptian astronomer and mathematician.</note> and other most approved mathematicians, that the moon is smaller than the earth, and that he rightly rejected Pliny's sophistry <note>original: "cavillum," a mocking or deceptive argument.</note> which attempts to prove the opposite. However, Hermolaus did not write correctly, nor in harmony with Ptolemy, when he states that the earth is only three and nearly two-fifths times larger than the moon. For that proportion exists between the diameters <note>The straight line passing from side to side through the center of a body.</note> of the earth and moon, but not between the spheres themselves. Geometric reasoning proves that spheres possess a triplicate <note>In modern terms, "triplicate proportion" means the ratio of the volumes is the cube of the ratio of the diameters.</note> proportion of their diameters. From this reasoning, it is gathered that the earth is larger than the moon not by three and nearly two-fifths parts, as Hermolaus writes, but by thirty-nine and nearly one-third parts. 

If Pliny's defender intended to point out this error of Hermolaus when he notes him concerning the size of the sun, moon, and earth, we would embrace the man not only as a physician but also as a mathematician. But since he also criticizes the same Hermolaus regarding the sun—where Hermolaus provided not even the slightest suspicion of error—we greatly fear that this remark savors of grammatical rather than mathematical subtlety. For even petty grammarians dare to dispute astronomy based on singular and plural numbers, or natural history through the use of the genitive or ablative case. 

<margin>The plant bearing strawberries.</margin>

<margin>Lysimachion <note>Commonly known today as Loosestrife.</note></margin>

Which is what Pliny’s defender ought to have done before saying the flower of **lysimachion** was common; otherwise, let him know he has spoken contradictions. For how can a flower be commonly known if the herb itself from which the flower grows is unknown? As I certainly know it to be ignored not only by the common folk, but even by the physicians of our age, just as many other things that were in medical use among the ancients are ignored.

If, however, I wished to speak in the manner of the sophists <note>Here used to mean those who use clever but fallacious arguments.</note>—not the elegant ones, but the barbarians—I could say both that the common people and physicians know the herb **lysimachion**, and yet they do not know the herb **lysimachion**. But I least think that Pliny's defender, a physician not only skilled but also learned, would have spoken thus; yet if one were allowed to speak so, it would be a true sophistical discourse. ...as Dioscorides describes. I truly testify that I have frequently seen the herb **corneola** <note>original: "corneolam"; likely a local Italian name for a species of Loosestrife</note> growing in the marshes of Ferrara, or on the banks of the Po. In addition, it has thin, green leaves, like those that sprout on a willow, which, if burned, emit a sharp smoke that bites the nostrils; and—this condemns Pliny’s account—it is seen marked not with a purple flower, but a golden one. Indeed, even Pliny is forced to admit that the flower of the **lysimachium** herb is golden, unless he wishes to claim that the stone of the same name, **lysimachus**, which is marked with golden veins as he himself describes in Book 37, Chapter 10, happened to share the same name by mere chance. Although the same Pliny can be criticized not only regarding the color of the flower, but also for the scent of the herb, which he writes is perceived as heavy <note>original: "gravem"</note>, and not sharp <note>original: "acrem"</note> as Dioscorides does; nor does he show how such a scent is perceived—namely, through the smoke of the burned herb. Dioscorides carried out all these observations most diligently, and furthermore taught the use of the herb in medicine, which Pliny neglected to do in the passage where he describes **lysimachion**.

However, I certainly do not remember reading in any Greek or Latin author that **lysimachium** is a dyeing herb <note>original: "herbam infectivam"; a plant used to produce dyes for textiles</note>, except for what Pliny writes in Book 26, Chapter 16: that it makes the hair blond. Dioscorides, however, says that **lysimachium** is called by another name, **lytron**, which name I suspect has been corrupted either in the texts of Dioscorides or in those of Pliny,

-># NICOLAUS LEONICENUS #<-

However, it might seem strange if the plant is called **yellow** or **weld** <note>original: "lutea" or "luteum"; names associated with the dye-plant Weld (*Reseda luteola*)</note>, since it produces a green color rather than yellow—unless it also produces a yellow or golden hue when used by itself and not layered over blue. Perhaps the name **lytron** <note>a Greek name for the plant</note> was given to it not from the color it dyes, but rather from its yellow flower. 

Furthermore, Avicenna—in the sixteenth Section <term>Fen: a subdivision of the "Canon of Medicine"</term> of his third book, in the chapter on the stripping of ulcers—mentions a certain plant which he calls the "dyer's herb" and the "citrine herb." He writes that its juice, when drunk or administered by enema, is beneficial for ulcers of the intestines. I do not believe he is referring to any plant other than **loosestrife**, since Dioscorides likewise states that the juice of its leaves, whether drunk or injected via enema, is helpful for those suffering from dysentery. 

However, the ancient commentator on Avicenna—whether it be Gentile <note>Gentile da Foligno (d. 1348), a prominent medical scholar</note> or someone else whose printed expositions on the cited passage are available—seems more eager to cut the words of Avicenna into parts (marking "the first point here," "the second there," "the third there") than to clarify their meaning, which would be of greater use to physicians. This commentator did not seek to illustrate with his learning this "dyer's citrine herb," nor the other plant which Avicenna mentions immediately after as having the same effect. Avicenna says that some call this second plant **alacohen’s foot** <note>original: "pedem alacohen"; a Latinized Arabic name</note>, and he himself believes it to be **crow’s foot** <note>original: "pes corui"; likely a species of Ranunculus</note>, although others before him, as he himself testifies, had said that Hippocrates understood **alacohen** to mean fig leaves. Gentile passed over both of these plants in his exposition without touching them, as if they were perfectly well known or as if knowledge of them offered little utility, even though they appear to have been famous in ancient medical practice and therefore necessary to know. 

The modern commentator on Avicenna, however, did not seem to neglect these matters entirely, yet the reader is left more uncertain than before by his explanations. For he says that the dyer's herb is **memite** <note>original: "memite"; likely *māmīthā* or the Horned Poppy</note>, the juice of which is used by dyers. Nor is the fact that Avicenna writes in his first book that **memite** is "cold and dry" a sufficiently effective argument to prove that **memite** is the "dyer's herb" which Avicenna mentions in the sixteenth Section <term>Fen: a subdivision of the "Canon of Medicine"</term> of his third book, in the chapter on the stripping of the intestines.
