### ON HERBS AND SHRUBS. ###

"...a poisonous potency, from which some were healed. But I never dared to give this by mouth, although I know of certain things which, when applied externally, cause blisters and ulcers, and do harm if eaten, such as garlic and onions."

Thus says that author: who, although he fears—as indeed he ought to fear—giving the root of **crow’s foot** <note>original: *pes coruinus*; a name applied to various species of buttercup (*Ranunculus*), which are known to be caustic and toxic</note> by mouth, which is a poison (as we shall declare later), nevertheless seems to suggest by his final words that if it were to be given by mouth, it should be administered with some degree of reason, and not without the authority of a Ruler <note>The author uses "Princeps" here, likely referring to a high-ranking medical authority or "Prince of Physicians"</note>. However, Giovanni Matteo de Grado <note>A 15th-century Italian physician and influential commentator on Arabic medicine</note>, another modern commentator on Avicenna, writes these words rather more boldly in his explanation of this root:

"Understand that when authors use **crow’s foot**, even in this case they always use its root and not its leaves; so also Master Avicenna, in the second book of the *Canon* <note>The *Canon of Medicine*, the standard medical encyclopedia of the Middle Ages</note>, sets forth the benefits of its root."

These words of the Commentator indicate to us that he himself feared the leaves of this herb, but not the root, because Master Avicenna had specifically approved the use of that root—and not the leaves—in the second book of the *Canon*.

I pity human life, which I see daily endangered under Avicenna—not as a 'Prince of Physicians,' as the younger doctors call him, but as a cruel tyrant. For if he orders a poisonous root to be used even inside the body, some physicians do not hesitate to use it on the sick; conversely, if he forbids a healthy root that resists poisons, treating it as if it were a deadly medicine, even famous doctors do not dare to give it.

The root of **crow’s foot**, which has the power to cause ulcers and acts like a poison (and should thus be avoided in medical practice except for external application), another modern commentator on Avicenna does not fear to <margin>† say</margin> should be taken internally, relying on the authority of Avicenna in both the second book of the *Canon* and the sixteenth book of the third, where Avicenna prefers it over **hermodactyls** <note>original: *hermodactylis*; likely meadow saffron (*Colchicum*), a potent treatment for gout that can also be toxic</note>.

Does not this same Avicenna—if there are any so foolish as to wish to believe him in everything—write in the second book of the *Canon* that **monkshood** <margin>Monkshood</margin> <note>original: *napellum*; a highly toxic plant also known as wolfsbane or aconite</note> is a destructive poison? However, the poison which in our age is called **monkshood** by the herbalists is called **aconite** by the Greeks and Latins, about which Virgil says:
> Step-mothers mix the **aconite**. <note>A famous line from Virgil's *Georgics* (2.128), referring to the plant's reputation as a tool for poisoners</note>

So it now appears that Avicenna imitates the character not just of a tyrant, but even of a step-mother. In contrast, Galen <note>The influential 2nd-century Greek physician whose authority Leoniceno sought to restore over Arabic commentators</note> praises aconite if something needs to be purged from the body, but says that one must be careful, saying it should not be taken in food or drink. This same Avicenna writes in the second book of the *Canon* that the root of **cinquefoil** <note>original: *pentaphyllum*; literally "five-leaf"</note>—which was recommended by Dioscorides <note>The ancient author of *De Materia Medica*, the primary pharmacological text of the era</note> against deadly poisons—is itself a destructive medicine. This belief is so strong that Michele Savonarola <note>A renowned 15th-century Italian physician and grandfather of the famous friar Girolamo Savonarola</note>, a physician famous in his own time and ours for the medical writings he published, did not dare to give it in cases of **quartan fever** <note>A fever that recurs every third day, typical of malaria</note>, for no other reason than because it was condemned by the Prince <note>Referring to Avicenna as the "Prince of Physicians," the title given to him in medieval universities</note>. Avicenna holds such authority among the physicians of our time, as I was saying recently, that he makes a deadly medicine healthy—like **crow’s foot**—and a healthy medicine destructive—like the root of **cinquefoil** or its juice. For even Jacopo de' Dondi, nicknamed "the Aggregator" <note>A 14th-century physician known for compiling diverse medical opinions</note>, numbers the juice of this root among destructive poisons based on the authority of Avicenna. Perhaps, however, as far as the root of **crow’s foot** is concerned, it is not so much Avicenna who should be blamed, but rather the physicians themselves for not correctly understanding Avicenna. For who compels them to think that the herb which the herbalists of our age call **crow’s foot** is the same one that the ancient physicians—namely Paul <note>Paul of Aegina, a 7th-century medical encyclopedist</note> and Dioscorides—celebrated under that same name? As if it were truly necessary that the names of herbs used now were also the same in a previous century! It would have been proper for those Commentators on Avicenna whom I noted above to have said...

### NICOLAI LEONICENI ###

...anywhere the herb **crow’s foot** <note>original: *coronopoda*; from the Greek *koronopous*</note>—for that is what the Greeks call the plant we name "crow's foot"—is compared to **hermodactyls** <note>original: *hermodactylis*; a bulbous root, likely a species of *Colchicum*, famously used since antiquity to treat joint pain</note> in its effectiveness for helping those with **gout** <note>original: *podagricos*; sufferers of *podagra*, a painful inflammatory arthritis</note>. However, he prefers the composition which the Greeks call <gloss>through crow’s foot</gloss> <note>original: *διὰ κορωνοπόδος*</note> over the other which the same Greeks call <gloss>through hermodactyls</gloss> <note>original: *δι’ ἑρμοδακτύλων*</note>. Paul <note>Paul of Aegina, a 7th-century Byzantine Greek physician</note> describes both of these in his seventh book, in which he treats simple and compound medicines, marking both with their proper titles.

The title and description of the first composition is as follows:

->**Gout Medicine via Hermodactyl.**<-

**Hermodactyls**, 4 <term>ounces</term> <note>original: *uñz*; abbreviation for *unciae*</note>; **anise**, **Ethiopian cumin**, **bishop's weed** <note>original: *ameos*</note>, **clusters of thyme**, **long pepper**, and **ginger**, three **obols** <note>original: *obolos*; a small unit of weight derived from the Greek coin</note> each; **epithyme** <note>a parasitic plant, often clover dodder</note>, half an ounce. The dose is 4 or 6 obols, given in the morning with seasoned wine or **hydromel** <note>a mixture of honey and water, like mead</note>. The title and description of the second composition, "through crow’s foot," is as follows:

->**A composition via crow’s foot, which serves the same purposes**<-
->**as the one via hermodactyl, and is beneficial to the stomach.**<-

**Ginger**, two obols; **pepper**, three obols; **agaric** <note>a medicinal fungus</note>, one obol; the inner part of <term>cinci</term> <note>possibly a corruption of *cnicus* (thistle) or a specific bark; in Paul of Aegina's original Greek, this often refers to the inner pith of a plant</note>, four obols; **root of crow’s foot**, six obols. The dose is eight obols. For those whose bowels are not easily moved, adding twenty-three **carob pods** <note>original: *siliquae*</note> causes about seven or eight bowel movements. Paul, in the third volume of his book on medicine, says on the authority of **Alexander** <note>Alexander of Tralles, a 6th-century physician</note> that this second recipe, named "through crow's foot," is better than the first, because it achieves the same evacuation and equally soothes the pain, while also doing no harm to the stomach. 

**Avicenna** <note>The influential 11th-century Persian physician Ibn Sina</note>, in the two places cited earlier, wrongly interprets the meaning of these words as referring to crow's foot alone. He compares the herb itself to hermodactyls, as if the root of the crow's foot of which Paul speaks were equal in purging the bowels to the root of hermodactyls—rather than possessing an **astringent** <note>original: *adstringendi*; the power to shrink tissues and stop secretions</note> quality, which is how **Dioscorides** <note>The primary ancient authority on botany</note> views it, testifying that it is beneficial for those with **celiac disease** <note>original: *coeliacis*; here referring to chronic abdominal or intestinal flux</note>.

Nor should anyone wonder that a purgative composition takes its name from a medicine that binds the belly. For in **gouty** <note>original: *podagricis*</note> and **sciatic** <note>original: *ischiadicis*</note> pains, we seek no less to restrain the flow of **humors** <note>bodily fluids believed to cause disease when out of balance</note> to the painful areas than to evacuate those that have already flowed there.

...which **Paul** <note>Paul of Aegina, a 7th-century Byzantine physician</note> had previously noted, it may seem so to those wishing to compare them. Here, however, someone will come forward and object to me with the very same point that I previously raised against **Avicenna** <note>The 11th-century Persian physician Ibn Sina</note> himself and his commentators: namely, that it is not clear from their explanations what the **dyer's herb** or **yellow herb** <note>original: *herba tinctorum siue citrina*</note> is, nor what the **crow's foot** <note>original: *pes coruinus*</note> is, which Paul understood, however poorly he was cited by Avicenna. Since, therefore, we have previously taught both what the "dyer's herb" mentioned by Avicenna is and what its nature is, and by what name it was distinguished among the ancients—just as we also did for the herb that our modern herbalists call "crow's foot"—it remains for us to teach what "crow's foot" was to the ancients, specifically to **Dioscorides**, Paul, and Avicenna. <margin>Coronopus</margin>
**Coronopus**—that is, "crow’s foot"—says **Dioscorides** <note>A 1st-century Greek physician and author of the foundational herbal *De Materia Medica*</note>, is a small herb, oblong, spread flat upon the ground, with divided leaves; this is also boiled as a vegetable. Some call it *amnodes*, some *astrium*; the Africans call it *atorsum*, the Romans *cacatricem*, some *stillago*, and some *sanguinari*. The root of this plant, when taken in food, is beneficial for those with **coeliac conditions** <note>digestive disorders</note>; it grows in uncultivated places, in thickets, and along paths. Setting aside the foreign names for this herb (concerning which we cannot judge whether they were written correctly or incorrectly), let us inspect the Roman names more diligently, so that if any of them are corrupted, we may correct them, and from there arrive at a true knowledge of the herb we seek. *Cacatricem* certainly seems to be a corrupted word; for it is neither Greek nor Latin. Therefore, I think it should be read as *galitricem*, or

...just as <note>original: *cuti* (likely a fragment of *sicuti*)</note> among the Greeks this herb was named **coronopus** <note>Greek: κορωνόπους, literally "crow's foot"</note> because it represents the image of a crow’s foot, for a similar reason among the Romans it would have been called **cock’s spur** <note>original: *galli crus*</note>. For there is a herb mentioned by the author of *On Simple Medicine*—whom some believe to have been **Apuleius** <note>likely referring to Pseudo-Apuleius, the author of a famous 4th-century illustrated herbal</note>—called **cock’s spur**, and also named **sanguinaria** <note>a name derived from the Latin *sanguis*, meaning blood</note>. He adds, however, the reason why it is named both "cock’s spur" and "sanguinaria": specifically, because when placed in the nostrils it makes blood flow, and it has, as he says, a cock’s foot at its tip.

Now, if I were to reveal how well-known this herb is among the common people, and at the same time its common name, I fear I would bring great disgrace upon **Avicenna** <note>the 11th-century Persian physician Ibn Sina</note> and his commentators, who hesitated over a matter well-known even to children. Truly, to hide these things is not so much to spare the ancients as it is to neglect life itself, which, as we said before, is endangered under the authority of Avicenna and his commentators. -> # NICOLÒ LEONICENO # <-

...of herbs, which Pliny knew by their Latin names, he remained ignorant of their Greek nomenclatures. We have already demonstrated Pliny’s ignorance regarding **isatis** and **woad** <note>original: *isatide & glasto*</note>, **pellitory** and **bindweed** <note>original: *elxine & conuoluolo*</note>, **prickly myrtle** and **butcher’s broom** <note>original: *oxymirsine & rusco*</note>, and **French nard** and **celtic valerian** <note>original: *nardo gallica & saliunca*</note> in our other short book published on the errors of Pliny and others.

Because this dispute between myself and Pliny’s defender <note>Leoniceno refers here to his famous intellectual debate with Pandolfo Collenuccio over the reliability of ancient texts</note> arose from the frequent errors found throughout every book of Pliny, and because that defender thought he could fix the mistake here by a single textual correction—specifically by changing the word "darnel" <note>original: *aeram*, referring to a weed often found in grain</note> into "herb" <note>original: *herbam*</note>—I now wish to show this same defender how many other corrections he must devise for Pliny’s text. This is necessary if he truly wishes to root out the error from the entirety of Pliny’s work, which caused our disagreement. Pliny is found to have committed this same error quite frequently, not only regarding herbs and the whole nature of plants, but also concerning animals and metals, as I shall demonstrate briefly across each category.

### PLINY’S ERRORS CONCERNING ANIMALS AND METALS ###

**PLINY**, in Book 20, writes that **black horehound** <note>original: *marrubium nigrum*</note> is called *prasion* <note>Greek: πράσιον, a general term for horehound</note> by the Greeks, though it would have been better if he had written *melan prasion* <note>Greek: μελανπράσιον, literally "black horehound"</note>; for the name *prasion* is a general term applied to both the black and white varieties. Later, in Book 27, he discusses the same black horehound under the name *ballote* <note>Greek: βαλλωτή, stinking horehound</note>, yet he does not realize that the very herb the Romans call black horehound is the one the Greeks call *ballote*. It is proof of his ignorance that Pliny claims in the same passage that the Greeks call *ballote* by another name, "black leek," rather than black horehound. I have also mentioned this error in my other book: Pliny often writes *prasson* <note>Greek: πράσον</note>, meaning **leek**, instead of *prassion*, meaning **horehound**, having been deceived by the similarity of the names.

<meta>This page continues Nicolò Leoniceno’s detailed critique of Pliny the Elder’s botanical errors. Following the previous page’s introduction on how Pliny frequently misidentified plants by failing to recognize their Greek names, Leoniceno now examines specific examples: orache (atriplex) and elder (sambucus). He uses these to argue that Pliny’s Natural History contains internal contradictions caused by a lack of linguistic and botanical precision.</meta>

<page-num>129</page-num>

### ON ANIMALS AND METALS ###

Pliny writes about **orache** <note>original: *atriplice*; likely *Atriplex hortensis* or Saltbush</note> in many places, but especially in Book 20, where he explains its powers and properties. However, Pliny seems to have been unaware that the Greeks call this vegetable **golden-vegetable** <note>original: *chrysolachanon*</note> because of its golden color. This is evident because later, in Book 27, he treats the "golden-vegetable" as a herb entirely different from orache. He goes so far as to assign to it powers that are completely opposite to those he previously attributed to orache. For instance, in Book 20, he reports on the authority of **Pythagoras** <note>The famous Greek philosopher, often cited in ancient medical texts</note> that orache causes **jaundice** <note>original: *morbos regios*; literally "the royal disease," so-called because it required expensive treatments or due to the golden hue of the skin</note> and a pale complexion. Yet, later in Book 27, when discussing the "golden-vegetable," he says there were some who claimed that if this herb were tied to those suffering from jaundice, it could be seen to cure the ailment. **Dioscorides** <note>A 1st-century Greek physician and the most important pharmacological authority of the era</note>, a most weighty authority, testifies to this same effect if the seed of the golden-vegetable is drunk. Truly, the fact that the same herb is meant by the Greeks under the name *chrysolachanon* and by the Latins as *atriplex* is clearly indicated—not only by the authority of Dioscorides asserting the same thing, but also by the color of the orache herb itself, which displays a golden hue. This is clearly why the name "golden-vegetable" was given to it by the Greeks.

<margin>Elder</margin> Pliny places the **Elder** <note>original: *sambucus*</note> among the trees in Book 24, where he explains its primary medicinal effects. Then, in Book 27, he describes this same small tree under the name <margin>Actea</margin> **Actea** <note>original: *actea*; the Greek name for the elder tree, *aktē*</note>. He describes it as having a heavy scent from the flowers, rough and jointed stems, and black seeds similar to soft ivy berries; he claims it grows in shady, rough, and watery places. All these signs point to the elder, especially since Pliny prescribes this same *actea* for the internal diseases of women, just as he does for the root of the elder. Nor will a defender of Pliny be able to respond on his behalf by saying that Pliny understood *actea* to mean **dwarf elder** <note>original: *ebulum*; a smaller, herbaceous relative of the common elder</note>, and thus was not treating the same plant, but two different ones under various names (one Greek, the other Latin) in different passages. One cannot, I say, say this for Pliny, because the Greeks do not call the elder *acten*, but rather they call the dwarf elder **ground-elder** <note>original: *chamæacten*</note>. And these...

# NICOLÒ LEONIČENO #

Indeed, as far as plants are concerned, let what has been said suffice—plants which Pliny seems to have thought were different not only in name but also in their very nature. However, the author of that book titled **The Horn of Plenty** <note>original: *Cornucopia*; likely referring to the work of the humanist Niccolò Perotti</note> is amazed at Pliny—a man of such great learning and authority—who, in the category of animals, made the **rough-foot** <note>original: *dasipodem*; from the Greek *dasypus*</note> distinct from the **hare**, even though, as he says, it is one and the same animal. He is amazed, I say, as one who had not noticed many other similar errors by the same author, even in other matters and not only regarding the hare. He attempts to show with many arguments that the "rough-foot" is not different from the hare, both from the reasoning of their names and from those things which **Aristotle** writes about the "rough-foot" that are consistent with the hare, and also from the common Greek and Latin proverbs concerning both the "rough-foot" and the hare.

All these arguments I—who very gladly defend Pliny’s authority wherever I can—am able to refute by this reasoning: nothing prevents two animals of a very similar genus from being found, to which all the same things that the aforementioned author brings forward might apply because of their natural affinity. For example, the hare and the **rabbit** <note>original: *cuniculum*</note>, the latter of which I think is called the
<margin>The "rough-foot" is the rabbit.</margin>
"rough-foot" by the Greeks. But if Pliny is excused for this error in such a way, he will still be completely liable for another error familiar to him: because he makes mention in his books of both the "rough-foot" and the rabbit as if they were different, even though they are one and the same animal. He does the same regarding the **roe deer** <note>original: *caprea*</note> and the **gazelle** <note>original: *dorcade*</note>, the **bat** <note>original: *uespertilione*</note> and the **nocturnal-flier** <note>original: *nycteride*</note>, the **catfish** <note>original: *siluro*</note> and the **glanis** <note>original: *glani*; a Greek term for a type of catfish</note>, and the **plaice** <note>original: *passere*</note> and the **psitta** <note>original: *psitta*; the Greek name for the same flatfish</note>. He names these animals sometimes in Greek and sometimes in Latin, but he never warns the reader whether they are the same or different, so that he clearly seems to have thought they were not the same.

Just as among metals, Pliny is clearly convicted of having thought that **quicksilver** <note>original: *argentū uiuum*</note> was different from **mercury** <note>original: *hydrargyro*</note>. <margin>The nature of quicksilver.</margin>
...they agree, even when those things which **Pliny** writes concerning the nature of quicksilver <note>original: *argenti uiui*</note>—such as it being a poison to all things, and that it eats away and breaks through all vessels with a dreadful wasting—are likewise reported by Greek authors, and especially **Dioscorides**, regarding **hydrargyrum** <note>original: *hydrargyro*; literally "water-silver"</note>. Therefore, let no one perhaps think that "quicksilver" is the natural form while *hydrargyrum* is the artificial one, and imagine that Pliny used various names for that reason. For as we have said, whether made by art or by nature, it is called by one name—*hydrargyros*—by the Greeks, just as it is named *argentum vivum* (quicksilver) by the Latins. If the defender of Pliny knew how to excuse these and other errors of the same kind—that is, similar to the one we recorded about **darnel** <note>original: *æra*; refers to *Lolium temulentum*</note> and **rye-grass** in our other booklet—he would have done better than he did in his own preface. By turning brass <note>a pun on the Latin *aes/aera* (brass/bronze) and *aera* (darnel)</note> into a weed, I shall confess that he may rightly boast among his fellow citizens and deserves to be crowned with the **civic crown** <note>a military honor in Rome</note> for restoring his fellow citizen to his former dignity. Otherwise, from his defense regarding brass alone, let him know that he has triumphed over only a single straw—if indeed he even triumphed over a straw—which we have previously demonstrated through many arguments against Pliny’s defender to have been wrongly changed into a weed.

Not much different, indeed almost a twin to those errors we recently touched upon, is Pliny's error regarding the **ant-like spider** <note>original: *phalangio myrmecio*</note>, which **Hermolaus** <note>Hermolao Barbaro, a famous 15th-century scholar who "corrected" Pliny</note> thinks happened through a slip of memory. We, however, believe it arose from the same cause 
<margin>Pliny was not sufficiently learned in Greek.</margin>
as the previous ones: namely, Pliny's lack of Greek erudition. Because he did not know what the word *myrmecion* <note>from the Greek *myrmex*, meaning ant</note> signified among the Greeks, he enumerated more types of *phalangium* spiders in Book XXIX than was necessary. For although in the fourth chapter of that same book he had written:
> "the phalangium is unknown to Italy and is of several types; one is similar to an ant, but much smaller, with a reddish head, and so forth:"
yet a few lines below, as if forgetful of what he had previously said, he pointlessly repeated the same type, writing thus: "the *myrmecion* is [similar to] an ant..."

...with a similar head, a black belly, and distinct spots. <margin>Phalangion.</margin>

<margin>Tarantula.</margin>
Arabs call a **rutela** is that kind of spider which is commonly
<margin>Rutela.</margin>
called a **tarantula**, as indicated by many properties which ancient authors handed down concerning *phalangia*, and which we also observe in them in our own age—such as their home in the small caverns of the gaping earth, and the great number of their offspring, which kill the parent once they emerge. Consider also the occurrences that follow a person touched by a tarantula: namely, stupor, a weakening of the knees, and a trembling of the entire body. From this, a proverb even arose: we say of people who cannot stand still in one place that they have been "bitten by a tarantula." <note>original: *à tarantula morsos*</note> I shall pass over other signs, not so well known to everyone, which the ancients recorded regarding the bite of *phalangia*, and which the physicians of our time have learned to be true through the "teacher of experience" <note>original: *experientia magistra*</note> regarding tarantulas. These doctors have observed even more than the ancients concerning the nature of this creeping thing <note>original: *reptilis*; used here generally for a crawling creature like a spider</note>: for instance, that it affects a person with such imaginings as it finds him occupied with at the very moment it bites. Thus it happens that if someone were thinking of himself as a king at the moment he is bitten or struck, he persists in that same thought after the strike; nor could anyone easily persuade him—even if he is a man of humble status—that he does not possess royal dignity. Indeed, I marvel that **Pliny** recorded that this animal, whose bite affects a person in such varied ways, was unknown to Italy in his times—unless someone might suspect that men in the following years were so wicked that they brought this poison from abroad...

Similarly, these same Greeks were the reason that the pain of the "loose intestine" <note>The large intestine or colon</note> was first called **colic**—a name we still use today. Pliny writes that the Emperor **Tiberius** was the first prince to experience this malady in Italy. I believe the same thing happened in the case of the **phalangium** <note>The venomous spider/tarantula discussed on the previous page</note>: namely, that the *meaning* of this word was unknown to Italy in Pliny’s time, rather than the venom or the venomous creature itself.

Indeed, this very point gave me more cause for suspicion than anything else—the ignorance of certain physicians of our own age (or those who flourished a little before it), which once made me an object of ridicule. For a conversation was being held among physicians, of whom I was one (though I was younger than the rest at the time and therefore of less authority), in the presence of a most distinguished and powerful man who had been educated from boyhood in the court of the most illustrious **Alfonso, King of Aragon**. # BY NICOLÒ LEONICENO #

...poisonous <note>original: *venenato*</note> creature which especially infests **Apulia**, commonly named the **tarantula**. While all the other senior physicians who were present asserted that no mention was made of this animal among the ancients, I alone contradicted them. I contended that it was named *phalangion* <note>original: *phalangion*; a Greek term for a type of venomous spider</note> by the ancient Greeks and *rutella* by the Arabic authors. Because of this, I seemed almost to be raving in the eyes of the man I mentioned—a man powerful in status and fortune <note>Likely King Alfonso of Aragon</note>, before whom this dispute was being held—who delivered a verdict against me. He said that he had heard with his own ears the physicians of **King Alfonso of Aragon** asserting that the ancient doctors had left nothing written in their books regarding the tarantula.

Indeed, this assertion by those physicians contains far more error than **Pliny’s** does. While Pliny’s error makes the tarantula unknown only to **Italy** in a previous age, their assertion makes it unknown to all lands. Otherwise, some mention of it would be found among the ancients under some name, whether Greek or foreign; yet they seemed to have utterly denied that it had ever been recorded.

However, certain physicians—even among the more recent ones who left behind treatises written on poisons—do mention *rutellae*, *phalangia*, and furthermore tarantulas. Yet, they do not refer to tarantulas under the chapter <term>On Rutellae</term>, but rather under the chapter <term>On Scorpions</term>. They testify that one kind of scorpion, which they list as the third type, is even called "tarantula" by **Rhazes** <note>original: *Rasi*; the 9th-century Persian physician Al-Razi</note>, but is called *sebel* or *sebegi* by **Avicenna** <note>The famous Persian polymath Ibn Sina</note>.

But, as I said, what is today named the "tarantula" is celebrated among the Greeks by the name *phalangium* and among the Arabs by the name *rutella*. The proof for this is that almost everything the Greeks write regarding *phalangia*, **Avicenna** writes the same regarding *rutellae*. Furthermore, he cites **Galen** writing about the species of *rutellae*, which that same author <note>Galen</note> had actually written regarding the types of *phalangia*. 

But let us return to **Pliny**, from whom we freely make this digression to these famous physicians so that we might show his errors to be much lighter in comparison to those of others—except that to this error of Pliny’s regarding the *phalangium* (which we touched on above), another certainly more serious one can be connected:

### ON ANIMALS AND METALS. 135 ###

In this matter, **Pliny** himself seems to disagree with his own writings. Indeed, in Book 11, when dealing with the various kinds of spiders <note>original: *araneorum*</note>, among which he lists the venomous spiders <note>original: *phalangia*; a Greek term for a type of spider believed to be highly toxic</note> first, he nevertheless considers any mention of them to be superfluous because, as he says, they are so well known. This makes it appear that **Pliny** had forgotten what he said in Book 11, for he later wrote in Book 29 that venomous spiders were unknown to **Italy**.

Someone might perhaps argue that those venomous spiders which **Pliny** describes in this later book as unknown to **Italy** are different from those he categorized among the types of spiders in Book 11. However, this interpretation is contradicted by all the authors who have written on the complete variety of venomous spiders, and it is especially contrary to **Pliny** himself. He mentioned a specific type of venomous spider which is called *myrmecion* <note>original: *myrmecion*; from the Greek for "ant," referring to an ant-like spider</note> in Greek due to its resemblance to ants; he counted this among the creatures unknown to **Italy** in Book 29, yet he equally placed it among the types of spiders in that same book.

Likewise, **Aristotle**, in the eighth book of his *History of Animals*, divides the genera of spiders and venomous spiders under a single classification. Thus, these creatures could not be matters of common knowledge—and therefore not worth mentioning—if the genus of venomous spiders had been unknown to **Italy**, as **Pliny** writes in the cited book.

But now, having left behind the study of herbs and creeping things <note>original: *reptilibus*; in this period, the term "reptile" often included insects, spiders, and any small crawling creature</note>, I come to another dispute. Although it may seem to be merely about names, it nevertheless pertains to two parts of medicine, which the Greeks call <term>anatomy</term> <note>the study of body structure</note> and <term>pathognomy</term> <note>original: *pathognomice*; the study of the specific signs and symptoms that characterize a disease</note>. Regarding these subjects, I could wish that **Hermolaus** <note>Hermolao Barbaro (1454–1493), a famous Venetian scholar who sought to "cleanse" ancient texts of medieval errors</note> had been as well-practiced as he was in the other field concerning the knowledge of herbs.

Nevertheless, I will not lack an excuse for so distinguished a man, just as we previously excused **Pliny** when he erred regarding herbs. We said that it should seem less surprising that **Pliny**—a man most occupied in the administration of the **Roman Republic**—was ignorant of such things, especially since even **Avicenna** <note>The 11th-century Persian "Prince of Physicians," whose Canon of Medicine was the standard textbook in Europe for centuries</note>, who is regarded by the physicians of our age as the prince of medicine, is found to have erred not a little in these matters. Why then should I not be able to say that **Hermolaus**, who was no less...

# NICCOLÒ LEUNICENO #

If, in matters pertaining to medicine, he is rebuked by the "Defender of Pliny" <note>likely referring to a contemporary critic who championed Pliny's authority against Leoniceno's corrections</note> for either holding a false opinion or for foolishly excusing the errors of others, such as regarding the **epiglottis** <note>original: *epiglosse*</note>, the **windpipe** <note>original: *arteria*; in this context, the trachea</note>, and the **gullet** <note>original: *gula*</note>, as well as in the **mesenteric vessels** <note>original: *lactibus*; referring to the "milky" vessels of the digestive system</note>—where **Hermolao** tries to protect **Theodorus Gaza**—or in **ulcers of the eye** <note>original: *argemis*</note> and **white spots on the cornea** <note>original: *albuginitibus*</note>, in **scrofula** <note>original: *strumis*</note>, and many other things: although these topics appear to belong to the medical art, because the dispute is more about names than about the things themselves (being matters of minor concern), I will intentionally leave them undefended.

However, I do not understand why the Defender of **Pliny** thinks **Hermolao** erred regarding the **epiglottis**, the **windpipe**, and the **gullet**. I have found nothing written by him on these matters, neither in his *Plinian Corrections* <note>original: *Plinianis castigationibus*; Hermolao Barbaro's famous work correcting thousands of errors in Pliny's text</note> nor in his notes to **Pope Alexander** <note>Alexander VI</note>. Perhaps the Defender of **Pliny** blames **Hermolao** for being a careless corrector of **Pliny’s** manuscript, because he left uncorrected that passage in Book 11, Chapter 27, where **Pliny** mentions the **epiglottis**, the **windpipe**, and the **gullet** among other parts of the human body. The Defender of **Pliny** thinks he has correctly emended the passage by writing it thus:

> Under [the tongue] is a smaller tongue, which none of the egg-laying animals possess. Its function is twofold, placed between two pipes: the inner of these is called the **windpipe** <note>original: *arteria*</note>, leading to the lungs and the heart. The **epiglottis** <note>original: *epiglossis*</note> covers this during eating, while the breath and the voice pass through it, lest food or drink, straying into the wrong path, should cause choking. The other pipe is on the outside and is called the **gullet** <note>original: *gula*</note>, through which food and drink are swallowed; this extends to the throat <note>original: *stomachum*; here meaning the esophagus</note>, and from there to the belly.

By reading the words of the manuscript in this way, the Defender of **Pliny** believes he has restored the true meaning to **Pliny**. Yet he does not see how much error those very words, even as "corrected," still contain. To say nothing of what we attributed to **Pliny’s** error regarding **darnel and tares** <note>original: *æra ac lolio*; referring to a botanical error</note>, it is not fitting for **Pliny**, a man...

<meta>This page continues Niccolò Leoniceno’s critique of anatomical inaccuracies in classical and contemporary texts. He is specifically targeting a contemporary scholar (the "Defender of Pliny") who has confused the relative positions of the trachea and the esophagus, an error Leoniceno traces back to a misunderstanding of Pliny the Elder.</meta>

### ON ANIMALS AND METALS ###

...it is considered quite Latinate to name the same thing now in Latin and now in Greek in almost the same line. Another error is found in these matters—and indeed a very great one—which even the "Defender of **Pliny**" included in his own work on *Anatomy* <note>original: *Anatomice*; likely referring to Alessandro Benedetti's *Historia corporis humani sive Anatomice*</note>. Thus, he has no room for excuse regarding this error, as he not only appeared to agree with it in his correction of **Pliny**, but also confirmed it in his own original work. In that work, following the example of **Pliny** (or a manuscript of **Pliny** he poorly corrected), he claimed that of the two tubes, the **windpipe** <note>original: *arteriam*; here specifically the trachea</note>—which pertains to the heart and lungs—is the inner one, while the **gullet** <note>original: *gula*</note>—through which food and drink are swallowed—is the outer one.

This is contrary to the arrangement of nature, which made the path for the voice and breath exterior <note>meaning closer to the front of the body</note> and the path for food and drink interior <note>meaning deeper or closer to the spine</note>. This fact can be recognized even in a living human being without dissection: it reveals itself first in the throat, from which the voice and breath proceed, in the anterior [front] part of the neck. However, the words of the "Defender of **Pliny**" in the eighth chapter of his third book indicate that he placed this throat in the posterior [back] part, both in his corrections of **Pliny** and in his *Anatomy*, written in this manner:

> Two small channels meet from the jaws of the mouth; one of these is shorter and more internal, which the **Greeks** call the **trachea** <note>original: *tracheam arteriam*</note> or **pharynx**, and the **Latins** call the **throat** <note>original: *guttur*</note> or the **breathing tube** <note>original: *spiritualem fistulam*</note>. The other, however, is longer and more external, which the **Greeks** call the **esophagus** <note>original: *isophagum*</note> and **stomach** <note>original: *stomachum*; in ancient anatomy, this often referred to the esophagus rather than the organ we call the stomach today</note>, and the **Latins** call the **gullet** <note>original: *gula*</note> or **feeding tube** <note>original: *cibalem fistulam*</note>.

In these words there are several errors, but we will first pursue the most serious one, in which the "Defender of **Pliny**" contradicts himself. For in the book and chapter mentioned, he places the gullet in the anterior part of the neck—otherwise it would not be "external" when compared to the "internal" trachea—unless perhaps he thinks that which is further back and closer to the spine is "external," while that which is in front and faces the chest should be called "internal." No naming convention could be more absurd than this! Later, in the seventeenth chapter of the same book, he writes this regarding the gullet:

> And now an account of the gullet must be given, which holds the posterior place, behind the trachea.

From this statement...

<meta>This page continues Niccolò Leoniceno’s detailed anatomical critique. He is refuting the "Defender of Pliny" (Alessandro Benedetti) regarding the relative positions of the windpipe (trachea) and the gullet (esophagus). Leoniceno argues that his opponent’s corrections of Pliny have created a physical impossibility, and he proposes his own emendation of the ancient text to restore its accuracy.</meta>

# NICCOLÒ LEONICENO #

it follows that the **windpipe** <note>original: *tracheam arteriam*</note> is exterior in comparison to the **gullet** <note>original: *gulæ*</note>, and consequently in the front; yet in his correction of **Pliny**, he made it [the gullet] the front one, and thus [the windpipe] the back one. Thus it happens that the same part of the neck—whether the windpipe or the gullet—is assigned positions that are both inner and outer, posterior and anterior. However, this contradiction appears not only in different chapters, but even in one, namely the eighth chapter of the same book. For near the end of that chapter, the defender of **Pliny** writes these words, speaking of the windpipe:

> It is placed before the gullet, because the heart is located in the front part. <note>original Latin: *Ante gulam poſita est, quia cor in priore parte collocatum est.*</note>

Although this same contradiction may not appear in the words of **Pliny’s** eleventh book as corrected by the defender of **Pliny**, the error is nonetheless not small—indeed, in my judgment, it is very great—if **Pliny** believed that food and drink are swallowed through the front part of the neck, while breath and voice pass through the back. Truly, it must be admitted that he believed this, unless those words are corrected differently than they were by **Pliny’s** defender. Therefore, we—who judge that whenever possible the blame for errors found in **Pliny’s** volumes (whether printed or manuscript) should be cast upon the printers, scribes, and those who poorly correct **Pliny**, rather than ascribed to the author himself—believe this entire passage of **Pliny**, about whose truth we are debating, should be written thus:

> Under it is a smaller tongue called the **epiglottis** <term>epiglossis: a Greek-derived term for the flap of cartilage that covers the windpipe during swallowing</term>; its function is twofold, placed between two pipes. The exterior of these is the **artery** <note>original: *arteria*; here referring to the trachea or windpipe</note> reaching to the lung and the heart; she [the epiglottis] covers this while eating, lest while breath and voice are passing through, food or drink should stray into the wrong path and cause choking. The other is interior, called the **gullet** <note>original: *gula*</note>, through which food and drink are swallowed; this leads to the stomach, and so forth.

By reading **Pliny’s** words in this way, that error is avoided which someone might rightly charge against **Pliny**—naming the same part of the throat now "the smaller tongue" and now "the epiglottis." For in our correction, in which the words "smaller tongue" are followed immediately by...

# ON ANIMALS AND METALS #

We add the other term, called the **epiglottis** <note>original: *epiglossis*. A flap of cartilage at the root of the tongue, which is depressed during swallowing to cover the opening of the windpipe.</note>, not as an affectation of Greek style, but as a clarification of how the "lesser tongue" is named with a single word by the Greeks. This clarification, I say, is frequently used not only by **Pliny** but also by other Latin authors. Furthermore, this removes another very serious error: we might have judged that **Pliny** thought the **windpipe** <note>original: *tracheam arteriam*</note> was located in the back of the neck if he had written—as the words of a poorly corrected manuscript suggest—that this was "interior" while the **gullet** <note>original: *gulam*</note> was "exterior." Our emendation also removes another contradiction in **Pliny’s** words, different from the one we recently charged against **Pliny’s** defender. For if the prohibitive particle "**lest**" <note>original: *ne*</note> is placed before those words "if drink," as **Pliny’s** defender places it in his own emendation, and not earlier in the passage (as we believe it should be read), the following absurdity would result: that the windpipe is covered and open at the same moment in time, since it is covered during dining but opened when the breath and voice are passing through. For when it is covered by the "lesser tongue" <note>the epiglottis</note>, neither voice nor breath can pass through it. This emendation of ours regarding **Pliny's** manuscript in this location is wonderfully confirmed by the author of that book titled *Cornucopia*. This man was renowned for his knowledge not only of words but of many subjects (as the title of his book indicates) and was a particular imitator of **Pliny**, so much so that he can be seen in many places as his paraphraser. On these same matters, he wrote about **Pliny** in this manner: 

<margin>Perotti is a paraphraser of Pliny in many places.</margin>

> “The **artery** <note>original: *arteria*. In ancient anatomy, the windpipe was often called the 'rough artery' because it was believed to carry air.</note> is that which leads to the lung and is covered by the **epiglottis**, which they also call the ‘lesser tongue,’ **lest** <note>original: *ne*</note> if drink or food should stray into the wrong path during a meal while the voice is passing through, it might cause distress. And this [the windpipe] is **exterior**, while the **gullet** <note>original: *gula*</note> is **interior**, through which food and drink are swallowed; this extends to the throat <note>original: *stomachum*</note>, and from there to the belly.”

This learned man saw that if he placed the windpipe on the inside and the gullet on the outside, he would be making a monster out of a man.

Even if he [Pliny’s defender] were to place the adverb of prohibition **"lest"** <note>original: *ne*</note> in the same order as he did, he would still be attempting something impossible—namely, that men could speak while the passage from the **epiglottis** <note>original: *epiglossis*</note>, which leads to the lung, is covered. Indeed, learned physicians and even philosophers, who are not ignorant of how an animal produces sound, know the impossibility of this thing. In this way, I and the author of the ***Cornucopia*** <note>Niccolò Perotti (1429–1480), whose work *Cornu Copiae* was a massive commentary on Martial and a standard reference for Latin usage.</note> have freed **Pliny** from such gross errors, to which Pliny’s defender had made him liable. Would that we were able to emend many other errors in the same book and the same chapter so easily, so that the fault might be attributed more to the scribes than to the author himself. 

But since we frankly confess that we do not know how to do this, and since many of these errors pertain to **anatomy** <note>original: *anatomicen*</note>, both of the human body and of other animals, it pleased me to test the wit of Pliny’s defender—a man who not infrequently boasts of his own anatomical knowledge—to see if he himself knows how to defend Pliny in those matters which will be noted by us, even in those things which he has taken under his own protection. These excerpts will be taken from the same eleventh book and the same thirty-seventh chapter <note>Referring to Pliny the Elder’s *Natural History*, Book 11, Chapter 37.</note>, in which Pliny speaks of the **windpipe** <note>original: *arteria*; in this context, the *arteria aspera* or trachea.</note>, the **epiglottis** <note>original: *epigloffe*</note>, and the **gullet** <note>original: *gula*; the esophagus.</note>. This is so that no one might perhaps suspect that we wish to wander afield, diligently searching for more of this author’s errors from various books of Pliny, which we might pile one on top of the other. 

Even if we had striven to do that, we would not have done it with ill will toward **Pliny**, but rather with good intent, so that we might incite Pliny’s defender to devise other emendations for the Plinian codex which would better vindicate the author himself from errors. But these present examples will suffice, from which a prudent reader will judge how much labor we could have prepared for Pliny’s defender if we had wished to inquire not into one chapter of a single book, but into many chapters of many books, and had wished to leave nothing untouched or undiscussed.

<meta>This page continues Niccolò Leoniceno’s critique of Pliny the Elder’s *Natural History*, shifting focus from the anatomy of the throat to the nature and attachment of animal horns. ### ON ANIMALS AND METALS

He speaks of the horns of animals, saying that in the herds of **Phrygia** <note>A region in central Asia Minor, modern-day Turkey.</note> these are movable like ears; then, a few lines later, he writes the following concerning these same horns: "In other animals, they adhere to the bones; in **deer** <note>original: *ceruorum*</note> alone, they grow from the skin." But let **Pliny's defender** <note>Likely referring to the scholar Hermolao Barbaro, who had recently published a massive volume of "corrections" to Pliny's text.</note> answer on Pliny’s behalf: in what way will the horns in Phrygian herds have the mobility of ears, unless in these animals—just as in deer—they grow from the skin? For they cannot originate from the flesh beneath the skin, since **Aristotle** <note>The Greek philosopher (384–322 BC) whose works on biology remained the standard for nearly two millennia.</note> is the authority in the third book of his *History of Animals* who states that the skin covers the head with no intervening flesh.

For this reason, it remains that they must originate from the bones of the head, and because of the continuity and solidity of that origin, they should maintain the same immobility as the bones themselves. Therefore, if horns grow from the skin only in deer, as Pliny seems to believe, then only in these—and not in the Phrygian herds—will they be movable like ears.

Indeed, Aristotle, in the third book of the *History of Animals*, proves that horns adhere to the skin rather than to the bone by this argument: because in Phrygia and elsewhere, there are **oxen** <note>original: *boues*</note> that move their horns just as they do their ears. In that same passage, he shows that the horns of deer do not differ from others because they grow from the skin (while in other horned animals they grow from the bones of the head), but rather for this reason: that most horns are **hollow** <note>original: *caua*</note> for the most part starting from the root, insofar as they surround a bone that grows from the head and is inserted into the hollow horn, filling it entirely. Nevertheless, they end in a solid point and consist of a simple material at the very tip. In deer alone, the horns are entirely solid and spread out into branches.

For Aristotle had clearly taught in the second book of his *History of Animals* that the hollow part of the horns in other animals grows from the skin, and he confirmed this with the example of oxen. Aristotle repeats this same nature of horns and the differences between animal types in the third book of ***On the Parts of Animals*** <note>One of Aristotle's primary biological texts focusing on the "why" of animal structures.</note> with these words: "In deer alone are the horns entirely solid and shed, both for the sake of utility—so that they may be relieved of the burden—and by necessity to some extent because of the weight..."

Now, from these words and others cited a little above from *Aristotle’s History of Animals*, it is easily seen that the horns of other animals, as well as those of **deer** <note>original: *ceruorum*</note>, adhere to the skin rather than to the bones. ...this same **Aristotle** <note>Aristotle (384–322 BC), the Greek philosopher whose biological works were foundational to Renaissance science.</note> says in the second book of his *History of Animals*.

Shortly thereafter, in the second book of *On the Parts of Animals*, he provided a certain general explanation. Therefore, **camels** <note>original: *cameli*</note> are not the only ones among the non-horned animals to have teeth on only one side <note>Referring to the lack of upper incisors, a trait common to many ruminants</note>, since **female deer** <note>original: *ceruæ*</note> are also not horned and likewise lack upper teeth.

If someone were to say that **Pliny** <note>Gaius Plinius Secundus (AD 23–79), author of the *Natural History*.</note> meant males and not females, and therefore excepted only camels, let them remember that many animals of both the female and male sex lack horns. Thus Pliny, even though he wrote "camels alone," included female camels under that exception; for as the grammarians say, the masculine gender encompasses the feminine. Since both females and males are included under the category of "non-horned," he who excludes one category must exclude the other.

For this reason, Pliny says "from those things which are not horned" <note>original: *ex hijs quæ non sunt cornigera*</note>, rather than "from those males who are not horned" <note>original: *ex hijs qui non sunt cornigeri*</note>, so that he might signify both natures by using a word of the neuter gender. This refers to females lacking horns—such as both deer and camels—and camels, whom alone Pliny writes lack teeth among the non-horned animals. He seems to have forgotten what he had previously discussed regarding female deer, when he did not hesitate to refute **Aristotle** using them as an argument. 

Aristotle had provided a reason why no horned animal has teeth on both jaws: that the material for the upper teeth, which they lack, is instead consumed to grow the horns. Pliny, however, says: "Those who think"—referring to the front teeth of the upper jaw, for he was speaking of these—"that they are consumed by the horns, are easily refuted by the nature of female deer, which have no teeth (just like the males) and yet have no horns." 

However, it would have been more proper for Pliny to think more soundly regarding the **Prince of Philosophers** <note>A traditional Renaissance title for Aristotle.</note>, and not to pronounce that he could be so easily refuted—especially on a matter where Aristotle himself raises the objection against himself and provides a satisfying solution in the book...

> ...and in the second book of *On the Parts of Animals*, where he writes: "The reason why **female deer** <note>original: *cervae*</note> lack horns, although they have the same teeth as the males, is that the nature of both sexes is [potentially] horned; but horns have been denied to the females because they are not truly useful even to the males—though males are less burdened by them thanks to their superior strength."

Either **Pliny** <note>Gaius Plinius Secundus (AD 23–79), Roman author of the *Natural History*.</note> did not see these words of **Aristotle** <note>Aristotle (384–322 BC), the Greek philosopher whose biological works were foundational to science in the Renaissance.</note>, or he pretended not to have seen them, so that while he wished to appear to have easily refuted Aristotle, it would not also become obvious to his readers that the greatest philosopher could be easily defended by his own words, rather than by those of another. Therefore, let any defender of Pliny choose in this matter which fault he would rather attribute to him: either negligence, for not having read all of Aristotle’s books on the nature of animals; or unfairness, for having sought to condemn—without a proper hearing—the very man he admits was his teacher in the recording of animal history. 

Pliny pronounced him proven wrong by the argument concerning deer, yet he failed to refute the reasoning Aristotle himself had provided regarding those same deer, should anyone—as Pliny indeed does—wish to raise them as an objection. Furthermore, Pliny writes in the same part of the book and chapter that **cloven-hoofed animals** <note>original: *bisulcis*</note> have two horns. If this statement is taken as a universal rule, it is not entirely true; for **swine** belong to the category of cloven-hoofed animals, and yet they possess no horns. 

Therefore, Aristotle wrote more accurately concerning these same animals: "The greatest part of horned animals are cloven-hoofed." Nor do all cloven-hoofed animals, if they are horned, possess two horns: for the **oryx** <note>A type of large antelope with long, straight horns, often mentioned in ancient natural histories.</note>—as Pliny himself admits in the following passages—is a cloven-hoofed animal, and yet it has only a single horn. Thus, in this place where he says nature bestowed two horns upon cloven-hoofed animals, he ought to have excepted the oryx, which is armed with only one horn—just as in almost the same line he had excepted the **Indian ass** <note>Ancient writers often used this term to describe the rhinoceros or a unicorn-like creature.</note>, which alone among the <term>solid-hoofed animals</term> <note>original: *solipedes*; animals like horses or donkeys that have a single, undivided hoof.</note> has a single horn.

<header>NICCOLÒ LEONICENO</header>

...however, **Aristotle** <note>Aristotle (384–322 BC), the Greek philosopher and scientist.</note> judged [the ostrich] to be of a dual nature, relating it no more to the birds than to the quadrupeds; indeed, perhaps more to the quadrupeds, because he speaks of its upper **eyelid** <note>original: *palpebra*</note> as a quadruped has. Here, I say, the error—if it should even be called an error—can easily be forgiven in **Pliny** <note>Gaius Plinius Secundus (AD 23–79), author of the *Natural History*.</note>, since there is another more serious error in Aristotle himself regarding these same eyelids or **eyelashes** <term>cilium</term> <note>Leoniceno distinguishes between the eyelid (palpebra) and the hair on the eyelid (cilium).</note> of animals, in which Aristotle seems to contradict himself. For in Book II of *On the Parts of Animals*, with **Theodore Gaza** as translator <note>Theodore Gaza (c. 1398–1475) was a leading Greek scholar whose Latin translations of Aristotle were standard in the Renaissance.</note>, he writes these words:

> » And among all creatures that have hair, man alone has eyelashes <note>original: *cilium*</note> on both eyelids.

This author writes the opposite here in Book II of the *History of Animals* in these words:

> » Although other quadrupeds do not have eyelashes on both eyelids, **monkeys** <note>original: *simiae*</note> do have them, though they are very thin, and longer especially on the lower one.

Therefore, since monkeys have hair on the rest of the body, and also on both eyelids as Aristotle writes in this place, but elsewhere—specifically in Book II of *On the Parts of Animals*—he writes that among all hairy creatures only man has eyelashes on both eyelids, he clearly contradicts himself. Let the Greek grammarian resolve this contradiction in Aristotle's words, while preserving Theodore Gaza's interpretation; or if he cannot do this, let him patiently allow me to sometimes differ from that same interpretation, so that I may restore the true meaning to Aristotle, the prince of philosophers. Nor should he take it so poorly if I have written that the good Theodore occasionally **nods** <note>original: *dormitare*, literally "to sleep." This is a reference to the Roman poet Horace’s famous line, *quandoque bonus dormitat Homerus*—"even the good Homer sometimes nods."</note> in his translations, just as **Horace** <note>Quintus Horatius Flaccus (65–8 BC), Roman lyric poet.</note>, the leader of poets, wrote the same words regarding **Homer**, and it is nevertheless tolerated by all learned men. 

Who thinks more highly or better of Pliny than **Hermolaus**? <note>Hermolaus Barbarus (1454–1493), a Venetian scholar famous for his *Castigationes Plinianae* (Corrections of Pliny), which identified thousands of errors in the *Natural History*.</note> Whose reputation he admits can in no way be shaken, and those to whom Pliny does not appeal, he considers clearly unlearned. Yet in his work *Corrections of Pliny*, in the preface of which he writes those words about Pliny, he frequently says that the same Pliny **hallucinates**...

But let these things be said in passing against the grammarians, both Latin and Greek, some of whom have striven to make gods out of **Pliny** and others out of **Theodore**. I am surprised that a serious physician and philosopher, a supporter of Pliny, fell so easily into their opinion. ...or when leaves fall from trees; the latter is called "leaf-shedding," <note>original: *defrondescere*</note> the former "feather-shedding," <note>original: *depennescere*</note> but it is not called "going bald." <note>original: *calvescere*</note> This is why **Aristotle**, <note>The influential Greek philosopher (384–322 BC) whose works on natural history were foundational to Renaissance science.</note> speaking of a similar condition in the **ostrich** <note>original: *struthiocameli*</note> in the fourth book of *On the Parts of Animals*, indicated that it is "smooth" <note>original: *glabrum*</note> on its head and upper neck, but not "bald." Leoniceno is famous for pointing out Pliny's errors.</note> writes a little further on in this manner:

> "All animals that have blood also have a brain; likewise those in the sea which we call 'soft-bodied' <note>original: *mollia*; referring to cephalopods like octopuses.</note>, such as the **polyp**." <note>An ancient term for an octopus.</note>

However, Aristotle—from whom Pliny translated this entire history of the parts of animals, though sometimes not faithfully enough—did not attribute a brain to the polyp and other bloodless creatures, but rather something "proportional" to a brain. Indeed, these are the words of the same author in the second book of *On the Parts of Animals*:

> "Since all things require a counter-balance through which they achieve a middle state—for essence and reason consist in this, and not in either extreme placed by itself—nature fashioned the brain as a counterpart to the seat and heat of the heart. For this reason, that part is joined to animals, possessing a nature common to both water and earth. Because of this, all creatures endowed with blood have a brain; of the others, almost none have one except by proportion, such as the polyp; for that whole genus possesses little heat due to its lack of blood. Therefore, the brain moderates the heat and boiling of the heart and brings it to a proper temperament."

From these words of Aristotle, it is easily established that the soft-bodied creatures, such as the polyps found in the sea, do not have a brain because they lack blood and therefore lack the "boiling" of a heart. Otherwise, nature would have fashioned something superfluous in them, which is considered absurd by all who study philosophy. Furthermore, it matters greatly whether one says a brain is present in a bloodless animal, or merely something proportional to it—just as fish have bones or spines which, according to Aristotle, are proportional to bones; whence...

Although **Aristotle**, in the second book of *On the Parts of Animals*, provides the same reason as Pliny—namely, that dolphins consist of bones rather than spines because they belong to the class of live-bearers <note>original: *uiuiparorũ*; animals that give birth to live young rather than laying eggs.</note>—he nevertheless immediately adds the reason why all cartilaginous creatures have a spine made of cartilage: because their movement is more supple. Therefore, the supporting structure needed to be not rigid, but soft. This is a reason Pliny also ought to have provided, lest he seem to contradict himself without any excuse—as he clearly does in the eighth book. There, he writes that among those lacking hair, only dolphins and **vipers** give birth to live animals; and yet Pliny (along with Aristotle, as we just mentioned) believes that fish of the cartilaginous kind, which are also not covered in hair, do the same.

But, so that we do not stray from our intended order, let us return to the **brain**, which Pliny believes animals lack if they are thought not to sleep. However, as **Aristotle** writes in his book *On the Parts of Animals*, there are many creatures that do not have a brain and yet sleep anyway, because they possess a "proportional" equivalent <note>Aristotle argued that while some lower animals lack a complex brain, they have a functionally equivalent organ or substance that allows for rest.</note>.

From this, one might finally prove that the brain differs from marrow, whose nature is a combination of fire and air, because its fattiness...

and animal fat <note>original: *assungia*, referring to soft animal fat or lard</note> indicate. **Pliny** says that most skilled authors record a vein extending from the eyes to the brain. This is not far from the truth, since both the nerves—which bring the power of sensation to the eyes—and the veins—which bring nourishment—reach those same eyes. However, **Pliny** also states his belief that a vein likewise descends from the eyes to the stomach. His evidence for this is that no eye can be torn out without a reaction <note>original: *redundatione*, suggesting a surging of fluid or nausea</note> in the stomach. Yet, this testifies to nothing other than the shared sensation <note>original: *patiendi consensum*; the physiological idea that organs are linked in their reactions</note> that exists between both members and the brain, through the nerves emerging from that same brain—a concept the Greeks call by the single word <term>sympathy</term> <note>original: *sympathiam*; in ancient medicine, this refers to the "interconnectedness" of the body where one part is affected by another.</note>.

Since we previously mentioned the eyelids of the **ostrich**, the planned order now requires that we reveal the remaining errors of **Pliny** regarding that same small part of the body. In order for all these things to appear more clearly—namely, what **Pliny** understands by "eyelids" <note>original: *genas*, which usually means "cheeks" but which Pliny uses for the lids themselves</note> and what he understands by "eyelashes" <note>original: *palpebras*</note>—let us declare it using no other words than **Pliny’s** own, which are read both in this place and elsewhere. **Pliny** calls those small membranes that cover the eyes "eyelids" [*genas*], which the Greeks call <term>blephara</term> <note>original: *βλέφαρα*</note>. **Theodore** <note>Theodore Gaza (c. 1398–1475), a Greek scholar whose translations of Aristotle's biological works were standard in the Renaissance.</note>, in his translation of **Aristotle's** *On Animals*, translates this as *palpebras*. Such a meaning for this word in **Pliny** is indicated by **Pliny’s** own words written in this very passage:

> Fish and insects do not have eyelids [*genas*], nor do they cover their eyes; a membrane as transparent as glass is stretched over them all. Also in the tenth book, where he discusses the sleep of aquatic animals, he writes in this manner: Even those who doubt other things believe that they do sleep; this is not evidenced by their eyes, because they do not have eyelids [*genas*].

**Pliny**, however, gives the name "eyelashes" [*palpebras*] to the hairs arising from the edges of the eyelids. These, as he himself says, nature had given to humans as a kind of palisade for sight, and a prominent fortification against attacking insects or other things falling in by chance. Women, however—so great is the desire for beauty—dye them. These lashes [*pal-*] also fall out...

I would have wished for these and other passages of **Pliny**, in which he seems most obviously to contradict himself, to have been corrected by a "patron" of Pliny. This would prevent someone—after the diligence of so many and such great men in correcting the manuscripts of **Pliny**—from having to undertake the same work anew, lest they seem to labor in vain, as if trying to reshape a statue of **Minerva** just to change her sandals, or repainting a picture by **Apelles** <note>A famous painter of ancient Greece</note> from scratch just to supply the straps for a few sandals. <note>original: *setarum*</note>. 

Pliny writes this of **elephants** in his eighth book, agreeing indeed with **Aristotle**, who in the second book of his *History of Animals* writes that the elephant is the least hairy <note>original: *hirtum*</note> among the genus of quadrupeds. But let us return to the cheeks <term>genas: In this context, Leoniceno and Pliny use this term to refer to the eyelids or the margins of the eye where the lashes grow.</term> and eyelashes of animals, regarding which I could wish Pliny could be defended as easily, lest he seem to write things contrary both to Aristotle and to common sense. This second statement will hold true if only monkeys are excepted, which are the only quadrupeds (as Pliny himself later teaches) that have eyelashes also on the lower lid. However, the things Pliny adds immediately after these words have no refuge of exception or other excuse. For he says that birds have eyelashes only on the lower lid, as do those with soft skin like snakes, and egg-laying quadrupeds like lizards; but that the **ostrich** <note>original: *struthiocamelo*</note> has them on both sides, like a human. Both observation and reason find all these claims to be false. For birds do not have hair on the lower lid, nor do snakes, nor lizards; nor does the ostrich have anything worth mentioning on both lids, but rather like a quadruped (as we noted before) only on the upper lid. All the rest of what Pliny adds is equally false: not even the lids themselves are present in all...

...therefore, blinking does not occur in those animals which bring forth live young. For Aristotle would have written more truthfully concerning these matters, just as he did in the second book of *The Generation of Animals*:

> The genus of humans, birds, and quadrupeds, both those that bear live young <term>viviparous: animals that give birth to live young rather than laying eggs.</term> and those that lay eggs <term>oviparous: egg-laying animals.</term>, cover their eyes for the sake of protecting their sight, but they do so in different ways. For those that bring forth live young have a double cheek <note>original: *genam*; here referring to the eyelids.</note> and are accustomed to blink with both. Birds, both the lighter and the heavier kinds, and egg-laying quadrupeds blink with the lower cheek; however, birds also blink <note>original: *nictantur*; specifically referring to the use of the nictitating membrane or "third eyelid."</note> from the corners of the eye by means of a membrane that passes over it.

At this point, I would wish the reader to be advised that the word *blepharon* <note>original: *βλέφαρον*</note>, which Theodorus <note>Theodore Gaza, a 15th-century scholar famous for translating Aristotle from Greek into Latin.</note> translates as "eyelid" <note>original: *palpebra*</note>, I interpret—following the imitation of Pliny—as "cheek" <note>original: *gena*</note>. But if anyone should apply those words of Pliny, "those which generate live animals," to the following clause, so that the meaning becomes: "those which generate live animals and the heavier birds blink with the lower cheek," then Pliny would still not be truthful in every respect, nor would he be in agreement with Aristotle on these same matters. For Aristotle, as is apparent from his words quoted just a moment ago, maintained that those which bring forth live young blink with both cheeks, while the heavier birds use only one—namely, the lower. The outer

<margin>The eyelash or eyelid margin.</margin>
edge of the upper cheek is called the "cilium" <note>original: *cilium*; here meaning the eyelash or the lid's edge.</note> by the ancients, as Pliny records, and he notes that if it is divided by some wound, it does not grow back together. Aristotle, however, writes that the same thing happens not only to the extreme edge of the upper cheek, but to the entire cheek—and equally to the lower as to the upper—just as it does to the jaw and the foreskin; for these parts, once wounded, do not heal into a solid whole.

<margin>The regrowth of canine teeth.</margin>
Pliny is the sole authority for the claim that canine teeth, if lost by some accident, never grow back; for I have read no one else who asserts the same thing, as far as I can remember. Aristotle, certainly, in the second book of his *History of Animals*, records that these same teeth are changed <note>meaning they are replaced as "baby teeth" by "adult teeth."</note> in humans, in dogs, and also in other beasts, but that the molar teeth <note>original: *maxillares*</note> are changed in no animal. Therefore, it would be more reasonable to believe this regarding the molars—that if lost by accident, they do not regenerate—rather than regarding the canines. In the same book, Aristotle writes that the seal <note>original: *vitulum marinum*; literally "sea-calf."</note> has a split tongue, while Pliny says it is double. Whether they both say the same thing...

...let the learned decide what they think: In this they certainly disagree, because Pliny asserts as a true fact that hares around Briletum and Tharnon, and in the Chersonese <note>The Gallipoli Peninsula.</note> near the Propontis <note>The Sea of Marmara.</note>, have two livers. Aristotle, however, thinks it is an error of those who, looking at the size, believe there are two livers when there is only one. Pliny also writes not much further down that in that membrane which the Greeks call *phrenas* and *diaphragma*, and the Latins call the *septum* <term>diaphragm: the muscular partition separating the chest from the abdomen.</term>—which is not actually a membrane but rather a muscle, as Galen the most noble physician feels—there is no flesh. The logic of its own nature indicates this is equally false, since a muscle is nothing other than flesh interwoven with nerves <note>original: *neruis*; in this period, the term could refer to nerves, tendons, or sinews.</note>.
<margin>What a muscle is.</margin>
Aristotle, moreover, where he speaks of this part of the human being, namely in the second book of *The Parts of Animals*, clearly indicates that it is fleshy, writing thus:

> >> This septum, or belt, is joined to the ribs at its fleshier and stronger part, but is more membranous in the middle. For in this way it is better suited for strength and as a shield against the heat rising up; that this is, as it were, the source of the matter is said to be proven by those things which happen for the most part: for when, because of their proximity, they have drawn in hot humor, they immediately and plainly disturb the sense of the mind, for which reason they are called *phrenes* <note>Greek: *φρένες*; the ancients believed the diaphragm was the seat of the mind or closely connected to it, hence the word "frenzy" or "phrenic nerve."</note>, as if they were participants in prudence. Yet they are in no way participants, but they are close to those things which possess that power, and from here they reveal the changing of the mind. For this reason they are thin in their middle part, not only out of necessity—because since they are fleshy in the part moved toward the ribs, they must be fleshier there—but so that they might receive less vapor; for if they consisted of fuller flesh, they would both possess and attract a great deal of vapor.

From these words of Aristotle, I think it is clear to everyone that the septum, or *phrenes*, is fleshy, even though they are thinner in their middle part and have less flesh. # NICOLÒ LEONICENO #

[Aristo]tle asserts that [the diaphragm] itself has no share in reason, yet it is called *phrenas* <term>phrenes: a Greek term for the diaphragm, from which we get words like "phrenic nerve"; it shares a root with the word for "mind" or "intellect."</term> by the Greeks because it is located near those parts which do possess that power. Therefore, according to Aristotle, the refinement of the mind is attributed to the heart; however, because of its proximity to the septum <term>septum transversum: another name for the diaphragm.</term>, this name is given to the partition itself by the Greeks. I also believe readers should be warned in this section that nothing has been changed from the translation by Theodore <note>Theodore Gaza (c. 1398–1475), a foundational translator of Aristotle from Greek into Latin.</note> in the words recently cited, except that for the word *hymenodesteron* <note>original: ὑμενοδέστερον</note> in Aristotle’s text, we have used the Latin *membranosius*, which means "more like a membrane," or "closest to the nature of a membrane." This interpretation seemed more faithful to us; otherwise, if we said (as Theodore translated) that the diaphragm consisted of a "thinner membrane" in its middle part, we would make Aristotle openly contradict himself. For he proves that the entire diaphragm is necessarily fleshy—which is also evident from dissections—even though the parts moved toward the ribs are fleshier. And a little later, where he writes that all the internal organs are enclosed in membranes, he teaches that the nature of membranes is such that they are entirely devoid of flesh. However, this contradiction is removed if we grant that the diaphragm is fleshier in some parts and more membranous in others, since this is the nature of all muscles: they are not equally fleshy in every part, but are thinner and more like a membrane in some places, and fleshier in others. Moreover, it is of no small importance whether one says a part of our body *is* a membrane, or merely has a *resemblance* to a membrane. Therefore, the diaphragm is not a membrane, as Pliny incorrectly names it, but is similar to a membrane in one specific part of itself.

In the aforementioned book, when discussing aquatic creatures that lack blood, Aristotle asserts that the parts pertaining to food—in which number the stomach is included—are necessarily present in all such aquatic creatures. Indeed, regarding the octopus and the cuttlefish, which Pliny brings forward as examples of bloodless animals lacking a stomach, Aristotle writes in that very place:

> The esophagus, or gullet, starting from the mouth, is quite long in the soft-bodied creatures <term>mollibus: refers to "mollusks," literally "soft ones."</term>; a crop follows it, just as in birds, then the stomach is joined to it, and the intestine, attached to the stomach, extends simply all the way to the exit.

But here indeed Pliny has gone astray, because he denied the stomach to the entire class of aquatic creatures, even though nature granted it to them as a necessity; yet for the elephant, he granted more stomachs than either Aristotle or nature itself, the mother of all things, allowed. For Pliny reports that the elephant has four stomachs,

Stomachs of the elephant.
