whereas Aristotle writes that the intestine in elephants is so winding that they *seem* to have four stomachs. Therefore, since it matters quite a bit whether something actually *is* or only *seems to be*, Pliny multiplied the stomachs in elephants by the same error with which he also multiplied the livers in hares. 

Pliny is also the authority for the claim that fat emerges from the middle of each kidney, except in the "sea calf" <term>vitulo marino: the seal.</term>. Aristotle, however, describes the kidneys as being entirely covered in fat, and says that not fat, but a certain cavity, emerges from the middle of each kidney—he himself also making an exception for the seal, as Pliny did.

Pliny takes all these points about the viper from Book VI of Aristotle’s *On the Generation of Animals*, but with little accuracy. For as to Pliny saying that the viper hatches young, this is true and in agreement with Aristotle, who maintains that the viper is the only one among all types of serpents that gives birth to a live animal. However, his claim that it does this on the third day does not agree with Aristotle, who attributes this three-day period not to the delivery of the young outside the womb, but rather to the bursting of the membranes after they have been hatched while still enclosed in them, as the more accurate translation by <term>Theodore: referring to Theodore Gaza (c. 1398–1475), a Greek scholar whose Latin translations of Aristotle were prized for their precision compared to older medieval versions.</term> shows, which goes like this:

> The viper is the only one of the serpents that produces a live animal, although it first produces <note>original: *pererit*—the text breaks here mid-word</note> eggs within itself...

From these, not only *Pliny* but even *Aristotle* is dragged into a contradiction, which is as follows: 

If the viper is the only serpent that brings forth a live animal <note>original: *animal edit*</note>, since it first produces eggs within itself, as *Aristotle* says—or if it is the only land animal that produces eggs internally and then hatches the young, as *Pliny* claims—yet the **marassus** <note>A local name for a type of snake, likely a variety of viper or asp common in Italy.</note>, or serpent, which is commonly called the **scurtio** <note>A regional Italian term for a venomous snake, possibly derived from "scorzone."</note> by another name, does this very same thing: namely, it first produces eggs within the womb, then sends the live animal out into the light, as people testify to have seen with their own eyes a thousand times over; it follows necessarily that the **marassus** and the viper are the same species of serpent, called by different names in the common tongue among different nations. 

The first words of both *Aristotle* and *Pliny* demonstrate this; however, their final words prove the opposite, in this manner: "The viper gives birth to young one by one on successive days, roughly twenty in number." But the **marassus** gives birth to twenty or even more young, but not one by one on successive days; rather, it gives birth to them all on a single day, as has frequently been observed. Therefore, the viper and the **marassus** are not the same species of serpent. This **syllogism** <note>A form of logical reasoning where a conclusion is reached from two premises.</note> is constructed in the **second figure** <note>In formal logic, a specific arrangement of terms used here to prove a distinction between two things based on differing properties.</note>. Let the defender of *Pliny* strive to protect *Pliny* from this contradiction as easily as we have cleared the "Prince of Philosophers" <note>Aristotle.</note> from the suspicion of this most serious error. For the viper does not have a double womb <note>original: *uuluam*—here referring to the uterus</note>, but rather only one; just as in other animals that produce eggs internally but give birth to a live animal externally <note>A reproductive method known today as ovoviviparity.</note>, that part where the eggs are contained is attached below the loins, and the opening is located above the intestines, as **Aristotle** is a most abundant witness both in his books *On the Parts of Animals* and also *On the Generation of Animals* in many other places. 

But if by a "double womb" Pliny implies one that is bifid <note>split into two parts</note> or bipartite, this will not be a feature peculiar to vipers and animals of a similar nature, but rather common to all others that generate both internally and externally. Pliny even affirms this in this same passage regarding cows and women. For he says that women have twin cavities <note>original: *geminos sinus*</note> on both sides, but that pregnant cows carry only in the right cavity, even when they are carrying twins. 

Pliny also notes the difference between suet <note>original: *sebum*—hard animal fat found in ruminants</note> and fat <note>original: *adipem*—softer fat</note> poorly, and contrary to Aristotle. For Pliny writes that the latter [fat] is congealed and brittle when cooled, and always at the edge of the flesh. However, Aristotle writes these things about suet, not about fat, in the third book of the *History of Animals* and the second book of *On the Parts of Animals*.

<margin>In which animals fat is found in the eyes.</margin>

> The constitution of the pupil is common to all animals: for in all those that possess this part and do not have hard eyes, it consists of fat <note>original: *adipe*</note>.

For no one doubts that birds are counted among those endowed with blood, not among the bloodless animals. Therefore, since blood (according to the aforementioned book by **Aristotle**) has no other containers besides the heart and the veins, if birds have blood, as sight demonstrates, and since blood cannot exist without a vein, birds will necessarily have veins as well. 

These are errors partly of the manuscript <note>original: *codicis*</note> and partly of the author himself, which we have decided should be gathered from just one chapter of a single book, so that we might warn **Pliny’s** defender that he has boasted in vain among his fellow citizens—as if, by a single defense of **Pliny** in one passage against us, the author was liberated from all suspicion of error. <meta>This page continues Nicolò Leoniceno’s philological and anatomical critique of Pliny the Elder. Having previously discussed botanical errors regarding the plant "lolium," Leoniceno here shifts to a detailed argument about anatomical nomenclature, specifically the distinction between the pharynx, larynx, and trachea, using authorities like Galen, Hippocrates, and Theodore Gaza to correct contemporary misunderstandings.</meta>

### ON ANIMALS AND METALS ###

> ...certainly, with no swelling existing in the pharynx—that is, the throat—for

so even **Theodorus** <note>Theodore Gaza (c. 1398–1475), a Greek scholar and translator of Aristotle and Galen whose Latin versions were standard in the Renaissance</note> translates this word. The head of the artery <note>term: *trachea arteria* — literally "the rough artery," the ancient name for the windpipe, distinguished from the "smooth" arteries that carry blood</note> is called the **larynx** by the Greeks—that is, the throat. Indeed, **Theodorus** likewise names the larynx in Latin as the *guttur* [throat]. But that space which is before the larynx and the esophagus—that is, the throat and the gullet—is properly named the **pharynx** by those same Greeks. In this sense, **Galen** <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–c. 216 AD), the most influential physician of antiquity whose works dominated Western medicine for centuries</note> also says this name was used by **Homer**, where the same **Homer** says that wine and fragments of human flesh erupted through the *pharynx* of the **Cyclops** <note>A reference to Book 9 of the *Odyssey*, describing the drunken Polyphemus vomiting</note>. Therefore, let the defender of **Pliny** take care, lest while he condemns the opinion of **Plato** (who believed that drink flows down through the windpipe to the lungs), he makes Homer's description far more absurd, if he wanted not only drink but even food to be vomited by the **Cyclops** through the *pharynx*—if he intends that word to be named by the Greeks as the windpipe, as the defender of **Pliny** would have it. **Galen** also, in Book IV of *On Affected Parts* (which is titled *On Interior Parts* among the Latins), declares what he understands by the pharynx in these words:

> "But I name the **pharynx** the interior space of the mouth, to which the end of the gullet and throat reaches."

Nor does **Galen** understand anything else by the pharynx when he says in Book VII of *On the Utility of Parts* that the windpipe is joined to the pharynx through the larynx. Although later the same **Galen** writes near the beginning of Book VIII of the same treatise that the windpipe is named "pharynx" equivocally <note>original: *equiuoce* — meaning the word is used loosely or has a double meaning</note> with that space which is before the larynx. But here we are disputing the proper and common meaning of the word **pharynx**. # THE WRITINGS OF NICOLÒ LEONICENO #

> ...signifies in this place, he declares it thus: By the *cervix* [nape], the neck is understood; by the **pharynx**, however, is understood that space which presents itself to the eyes if the mouth is opened and the tongue is pressed down, in which two openings are contained: one for the stomach <note>original: *stomachus* — in this context, the esophagus or gullet</note>, the other for the **larynx**.

That is, if we wish to speak in Latin, one belongs to the **gullet** [*gula*], the other to the **throat** [*guttur*]. For in this way **Theodorus** <note>Theodore Gaza (c. 1398–1475), a key Byzantine scholar whose Latin translations of Aristotle and Galen were prized for their elegance</note>, a man most learned in Greek and Latin, everywhere interprets these words in his translations; just as he also translates the Greek word *pharynga* as the Latin *fauces* [jaws or throat], although

**Pliny** says that the top of the gullet is called the *fauces*, and the furthest part the stomach. We, however, following the authority of **Galen**, say that the Greeks use the term "pharynx" not for the top of the gullet, but for the place where both the top of the **trachea** <note>term: *trachea* — the windpipe. I am moved by this passage—I who am usually more inclined to argue against "barbarous" men <note>Leoniceno often criticized medieval Scholastic authors and translators from the Arabic, whom he called "barbarians" for their perceived lack of Greek linguistic precision</note> than against Latinists, especially those who are living and are my friends (whom I would not criticize unless they had first broken the bond of friendship and begun to find fault with me)—to expose the error of **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the Persian physician whose "Canon of Medicine" was the standard textbook in European universities</note>, or at least of his **Commentators**. When writing about these parts of the human body that we are now discussing in their books or commentaries, they seem to disagree with **Hippocrates** and **Galen**. Indeed, **Avicenna**, in the third book of his *Canon*, in the ninth **Fen** <note>term: *Fen* — a specific division or section within Avicenna’s *Canon of Medicine*, derived from the Arabic *fann*</note>, in the chapter on the discussions of the throat, writes these words:
> By "throat" [*guttur*] we understand the space in which the passages for breath and food are located.

In these words, it seems to me that **Avicenna** intended to say the same thing as **Galen**, when he writes in Book IV of *On the Internal Parts*:
> I call the **pharynx** the inner space of the mouth, which the end of the gullet and the throat reach.

For Latin translations from the Arabic are accustomed to use the Latin word *guttur* [throat] for the word *pharynx* used by Greek authors; this is certainly how the Arabic-to-Latin translation of the *Book of Prognostics* <note>A famous work by Hippocrates on predicting the course of diseases</note> reads in the passage we cited above where **Hippocrates** names the "pharynx." For let it be permitted to me, wishing to refute the "barbarians" <note>Leoniceno frequently used the term "barbarians" to describe medieval Scholastic and Arabic-influenced authors whose Latin was, in his view, imprecise or corrupted</note>, to use those words which they themselves use in their books. I do this lest, if I speak differently than they do, I appear to have criticized them through false accusation, as if I were speaking of something other than the matter they discuss. I must entirely avoid the suspicion of this fault, both in all my work and especially in this one, in which I defend myself against the patron of **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder (23–79 AD), the Roman naturalist. Leoniceno’s career was defined by his "Errors of Pliny," where he used Greek sources like Galen to correct Pliny's botanical and anatomical mistakes</note>, who accuses me in his preface of shamelessly slandering Pliny.

Moreover, **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the Persian "Prince of Physicians." Most clearly, however, one of the more recent authors, who has lately begun to be held in high regard, writes thus in his exposition of this passage of Avicenna:

> » In the first part he says first that the **throat** [*guttur*] is the space, or part of the body, which extends below from the root of the chin to the bones of the *furcula* <note>term: *furcula* — the "little fork," referring here to the collarbone or the hollow of the throat</note>, and contains within itself the passage of breath (which we are accustomed to call the pipe of the lung, the vocal artery, and the **trachea**) and the passage for food, which physicians call the **gullet** [*meri*], the **esophagus**, and the **uvula** [*uua* or *uula*], which covers the **epiglottis**, and the two **tonsils** [*amigdalæ*], which are the two small "little ears" at the root of the tongue, and the *gassamat* <note>original: *gassamat* — a transliteration of an Arabic anatomical term, likely referring to the structures of the larynx or the "roughness" of the throat</note>.

This Expositor counts all these as parts of the throat; however, some belong to the neck, and some to the mouth. The **trachea**, or pipe of the lung, and the **esophagus**, or gullet, belong to the neck; but the uvula and the two tonsils belong to the mouth, and as I believe, so does the *gassamat*; although I do not wish to decide on a "barbarous" term.

All these things Galen says, according to the translation currently in use, praising the craftsmanship of nature in the appropriate formation of the parts of the mouth. Among these, as can be seen, he places the internal openings of the nose, the column (that is, the **uvula**), the epiglottis, the larynx (that is, the **throat** [*guttur*]), and the orifice of the stomach (that is, the ***meri*** <note>original: *meri* — a medieval term derived from Arabic to designate the esophagus</note>, or gullet), together with the tongue and teeth. <meta>This page continues Nicolò Leoniceno’s rigorous anatomical critique, transitioning from the general structure of the neck discussed on the previous page to a specific debate over the boundaries between the mouth and the throat. He contrasts the definitions found in Aristotle, Avicenna, and Galen to resolve confusion caused by medieval translations.</meta>

# ON ANIMALS AND METALS #

<note>Aristotle’s</note> *History of Animals* states that what is described within the jaws and lips is the mouth; the parts of the mouth, however, are the palate, the throat <note>original: *fauces*</note>, the tongue, the tonsils, and the teeth. He maintains that the parts of the neck are the anterior artery <note>the trachea or windpipe</note> and the posterior gullet <note>the esophagus</note>. However, according to the declaration of the "New Expositor" <note>likely a reference to a contemporary commentator on Arabic medicine</note>, Avicenna seems to group together as parts of the same member called the throat <note>original: *guttur*</note> not just the passage or duct of the **larynx** (which more recent writers mistakenly call the **epiglottis** by misusing the term), but the entire **windpipe** <note>original: *tracheam arteriam*</note>; and not just the uppermost opening of the gullet or esophagus <note>original: *meri*</note>, but the whole esophagus along with the **uvula** <note>original: *uua*</note>, the **epiglottis**, and the two **tonsils** <note>original: *amigdalis*</note>. 

Galen, however, separated these and assigned them to different members: some to the neck, such as the windpipe and the esophagus; others, such as the openings of the throat and gullet together, as well as the **little column** <note>original: *columnellam*</note> (which more recent writers call the **uvula**), he assigned to the mouth. For that Galen intends the little column or uvula to be a part of the mouth and not the neck or throat is indicated by his words in Book I of *On the Differences of Diseases*, in which he shows that a cut-away uvula is an affliction of the palate, and not of the neck or throat. 

In this place, I would like to caution the "defender of Pliny" <note>a reference to a contemporary scholar defending the terminology of Pliny the Elder</note> that he is incorrect in his anatomical work to call that part of the palate a *columella* <note>a small column</note>, which the Greeks call *chionida* <note>original Greek: κιονίδα, meaning "little column"</note>, after the shape it represents. He ought to have said *columnella* rather than *columella* for the same reason. However, we do not labor much over names, except that for a man professing knowledge not just of things but also of names in that treatise, we would wish him to have been more diligent than "barbarians" <note>Leoniceno’s common term for medieval scholastic scholars</note> usually are, even in matters of nomenclature. 

It is not, however, a matter for wonder if Galen assigned the bodies of the windpipe and the esophagus (or *meri*) to the neck, but their openings or passages to the mouth. For these two, as he says in the commentary on the *Book of Prognostics* cited above, are contained in the throat <note>original: *faucibus*</note>. Although the throat is on the border of the mouth and the neck, it nonetheless seems to belong more to the mouth, just as the palate does.

->### NICOLAI LEONICENI ###<-

Therefore, if we wish to bring Galen and his interpreter Avicenna into agreement—or at least make them less discordant—we must say (as we mentioned above, setting aside the barbarous <note>Leoniceno uses "barbarous" to refer to medieval Arabic-to-Latin translations that he felt corrupted original Greek medical concepts</note> interpretations) that by "throat" <note>original: *guttur*</note> Avicenna understood the **pharynx**, that is, the **jaws** <note>original: *fauces*</note>. This is, as he himself declares, that space in which the passages for breath and food are located—namely, the very openings of the **windpipe** <note>original: *tracheæ arteriæ*</note> and the **esophagus** <note>original: *meri*; from the Arabic *merī*</note>—and not the entire structures which, as we have said, belong to the neck and not the jaws. This interpretation of ours is confirmed by the words of Avicenna himself, if they are considered more diligently, added shortly after the previous passage: "And you already know the anatomy of the esophagus, and the anatomy of the epiglottis." For he did not say the "anatomy of the windpipe," but of the **epiglottis**, by which he meant the **larynx** <note>original: *laryngis*</note>, or the uppermost part of the windpipe which consists of three cartilages. This is what the Greeks call the *larynx*, but the barbarians call the *epiglottis* (misusing the term, as we said); Latin speakers can conveniently name it the "throat" <note>original: *guttur*</note>. According to Galen, the passage of this larynx (or "epiglottis") is contained within the jaws as part of the mouth. By this, Avicenna intended to suggest to us that by "passage of the spirit," he did not mean the entire windpipe, but only the opening of the larynx.

We must likewise think that Avicenna felt the same regarding the uppermost opening of the esophagus, which he calls the "passage of food," rather than the entire esophagus. And so, regarding these two parts of the throat, by understanding "throat" to mean the "jaws"—just as the barbarians use the word—Galen and Avicenna will be in agreement. However, they are certainly in disagreement in that Galen placed the **uvula** <note>original: *uuam*</note> not in the jaws, but in the palate; just as he placed the two **tonsils**—which he calls **paristhmia** in Greek—not in the jaws themselves, but in a location very nearby, or rather, adjacent to them. I know, however, that there is a disagreement between **Gentile** <note>Gentile da Foligno, a 14th-century physician</note> and **Mundinus** <note>Mondino de Liuzzi, a pioneer of medieval anatomy</note> concerning the position of the two tonsils. We reserve the discussion of this for another treatise, in which we shall address the errors of Mundinus in anatomy. But since mention has been made of Gentile...

These final words of Gentilis concerning the third definition of the throat certainly attempt to make Avicenna consistent with Hippocrates and Galen. However, we have already sufficiently shown above how much they actually disagree if the throat is understood in this place as Gentilis thinks, since we have declared what Hippocrates understood by the **pharynx**—for which the Arabic translation uses "throat"—according to the exposition of Galen. For this reason, all that we have said against the "new" commentator of Avicenna also applies to the older one, who errs even more significantly insofar as he cites a passage from the third book of the *Prognostics* which is entirely contrary to his own interpretation.

Indeed, the first definition of the throat provides a great opportunity for uncovering the discords between Galen and Avicenna; because in that chapter of the first book "On the Anatomy of the Throat," where Gentilis cites Avicenna regarding the throat, Avicenna speaks equivocally <note>Using the same word to mean different things</note>. For first, when he says the throat has two pairs of muscles which pull it downward, he understands the "throat" to be the **trachea** <note>original: *tracheam... arteriam*</note>. But when, later at the end of the chapter, he says: "the muscles of the throat, however, are two..."

» the **throat muscles**, which are two muscles positioned at the gullet aiding in swallowing. These are the words of **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina, the 11th-century Persian physician whose *Canon of Medicine* was the standard medical textbook in Europe at this time</note>. However, the pair of muscles that he claims to have mentioned in the chapter on the **epiglottis** is that same pair he discussed in the preceding chapter. He stated that their origin is deep within the **thorax** <note>the chest</note> and extends to the **peltate cartilage** <note>the shield-shaped or thyroid cartilage</note>. This is the "second pair" according to **Galen**, who says that two other muscles arise from the sides and lower parts of the cartilage shaped like a shield—which Avicenna calls the "peltate" cartilage—and says they terminate at the breast. Although Avicenna disagrees with Galen on this point, he places the origin where the termination of these muscles actually is, and conversely says they extend toward the place from which they actually originate.

He errs with a similar discrepancy regarding the second pair (which is the first pair according to Galen). Avicenna says these also arise from the chest and are raised up, connecting first with the **hyoid bone** <note>original: *lauda*; the U-shaped bone at the base of the tongue</note> and afterwards with the throat, pulling it downward. Yet Galen says these two muscles take their origin from the lower edge of the bone shaped like the Greek letter **upsilon** <note>the hyoid bone, often called the "hyoid" because it resembles the Greek letter *υ*</note>, and then, spreading out along the length of the entire **trachea** <note>the windpipe</note>, they are attached to the breast. These words of Galen differ significantly from the words of Avicenna, who says they are raised up and connect first with the hyoid and then with the throat.

Avicenna disagrees with Galen not only regarding the origin and termination of these muscles but also regarding their **function**. Galen maintains they were created to contract and narrow the **trachea**; Avicenna, however, claims they serve to pull it lower. In this matter of usage, as well as in their origin and end, although **Ali Abbas** <note>Ali ibn al-Abbas al-Majusi</note> seems to support Avicenna, I nevertheless place greater faith in **Galen**—the most skilled authority in this branch of medicine—than in the Arabic authors when it comes to matters of **anatomy**. This is especially puzzling since the muscles of only one of them—namely the epiglottis—are nearly twenty according to Galen, and eighteen according to Avicenna. If the two muscles aiding in swallowing are added to these, the total would become either twenty or twenty-two, depending on which opinion one follows.

If Gentilis should respond that Avicenna, in that same chapter, is only dealing with those muscles that move the structure joining the epiglottis and gullet during the act of swallowing, and not the other muscles serving different movements of the gullet or epiglottis, we shall further trouble Gentilis with another question: why does Avicenna name only two pairs of muscles that pull the throat downward, and not just as many others that pull it upward? After all, the "throat"—that is, the body joining the epiglottis and gullet—moves both up and down during the time of swallowing. It seems impossible that two contrary movements could be performed by the same muscles, since each individual muscle draws the part it moves toward its own origin, as Galen teaches both in the eleventh book of *On the Usefulness of the Parts* and in many other places. 

I wish that Gentilis were alive to answer these questions or doubts of mine. We have also shown above that the throat is one thing and the esophagus is another, since we have proved from the authority of Galen that the throat belongs to the mouth, whereas the esophagus belongs to the neck. 

Furthermore, in the fourteenth *Fen* <note>A division or chapter in Avicenna's *Canon*</note> of the third book, in the fourth chapter *On the Causes Preventing Swallowing*, Avicenna discusses various causes arising from the esophagus itself or from neighboring organs. If he had believed that muscles existed in the esophagus, he certainly should have included their **paralysis** (which can occur) among those causes. ### NICOLÒ LEONIENCO

According to **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the Persian physician whose *Canon of Medicine* was a standard textbook</note>, it necessarily follows that among the organs which serve as the passage for food—such as the intestines—not only the **esophagus** <note>original: *meri*, a Latinization of the Arabic *mari’*</note> and the **sphincter** <note>original: *sincteris*</note>, but even the **colon** <note>the large intestine</note> are moved by **muscles** <note>original: *lacertos*, typically referring to voluntary or skeletal muscles</note>. Otherwise, it would not be possible to suffer <margin>Paralysis.</margin> **paralysis** while sensation remained unharmed; for paralysis indeed attacks either sensation, or motion, or both. But we have demonstrated more extensively elsewhere where this error of Avicenna’s originated and how it arose. He also speaks of the internal muscles of the esophagus—in which Avicenna claims the third type of **abscessed suffocation** <note>original: *suffocationis apostemosæ*, a condition where an internal swelling or abscess blocks the throat</note> occurs—likewise in Book III, Fen VIII, Chapter III, "On Suffocations." From all these passages brought forward by us, it can be proven that Avicenna intended the esophagus to have muscles, and thus that it is moved not only by its own **natural power** <note>involuntary biological force</note> but also by the **animal power** <note>the "animal" or "soul" power responsible for voluntary movement</note> which operates through the muscles. 

However, regarding how many these muscles are, and in which layer of the wall they reside—the internal or external—he left nothing written in his books, at least as far as I know. Neither did **Haly Abbas** <note>Ali ibn al-Abbas al-Majusi (died c. 982–994), another influential Persian physician</note>, who only speaks of the muscles of the **throat** <note>original: *gurgulionis*</note> that serve both the voice and swallowing. If anyone wished to place these muscles in the body of the esophagus, it would follow that not only the **windpipe** <note>original: *tracheam arteriam*</note> and its head, which the Arabs call the **epiglottis** <note>original: *epiglotton*</note>, but also the **esophagus** <note>original: *isophagum* or *meri*</note> and its head (that is, the orifice) would be instruments of the voice. This is something that all physicians and philosophers admit regarding the windpipe and the epiglottis. However, concerning the esophagus and its orifice—which nature crafted solely for food and drink—no one has dared to write such a thing. 

This error of Avicenna—claiming the esophagus has internal muscles, from whose swelling or abscess a creature might be strangled—was followed by **Jacopo da Forlì** <note>Iacobus Foriliuiensis (c. 1364–1414), a famous Italian commentator on medical texts</note> in his exposition of the fourth **aphorism** <note>a short medical principle by Hippocrates</note> of the fourth section of the *Aphorisms*. The beginning of that aphorism is: "If one is held by a fever, while no swelling exists in the **jaws** <note>original: *faucibus*</note>." There, the same Jacopo enumerates four species of **quinsy** <note>original: *squinantiæ*, a severe and potentially suffocating throat inflammation</note>, and he lists as the third type that which occurs in the internal muscles of the esophagus. However, Jacopo’s error in that place is doubled,

# ON ANIMALS AND METALS.

...because [Avicenna] not only falsely names "internal muscles of the esophagus," <note>original: *musculos meri intrinsecos*. The term *meri* is a Latinization of the Arabic *mari’*, meaning esophagus.</note> which do not exist, but also falsely cites both **Hippocrates** in the third book of *Prognostics* and **Galen** in the fourth book of *Internal Parts* <note>original: *interiorum*, referring to Galen's *De Locis Affectis* (On the Affected Parts)</note> as making mention of a type of **quinsy** <note>original: *squinantiæ*, a severe inflammation of the throat or tonsils</note> involving these internal muscles of the esophagus. However, neither Hippocrates nor Galen, in their own commentaries—whether on the third book of *Prognostics*, or in the previously cited aphorism, or even in the fourth book of *Internal Parts* where Galen himself provides the physicians' four-fold division of **angina** <note>a general term for throat inflammation or choking</note>—speaks at all of a type where the internal muscles of the **esophagus** <note>original: *isophagi* (Greek) or *meri* (Latinized Arabic)</note> are **abscessed**. <note>original: *apostemati*</note>

For let me be permitted, while disputing against the **barbarians**, <note>Leoniceno, a Renaissance humanist, used "barbarians" to describe medieval Arabic and Scholastic Latin authors who he believed corrupted classical Greek medical knowledge.</note> to occasionally use the same vocabulary that they use in all their discourse. For I disagree with these "barbarian" medical authors not so much in names, but in the facts themselves. I attribute to them an ignorance not of words, but rather of **anatomy**, since they assign muscles to the esophagus which it simply does not have—namely, internal ones.

If indeed there are any muscles touching it from the outside—two in the front part toward the throat, and two in the back part toward the vertebrae of the neck—neither pair serves the movements of the esophagus. Instead, the pair touching the front provides movement to the **shield-shaped cartilage** <note>original: *cartilagini clypealis*, now known as the thyroid cartilage</note> of the throat; the other pair, touching the outside, serves the bending of the neck, as can be gathered from Galen’s anatomical writings and the seventh book of *On the Utility of Parts*.

Therefore, it remains that the movement of the esophagus is **natural** <note>involuntary or biological</note> in itself and not through any other means, as Galen clearly believes in the fourth book of *On Natural Faculties*. Or rather, the esophagus itself performs the function of a muscle in animals, rather than being moved by muscles—an idea Galen suggested to us in the first book of *On the Movement of Muscles* that some might hold. Regarding the **natural attractive power** <note>the biological force that draws food down</note> which we believe exists in the esophagus alone without **animal power**, <note>voluntary or "soul-driven" motion</note> whether we wish to use the Greek *esophagus* or the Latin *gula* [gullet], even the **champion of Pliny** <note>original: *Plinij patronus*. Indeed, I praise the man who, in the act of swallowing, attributes no other force to the esophagus than a natural one, which the Greeks call **drawing-down** <note>original: *cathelticem*</note>, drawing the food by the oblong warp of fibers. But he is subject to another mark of error, because since in another place of his work he attributes muscles to the esophagus in the same way as he does to the **epiglottis** and the **trachea** <note>original: *tracheæ arteriæ*, the "rough artery," the standard Renaissance term for the windpipe.</note>, he can be judged to think that nature has made something in vain—namely, the muscles of the esophagus. For to what use did nature give those muscles of the esophagus, if not either for drawing in or expelling food? 

Unless, perhaps, he believed that the oblong fibers of the interior membrane, or the broad ones of the exterior, were the fibers of the muscles proper to each membrane; which estimation would be false, and contrary to both **Galen** and **Avicenna**, who maintain that these same fibers serve two natural powers, named one "attractive" and the other "expulsive."

This, therefore, is that accidental motion <note>original: *motus per accidens*; a movement that occurs as a side-effect of another part moving, rather than by its own power.</note> by which **Galen** says, in his book *On the Movements of Liquids*, that the epiglottis is moved at the time when food is swallowed. It is not at all as **Mondino** <note>Mondino de Luzzi (c. 1270–1326), a pioneering Italian anatomist.</note> and **Gentile** <note>Gentile da Foligno (d. 1348), a famous physician and commentator on medical texts.</note> seem to imagine—namely, that when the esophagus <note>original: *meri*; a term derived from Arabic commonly used in medieval Latin for the esophagus.</note> lifts itself toward the upper parts, the epiglottis is also lifted, and when it lowers itself, the epiglottis is lowered. On the contrary, as can be gathered from **Galen’s** words, it is quite the opposite; nor are these two movements of ascent and descent of the esophagus and the epiglottis "animal movements" <note>original: *motus animales*; movements controlled by the soul or will, which we would today call voluntary muscular movements.</note>—that is, performed by muscles, as **Gentile** also seems to have believed when he said the throat is sometimes taken as the body joining the epiglottis and the esophagus, which is moved up and down during swallowing. He takes this from the first *Fen* <note>A division or "branch" of Avicenna’s *Canon of Medicine*.</note> of the first book of the *Canon*, in the chapter *On the Anatomy of the Muscles of the Throat*. Instead, these movements are "natural" <note>original: *naturales*; involuntary or biological movements not controlled by conscious will.</note>—that is, performed by the power of the fibers <note>original: *uillorum*; refers to the thread-like tissues or fibers within a membrane.</note> of the esophagus, which contract during the time of swallowing and relax when it ceases. This is so even though the movement of the esophagus is primary <note>original: *per se*</note>, while the movement of the epiglottis is accidental, as **Galen** also feels in his book *On the Movements of Liquids*.

I am amazed, however, that **Gentile**—otherwise a diligent reader and even an expositor of **Avicenna** <note>The Latinized name of Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the influential Persian physician.</note>—did not notice these movements of ascent and descent, both in the epiglottis and in the esophagus, or at least learn from **Avicenna’s** teaching that they are not performed by the "animal" force of the muscles, but rather by the "natural" force of the fibers of the tunic <note>A layer of tissue or membrane.</note> lining the mouth of the esophagus and the epiglottis. Indeed, **Avicenna** himself teaches this very thing in the thirteenth *Fen* of the third book, in the first chapter *On the Anatomy of the Esophagus and the Stomach*, where he gives the reason why this tunic lines the inner part of the esophagus, just as it does the epiglottis and the mouth, as we have said,

# NICCOLÒ LEONICENO

“And it consists of two tunics <note>original: *tunicis*; the layers or membranes of an organ.</note>, of which the inner one has longitudinal fibers <note>original: *uillos*; literally "hairs," used here for the grain of the tissue.</note>, because of what is known regarding the necessity of attraction; and for this reason the stomach contracts when swallowing occurs, and the epiglottis is raised.” In these words, **Avicenna** <note>The Persian physician Ibn Sina (980–1037), author of the *Canon of Medicine*.</note> intended nothing other than what **Galen** <note>The influential Greek physician of the 2nd century AD.</note> suggested: that when the esophagus <note>original: *meri*; a medieval Latin term for the esophagus derived from Arabic.</note> descends during swallowing, the epiglottis rises, and vice versa. He believed both movements to be natural, as they are performed by the membrane—the thin tissue covering the mouth, the esophagus, the stomach, and the epiglottis all at once. Otherwise, the epiglottis would not be moved accidentally by the motion of the esophagus unless it also shared this same membrane with the esophagus.

Furthermore, I wonder that the defender of **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder (23–79 AD), author of *Natural History*. Leoniceno often criticized his lack of anatomical accuracy.</note> did not hesitate to write, in his own anatomical description, something different from all others who have written on anatomy: that the throat, of which the uvula <note>original: *gurgulio*; while usually meaning the uvula, Pliny sometimes used this for the windpipe or throat region.</note> is a part, pulls the esophagus upward during swallowing. This contradicts **Mondino** <note>Mondino de Luzzi, a 14th-century anatomist.</note>, who held that it is not the epiglottis that pulls the esophagus, but the rising esophagus that causes the epiglottis to rise. 

According to **Galen** and **Avicenna**, however, the esophagus (or *meri*) forces the epiglottis to rise by contracting and descending. Yet according to **Gentile** <note>Gentile da Foligno, a prominent 14th-century medical commentator.</note>, the epiglottis and the esophagus move upward or downward together during swallowing. If they had the same muscles serving their movements, as **Gentile** clearly seems to think, I certainly do not see how this movement of the body—uniting the epiglottis and the esophagus—could happen otherwise. This is especially true since muscles always pull the part they move back toward their own origins <note>The "origin" is the fixed end of a muscle; muscles only pull, they do not push.</note>, as was demonstrated by us above when arguing against **Gentile** using **Galen’s** authority.

Nevertheless, the same **Gentile**, in the tenth *Fen* <note>A division or chapter of a book.</note> of the third book, in the chapter on the anatomy of the epiglottis and the windpipe <note>original: *cannae*; literally "the reed," a common term for the trachea.</note>, writes these words: “It should be considered that the part of the windpipe of the lungs which is called the epiglottis—where there is no such reduction of cartilage—rises upward at the hour of the bolus's <note>original: *boli*; the chewed mass of food.</note> descent, and therefore it is not compressed by the mouthful, and thus it does not suffer pain...”

> “...the man suffers, nor is the breath harmed, but it was not possible for the whole tube <note>original: *canna*; likely referring to the *canna pulmonis* or trachea.</note> to be drawn higher, and therefore so that a conjunction of the bolus <note>A rounded mass of chewed food.</note> passing through does not occur during the act of breathing, and so that pressure does not occur in the tube, they were not of perfect circulation.”

Therefore, considering the matter more diligently, we will find a contradiction between the words of the first explanation and the second. For the second explanation suggests to us that the movement of the epiglottis when the bolus descends is natural. Indeed, as was declared before, the cause of this movement is the longitudinal fibers <term>villi; used here to describe the grain or texture of the tissue</term> of the inner tunic of the esophagus, which is a tunic shared with the epiglottis.

The first explanation, however, as we have proven, shows the same movement to be "animal" (voluntary). According to physicians who distinguish the animal power from the natural power, this cannot happen, even though two powers can be joined to perform the same movement. This is similar to how, in the emptying of the lower bowel, both the natural expulsive power of the intestines and the "animal" power of the muscles located in the upper part of the belly act together. We concede that these two powers also assist in the work of swallowing, yet we deny that the esophagus has muscles, just as the intestines do not have them—except for the very last part of the intestine, named the **Rectum**. This part, in its final section called the "seat" <note>The anus.</note>, possesses a muscle which prevents [waste] from exiting against our will.

Likewise, we also say that the movement of food from the opening of the throat down to the bottom of the stomach is, by the same reasoning, only natural, and that the animal force has no place in this, but only in moving the food toward the opening of the throat. For the movement of the tongue and the two muscles located in the throat work toward this end; and to that extent, swallowing can be called an animal movement, because if this operation did not precede it, the food could not afterwards descend to the lower parts by the natural attractive force of the esophagus <note>original: *meri*; a medieval term for the esophagus derived from Arabic</note>. > And similarly, the operation of swallowing is completed by two powers: one is natural attraction, and the other is voluntary attraction. The first indeed completes its operation through the fiber <note>original: *uillum*; referring here to longitudinal muscle fibers</note> that extends lengthwise, which is in the mouth of the stomach and the esophagus; and the operation of the second is completed through the fiber of the swallowing muscle.

I could wish, however, that in this place Avicenna—just as he clarified for us what was not particularly obscure, namely where the oblong fiber was located through which the natural attractive power exercises its operation (which he said was in the mouth of the stomach and the esophagus)—had also revealed what was more hidden: namely the position of the swallowing muscle's fiber. Specifically, whether it was in the esophagus or in the pharynx (that is, the throat), in which Galen undoubtedly placed it, as has been sufficiently explained by us above. ...words, which we also recounted above: "And none of these members which are the path of food is moved by muscles, except the two extremes, namely the head, which is the esophagus <note>original: *meri*; a medieval term for the esophagus derived from Arabic</note>, and the lower part, which is the sphincter <note>original: *ficteris*; a medieval variation of the Greek *sphinkter*</note>."

The pharynx, however, is not the head of the esophagus <note>original: *isophagi*</note>, nor the "head of the *meri*" according to Galen, but rather that space of the mouth where the top of the esophagus terminates, as was also declared by us above. I am surprised by the commentators of Avicenna, both the older and the more recent ones, who have departed from the common opinion of Galen and Avicenna in those matters where they actually agree—such as the contraction of the stomach during swallowing and the simultaneous lifting of the epiglottis. Yet, where they were actually in disagreement—such as regarding the muscles of the throat and the esophagus—these commentators noted no discord between them, nor did they strive to bring these two "princes of medicine" into harmony. 

Jacques Despars <note>original: *Iacobus de partibus*; a famous 15th-century French physician and commentator on Avicenna</note>, the most recent of Avicenna’s commentators, seems to have applied himself to this study, yet in this particular section he seems to have "nodded off." He appears to agree with Avicenna, thinking that Galen and Avicenna say the same thing about these muscles, which are specific to these two extremities: the upper one, called the head of the esophagus or the "gullet," and the lower one, which younger physicians (speaking partly in jargon and partly in Latin) call the "anus" and "sphincter." 

Nevertheless, in the first book of the *Canon* <note>Avicenna’s *Canon of Medicine*, the standard medical textbook of the era</note>, in the first *Fen* <note>A division of the *Canon*, from the Arabic word *fann* meaning "part" or "specialty"</note>, in the chapter "On the Anatomy of Muscles," this same Jacques does notice the point on which Galen and Avicenna agree: the upward movement of the epiglottis and the downward movement of the esophagus during swallowing. He even cites Galen on these movements from Book VI of *On the Usefulness of the Parts* <note>original: *De iuuamentis membrorum*</note>. But he himself, just like Gentile <note>Gentile da Foligno, a prominent 14th-century Italian physician</note>, fails to remember that later, in the third book of the *Canon*, he attributed these same opposing movements—namely of the esophagus and the epiglottis—not to the muscles (which are the instruments of the "animal" or voluntary motive power), but rather to the fibers of the inner lining of the esophagus, which serve the natural "attractive" power <note>The "attractive power" was the biological force believed to draw nourishment into an organ, functioning independently of conscious will.</note>. Therefore, to those considering the matter more diligently, the doctrine of Avicenna, along with so many of his commentators, who

We forgive the Patron of Pliny for such things so often in his <term>anatomy</term> <note>original: *anatomice*; here referring to the study or description of bodily structures</note>, judging that in writers, it is not an ignorance of words, but rather an ignorance of things that ought to be refuted.

<page-num>690</page-num>

<margin><term>Ekphysis</term> <note>Greek: ἐκφύσις; meaning an "outgrowth" or "offshoot."</note></margin> That is to say, it is called an "outgrowth" because it first arises from the <term>pylorus</term> <note>The opening from the stomach into the small intestine.</note>, or the *dodecatylum*, or as doctors now call it, the **duodenum**, because it extends to a length of twelve fingers. Avicenna also, in Fen 16 of Book 3, in the chapter "On the Anatomy of the Intestines" (which are six in number), says the first is the duodenum. Yet earlier, in Fen 13, in the chapter "On the Anatomy of the Esophagus and the Stomach," he had written these words concerning the <term>portanarius</term> <note>Latin: *portanarius*; a medieval term for the pylorus, literally meaning "gatekeeper."</note> and the duodenum:

>> "And in the lower part of the stomach is an opening to which the twelve-finger intestine is connected, and this opening is called the *portanarius*, and it is narrower than the upper opening, because it is the passage for that which is contrary to it <note>Likely referring to the passage of digested food (chyme) vs. the intake of food.</note>, and this passage is indeed closed until digestion is complete."

From these words of Avicenna written in this place, two things can be gathered which Galen also believes: that the *portanarius* is not the first intestine, but rather the opening to which the first intestine is joined; and that it is located in the lower part of the stomach, such that it should be judged as part of the substance of the stomach rather than the intestines. However, the same Avicenna later, in the previously cited Fen 16, determined the opposite, writing in this manner:

>> "And the duodenum intestine is connected to the bottom of the stomach, and has an orifice following the stomach, and it is called the *portanarius*."

Likewise, a little further down in the same chapter, "On the Width of the Orifice of the Duodenum":

>> "And its width is indeed the width of its orifice, which is called the *portanarius*."

But Avicenna, besides the fact that he seems to contradict himself in various places, is also in this matter contrary to Galen. Galen indicates in many places that the pylorus is the lowest part of the stomach, as in the second book of the *Art of Medicine* <note>Latin: *Ars Parva* (The Small Art), one of Galen’s most influential introductory texts.</note>, where he says a phlegmatic man who vomited bile every day was subject to this condition because the passage that belches out the bilious humor transmitted a large portion of it to the pylorus of the stomach. But the same Galen declares even more clearly that the pylorus is made of the substance of the stomach, not the *dodecatylum* or duodenum.

Furthermore, the bile is not transmitted to the pylorus, but a little lower—that is, to the 'beginning' or the duodenum—through its own duct proceeding from that bladder which is called the bile receptacle. 

Regarding this duct—whether it be one or double, and where it terminates—I know that most of the younger doctors are ignorant. Following <term>Mundinus</term> <note>Mondino de' Liuzzi (c. 1270–1326), a medieval Italian physician known as the "Restorer of Anatomy."</note>, they think that this duct is single near its beginning, but in its course is split into two branches. They believe the larger branch in most humans is carried to the duodenum, while the other smaller branch goes to the bottom of the stomach, so that the stomach might be made stronger for digesting food by the heat of the bile reaching it. However, Galen made no mention of such a function, neither in Book IV of *On the Usefulness of the Parts* nor anywhere else in his writings. Rather, in Book V of *On the Usefulness of the Parts*, he asks why nature did not similarly create a duct carrying bile that reached the stomach, just as it does for the 'beginning' or the duodenum. ...but rather to her kindness, which did not wish for a small benefit—which the stomach <note>original: "ventriculus"</note> would have received from such a passage—to be outweighed by another much greater disadvantage: namely, the constant vomiting of food. For if the stomach were irritated by the sharpness of yellow bile, it would be unable to retain food for the time required for it to be digested. 

Therefore, it is the opinion of Galen, which he also expresses in Book II of *On Temperaments* <note>original: "De temperamentis," also known as "On Complexions."</note>, that this passage is not always double, as **Mundinus** <note>Mondino de Liuzzi (c. 1270–1326), a medieval anatomist whose textbook was standard in Leoniceno’s time.</note> seems to believe. Mundinus knows no other way to resolve Galen’s dilemma in Book III of *On Natural Faculties* <note>original: "De uirtutibus naturalibus."</note> regarding how the gallbladder <note>original: "cystis fellis"</note> attracts and expels bile through the same neck. Galen's view is that the duct is sometimes single, and when it is single, it reaches the middle intestine between the <term>pylorus</term> and the <term>jejunum</term> <note>The second part of the small intestine, from the Latin "jejunus" meaning "empty."</note>—that is, it reaches the beginning [of the intestines], or the **duodenum**. 

When the duct is indeed double, its larger branch reaches the aforementioned beginning or duodenum, while the other smaller branch reaches the bottom of the stomach a little above the pylorus; this occurs in the majority of cases. It happens only very rarely that the locations are switched, so that the larger branch reaches the bottom of the stomach and the smaller reaches the beginning or duodenum. 

He says that from this switch, a great disadvantage occurs, because the stomach continuously receives yellow bile and is subsequently forced to vomit before it can even take in food; and if it should retain the food, it suffers great harm from the bile. For those in whom the passage is entirely single, Galen says all the bile flows down to the jejunum. 

From these words of Galen we can gather several points: 
1. First, that a single duct is more suited to human nature than a double one. 
2. Second, if a double duct is present, it is more appropriate for the larger branch to reach the first intestine (called the "beginning" or the **duodenum**). 

For if the opposite occurs, it is an error of a greatly straying nature—just as she strays only slightly when she makes a double duct out of a single one but sends the smaller branch to the bottom of the stomach so that it might do less harm. This opinion of Galen, however...

<meta>This page continues Nicolò Leoniceno’s critique of medieval and contemporary anatomical descriptions. He is specifically addressing the structure of the gallbladder's ducts and correcting the terminology used by Mundinus and a contemporary scholar whom he calls "the defender of Pliny."</meta>

<page-num>195</page-num>
# ->ON ANIMALS AND METALS.<-

**Mundinus** <note>Mondino de' Liuzzi (c. 1270–1326), a medieval Italian physician whose anatomical manual was the standard text for centuries.</note> is in error. For in his anatomical work, he described this "neck" <note>the duct of the gallbladder</note> as not only "bifurcated" (to use **Mundinus’s** own word) but even "trifurcated" <note>split into three branches</note>. He says that the first of these branches is directed into the middle of the liver; a second, more obvious one, is carried to the **pylorus**; and the largest of all is extended to the intestines called the **lactes** <note>original: "lactes"; a historical term for the small intestines or mesenteric vessels, so called because of the milky-looking chyle they contain</note>. Regarding the second branch which leads to the pylorus, he says it is reported by some that another branch arises from it which tends toward the bottom of the stomach, though others deny this.

That this arrangement is not a constant rule is asserted by the same defender of **Pliny** <note>Referring to a scholar, likely Pandolfo Collenuccio, who defended the accuracy of the Roman naturalist Pliny the Elder against Leoniceno's criticisms.</note>, and he is quite right; for this is also **Galen’s** opinion, as we have declared previously. However, he was not correct—and indeed was entirely out of harmony with **Galen**—when he wrote that, besides the duct carried to the pylorus, another and indeed the largest duct is extended to the intestines called the **lactes**.

For among the small intestines, besides the **jejunum** <note>the middle section of the small intestine</note> and the "thin" intestine <note>the ileum</note>, there is also the **pylorus**, which has a measure of "twelve fingers" <note>referring to the duodenum</note>, as the defender of **Pliny** himself writes in the chapter *On the Three Thinner Intestines*. In that same chapter, he also writes that the bile duct belongs to this very intestine. Since he had written this, he ought not later, in another chapter, create a second "largest" duct leading to the **lactes** in addition to this bile duct carried to the pylorus (that is, to the first of the intestines that make up the **lactes**).

For the ancient physicians, such as **Galen** and **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the influential Persian physician</note>, as we have shown above, recorded only one bile duct. This duct leads from the bladder <note>the gallbladder</note>—which is the reservoir for bile—to the first of the intestines. The defender of **Pliny** calls this intestine the "pylorus," but **Galen** calls it the "outgrowth" <note>original: "exortum"</note> and the *dodecatylon* <note>Greek for "twelve fingers long"</note>, while **Avicenna** and the other more recent physicians call it the **duodenum**. 

Although I am aware that the defender of **Pliny** could defend himself on this point by the authority of **Avicenna**, who in the third book of the *Canon*, Section 16, in the chapter *On the Anatomy of the Intestines*, writes that "yellow bile" <note>original: "cholera citrina"</note> comes to the **jejunum** intestine. From this, perhaps the defender of **Pliny** could argue that another bile duct extends not only to the pylorus, but also to the jejunum. But let the defender of **Pliny** remember...

# NICOLÒ LEONICENO

[The] defender [of Pliny] <note>original: "patronus"; likely referring to Pandolfo Collenuccio, who defended the Roman naturalist Pliny against Leoniceno's corrections.</note> argues that no other duct is necessary for the **jejunum** <note>the middle section of the small intestine</note> for the reception of **yellow bile**, since more than enough of it descends to that organ from the first intestine, whether that intestine be called the **pylorus**, the origin, or the **duodenum**. Wherefore **Galen** speaks more accurately when he writes in the second book of *On Temperaments* <note>original: "De temperamentis"; also known by the Latin title "De complexionibus"</note>, which I cited above, that this simple duct allows all the bile to flow down to the jejunum. He speaks more accurately, I say, than **Avicenna** did when he wrote that such a humor "flows down" rather than "comes to" the jejunum intestine; for Galen knew that the movement of this humor was a descent from another higher intestine rather than an arrival [from the duct itself]. **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the Persian physician whose "Canon of Medicine" dominated European universities for centuries.</note> ought also to have known this, lest he otherwise seem to contradict himself in various places; for the same **Avicenna**, in Fen 15 of Book 3, in the chapter "On the Anatomy of the Gallbladder," writes that in most humans the gallbladder duct is continuous with the **duodenum**.

Let these remarks suffice concerning the biliary ducts, in which the defender of **Pliny** has, in my judgment, erred significantly, as I have shown. He has erred even more than those other physicians who, professing "barbaric" medicine <note>original: "barbaram medicinam"; Leoniceno’s dismissive term for the medieval scholastic tradition based on Arabic translations, which he sought to replace with original Greek sources.</note>, believed—through a poor understanding of the words of **Avicenna** and **Galen**—that there are two ducts even in the natural state: one leading to the **pylorus** and another to the **duodenum**. I say he should be excused even less because he wishes to be regarded not as a follower of the "barbarians," but as a follower of **Galen** especially, both in other matters and particularly in those pertaining to anatomy.

But this same defender of **Pliny** departs no less from the truth and from the opinion of **Galen** regarding the intestines themselves, such as when he writes that the **jejunum** intestine is not as tangled <note>original: "implicitum"; referring to the complex folding and coiling of the intestinal tract.</note> as the others. This is entirely false, and completely contrary both to the writings of the authorities and to those things which are made manifest to the senses. For the first intestine—which the same defender of **Pliny** calls the **pylorus** and others call the **duodenum**—is much less tangled; indeed, it is not tangled at all. For which reason some, such as **Galen**, in not just one place but in several...

...left it attested, nor did they think it should even be called an intestine; nor, if we believe the same **Galen**, is the **small intestine** <note>original: "tenue intestinum"; here referring specifically to the ileum</note> more coiled than the **jejunum** <note>the middle section of the small intestine, traditionally called "empty" because it was often found so during dissections</note>. In fact, it is either equally or even less coiled. Indeed, the many windings of the intestines are necessary for various reasons, but specifically so that more veins may terminate in them. 

This view is held not only by **Galen**, who writes in his anatomical works that the jejunum intestine is bent into many coils containing a great number of vessels, but also by **Avicenna** <note>the influential Persian physician Ibn Sina</note>, who says that one reason for these windings is the continuous arrangement of the openings of the **sucking veins** <note>original: "venarum sugentium"; the mesenteric veins that absorb nutrients</note>. Therefore, where there are more veins, it is not only likely but almost necessary that there be more windings. 

**Galen** also testifies that there are more veins in the jejunum than in the small intestine in the sixth book of his **On Anatomical Procedures** <note>original: "De aggressibus anatomicis"</note>, where he writes that the small intestine has the same substance as the jejunum. He notes they differ in only two ways: first, because it is never found empty <note>Leoniceno is likely debating the naming conventions of the "jejunum" here</note>, and second, because it does not have such a great multitude of vessels. 

**Avicenna** also confirms this greater number of veins in the jejunum in the chapter cited above. However, he disagrees with **Galen**—and even with himself—in that he claims the **duodenum** has more veins than the remaining intestines after the jejunum. **Galen** did not suggest the duodenum, but rather hinted to us that the small intestine <note>the ileum</note> holds the second place in the abundance of veins, when he spoke the words we recently cited: *The jejunum intestine is bent into many coils, having a great many vessels.* **Avicenna** is also forced to agree with this if he wishes to maintain his other reason for the multitude of windings in the intestines—which, according to him, is the arrangement of the openings of the sucking veins. For where there are many veins, there must also be many windings. Consequently, if there are no windings anywhere, one should not think there is such a great multitude of veins there. ...[convo]lutions, as **Avicenna** likewise admits in *Fen* 16 <note>a "Fen" is a division or "branch" of Avicenna's *Canon of Medicine*</note>, in the chapter **On the Anatomy of the Intestines**, where he writes these words: <margin>,,</margin> "And the <margin>,,</margin> part of the small intestine <note>original: "intestini subtilis"</note> that follows the duodenum is <margin>,,</margin> named the **jejunum** <note>the middle part of the small intestine, from the Latin *ieiunus* meaning "empty"</note>. For this reason, if **Avicenna** did not wish to contradict his own opinions, he ought to have said that after the jejunum, in the thin intestine <note>original: "in tenui"; referring to the ileum</note>, there is a multitude of **mesenteric veins** <note>original: "venarum messaraicarum"; the veins that absorb nutrients from the gut</note>, where **Avicenna** himself also admits there is one revolution after another. For this reason, he calls it not only the "long intestine," but also "convoluted and revolved," as if it possesses even more revolutions than the jejunum intestine. From this, one might conclude that there is a greater multitude of veins in it than in the jejunum, let alone the duodenum.

Moreover, **Celsus** <note>Aulus Cornelius Celsus, a 1st-century Roman medical encyclopedist</note> also concedes that the thin intestine <note>the ileum</note> has more revolutions than the jejunum. The defender of **Pliny** <note>Leoniceno refers to a contemporary critic who defended Pliny the Elder against Leoniceno’s charges of scientific inaccuracy</note> sought to imitate this author [Celsus] not only in his opinions but even in his phrasing, although he erred more than Celsus did. In the fourth volume of his work *On Medicine*, Celsus does not write that the jejunum is less "entangled" <note>original: "implicitum"; coiled or folded</note> than the rest. From such words, it would follow that the duodenum is the most entangled—which **Galen** and **Avicenna** both deny, as Avicenna maintains that the revolutions first begin in the jejunum intestine. I say that Celsus does not write what the defender of Pliny claims, but only these words: <margin>,,</margin> "From that junction which they call the **pylorus** <note>the opening from the stomach into the duodenum</note>, the <margin>,,</margin> **jejunum** intestine is not so entangled; from there, the thinner intestine <margin>,,</margin> [the ileum] is violently entangled into loops." Thus, we must understand that this comparison is made not between the pylorus and the jejunum, but only between the jejunum and the thin intestine, regarding which of them is more or less entangled...

...[pre]paration, which **Pliny’s** advocate <note>original: "Plinii patronus"; likely referring to an authority Pliny followed or a contemporary defender of his text</note> claimed also occurs at the **pylorus** <note>the opening from the stomach into the small intestine</note>, and that the pylorus is more convoluted than the **jejunum** <note>the middle section of the small intestine</note>—a claim he declared entirely false in his *Anatomy*. That, however, I would dare to affirm for certain: that **Mundinus** <note>Mondino de Luzzi (c. 1270–1326), a medieval anatomist</note> errs in his *Anatomy* when he writes that the jejunum intestine has the same straightness as the **rectum**. This is just like his other claim: that more **mesenteric veins** <term>venæ messaraicæ; the blood vessels that absorb nutrients from the gut</term> go to the **ileum** (or thin intestine) than to any other intestine. **Galen** and **Avicenna** assert the contrary: namely, that the jejunum is the first of the slender intestines to receive convolutions. 

**Galen** clearly separates the jejunum from the thin intestine by two differences: because the thin intestine is not found empty <note>the name "jejunum" comes from the Latin for "empty," as it was often found empty during autopsies</note>, and because the same thin intestine does not possess such a great multitude of veins. Nor will I be afraid to say—though I do so less willingly when dealing with errors, making mention of eloquent men—I will not, I say, be afraid to say that **Pliny’s** advocate, along with **Celsus**, goes astray. They write that the **pylorus** intestine received this name among the Greeks because, like a gate <note>from the Greek *pyloros*, meaning "gatekeeper"</note>, it emits through the lower parts those things which we are about to excrete. 

For the intestines, especially the slender ones, were not made by nature for this end—to emit the excrements of the lower belly—but rather to be instruments for the distribution of food, which must be transmitted through the **mesenteric veins** to the **liver** <note>original: "epar"</note>. Therefore, our **Galen** more correctly says that the pylorus was so named for this reason (whether the term is used for the lowest part of the stomach or for the first intestine annexed to it): so that, like a just gatekeeper, it permits nothing to exit which has not first been **converted** into **chyle** <note>original: "chylum"; the milky fluid of digested food</note>...

I, however, do not see why waste generated in the stomach could not produce the same symptoms as those caused by waste ascending from the intestines to the stomach. Therefore, if waste had its being in the stomach—as the aforementioned men wish to claim—a person would suffer from **ileus** <note>a painful intestinal obstruction that can lead to "fecal vomiting"</note> every day; every day he would vomit and hiccup. > It has been shown previously that nothing is suddenly transformed into a contrary quality. How, then, will bread become blood? How will a beet, or a bean, or anything else, unless it first undergoes some other alteration? And how will waste be generated suddenly in the small intestines? Is there something in those intestines more powerful for alteration than in the stomach? Is it the thickness of the membranes, the proximity of neighboring organs, the length of time, or some innate heat in the organs?

Likewise, further down in the same book, Galen writes similar words. From these, we can gather that, according to him, waste is first generated in the small intestines and not in the stomach. These are his words:

> For food does not change its old quality so swiftly that it becomes waste the moment it falls into the small intestines. Bile, however, or urine, change their quality much more readily; once they have exited the veins, they undergo transformation and putrefaction very quickly.

**Jacob of Forlì** <note>Iacobus Foriliuiensis (1364–1414), an influential Italian physician and commentator on medical texts</note> wrote in a certain conclusion of his regarding a question touched upon in the second part of the *Aphorisms* <note>The *Aphorisms* of Hippocrates, which Jacob commented upon</note>, in which he asks in what place the waste or excrement receives its form. He argues, I say, that this happens not through separation and purification, but rather through an alteration that results in a change of substance. From this, the same Jacob writes a third conclusion, which he says can probably be sustained: that sometimes waste is acquired in the intestines, both in its substantial and accidental form. 

However, this does not happen "sometimes," but always in healthy humans, as can be seen from the words of **Galen** <note>the famous Greek physician whose theories dominated Western medicine for centuries</note> cited above. Nevertheless, Jacob attributes a contrary opinion to Galen: namely, that the **substantial form** <term>substantial form: the essential nature that makes a thing what it is (e.g., turning food into waste)</term> is acquired in the stomach when the body is naturally and properly disposed. For this is Jacob's first conclusion in the aforementioned question. 

His second conclusion (the other one touched upon) is that the separation and purification of waste from the **chyle** <term>chyle: the milky fluid of digested food before it is converted into blood</term>, and the acquisition of the **accidental dispositions** <term>accidental dispositions: the non-essential qualities like color, smell, or texture</term> by which waste is distinguished from chyle, are acquired in the intestines. Through these two conclusions, Jacob thought he had created a harmony between Galen and **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the Persian "Prince of Physicians" whose *Canon of Medicine* was a standard text</note>, as if the first conclusion were according to Galen's opinion and the second according to Avicenna's, and that neither contradicted the other. 

If it were as Jacob thought, then every contradiction between Avicenna and Galen would be removed. But the matter is quite the opposite. For as appears from what was said before, Galen himself is the one who feels that dung is generated in the small intestines, while Avicenna believes it happens in the stomach. I can nonetheless demonstrate from many of Avicenna's own words that this is his opinion. Resolving this doubt, he writes these words: 

>> The primary attraction of food by the intestines occurs so that the intestines may find "pleasure" and take something from it; and because the waste in the intestines is proportional, just as urine is in the bladder, therefore the waste, which comes from the bulk of the food, aids this attraction. 

Likewise, shortly after, Gentile, resolving another doubt as to whether the intestines possess an attractive power, writes in the same vein with these words: 

>> It must be said that there is an attractive power in the intestines; for if there is any "pleasure" for the intestines in what is within them, then they attract it. For attraction depends on pleasure, since the attractor draws for the sake of enjoying pleasure; but the intestines take pleasure in what is in them, since they receive some refreshment from it—at least the "slender" [small] intestines—and even the "gross" [large] ones take some pleasure in the waste. Just as dogs [take pleasure] in their excrement, so the intestines in waste, the bladder in urine, and the gallbladder in bile, as stated in Book III of *On the Natural Faculties* <note>original: "De uirtutibus naturalibus," a key work by Galen explaining how the body's organs function</note>. 

These are the views of Gentile, who in his own words seems to believe that waste is drawn by the intestines just as urine is drawn by the bladder. 

**Galen** <note>the 2nd-century Greek physician whose authority Leoniceno is defending against later medieval interpretations</note>, however, does not even want the **chyle** <term>chyle: the milky fluid of digested food before it is turned into blood</term> to be drawn in by the intestines from which they are nourished, let alone the waste. Nor, indeed, does he believe urine is drawn by the bladder. Rather, he holds that the former is propelled from the stomach through the **pylorus** <note>the muscular opening from the stomach into the small intestine</note> to the intestines, while urine is propelled from the kidneys to the bladder through the urinary passages [ureters]. Galen himself testifies to this in many places concerning the intestines; he maintains they have no attractive power at all, and therefore lack fibers or villi...

Concerning the bladder, however, he clearly declares this in Book VI of *On the Affected Parts* <note>original: "De interioribus", a work by Galen</note>. **Avicenna** also, a little further back, offers a similar reason for why the **duodenum** <term>duodenum: the first part of the small intestine immediately following the stomach</term> is narrower than the **esophagus** <term>esophagus: original "meri", the tube leading from the mouth to the stomach</term>, writing these words:

>> "And that which penetrates into this intestine is smoother, and flatter, and of a more subtle quantity because of its digestion in the stomach, and the mixture of watery foam with it."

Explaining these words, **Jacques Desparts** <note>Iacobus de partibus (c. 1380–1458), a French physician known for his massive commentary on Avicenna</note>, a modern commentator on Avicenna, writes in this manner:

>> "And the things which pass through the **pylorus** <term>pylorus: original "portanarium", the opening from the stomach into the small intestine</term> and the duodenum are smoother than these and flatter—that is, less rough, or more gentle and of a finer substance, or of smaller or more slender mass. First, because of the digestion they acquired in the stomach, which there mixed the fine with the coarse and made them equal. Second, because those things which have been mixed with watery foam are thinned out."

These are his words. But Avicenna's reasons, which attempt to prove that the first intestine is narrower than the esophagus, besides appearing sufficiently absurd, are also otherwise flawed because they contradict another point. By this other point, Avicenna later tries to prove that the second intestine is always found empty, from which it is named the **jejunum** <term>jejunum: the middle part of the small intestine; its name comes from the Latin "jejunus," meaning hungry or empty</term>. 

<margin>How the jejunum intestine got its name.</margin>

This is because, namely, pure **yellow bile** <term>yellow bile: original "cholera citrina", one of the four humors of ancient medicine</term> comes to this same intestine—that is, unmixed with waste—as the commentators of Avicenna explain. For if the waste mixed with **chyle** <term>chyle: the milky fluid of digested food</term> is drawn from the duodenum, from which it immediately descends to the following intestine called the jejunum, how can the yellow bile reach the jejunum pure (that is, unmixed with waste)? In the jejunum, it would encounter waste mixed with chyle, just as in the other following intestines. Nor can they say that a complete separation of waste from the chyle occurs in the intestine called the duodenum, since they say that waste mixed with chyle reaches even the **cecum** <term>cecum: original "monoculum" (one-eyed), the pouch at the beginning of the large intestine</term> and the **colon** as well. This is indicated by Avicenna’s own words in the cited chapter written on the cecum, in this manner:

>> "And of these matters, it is because this intestine is..."

<summary>Leoniceno critiques Avicenna’s theory that the jejunum is empty because it contains "pure" bile, arguing that if food waste moves from the stomach through the duodenum, it must also be present in the jejunum.</summary>

We do not, however, say for that reason that either urine or sweat receives its substantial form in the stomach; rather, the one is formed in the veins, or more properly in the **kidneys** as **Theophilus** <note>Theophilus Protospatharius, a 7th-century medical writer</note> prefers, and the other in the limbs, at
