which the same watery superfluity <note>original: "superfluitas," referring to the excess fluid not used by the body</note> sends along with the blood. For this is the vehicle of nourishment, both that which is carried from the **stomach** <note>original: "ventriculo"</note> through the **mesenteric veins** <term>mesenteric: the veins that transport absorbed nutrients from the digestive tract to the liver</term> to the **liver** <note>original: "epar"</note>, and that which is transmitted from the liver to nourish the entire body. Therefore, the reasoning of **Gentile** <note>Gentile da Foligno (d. 1348), a prominent medical commentator</note> and **Jacopo da Forlì** <note>Jacopo da Forlì (d. 1414), an Italian physician and philosopher</note>, by which they strive to prove that dung receives its **substantial form** <term>substantial form: a philosophical term for the essential nature that makes a thing what it is</term> in the stomach—on the grounds that the same thing gives form to both what is helpful and what is harmful—we can refute in this way: **Sweat** is the wateriness of the blood, as not only **Galen** in Book XI of *On Simple Medicine* and Book I of *On Healthful Matters* attests, but also **Avicenna** in the second book of the *Canon*; and yet blood receives its substantial form in the liver, while sweat [receives its form] in other parts of the body. We can make a similar argument from **urine**, which has the same matter as sweat, as **Galen** holds in the previously cited Book XI of *On Simple Medicine*; and yet it is formed in the **kidneys** <note>original: "renibus"</note>, as we said was the opinion of **Theophilus** <note>Theophilus Protospatharius, a 7th-century Byzantine medical writer known for his work on uroscopy</note>, which **Aegidius** <note>Likely Aegidius of Corbeil (d. 1224), a physician famous for his poems on urine</note> also confirms; and yet blood, of which urine is the superfluity, is generated in the liver.

Why indeed we can judge the condition not only of the kidneys, but primarily of the liver and the veins, from the urine is not difficult to understand by reason, since that watery matter from which urine is made in the kidneys undergoes much from the veins and liver before it is drawn by the kidneys and converted into liquid urine. In the same way, from the **dung** <note>original: "stercore"</note> we judge the conditions of both the stomach and the intestines: because although dung is generated in the intestines, the matter from which it is made previously underwent the most alteration in the stomach itself. We have shown this above by the authority of **Galen’s** third book of *On Natural Powers*, in the passage where he writes that many necessary alterations occur before bread is transmuted into dung.

But now let us leave this rank and fetid dispute over the generation of dross, which by its very odor might offend the nostrils of readers, and turn to that which in the second place

...as we had proposed to do, let us return to the defense of **Hermolaus** <note>Hermolaus Barbarus (1454–1493), a Venetian scholar famous for his "Corrections to Pliny" (*Castigationes Plinianae*)</note> in those matters pertaining to medicine. I see he is further rebuked by **Pliny’s defender** <note>Refers to Pandolfo Collenuccio, who wrote a defense of Pliny against Leoniceno’s criticisms</note> for saying that **strumae** <term>struma: a swelling of the neck, typically what we now call scrofula or tuberculous cervical lymphadenitis</term> are **adenes** <note>original: "adenas," from the Greek word for glands</note>. The critic objects that *strumae* are not *adenes*, but rather grow within them, and even then, not in all of them. I marvel at this objection made by Pliny’s defender, as I hear he interprets **Paul of Aegina** <note>A 7th-century Byzantine Greek physician</note>; in that author, he could have read that **choerades** <note>original: "choeradas," the Greek term for scrofulous swellings</note>—which in Latin we call *strumae* and in the common tongue **scrofulae**—are hardened *adenes* [glands]. Therefore, Pliny's defender cannot reproach Hermolaus for writing that *strumae* are *adenes* without equally condemning the very author he interprets. He also accuses Hermolaus of falsely believing that **leucomata** and **argemata** <term>leucomata and argemata: different types of white spots or ulcers on the eye's cornea</term> are the same thing. For that he himself unjustly rebuked Hermolaus—a man of no less stature in our age—is shown by Hermolaus’s own words concerning *argemata* and *leucomata*, written in this manner:

> **Argemata** <note>original: "Argemata," small white ulcers on the edge of the iris</note> seem to be almost the same as **leucomata** <note>original: "leucomata," a white opacity of the cornea</note>, that is, **white spots** <note>original: "albugines"</note>, although in the entry for the herb *lotos*, **Dioscorides** <note>A 1st-century Greek physician and botanist</note> seems to separate them, since he records that the herb is effective against both *argemata* and *leucomata*—unless one thinks that **glaucomata** <note>original: "glaucomata," referring here to a clouding of the eye</note> should be written in that place instead of *leucomata*.

In this passage, Hermolaus does not actually decide whether *argemata* and *leucomata* are the same eye defect, but because of a certain similarity in color between both conditions, he doubts not without reason. However, near the end of the entire work—that is, the *Cancellations and Glosses on Pliny*—where he reminds the reader how to judge his labor, he very clearly sets out the difference between **argemon** and **leucoma** based on the authority of Paul [of Aegina]. Although, as he later adds, "we have learned, as **Pausanias** <note>A 2nd-century Greek traveler and geographer</note> reports, that *argemon* was thought to be the same as *leucoma*." <margin>Argemon.</margin> ...what we have said is this: An *argemon* <note>A white ulcer on the edge of the iris</note> differs from a *leucoma*, which is to say, a white spot. Paul <note>Paul of Aegina, a 7th-century Byzantine physician</note> says that an *argemon* is an ulcer of that circle called the **iris**—that is, the "celestial bow" in the eye—which is red on the outside and white on the inside. 
<margin>Albugo.</margin> An **albugo** <note>A white opacity or "white spot" on the cornea</note> is a somewhat deep scar of the eyes, appearing like a small cloud on the surface. If only **Avicenna** <note>The famous Persian physician Ibn Sina (980–1037)</note> had distinguished *albugo* from *argemon* so clearly! For from the definition of *albugo* which that same Avicenna provides in the <term>Third Canon</term> <note>Referring to Book III of Avicenna's *Canon of Medicine*, which deals with localized diseases</note>, it is not apparent how *albugo* differs from *argemon*—unless Pliny’s defender can manifest this difference from Avicenna’s words in the same way I have revealed it from the writings of Hermolaus, who cited Paul. If he manages this, we shall tolerate his obvious slander against Hermolaus with a more even mind. 

But now I see that I have wandered further than I intended in describing the errors of Pliny’s defender and of other physicians. I have not even run through every single chapter of Pliny’s book or the anatomy of his defender, but have only noted those points that arose in the defense of ourselves or of Hermolaus. Indeed, what I thought at the beginning was a mere "game"—this dispute over Pliny’s errors—I now see has become a useful, or rather almost hateful, contention. 

Yet it was Pliny’s defender who first gave no small occasion for this. In the preface to his *Emendations of Pliny*, he strives to dishonor me—even though I am bound to him by an old friendship—simply because I criticized Pliny on the subject of metals. He did not do this with logic and arguments, which I could have borne with a calm mind, but with mockery and insults. He calls me a **smatterer** <note>original: *sciolum*, a "know-it-all" possessing only superficial knowledge</note> and a **babbler** against an author celebrated for so many centuries. He claims I am **summoning ghosts to a pointless fight**, calling me **unlearned and unrefined** (for not "tasting" the wisdom of Pliny), and labeling me a **shameless and licentious slanderer**. He has said many other things directed at me specifically that could have provoked even Socrates, the most patient of men regarding injuries, to anger. For my part, although I profess to follow moral philosophy as much as any other branch of philosophy...

For I do not hate those who contradict me, but rather those who slander me—especially because they incite me to do what I would otherwise not wish to do: to speak ill of others in return. Leoniceno is dismissive of critics who focus on minor linguistic points rather than scientific or medical truth.</note> recently turned my stomach; though they have barely progressed beyond their first ABCs, they dare to pass judgment on higher studies. But let them chatter as much as they like; my ears shall henceforth be closed to their noise, lest at my age, by disputing with them over the rules of grammar, I seem to be turning into a child again <note>original: "repuerescere."</note>. 

However, if there are those who wish to fight against me regarding matters of medicine or universal philosophy—fields in which I have offered broad ground for any who wish to duel—and if they choose to enter a glorious contest, not so much for Pliny as for **Avicenna** <note>The 11th-century Persian physician whose "Canon of Medicine" dominated European universities, often criticized by Humanists like Leoniceno for its "Arabic" corruptions of Greek medicine.</note> and the other medical followers of Avicenna whom I have noted in this work, we are ready to respond with the same modesty we desire from them. We are prepared either to retract our own errors, if they demonstrate that we and not they have erred, or to further confirm the errors of others if they are weakly defended—and even to heap up many more errors, just as we have recently done regarding Pliny.

## FRANCESCO TOTTI <note>original: "Franciscus Tottus." Totti was a student from Lucca who became a close associate of Leoniceno.</note> OF LUCCA,
## To Nicolò Leoniceno, sends his warmest greetings. <note>original: "S. P. D." (Salutem Plurimam Dicit), a standard Latin greeting meaning "sends many greetings."</note>

<image-desc>Ornate decorative initial 'D' featuring intricate floral and foliate scrolls within a square border.</image-desc>

I had already decided from my earliest years of study, once I had determined to devote my efforts to the science of healing, to choose for myself a teacher who surpassed all others in both talent and learning. Since it is the nature of virtue that it cannot remain hidden in the shadows, but instead brings forth and elevates men even of the lowliest condition into the light, it so happened that I desired you above all as my teacher. In the judgment of every learned man, you alone are considered in this age, throughout the entire world, as the foremost glory of medicine and, by the highest right, its finest father. 

For this reason, I came to Ferrara—a city made illustrious in those times by you alone as its professor—with the intention of having you as my sole guide, to whom I might entrust myself entirely. In your teaching, I hoped I would achieve everything I desired. Nor did the hope I had conceived of you fail me in any part; for the things I had heard of you from afar through constant report, the reality itself has confirmed to be far greater. 

For while I applied myself to the liberal arts <note>The "liberal studies" (grammar, logic, rhetoric, etc.) were the foundation of a Renaissance education before a student specialized in medicine or law.</note> and the medical craft under your guidance, I noticed nothing more pleasant than your company, nothing more excellent than your talent, and nothing more abundant than your learning—which indeed is adorned in a wonderful way by your integrity of character and innate kindness <term>humanitas</term> <note>A central Renaissance value combining classical learning with refined, compassionate behavior.</note>. 

To this is added the fact that in these times, nothing can be found or even imagined more acute in speaking than you alone, nothing more certain in responding, and finally, nothing more sublime in teaching the meanings of the ancient philosophers or physicians, or more beneficial in treating the sick. 

But I omit these things, which have been declared by you in many places, through which you have gained the favor of many nobles and other most distinguished princes. I do so especially lest someone might think I am saying these things merely to flatter your ears—I, who have always abhorred all flattery—even though I judge it to be my duty, out of my supreme devotion to you...

...would accuse Barbarus <note>Hermolao Barbarus (1454–1493), a famous Venetian humanist who, like Leoniceno, worked to correct errors in Pliny’s *Natural History*.</note>, a man who is both most friendly to you and most deserving in the field of literature, too sharply—I might even say too boldly. I am therefore wonderfully glad, since this is clearly honorable for you, and it makes you not only influential among many, but also more dearly loved. 

I also strongly congratulate you on the praise which you have won most fully among all men for this reason; but you will achieve a far greater and more solid fame, and commend your name to immortality, if (as everyone is now convinced) you will rescue medicine from all darkness and obscurity. I ask that you do not disappoint this expectation, adorned as you are with such great learning and talent; by whose labor and help alone we hope, without doubt, to be liberated from pestiferous barbarism <note>In the Renaissance, "barbarism" often referred to the corrupted medieval translations of scientific texts that humanists sought to replace with direct translations from the original Greek.</note> once you have translated all the works of Galen into the Latin language. 

Truly, this—which is most beneficial for the human race—is what Battista Egnazio <note>Giovanni Battista Egnazio (1478–1553), a prominent Venetian humanist and educator.</note> desires no less than I; his refined manners and distinguished erudition in both Greek and Latin could easily entice anyone to love him. This is what Lodovico Bonaccioli, Cesare Optato, Girolamo Menochio, and our own Lorenzo Bertolini—truly the most famous physicians—most greedily desire. To this, all the other brilliant minds among physicians exhort you; this, I say, is that one thing which all students of letters most especially demand and expect. I do not believe the expectations of all these men should be delayed any longer, so that we—and even posterity—may acknowledge ourselves to be greatly indebted to you for such a significant benefit. 

Farewell, and know that I will always be ready to serve you, in accordance with your unique kindness toward me, in whatever way I can be of use to you in deed or labor. 

Venice, the Ides of March <note>March 15th</note>, 1509.

# GIROLAMO MENOCHIO OF LU-
## cca, physician, to Niccolò Leoniceno, the preeminent
## Philosopher and physician, sends greetings.

<image-desc>A square woodcut ornamental initial 'C' containing a scene of a figure in a classical landscape. The figure appears to be kneeling or working on the ground in a garden. In the background, there is a building with a tower and rolling hills under a clear sky.</image-desc>

Since there are many things, most learned man, which entice men to love, virtue especially seems to hold the greatest power among them. Therefore, when in recent days I diligently read through your interpretation of **Galen’s Art of Healing** <note>original: *curativæ artis Galeni*, referring to Galen's *Methodus Medendi*</note>, which was granted to me by Constantius of Pistoia, the Chancellor; and when I also saw here some of your writings on the **dipsas** <term>dipsas: a species of viper in classical lore whose bite was said to cause an unquenchable, fatal thirst</term>, and also some pieces written against a certain Pistoian by our mutual friend Francesco Totti of Lucca, I was moved beyond measure to love you. This was so even though I had already begun to admire your excellence once before, when I spoke with you there regarding the disease they call the **French sickness** <note>original: *morbo, quem Gallicum appellant*. This refers to syphilis, which was a new and terrifying epidemic in Italy at the end of the 15th century</note>.

In these writings of yours, I truly found many things that were dear to my heart, but one especially regarding the **rabid dog** <note>the subject of rabies or hydrophobia</note>. I had spoken much on this subject once in the house of **Aldus the Roman** <note>Aldus Manutius (c. 1449–1515), the famous Venetian printer and humanist</note> in Venice, in the presence of the Venetian physician Niccolò Zoccha. At that time, because I had read **Dioscorides** <note>A 1st-century Greek physician and botanist</note> in Greek, as well as many other more recent Latin authors who set down such a grave disease and its cure according to their art, my experience actually conflicted with the words of **Aristotle**; yet I did not think it was permitted for me to rail against such a great philosopher. For this reason, I give you enormous thanks, and I am grateful because you have removed a most heavy doubt from my mind. 

Your work on the **dipsas**, truly, has struck me with an immense thirst—much like the disease itself—to read anything coming out of your "workshop" <note>Menochio is making a play on words: reading about a thirst-inducing snake has made him "thirsty" for more of Leoniceno's scholarship</note>. I urge you, therefore, so far as your busy schedule allows, to set about translating the remaining volumes of Galen; or, if you have already begun, that you hasten to publish them. For what is circulated that is more full of errors than his Latin books? Or what is more foul? Indeed, his books have been so corrupted that anyone even moderately learned in Latin would scorn to read them. And although one might sweat much over the reading of them, nevertheless from that effort...

...often no sense at all, and sometimes even a perverted sense, can be drawn out, whereas nothing is more elegant than a reading of Galen’s books in the original Greek. Strive, therefore, to rescue him from these Barbarians; for you alone are able to do so. But if you should disdain to do it, I fear that just as the Barbarians—I mean, of course, the Turks—have plundered and now hold a great part of Greece, so too the barbarian physicians of our own time will utterly ruin and tear Galen to pieces with their petty interpretations. Free such a great man, then, from such a calamity. If you do this, you will first do something pleasing to God, and then you will devise a certain healthy and common remedy for both the living and for future generations. For you know well how many errors, and of what great consequence, are daily committed in this medical art. But more on these things at another time. 

If I can do anything here for your Excellence, I offer you my labor, my home, and my whole self. And so that I might not await a response from you without great benefit to myself, I ask that you deign to explain to me by letter under which chapter in the Greek text of Dioscorides <note>original: *Dios.*, referring to Pedanius Dioscorides, the 1st-century author of the most influential pharmaceutical manual in history, *De materia medica*</note> that substance is found which we call **purging cassia** <term>cassia fistula: a tropical tree whose pods contain a sweet, dark pulp used in the Renaissance as a mild laxative</term>, and what name he gives to it. Likewise, I would wish to learn from your Excellence where the same Dioscorides treats of **manna**, and what he means by *manna baes* <note>original: Μάννα βάης. In ancient pharmacy, 'manna' could refer to frankincense grains or various plant exudates; the specific term here refers to a variety Leoniceno was debating</note>; also, what **ixias** <term>ixias: likely referring to the "birdlime thistle" (*Chameleon niger*) or a similar gummy plant described by Dioscorides</term> is. 

For I am not ashamed, nor have I ever been ashamed—even if I know only a little—to learn at last what I do not know from a learned man, such as I have long known you to be. Nor would I wish you to accuse me of greed, because I have decided to enter into friendship—or rather, to confirm it—to my own no small advantage. For my friend Francesco Totti—or rather, *our* friend—has declared to me that you are the sort of man who would gladly educate anyone, even a stranger. Furthermore, I thought it shameful for me to depart thirsty from such a fertile fountain of the clearest water, especially since, having been struck by your work on the **dipsas** <note>original: *dipsade ictus*. This is a clever pun; the 'dipsas' was a legendary viper whose bite caused unquenchable thirst. Menochio says he is "thirsty" for knowledge because he read Leoniceno's treatise on that snake</note>, I have long desired it. 

May your Excellence fare well, to whom I most highly commend myself. 

The twenty-seventh of November, 1503 <note>original: *Quinto Calendas Decembres. M. D. III.*</note>.

# NICCOLÒ LEONICENO to GERO-
# lamo Menochio of Lucca, most distinguished philosopher
# and physician, sends greetings.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'Q' depicting several animals (possibly dogs or hounds) in a natural landscape with trees.</image-desc>

The very eloquent letter which Francesco Totto of Lucca, our mutual friend, recently delivered to me, clearly showed me that you are not one of those who profess barbarian <note>In this context, "barbarian" refers to the medieval Scholastic and Arabic-influenced medical traditions that Leoniceno and other Humanists sought to replace with original Greek sources.</note> philosophy and medicine. Otherwise, you would not write so elegantly, nor would you so greatly approve of our translations or our writings, in which we especially criticize the barbarian authors. Indeed, having read your letter, I have begun to hope well for our age, seeing that I have such men who share my feelings about the whole of philosophy and the art of medicine. You are one such man, as is our friend Giacomo Costanzi of Pistoia <note>original: *Constantius noſter Piſtoriēſis*</note>, and certain others—few in number indeed, but possessing a "virtue living in war" <note>A poetic allusion, likely to Virgil, suggesting a small but brave group fighting against ignorance.</note>; if, due to my now advancing age, I am unable to fulfill all that you most desire and exhort me to do, it will at least be helpful to have held out the lamp and opened the path. By this path, that foul barbarism which long ago occupied all the liberal arts may be driven out or utterly routed.

Therefore, it will be the duty of you and others who take delight in proper studies to strive to achieve together with me what I cannot accomplish alone. We should claim for ourselves—far more justly—that praise which certain men of letters have recently claimed for the rescue of Italy from the Barbarians. For we are not merely recovering the Latin language; we are truly rescuing all people from the danger of death when, by dispelling the shadows of our century, we bring ancient medicine back into the light. This, indeed, seems to me to be true philosophizing: to contend with the Barbarians not over mere words, but over things most necessary for human health. Let them speak as they wish, and call a viper *tirus* <note>A medieval term for a specific type of snake used in medicine.</note> or by any other name, provided they are not ignorant of which serpent is the *tirus* that must be used in the composition of theriac <term>theriac: a famous ancient "universal antidote" made of dozens of ingredients, including viper flesh, which required precise identification of species</term>. ...ignorance, and we have demonstrated that both Albert, surnamed the Great <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a medieval scholar whose works on nature were being re-evaluated by Renaissance humanists.</note>, and also Avicenna <note>The Persian physician Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), whose *Canon of Medicine* was the standard medical textbook of the Middle Ages, but was criticized by Leoniceno for errors in Greek translation.</note>—to whom this age grants the sovereignty of medicine—labored in error regarding our *dipsas* <note>original: *dipsade*. The *dipsas* was a legendary serpent whose bite was said to cause unquenchable thirst. Leoniceno likely wrote a specific treatise on this subject.</note>. If this has induced such a thirst in you as you write, you could, by your own right—as if bitten by that serpent—drain the waters of our fountain with one gulp of the mouth. For why did you ask for so little at the end <note>original: *calce*, literally "the heel."</note> of your letter? Why also did you divide your questions, committing some to the letter and some to the manuscript? Was it because you feared you might too greedily abuse the beginnings—or rather the confirmation—of our friendship? Or was it because you suspect the truth: that there is no fountain here with us, but only a small stream bubbling up, which an immoderate drink could easily dry out?

Nevertheless, given the time available, I shall attempt to satisfy your most honorable desire regarding those things you wish to learn from me. Perhaps I shall fulfill it more abundantly at some time, if it should happen that you wander with me in the mountains of your homeland, which I have decided to visit for this very purpose: so that I may observe the herbs growing in them, both the healing and the harmful.

<margin>Tuscany is fertile in every kind of herb.</margin>

For it does not escape me that Tuscany is most fertile in both medicines and poisons; the same is confirmed by the authority of Theophrastus <note>The "Father of Botany" (c. 371–287 BCE), whose *Enquiry into Plants* was a key source for humanists.</note> in the ninth volume of his *History of Plants*, and by Aeschylus. I make Francesco Totto a witness that this has long been the intention of my mind—a man to whom, on account of his integrity of character and excellence of learning, I am accustomed to reveal all my thoughts. On account of this same purpose of my mind, I do not altogether reject those things which you offer me in your most kind letter. Perhaps I shall use them, if necessity requires, for that work which I hope will also please you—you who are not in that "heresy," as I believe, in which almost all younger physicians are engaged: thinking that this investigation of herbs and other <term>simples</term> <note>original: *simpliciũ medicamentorũ*. "Simples" refer to medicinal plants or minerals used on their own, rather than as part of a complex compound.</note> belongs not to physicians, but to <term>ointment-sellers</term> <note>original: *seplasiarios*. Specifically, sellers of perfumes and ointments in ancient Rome, used here as a derogatory term for uneducated druggists.</note> or <term>pharmacists</term> <note>original: *pharmacopolas*. At this time, physicians were trying to distinguish their "scientific" role from the "trade" of the apothecary.</note>. 

But if Hippocrates, that first parent of medicine, and the ancient physicians who succeeded him, had felt this way, it would not have pleased them to go through the wildernesses and seek herbs, some for one purpose and others for another...

### ON CASSIA FISTULA.

BUT lest I seem to imitate that very talkativeness which I so strongly condemn, let us now come to those things you asked of me at the end <note>original: *calce*, literally "the heel."</note> of your letter. The first of these is: under which chapter is *cassia fistula* <note>The "pudding-pipe tree" (*Cassia fistula*), a tropical tree whose seed pods were used as a laxative.</note> contained in the works of Dioscorides <note>A first-century Greek physician and author of *De Materia Medica*, the primary botanical authority of the era.</note>? And, as part of the same inquiry, under which chapter is *manna* <note>A sweet exudate from the flowering ash tree (*Fraxinus ornus*), used as a mild laxative.</note> found—both of which the more recent physicians use for softening the bowels? Therefore, I respond to both: that the Greek authors—I speak of the ancients—make no specific mention of either, either because they did not know of them, or perhaps they did not approve of them for medical use. Indeed, Galen <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–c. 216 AD), whose medical system dominated European medicine for over a millennium.</note> completely disapproves of a fruit similar to *cassia fistula*, which the Greeks call *ceratia* <note>original: *ceratia* (Greek: κεράτια), referring to the carob fruit (*Ceratonia siliqua*).</note> and the Arabs call—by a corrupted term, I think—*carnubium* <note>Carob.</note>. He goes so far in the second book of *On Foods* as to wish, or rather to think it better, that it were never brought to the people of his nation from the places where it grows. On account of these words, I am struck with wonder at how Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the Persian polymath.</note>, who claims to be an interpreter of Galen, nevertheless incorrectly cites him by saying that this fruit is *not* exported to other regions. For Galen would have wished in vain that it were not brought to his people if it were not already being exported to other regions from the soil where it is produced. Now, I said that *ceratia* <note>carob</note> is a fruit similar to *cassia fistula*, because the color of the bark is the same, and the pulp is also sweet just like *cassia fistula*; furthermore, the same pulp is divided by similar seeds. This is proven not only by the senses but also by the authority of Serapion <note>Serapion the Younger, a 12th-century Arab author of a treatise on medicinal "simples."</note>, who says in his chapter "On Cassia Fistula" that inside the canes of the cassia there are layers of black flesh, with walls dividing them, and between one layer and another there are seeds, just like the seeds of the *naxilocaractæ* <note>Likely a corruption of *xylocaracta*, meaning carob seeds.</note>, and of the same size, whose color is

...between gray-blue and redness. By *xilocaracta* <note>original: *xilocaracta*, from the Greek *xylokeraton*, literally "wood-horn."</note> we ought to understand the fruit which the Greeks call both *ceratia* and *xilocaracta*, the Latins call the "sweet pod" <note>original: *siliquam dulcem*, referring to the carob (*Ceratonia siliqua*).</note>, and the Arabs, as we said before, call *carnubium* [carob]. But the sweet pod and *cassia fistula* <note>The purging cassia or "pudding-pipe tree" (*Cassia fistula*), whose long pods contain a laxative pulp.</note> share the same properties. For the pulp <note>original: *medulla*, literally "marrow."</note> of both, when fresh, loosens the bowels; but when dried, it rather constricts them. Regarding the sweet pod, Dioscorides, Galen, and Paul <note>Paul of Aegina, a 7th-century Byzantine medical writer.</note>, as well as Pliny among our own Latin authors, testify to this. Regarding *cassia fistula*, it is established by the experience of doctors.

However, it is necessary to remind the younger doctors that in the books of the Greeks, such as those of Dioscorides and Galen, one indeed reads about *cassia fistula*, but not about the one you are asking about, which has the power to soften the belly. For that reason, it is named the "pharmaceutical pod" <note>original: *siliqua pharmaceutica*.</note> by some more recent authors. Instead, [the Greeks] speak of a certain species of "woody cassia" <note>original: *cassia lignea*, a fragrant bark similar to cinnamon.</note>, which is called <term>syrinx</term> <note>original: *σύριγξ*, meaning a pipe or tube.</note>—that is, "fistula"—by those same Greeks. Therefore, one must pay diligent attention so that when we find "cassia fistula" written in the books of the Greeks, we do not think it refers to the other one of which the Arab authors speak.

Indeed, I know that most of the more recent doctors are frequently entangled in this error, using the bark of the "Arabian" *cassia fistula* in medicine to stimulate menstruation, when they ought rather to use "woody cassia" for that purpose, following the authority of Dioscorides and other Greek doctors. These Greeks seem to have ignored the other *cassia fistula* [the laxative pod], just as they completely looked down upon other fruits of trees which the Arab authors, and the younger doctors who follow them, use frequently.

Certain Arab authors, especially Serapio <note>Serapion the Younger, a 13th-century physician who compiled Arab and Greek botanical knowledge.</note>, recommend "jujubes" <note>original: *iuiubas*, the fruit of the *Ziziphus jujuba* tree.</note> for many medical uses. Thus, younger doctors provide the water in which jujubes have been boiled as a drink for those suffering from "hot and thin phlegm" <note>In the humoral system, a condition where thin, irritating mucus was thought to cause illness.</note>. Galen, however, in his second book *On Foods*, in the chapter "On Serica"—that is, *zinzifis* or jujubes—frankly confesses that he has nothing to testify regarding them for the preservation of health...

He highlights how the medical tradition has shifted from Greek foundations to include Arabic botanical knowledge, such as the use of jujubes.</summary>

### OF CASSIA FISTULA ###

...preservation <note>original: *[con]seruationem*</note>, or the treatment of diseases. For they are, as he says, the food of unruly women and children, providing little nourishment and being indigestible. Together with this, because it is not a food that is good for the stomach <note>original: *eustomachum*</note>, it is clear that they also give little to the body. What is more common in the talk of doctors than "sebesten," or "eclegma" <note>A syrupy medicine intended to be licked or dissolved in the mouth.</note>, or—to use the terms common among younger doctors—the "electuary of sebesten"? Yet concerning this medicine, so famous among the Arabs and younger doctors, neither Dioscorides nor Galen mentioned anything at all. 

However, Paul <note>Paul of Aegina, a 7th-century Byzantine physician.</note>, who lived later than both, said only this about the <term>mixa</term> <note>original: *mixa*; the Assyrian plum or sebesten (*Cordia myxa*).</note>: that it is the fruit of a tree, smaller than plums, but similar in its properties. <margin>The *mixa* fruit.</margin> Now, we have very little doubt that the *mixa* is the fruit which the Arabs call <term>sebesten</term>; for our very senses prove it, with Paul's words confirming the same. For it is, as he says, a fruit similar to a plum, but smaller than it. 

Pliny also, in Book XIV of his *Natural History*—specifically in the chapter on the trees of Syria—speaks of plums grown on the mountains of Damascus and *mixas* together, and he says that both fruits are now familiar to Italy. Perhaps this study of ours will be of use to the science of medicine if I now identify with Latin or Greek names those things which more recent doctors are accustomed to announce only by foreign <note>original: *barbaris*; Leoniceno uses this term to refer to Arabic medical authorities whose influence he sought to replace with classical Greek and Latin sources.</note> names, and which they obtain only from foreigners, and if I demonstrate that they can even be found in Italy. 

For some time ago, we stripped the <term>tiris</term> <note>original: *tiris*, referring to the *tyrus* or viper.</note> of its reputation for high value, showing that there are other serpents in Italy far more useful than the Egyptian vipers for the composition of <term>theriac</term> <note>A famous ancient "universal antidote" made of many ingredients, including viper flesh.</note>. And we have already become hateful to those who sell names rather than true remedies. But we write these things for you and those like you, who do not seek profit from the art of medicine so much as the health of mankind, and who prefer to treat the sick in Italy in Latin rather than in Arabic.

### NICCOLÒ LEONICENO ON MANNA ###

**CONCERNING** manna—about which you also ask what it is according to Dioscorides <note>A 1st-century Greek physician and author of *De Materia Medica*.</note>—if I were to agree with the opinion of Simon of Genoa <note>A 13th-century physician and lexicographer.</note>, who in the letter M, in the chapter "On Honey," says that the ancient Greeks had no knowledge of the sugar <note>original: *zuchari*</note> which we use in various compositions, I would say what he suggests in his own words in the cited passage: that "manna" in Dioscorides is actually the "sugar" named by that same Dioscorides in the chapter "On Honey." However, I feel differently. I believe that sugar <note>original: *sacharum*</note> in his work, as also in Galen’s, is that which we commonly call sugar <note>original: *zucharum*</note>. Furthermore, while the ancient Greeks did indeed speak of sugar specifically as a certain type of honey, they spoke of manna only in a general sense, not specifically. This is true despite the fact that Mesue <note>An influential, likely 13th-century medical author often cited in the Middle Ages.</note> falsely alleges in three places that Galen speaks of manna: namely, in the chapter "On Manna," the chapter "On Scammony," and the chapter "On the Preparation of Manna According to the Invention of Galen." For manna, according to the Greek authors, is not a medicine that softens the belly <note>A laxative.</note>, but rather one that binds it <note>An astringent.</note>, and it is more frequently called 
<margin>Manna of frankincense</margin> 
manna of frankincense <note>original: *manna thuris*</note>, which is also simply called "manna." For, as Galen says in the thirteenth book of the *Art of Healing*, that which is called manna is the fragments <note>original: *concussio*; the small crumbs or dust created when frankincense is shaken or struck.</note> of frankincense, which possesses a small degree of binding power, and for that reason, it is better for certain uses than the frankincense itself. For frankincense has only the power to promote suppuration <note>The formation of pus to heal a wound.</note> and is not at all styptic <note>A substance that shrinks tissues or stops bleeding.</note>, especially the type that is fattier and whiter in color; just as that which is more yellow dries things out more. But to that which is called manna, a small amount of the bark of the frankincense tree is mixed in, from which it derives its binding power. Pliny writes to the same effect in Book XII of his *Natural History*, in the fifteenth chapter titled "On the Nature and Types of Frankincense." These are his words: 
> We call the crumbs shaken out by impact "manna." 
Though by a fault of the manuscript, "mammam" is read instead of "mannam"; thus, your third question has now been satisfied in passing.

<meta>catchword: -ctum (This likely completes a word like *satisfactum* on the following page.)</meta>

### CONCERNING MANNA ###

...stated <note>Connecting from the previous page: "which is... stated."</note> what manna of frankincense is according to Dioscorides <note>A 1st-century Greek physician and author of *De Materia Medica*.</note>. But above, I said that the Greek authors write about manna—a medicine comparable to purging cassia <term>cassia fistula: the 'pudding-pipe tree,' whose pods were used as a mild laxative</term>—if not specifically, at least in a general sense. This is because this manna which "loosens the belly" <note>Acts as a laxative.</note> can be referred to the chapter "On Honey" among those same Greek authors, just as sugar <note>original: "sacharum"</note> is, which is categorized as a species of honey both by Dioscorides and also by Galen <note>A Greek physician whose work formed the basis of Western medicine for centuries.</note>. Indeed, these are the words of Dioscorides concerning sugar:

> What is called "sugar" <note>original: "sacharũ"</note> is also a kind of honey that hardens in India and is found in "Happy Arabia" <note>Arabia Felix, the southern part of the Arabian Peninsula.</note> within reeds; in its substance it is similar to salt, and it crumbles between the teeth like salt.

Although Simon of Genoa <note>A 13th-century physician and lexicographer.</note>, as we noted above, thought that this sugar mentioned by Dioscorides was not what we call sugar <note>original: "zucharum"</note>, but rather a certain species of manna, this provides the only reason that Mesue <note>A common name for influential medical authors in the Middle Ages.</note> might be excused for alleging that Galen writes about manna—if by "manna" he understands the sugar which Dioscorides and Galen consider a species of honey. For manna, of which the Arabic authors speak more specifically, differs little from sugar and honey, as is clear from the authority of both Serapion <note>Likely Serapion the Younger, a 12th-century writer on medicinal plants.</note> and also Avicenna <note>A Persian polymath and one of the most significant physicians of the Islamic Golden Age.</note>. Nor does it stand in the way that honey is produced almost everywhere and is the work of bees, while manna is found in only a few places and is solely a gift of nature. Since if this reasoning were valid to prove that manna should not be categorized under the chapter "On Honey," it would also prove the same for sugar, which in the time of Dioscorides—as appears from the words of this author noted above—was found only in India and Happy Arabia in reeds, and yet it is numbered among the species of honey not only by Dioscorides but also by Galen. These two authors wrote about both in the same chapter. Although Avicenna seems to have distinguished "Indian salt" <note>original: "salem Indum"</note>—about which Dioscorides wrote—not only from honey but also from sugar. Indeed, in the fourth...

<meta>This page continues Nicolai Leoniceno’s analysis of pharmacological substances, specifically focusing on the distinction between various types of sugar and "Indian salt" as described by Avicenna and other medical authorities. # NICCOLÒ LEONICENO #

...in the Canon <note>original: "Canone." This completes the word from the previous page, referring to Avicenna's *Canon of Medicine*.</note> and he names both **Taberzeth sugar** <term>Taberzeth sugar: a highly refined, hard white sugar, the name of which derives from the Persian word for "axe-cut" because of its solidity</term> and **Indian salt** among the remedies that act against roughness of the tongue. However, he prescribes Taberzeth sugar when this roughness stems from viscosity <note>A sticky or thick quality of the fluids in the mouth</note>, and Indian salt when it stems from dryness. Thus, it appears that **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the most influential philosopher-scientist of the medieval Islamic world</note> considers Indian salt to be something different from Taberzeth sugar.

Nevertheless, the commentators on Avicenna, such as **Gentile** <note>Gentile da Foligno (d. 1348), a famous Italian physician known for his extensive commentaries on Avicenna</note> and **Herculanus** <note>Giovanni Arcolani (d. 1458), an Italian medical professor</note>, understand **sugar candy** <note>Crystallized sugar or rock candy</note> to be meant by "Indian salt." Yet, this interpretation contradicts the words of Avicenna himself in the fourth book of his *Canon*, in the chapter *On the roughness of the tongue in those with fever*, where he states that the salt imported from India has the color of salt and the sweetness of honey.

Avicenna—as well as **Paul** <note>Paul of Aegina, a 7th-century Greek physician whose works were a primary source for later Arabic medicine</note>, from whom Avicenna adopted this remedy almost word for word—means a white salt that is mixed into food as a seasoning. Sugar candy, however, is not described as being entirely white in color, but rather somewhat yellowish. One might also ask Avicenna and his commentators why Taberzeth sugar would be effective for roughness caused by viscosity, while sugar candy works for that caused by dryness, since according to the same Avicenna in the second book of the *Canon*, Taberzeth sugar has a soothing power. No authority or logic establishes this for sugar candy—unless by "sugar candy" we mean the red variety. For according to Avicenna, both *suimenum* <note>original: "suimenum," a term used in medieval translations of Arabic texts to refer to a specific sugar preparation</note> and red sugars have a more powerful soothing effect. However, sugar candy is distinguished from red sugar even by more recent physicians.

Perhaps this error of the commentators, who interpret Indian salt as sugar candy, is of little consequence to medical practice, since sugar candy is an artificial product made from <margin>Sugar candy</margin> white sugar. What is more worthy of investigation is whether sugar candy should be given to feverish patients to quench their thirst by being held in the mouth, as many physicians do in our time, and as **Montagnana** <note>Bartolomeo Montagnana (d. 1452), a celebrated professor of medicine at the University of Padua</note> suggests should be done in one of his *consilia* <note>A formal medical opinion or case study written for a specific patient</note>, where he says that sugar candy is used by illustrious men...

# ON THE POISON IXIA #

...matters <note>original: "bus." Completing the word "rebus" from the previous page.</note> that it is named "Constantinopolitan salt," and he says it should be collected in the first fen of the fourth book <note>Referring to the divisions of Avicenna’s *Canon of Medicine*</note> in the chapter *On the treatment of thirst in fevers*. However, it is clear from the authority of **Avicenna**—who writes these words concerning **haoscer sugar** in the second book of the *Canon*—that no species of sugar is suitable for extinguishing thirst, except perhaps for haoscer sugar, which is a certain species of manna:

> <note>original: "Et non facit sitim, sicut ĩ reliquæ species zuchari: quoniam eius dulcedo est parua, & est bonum stomacho & epati."</note> "And it does not cause thirst, as do the other species of sugar: since its sweetness is small, and it is good for the stomach and liver."

From these words we can gather two things: first, that **haoscer sugar** <term>haoscer sugar: a Persian term for a medicinal substance often identified as "shukkar-al-ushar," a sweet excretion found on the Calotropis procera shrub</term>—which is a manna that falls upon the **alusar** <term>alusar: likely the 'Ushar' or Sodom Apple shrub</term> and is like pieces of salt—is called both "sugar" and "manna"; and second, that the other species of sugar actually cause thirst by their excessive sweetness, with the exception of that which is called haoscer sugar. Therefore, since **sugar candy** <note>Crystallized sugar or rock candy</note> is a form of sugar distinct from haoscer sugar, it does not seem to have any efficacy for extinguishing thirst. And if we wish to speak the truth, Avicenna is poorly cited by **Montagnana** <note>Bartolomeo Montagnana (d. 1460), a Paduan physician</note> in the first fen of the fourth book, in the chapter *On the treatment of thirst in fevers*: for in that chapter there are no words from which we can conclude anything about sugar candy being named by Avicenna among the other remedies pertaining to the extinction of thirst.

### ON THE POISON IXIA. ###

Now, regarding the **ixia** <term>ixia: a term with multiple meanings in ancient botany, referring variously to birdlime, a genus of plants, or specific thistle-like plants like the Pine Thistle</term>, which you also ask about in your letter—what it is according to **Dioscorides** <note>A 1st-century Greek physician and author of *De Materia Medica*</note> and in the manuscript, and what it is according to Avicenna and the more recent physicians—it is not easy to answer. This is due to the ambiguity of the name, not only among the Greeks but also among the Arabs. For both the **white chameleon** and the **black chameleon** <term>chameleon: refers to types of thistles, likely Atractylis gummifera (black) and Carlina acaulis (white)</term> are called "ixias" by the Greeks; and furthermore, there is a certain kind of poison which is called not only "ixias" but also **ulophonos** <note>original: "ulophonos." From the Greek meaning "wolf-killer."</note>. Although this latter name is also attributed by these same Greeks to the root of the black chameleon, which is itself a poison. **Paul** <note>Paul of Aegina, a 7th-century Byzantine physician</note> treats both roots—that of the black chameleon and the ixia poison—in his treatise on poisons. Dioscorides, however, in the same treatise, speaks only of the ixia, a poison which he also mentions very often in his books written *On Simple Medicine*...

# NICCOLÒ LEONICENO #

<note>original: "meminit." This completes the sentence from the previous page: "...as Dioscorides mentions."</note> mentions it. For in the chapter *On Wormwood* <term>wormwood: *Artemisia absinthium*, a bitter herb used since antiquity for digestive issues and as an antidote</term>, he says that when taken with wine, it counteracts *ixia* and hemlock. Likewise, in the chapter *On Castoreum* or on the testicles of the beaver, he says they are drunk with vinegar against deadly drugs, but particularly against *ixia*. Writing also on how *oxymel* <term>oxymel: a traditional medicinal drink made from a mixture of honey and vinegar</term> is prepared, he later adds this among other benefits: that it helps those who have drunk poppy juice <note>original: "meconium," the juice of the opium poppy</note> or *ixia*. Likewise, in the chapter *On Goat-marjoram*, he says all its species are useful against the ingestion of *ixia* with wine—and in many other places, which we do not wish to recount except as they pertain to our purpose. **Dioscorides** <note>Pedanius Dioscorides (c. 40–90 AD), the primary Greek authority on botany and pharmacology in the Renaissance</note> speaks of *ixia* as a poison. Therefore, if you ask what *ixias* is in the fourth book of **Dioscorides**, I can answer for the present that it is a poison of its own kind, and a root itself, as **Paulus** <note>Paul of Aegina (c. 625–690 AD), a Byzantine physician whose works summarized ancient medical knowledge</note> testifies where he treats poisons; although he does not explain which plant the root belongs to, it is nonetheless different from the root of the black chameleon thistle, as is clear from the same **Paulus**, who creates two separate chapters among the poisons, one *On the root of the black chameleon* and the other *On ixia*, as we also indicated a little earlier. 

I notice that **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder (23–79 AD), whose *Natural History* was often criticized by Leoniceno for translation errors</note> very often in his books on natural history has named this same kind of poison "birdlime" <note>original: "viscum." In Greek, *ixia* can mean birdlime, a sticky substance used to catch birds. Leoniceno is pointing out that Pliny may have confused the specific poison *ixia* with the general substance birdlime</note>—I know not if correctly—and wrote that the same remedies work against birdlime which **Dioscorides** wrote against the poison *ixia*, of which we spoke just now. For in Book 20, Chapter 17, regarding *Goat-marjoram*, he writes thus:

> "Goat-marjoram <term>goat-marjoram: *Tragoriganum*, a pungent herb similar to oregano or savory</term> is similar to wild thyme; it promotes urine, disperses tumors, and is most effective when drunk against birdlime and the bite of a viper."

Likewise, in Book 23, Chapter 2:

> "**Oxymel**," he says, "the ancients admit to have been beneficial against birdlime."

Likewise, in Book 27, Chapter 7, he uses these words:

> "There are several kinds of **wormwood**; they are opposed to birdlime and hemlock when taken with wine."

Similarly, in Book 32, Chapter 3, he writes thus:

> "Beaver testicles, when drunk, heal against poisons; they specifically help against birdlime when taken with vinegar."

But also the same **Pliny**...

### ON THE POISON IXIA ###

In book 20, chapter 14, **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder (23–79 AD), author of the *Natural History*</note> says that leaves of **rue** <term>rue: *Ruta graveolens*, a bitter herb used in antiquity as a "universal" antidote</term>, crushed and taken with wine, are effective against **aconite** <term>aconite: a highly toxic flowering plant, also known as monkshood or wolfsbane</term>, and especially against **mistletoe** <note>original: "viscum." In this context, Leoniceno is arguing that Pliny uses the word for mistletoe/bird-lime to mean the poison *ixia*</note>. **Dioscorides** employs this same remedy in his book *On Poisons* against the drinking of the poison **ixia** <term>ixia: a toxic, gummy substance derived from the root of the chameleon thistle (*Atractylis gummifera*)</term>. Likewise, Pliny in book 23, chapter 6, praises resins as being effective against mistletoe. Dioscorides, in the same book, especially recommends fir resin against the poison *ixia*.

From all of these examples—the words of both Pliny and Dioscorides compared with one another—it appears clearer than light that Pliny called that kind of poison which the Greeks call *ixia* by the name **viscum** <note>original: "uiscum," referring here to the sticky substance or bird-lime</note>, as we have said. **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the influential Persian physician</note> also speaks of mistletoe as a poison in the fourth book of the *Canon*, and he describes almost the same signs and remedies that Dioscorides does regarding the potion of the poison *ixia*. 

However, many younger physicians, not noticing this, think that both Pliny and Avicenna are speaking of the **bird-lime** <note>original: "uisco," a sticky adhesive made from mistletoe berries used by hunters to catch birds</note> by which birds are deceived. But I do not see how it is fitting for either Pliny or Avicenna to number the bird-lime of fowlers among the poisons. Indeed, Pliny writes most accurately about the various kinds of mistletoe in the last chapter of book 16. He is so far from saying that any of them are poisonous that he says mistletoe grown on a hard-oak, if gathered with a certain ritual—according to the opinion of the **Druids** <note>The ancient Celtic priestly class; Pliny famously described their ritual harvesting of mistletoe with a golden sickle</note>—is a remedy against all poisons. 

In that same passage, Pliny disapproves of the superstitious nature of this opinion, yet he does not refute the idea that it is a remedy; this he certainly should have done if he had believed mistletoe to be a poison. Furthermore, Avicenna, in the second book of the *Canon*, reports many things about mistletoe as a healthy medicine, giving us no indication that it is a deadly poison. Therefore, one must admit either that both authors contradict themselves in different places, or that when they speak of mistletoe as a poison, they are misusing the term. For *ixias* taken as a poison is not mistletoe, even though the name is derived from it. In the same way, the white and black **chameleon** <term>chameleon: referring here to the chameleon thistle, not the animal</term> is named *ixias* for the reason that in certain places...

# NICCOLÒ LEONICENO #

...it produces bird-lime <note>original: "uiscum"</note> under the armpits of the leaves, as Pliny says in book 22, chapter 18. However, according to Dioscorides, it is found near the root; thus the poison **ixia** <term>ixia: a toxic, gummy resin derived from the root of the chameleon thistle</term> received its name from the outcome that follows its drinking. For just as bird-lime <note>original: "uiscum"</note> retains whatever sticks to it, so the poison *ixia*, once swallowed, contracts all the **superfluities** <term>superfluities: in Galenic medicine, excess bodily fluids or waste products believed to cause disease</term> of the body. We, indeed, thus vindicate **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder (23–79 AD), whose *Natural History* was a standard but often criticized reference</note> from the charge of contradiction by explaining his misuse of the word.

But let the younger physicians see how they may defend **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the Persian physician whose *Canon of Medicine* dominated European universities</note>, whom they claim spoke about the bird-lime used by **fowlers** <term>fowlers: hunters who used sticky "lime" on branches to trap birds</term> as being among the poisons in the fourth book of the *Canon*. For some of them, who have published quite a long treatise on poisons, cite Avicenna as writing remedies for such bird-lime taken internally. Nor indeed would it be very surprising if Avicenna was deceived by the similarity of names regarding this *ixia*, just as he was in another case—namely, in the root of the **black chameleon** <term>black chameleon: *Atractylis gummifera*, a thistle-like plant</term>. For we have said that the Greeks also call this root *ixia*, though for a different reason. Thus, Avicenna attributes the properties that belong to the poison *ixia* to bird-lime <note>original: "ixo," the Greek word for mistletoe/bird-lime</note> as if it were a poison in the fourth book of the *Canon*. Similarly, those characteristics which suit the white or black chameleon, the same Avicenna ascribes to another shrub, which the Greeks call **chamaelea** and the Arabs call **mezereon** <term>mezereon: *Daphne mezereum*, a flowering shrub used in traditional medicine</term>.

<margin>The origin of Chamaelea.</margin>
However, the *chamaelea* is very different from the white or black chameleon, not only in its shape but also in its medicinal properties. The *chamaelea* earned this name among the Greeks because it has leaves similar to an olive tree <note>The name is derived from the Greek "chamai" (on the ground) and "elaia" (olive)</note>. But the white and black chameleon, as **Dioscorides** <note>Greek physician (c. 40–90 AD) and author of *De Materia Medica*</note> says, resembles the *silybum* or *scolymus* <term>silybum/scolymus: types of thistles</term>. Those who have seen the herb still called *chameleon* by the Greeks on the island of **Crete** testify that it is prickly and bears bird-lime, just as both Dioscorides and Pliny recorded. They also say that the Cretans use this bird-lime to glue feathers onto their arrows.

<margin>The herb Carlina.</margin>
Furthermore, they say it is very similar to the herb we call **carlina** <term>carlina: the carline thistle</term>. Some think it is named *carlina* by our people because it was a discovery of **King Charles** <note>referring to Charlemagne; legend says an angel showed him the thistle to cure his army of the plague</note>. I, rather, [think] *carlina*...

<meta>This page continues Nicolò Leoniceno’s critique of the botanical and taxonomic errors found in the works of medieval Arab physicians, specifically regarding the confusion between the plants known as chameleon, chamælea, and mezereon. He is arguing that these authors conflated distinct species described by the Greeks (Dioscorides) and Romans (Pliny).</meta>

# ON THE POISON IXIA #

<note>original: "DE IXIA VENENO"</note>

...by changing one letter, I believe it was called *cardina* <note>original: "pro cardina dictam"</note> because it belongs to the genus of **thistles** <term>thistles: prickly plants of the family Asteraceae, often mentioned in ancient medicine</term>, or prickly herbs. The Greeks called the plant **chamæleon** <term>chamæleon: referring here to the chameleon thistle (Atractylis gummifera or similar species)</term> and it obtained this name among them because it changes its colors according to the earth in which it grows, just like the **chameleon animal** <note>a reference to the lizard known for color changes</note>, which itself does not have a stable color, but takes on whatever it is closest to, except for red and white. 

Although there is a difference not only in name but also in nature between the **chamælea** <term>chamælea: likely the "Dwarf Olive" or a species of Daphne</term> shrub and the **chamæleon** prickly herb, **Avicenna** and **Serapio** <note>Serapion the Younger, a 12th-century Arab physician</note>, and almost all the Arab authors, confused the properties of both in a single chapter. One can clearly detect this error in Serapio, in the chapter *On Mezereon* <term>mezereon: a term used by Arab physicians for Daphne species, which became confused with other plants</term>—that is, *chamælea*. In that chapter, he describes *mezereon* in the same way **Dioscorides** <note>Pedanius Dioscorides (c. 40–90 AD), the primary Greek authority on herbal medicine</note> describes *chamælea*, and he attributes the same medicinal properties to *mezereon* that Dioscorides (whom Serapio even cites) gives in his chapter on *chamælea*. 

But a little later in the same chapter, Serapio also brings in **Paulus** <note>Paul of Aegina (c. 625–690 AD), a Byzantine Greek physician</note> speaking about "white" and "black" *mezereon*. However, black and white are not varieties of *mezereon* (the *chamælea* shrub), but of the **chamæleon** prickly herb. These two types—one white, the other black—are distinguished not only by Dioscorides but also by **Pliny**; indeed, they are distinguished by Serapio himself, who later, in another place and a different chapter, writes almost the same things about the white and black chameleon as Dioscorides did about both. Yet, he does not remember that he had already mentioned the same herbs in the chapter *On Mezereon*. 

Avicenna likewise did what he himself usually objects to in others: he placed "a chapter within a chapter." For in Book II of the **Canon** <note>The *Canon of Medicine*, the most influential medical encyclopedia of the Middle Ages</note>, he includes the properties of both *chamælea* and the white and black *chamæleon* in a single chapter titled *On Mezereon*. He claims there are several species of it, even though *chamælea*—which the Arabs properly call *mezereon*—is a single species, fol...

...according to **Dioscorides**, **Galen**, **Paul**, and **Pliny**, who all classified white and black **chameleon** <term>chameleon: referring here to the chameleon thistles (Atractylis gummifera), not the animal</term> as herbs of their own kind, differing from **chamælea** <term>chamælea: likely the "Dwarf Olive" or a species of Daphne shrub</term> (that is, the **mezereon** shrub). Repeating this same error, **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the influential Persian physician whose "Canon of Medicine" was the standard textbook in Europe</note> also writes in the second book of his *Canon* under the letter K: "Chameleon," he says, "is a species of mezereon, black and deadly." He states furthermore in that same chapter, *On Mezereon*, that all species are administered for **morphea** <note>original: "morpheam"; a skin condition involving patches of discoloration</note>, **albaras** <term>albaras: an Arabic term for skin conditions such as vitiligo or leprosy</term>, and freckles <note>original: "lentigines"</note> when smeared on the outside; and sometimes sulfur is mixed in. Yet this medicinal use belongs to the black chameleon alone, as not only Dioscorides but even Avicenna himself testifies in letter C, in the chapter *On the Chameleon*. This statement is also false, just as before, because that property of cleansing foul ulcers and those that have a scab <term>eschar: a piece of dead tissue, or "slough," cast off from the surface of the skin</term> with honey does not belong to the white or black chameleon (which Avicenna falsely suggests in that chapter are species of mezereon), but only to *chamælea*, as is held by the authorities of both Dioscorides and Galen. Continuing this error even in the fourth book of his *Canon*, the symptoms and remedies which are assigned by **Paul** <note>Paul of Aegina, a 7th-century Byzantine Greek physician</note> to the poisonous root of the black chameleon are ascribed by Avicenna to *mezereon* (that is, *chamælea*).

### ON THE POISON IXIA.

...[white and black chamele]on <note>original: "tem" (finishing "chameleontem" from the previous page)</note> are species of **mezereon**, and he deals with them together with **chamælea** in the same chapter. At times he treats white and black **chameleon** separately; likewise, he refers to the poison **ixia** in the Fourth Book of his *Canon* in different chapters: one under the heading of **birdlime** <term>birdlime: a sticky substance, often called "viscus" in Latin, used to trap birds; here referring to a plant resin</term>, which we discussed above; the other under **thephisia**, which he interprets as the gum of mountain **rue**. Here also, Avicenna entangles himself in many errors. 

The first error is a false explanation, which is also found in the Second Book of the *Canon* in the chapter *On Thephisia*, where he likewise explains **thephisia** as the gum of wild rue. This error was followed in part by **Montagnana** <note>Bartolomeo Montagnana (d. 1460), a famous professor of medicine at Padua</note> in a certain medical counsel, in which he advises a man with leprosy and orders the application of a remedy made from a black snake, to which "moist" (that is, fresh) **thephisia** is added. In explaining **thephisia**, Montagnana says that it is wild rue; if that is unavailable, he instructs that cultivated or domestic rue be used in its place. 

But if Montagnana had compared the chapter on **thephisia** in Avicenna’s Second Book with the chapter *On Tapsia* in **Dioscorides** <note>The 1st-century author of "De Materia Medica"</note>, he would have undoubtedly understood that this name "**thephisia**" was a corrupted term in Avicenna’s text, and that "**thephisia**" had been written instead of **tapsia** <term>tapsia: Thapsia garganica, known as the "deadly carrot," a plant with a burning, irritating juice</term>. Thus, a false explanation took root from a scribal error. From that same Dioscorides, Montagnana could have learned that **tapsia** is called by another name—not wild rue, but rather wild **ferula** <term>ferula: a genus of tall flowering plants in the carrot family, such as giant fennel</term>. 

The second error is found in Avicenna, because those effects which **Dioscorides** and **Paul** <note>Paul of Aegina, a 7th-century Byzantine medical encyclopedist</note> attribute to the poison **ixia**, Avicenna attributes to **thephisia** (that is, the gum of wild rue). He did not notice that he was going to treat that same **ixia** in the chapter *On Aldibe* (that is, birdlime) in that same book—namely, the Fourth Book of the *Canon*—just a little later. Indeed, in the chapter on **thephisia**, he writes these words:

> This is the gum of mountain rue, and sometimes there is perceived in its flavor 
> something like the flavor of **albedagori** <note>original: "albedagori"; a corrupted term for a plant or resin</note>; it is hot, and there happens 
> to those who drink it a retention of all those things that flow from both 
> passages <note>This refers to a total suppression of both urine and feces</note>, and the tongue becomes abscessed, and rumblings and 
> bloating occur. All of which signs also...

# NICOLÒ LEONICENO

...Dioscorides writes concerning those who have drunk the poison **ixia** <note>ixia: the poisonous juice of the root of the chameleon plant (Atractylis gummifera)</note>. The third error is indeed much more serious than the previous ones, because **Avicenna** contradicts himself regarding **thephisia**: for in the Second Book of the *Canon*, in the chapter *On Thephisia*, he writes that a purging quality <note>original: "solutio"</note> exists in its root, its bark, and its resin <note>original: "lachrima" (tears)</note>. However, in the Fourth Book of the *Canon*, treating the same **thephisia** (that is, the gum of mountain **rue**) among the poisons, he says that it causes the retention of everything that flows from both passages <note>referring to the bowels and the bladder</note> in those who drink it. Therefore, since purging and the retention of wastes are opposite effects, the contradiction we noted in Avicenna’s words is clear. 

These things have been said by us about **thephisia** in passing, partly to show how many errors contemporary medicine is involved in, with junior physicians establishing **Avicenna** as their leader in it and admitting many things that the same Avicenna wrote as truth without any examination of reason—just as we indicated a little while ago regarding **Montagnana**, a physician illustrious in his own time. Partly, we mention this to demonstrate to you what we also hinted at from the beginning: that it is very difficult to identify what **ixia** is according to Avicenna and the junior physicians who follow him. This is because Avicenna seems ambiguous regarding this poison, calling it now **birdlime** <term>birdlime: Latin "viscus," a sticky substance used to trap birds, which Avicenna confused with plant toxins</term>, now **thephisia** (that is, the gum of mountain rue). 

Whence certain more recent authors treating poisons create two chapters in imitation of Avicenna: one on the bird-catchers’ **birdlime**, which is not a poison—or if it were, it is not **ixia**, which Avicenna seems to have wanted to address in the chapter *On Birdlime*. This is evident because he notes not only the same signs (though not all) in the drinking of birdlime that **Dioscorides** notes in the drinking of the poison **ixia**, but he even prescribes nearly the same remedies against it. The other chapter they create is on the gum of wild or mountain **rue**, which gum is found nowhere on earth. For it is an error of Avicenna’s, as we said, which those same recent physicians whom we just touched upon, noticing in their own treatises on poisons...

...those who attempt to explain it admit that the **gum of wild rue** <note>original: "gummi rutae agrestis"</note> is actually the **gum of thapsia** <note>original: "gūmi tapsiae"; Thapsia is a genus of poisonous plants in the carrot family, often called "deadly carrots."</note>. ## ON TURBITH.

Regarding the **turbith** <note>original: "turbit"; a root used as a purgative, likely *Operculina turpethum*.</note> about which you ask in your letter, it is difficult to determine by what name it is classified in the works of **Dioscorides**. For **turbith** is a foreign <note>original: "barbarum"; Leoniceno uses this term to refer to non-classical, typically Arabic or medieval Latin sources.</note> name. The foreign authors write about it in various ways; for **Serapion** <note>Serapion the Younger, a 12th-century author of a book on medicinal simples.</note> writes one thing about it, and **Mesue** <note>A name attributed to a series of influential medieval pharmaceutical texts.</note> another. Therefore, if you ask me what that **turbith** described by Serapion is in the work of Dioscorides, I can answer you without any hesitation that it is **tripolium** <note>Sea Starwort (*Aster tripolium*).</note>, even though this name has been corrupted in the version of Serapion where he cites Dioscorides. 

Indeed, the things that **Dioscorides** and **Pliny** wrote concerning **tripolium**—that it grows in maritime places where the wave strikes, neither in the sea nor on dry land; that it has a leaf thicker than that of **woad** <note>original: "isatidis"</note>; a stem the length of a palm and a divided tip; a white, fragrant root, hot to the taste, and so forth—these same things Serapion writes regarding **turbith**, which he erroneously calls **caricamum** <note>original: "caricamum vitiose"</note> instead of **tripolium**. Regarding this error, whether it belongs to the manuscript or the author, it is less surprising when we consider that even in **Pliny**, the text is corruptly read as **clover** <note>original: "trifolium"</note> instead of **tripolium**. This was to such an extent that **Simon** <note>Simon Januensis, author of the *Synonyma Medicinae*, a 13th-century medical dictionary.</note> doubted whether the chapter on **clover** in Pliny, the one on **tripolium** in Dioscorides, and the one on **turbith** in Serapion all referred to the same plant. Furthermore, **Pandectarius** <note>Matthaeus Sylvaticus, author of the *Pandectae Medicinae*, an encyclopedia of medicinal substances.</note> wrote two separate chapters: one on **tripolium** according to Dioscorides, and another on **turbith** according to Serapion, as if turbith...

...in the works of **Serapion** <note>original: "Serapionem"; Serapion the Younger, a 12th or 13th-century physician whose work "On Simple Medicines" was highly influential.</note> it may be something other than the **tripolium** <note>original: "tripolio"; likely Sea Aster (*Aster tripolium*).</note> found in **Dioscorides**. This error perhaps arose from the author of the *Pandects* <note>original: "Pandectarij"; referring to Matthaeus Silvaticus, author of the 14th-century medical encyclopedia *Pandectae Medicinae*.</note>, along with the uncertainty of **Simon** <note>Simon of Genoa, a 13th-century medical lexicographer and translator.</note>. The occasion for this was that in the Latin translation of **Dioscorides**, whose words the author of the *Pandects* cites, it is written that **tripolium** has leaves similar to **celery** <note>original: "apio".</note>. However, **Dioscorides** more accurately records that they are similar to the **woad plant** <note>original: "isatidi herbæ"; *Isatis tinctoria*, a plant used since antiquity to produce blue dye.</note>—that is, the plant we commonly call **woad** <note>original: "guadum".</note>, which is very famous for its use by dyers. In **Serapion**, however, this similarity is referred neither to celery nor to woad, but to a certain plant called **arasatis**. I believe this word has been corrupted among the **Arabs**, and that *arasatin* was written instead of *isatis*, just as in **Pliny** <note>Gaius Plinius Secundus, the Roman author of *Natural History*.</note> we find it erroneously written not as "the leaf of woad," but as "the leaf of *satis*, thicker by a palm's breadth." This passage was corrected by me some time ago in my book *On the Errors of Pliny and Other Physicians*.

<margin>Turbith.</margin>
If, however, you ask me what **turbith** <note>original: "turbit"; a purgative root, likely *Operculina turpethum*.</note> is—the substance described by **Mesue** <note>Yuhanna ibn Masawayh or "Pseudo-Mesue," an authority on pharmacy.</note>—it must be said that Mesue’s **turbith** is not the **tripolium** of **Dioscorides**, but rather the root of some herb that has a sharp, milky sap, belonging to the genus of **spurges** <note>original: "tithimalorum"; plants of the genus *Euphorbia* known for their irritating white latex.</note> or "milk-bearing plants" <note>original: "lacticinorū".</note>, as the younger physicians call them. For such is the turbith described by Mesue; it does not have a leaf like woad, but rather like **fennel** <note>original: "ferulæ"; specifically the Giant Fennel.</note>. For these are his words, as you know:
> Turbith is the root of an herb whose leaves are like the leaves of fennel, though smaller, and it is among those that contain milk.

Therefore **Actuarius** <note>Joannes Zacharias Actuarius, a 13th-century Byzantine physician.</note>—a medical author of great authority among the Greeks, though much later in time than **Galen** and **Paulus** <note>Paulus Aegineta, a 7th-century Greek medical writer.</note>, and who records many medicines of the Arabs under their own names—says that the substance called **turbith** by the "Barbarians" <note>Meaning non-Greeks, here specifically referring to Arabic-speaking medical writers.</note> is the root of the plant called **pityusa** <note>original: "pitiusa"; Pine Spurge (*Euphorbia pityusa*).</note> by the Greeks. Certain other Greeks besides Actuarius seem to have held this opinion; in the chapter *On Pityusa* in Dioscorides, where the root is mentioned, they inserted those words which I do not believe belong to Dioscorides, but are rather a gloss: <gloss>which they call tourpeit</gloss> <note>original Greek: "ἣν καλοῦσι τούρπειτ".</note>, meaning the root they call turbith.

A little further down, he writes another chapter "On Sebram," and in that same chapter he cites **Dioscorides**, as if *sebram* were a different medicine from *pitiusa*.
