### OF NICCOLÒ LEONICENO

[Dio]scorides <note>original: "Dioscoridem"; a reference to the 1st-century Greek physician whose "De materia medica" was the primary botanical authority.</note> states that it has leaves similar to woad <note>original: "isatidi"; Isatis tinctoria, a plant used to produce blue dye.</note>. By the same reasoning, it is proven that the herb **soldana** <note>Sea Bindweed (*Calystegia soldanella*), a coastal plant known for its purgative properties.</note> is not the **turbith** described by **Mesue** <note>Johannes Mesue (Masawayh), a 9th-century Persian physician.</note>; for that **turbith** has leaves similar to giant fennel <note>original: "ferulae"; Ferula communis.</note>, as was also stated before, while the leaves of **soldana** are entirely different from the leaves of giant fennel. By a similar argument in my book *On the French Disease* <note>original: "De morbo gallico"; Leoniceno’s famous 1497 work on syphilis.</note> written against **Gentile** <note>Gentile da Foligno (d. 1348), a famous medical commentator.</note>, we proved that the herb **soldana** is not the **cachile** mentioned in **Serapion** <note>Serapion the Younger, an influential 12th-century Arabic medical writer.</note>:

<margin>Cachile.</margin> since **cachile** <note>Likely Sea Rocket (*Cakile maritima*).</note>, according to the same **Serapion**, has leaves like watercress <note>original: "nasturtii".</note>, which bear no resemblance to the leaves of **soldana**. However, for the sake of more thorough teaching, we add here that the Arabic authors referred the herb **soldana** neither to the chapter "On Cachile" nor to the chapter "On Turbith," but, in imitation of the Greeks, to the chapter "On Cabbages" <note>original: "De caulibus".</note>. For the herb commonly called **soldana** by us is that which **Dioscorides** and **Galen** call **sea cabbage** <note>original: "brassicam marinam".</note>; which will appear clearly if one compares

<margin>Soldana is sea cabbage.</margin> what we observe with our own eyes in the herb **soldana** with what **Dioscorides** writes about **sea cabbage**. However, in [treating] this herb, it seems to me that the Arabic authors went astray in that they treated the domestic, the wild, and then the sea cabbage continuously in the same chapter, as if all these were species of the same immediate genus. This could be granted regarding the wild and domestic cabbage, since they differ only by the distinctions of "cultivated" and "wild." But this is by no means the case for the sea cabbage, which is entirely different from the other two, as not only **Dioscorides** but also **Galen** testify. In the opinion of these authors, "sea cabbage" and "cultivated cabbage" (or even the wild kind) are named equivocally <note>original: "aequivoce"; this means they share the same name ("cabbage") but do not share the same biological nature or essence.</note>. Yet, that the Arabs thought the cultivated, wild, and furthermore the sea cabbage possessed some affinity between them—not only in appearance but also in nature—is established by the fact that they include them all in the same chapter, as we have said. And besides this, the words of **Serapion** show the same, who writes thus regarding sea cabbages:

> Sea cabbages are further removed from the likeness of domestic ones than, clearly, the wild cabbages are. For concerning those...

# ON TURBITH OR TRIPOLIUM.

...as he had spoken of previously. <margin>»</margin> > Wild, marine, and domestic
<margin>»</margin> > [cabbage] ripens inflammatory swellings <note>original: "phlegmones".</note> and hard tumors.

Whatever effect is assigned by **Dioscorides** <note>Pedanius Dioscorides, the 1st-century author of "De Materia Medica".</note> to cultivated and wild cabbage in part; however, to sea-cabbage <note>original: "marino cauli".</note>, it is ascribed by no one, and is confirmed by no experience. But the truer opinion is that of the Greeks touched upon by us: that wild and cultivated cabbage are similar only in shape, color, and natural properties, except that the wild is whiter, hotter, and drier—just as all other wild plants are stronger than cultivated ones in the same genus, according to these two qualities, as **Galen** <note>Claudius Galenus (129–216 AD), the most influential physician in Roman medicine.</note> says. But sea-cabbage <note>original: "marina brassica"; often referring to Sea Bindweed in this context.</note> differs entirely from those two. We thought these things should be noted in the Arabic authors, so that no one might think we would list the herb **soldana** <note>Sea Bindweed (*Calystegia soldanella*).</note> among the species of cabbage—as they did, perhaps because they did not know that sea-cabbage was mentioned by **Dioscorides** and **Galen**. 

But since we have interspersed many things so that we might deserve your fuller favor, let us now return to that which was primarily asked from the beginning: what "turbith" <note>original: "turbit"; the root of *Operculina turpethum*, used as a purgative.</note> is in **Dioscorides**. Perhaps, amidst such a great diversity of opinions among both Arabic and Latin authors concerning this medicine, it would be better to ask what that root is in **Dioscorides** which they sell in the apothecary shops <note>original: "officinæ".</note> as turbith. Indeed, I have labored long and hard to see the green herb while it is still growing <note>original: "uirentē".</note> whose root is called turbith. For those who bring us only the dried root can say neither where it grows, nor what sort of leaf or flower distinguishes turbith—except that one pharmacist <note>original: "pharmacopola".</note> testified to me regarding the flower of turbith that which **Dioscorides** writes of the leaf of **tripolium** <note>Sea Aster (*Aster tripolium*).</note>: namely, that it appears white in the morning, purple at noon, and crimson <note>original: "phœniceus".</note> in the evening. If this was truly reported to me, without a doubt the turbith which we use is the tripolium of **Dioscorides**. But since this miracle concerning the flower could scarcely be believed of **Dioscorides** himself, let alone some pharmacist, we must strive by all means to inspect the green leaf itself, and [see] whether it is like the leaf of woad <note>original: "isatidis".</note>...

...or similar to fennel <note>original: "ferulæ"; referring to the giant fennel, *Ferula communis*, often used in classical botany to describe a plant's stalk.</note>, or even neither, let us consider more carefully. 

For it is possible that the root we use is neither the turbith <note>A purgative root, likely *Operculina turpethum*, used extensively in medieval medicine.</note> of **Mesue** <note>Pseudo-Mesue, an influential but anonymous 13th-century author whose medical works were attributed to an earlier Arabic physician.</note>, nor even the turbith of **Serapion** <note>Serapion the Younger, a 12th or 13th-century Arabic author of a famous work on simple medicines.</note>; I see such great carelessness in these matters which are in very frequent use by doctors. For if anyone should say it is **Serapion’s** turbith, we can object that turbith in **Serapion** is the same as tripolium <note>original: "tripolium"; likely Sea Starwort (*Aster tripolium*).</note> in **Dioscorides** <note>Pedanius Dioscorides, the 1st-century author of "De Materia Medica," the foundational text for Western botany.</note>. But the root of tripolium, according to the same **Dioscorides**, is fragrant. However, the one we use for the turbith root is completely lacking in odor. 

If, however, another asserts that this is the turbith described by **Mesue**—since that turbith, according to the same **Mesue**, belongs to the class of milk-bearing plants, or "milky" ones, that is, those plants that have a very acrid sap—we will ask him which of those described by **Dioscorides** or **Serapion** it might be, or whether it is some species of spurge <note>original: "tithimalorum"; plants of the genus *Euphorbia*, known for their irritating white milky sap.</note>. 

There are seven or eight of them, but none of them can be the turbith described by **Mesue**. Indeed, none of those has leaves similar to fennel, such as the turbith designated by **Mesue** has, as is clear from **Dioscorides** and **Serapion**, who describe the individual species of spurge by their leaves and flowers and other properties. 

Nor is it caper spurge <note>original: "lathiris"; *Euphorbia lathyris*.</note>, which more recent doctors call lesser cataputia <note>original: "catiputiã minorem".</note>. **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (980–1037), the Persian polymath.</note>, however, calls it *mendana*, as is evident from the similar things that **Dioscorides** wrote about caper spurge and **Avicenna** wrote about *mendana*. Nor is it purple spurge <note>original: "peplios"; *Euphorbia peplus*.</note>, which **Dioscorides** treats among others that emit an acrid milk. For the root of this is useless, as **Dioscorides** says; and **Avicenna** also treats this in the second book of the *Canon*, under the name *bebilis*, in a chapter distinct from the chapter "On Turbith." 

By the same reasoning, it is not *peplion*, that is, wild purslane. For **Avicenna** also names this *bilomon* in the second book of the *Canon*. Moreover, the translation of **Hippocrates'** books *On the Regimen in Acute Diseases* called it *felicinium*, and it is used in medicine not by its root, but by its leaf or fruit. It also has leaves similar to purslane—from which it gets its name—but not to fennel, like the turbith described by **Mesue**...

# ON TURBITH OR TRIPOLIUM.

###

[Me]sue. Finally, by examining each species of those plants that flow with a milky and sharp juice, it does not seem that the description of turbith found in **Mesue** <note>Pseudo-Mesue, an anonymous but highly influential 13th-century medical author whose works were often attributed to a much earlier Arabic physician.</note> fits any of them. Perhaps, however, it is not even correctly written by **Mesue** that turbith belongs to the genus of those that have milk. 

Indeed, this same author says that *mezereon* <note>original: "mezereon"; referring to the mezereon or spurge olive (*Daphne mezereum*), known for its toxic and irritant properties.</note> is a larger plant among the milky ones <note>original: "lacticiniorũ"; plants that produce a white, latex-like sap.</note>. Yet, this plant called *mezereon* by the Arabs is called *chamaelea* <note>original: "Chamælea"; likely *Daphne gnidium* or *Daphne oleoides*.</note> by the Greeks, as is clear to anyone comparing the chapter "On Chamaelea" in **Dioscorides** <note>The 1st-century author of "De Materia Medica," the primary authority for Leoniceno.</note> with the chapter "On Mezereon" in **Serapion** <note>Serapion the Younger, a 12th-century Arabic writer on medicinal simples.</note> and even in **Avicenna** <note>The famous 11th-century Persian physician and polymath.</note>. 

However, **Avicenna** himself, though under the name of *mezereon*, describes *chamaelea*—which is well known not to be among the milky plants—yet he claims that *mezereon* is a great milky plant. Thus, it appears that the Arabs—especially **Avicenna** and **Mesue**—fell into a double error in the chapter "On Mezereon": first, because they placed *mezereon* (called *chamaelea* by the Greeks) among the milky plants; and second, because they confused white and black *chameleon* <note>original: "chamæleontē"; referring to the Chameleon thistle (*Atractylis gummifera*), which produces a gummy juice.</note> with *chamaelea* or *mezereon*. 

That **Mesue** was also not free of this second error can be proven from the properties he attributes to *mezereon* at the end of the chapter. These properties were assigned by **Dioscorides** not to *chamaelea* (which the Arabs call *mezereon*), but rather to the white or black *chameleon*. For what **Mesue** writes about *mezereon*—that it kills intestinal worms <note>original: "lumbricos".</note>, that a mouthwash made from it with vinegar helps toothache, that an ointment is made from it for the "itch" <note>original: "scabiē"; a general term for contagious skin eruptions.</note>, and a liniment made from it and sulfur removes *morphea* <note>A skin condition causing hard, discolored patches.</note>, *albaras* <note>An Arabic term often used for white leprosy or vitiligo.</note>, and freckles—are almost exactly the properties attributed by **Dioscorides** to the white and black *chameleon*, but not to *chamaelea* (that is, *mezereon*). 

**Serapion**, however, although he made a similar confusion between the *chameleon* and the *chamaelea* in his chapter "On Mezereon" (as we showed when we discussed *ixia* <note>original: "ixia"; a term often used for the birdlime or gummy juice extracted from certain thistles.</note>), is more to be approved in this regard than **Mesue** or **Avicenna**, because he did not at all classify *mezereon* as a milky plant. And he who [recognized] the true *mezereon*, that is, *chamaelea*...

Indeed, the same Dioscorides says that the leaves of *crission* are longer than the leaves of *buglosson*. <meta>This page continues Nicolas Leoniceno’s detailed philological investigation into the botanical identity of bugloss. -># ON BUGLOSS<-

...in almost the same way that **Dioscorides** <note>Pedanius Dioscorides (c. 40–90 AD), the author of *De materia medica*</note> describes the same *crission* <note>original: "crission"; an ancient name for a type of thistle-like plant</note> as having leaves not longer than bugloss—or as he interprets it, "ox-tongue"—but rather it is written that they are smaller. I believe this error occurred because of the similarity of the Greek words and a flaw in the manuscript that **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder (23–79 AD), whose *Natural History* was a standard but often flawed Roman reference</note> possessed; for instead of *macrotera*, which means "longer," he found written *microtera*, that is, "smaller." However, in many Greek manuscripts, not only printed ones but also those written by hand, I found in Dioscorides *macrotera* <note>original: "μακρότερα"</note>, that is, longer, and not *microtera* <note>original: "μικρότερα"</note>, that is, smaller. 

It is clearly evident to the senses that the leaves of that herb, which is commonly called bugloss, are longer than the leaves of borage. Likewise, the same Dioscorides says that at the top of the stalk of the *crission* are purple heads which dissolve into downy fluff—which is also observed by sight in the herb we call bugloss—whereas in borage, blue heads are seen, and not purple ones. Furthermore, in the author of *On Simple Medicine* <note>A title attributed to various early medieval medical compilers</note>, these words are read:

> » The Romans call bugloss "ox-tongue" <note>original: "lingua bubula"</note>; the Lucanians call it *corago*; it
> » grows in cultivated and storied <note>original: "fabulosis"; likely a scribal error for "sabulosis," meaning sandy</note> places.

Perhaps, however, instead of the word *borago*, the word *corago* was erroneously written, or the name *corago* was changed by one letter into *borago*. As for the statement that it grows in cultivated and sandy places, Dioscorides records the same regarding his own bugloss. 

**Pandectarius** <note>Matthaeus Silvaticus (c. 1280–1342), a medical lexicographer known for his "Pandects" which attempted to sync Greek, Latin, and Arabic terms</note> also—if this man carries any authority—under the letter L, regarding *lisin altaur* <note>original: "lisin altaur," from the Arabic "lisan al-thaur," meaning ox-tongue</note> (which name among the Arabs signifies "ox-tongue"), interprets it as borage itself. Therefore, it might perhaps be better, when we employ bugloss for medical use—about which Dioscorides, **Galen** <note>The most influential Greek physician of the Roman Empire</note>, and Arabic authors all cite—to accept borage rather than that herb which is everywhere called bugloss. 

And so, that which **Montagnana** <note>Bartolomeo Montagnana (d. 1460), a famous professor of medicine at Padua</note> thought—that **Avicenna** <note>The Persian physician Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037)</note> said nothing about borage—will be proven false. For unless my opinion deceives me, the chapter *On Bugloss* or *Ox-tongue* in Avicenna is actually the chapter *On Borage*, just as it is in **Serapion** <note>Serapion the Younger, a 12th-century author on medicinal "simples"</note>. It will also be false what **Simon** <note>Simon of Genoa (13th century), a medical linguist</note> writes, who thought that no author wrote about both herbs at the same time.

<meta>This page continues Nicolas Leoniceno’s philological investigation into botanical nomenclature. The catchword at the bottom "fit Simo-" suggests the next page will reference the poet Simonides or a similar name.</meta>

-># BY NICOLÒ LEONICENO<-

Since **Dioscorides** <note>Pedanius Dioscorides (c. 40–90 AD), the author of *De materia medica*</note> among the Greeks, and **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder (23–79 AD), author of the *Natural History*</note> among us Romans, made mention of both bugloss <note>original: "buglossa"; literally "ox-tongue"</note> as well as *crission* <note>original: "crission"; an ancient name for a type of thistle-like plant</note>. It cannot be denied that borage <note>original: "borago"</note> is one of these two plants in Dioscorides—either *crission* or bugloss—especially by those who admit that borage is a species of bugloss, or bugloss a species of borage; since Dioscorides himself testifies that *crission* has leaves similar to bugloss, and that bugloss is called "great." 

If, however, borage is the plant the Greeks called *crission*, it will be true what is written by **Montagnana** <note>Bartolomeo Montagnana (c. 1380–1452), a prominent Paduan physician</note>: that so many things are rashly claimed about borage by the younger doctors. For Dioscorides reported only this concerning *crission*: that if its root is bound over a painful area, it soothes the pain. **Pliny**, however, recorded that the herb or the root, when bound to the body, heals the pains of varicose veins. Therefore, let the younger doctors choose whichever they prefer: either that borage is the true bugloss, as we believe, or that the use of this herb is not effective for those purposes for which they imagine it to be.

### ON SOW THISTLE.

<margin>Sow thistle <note>original: "Sonchus"</note></margin>
Now, concerning sow thistle <term>cicerbita</term> <note>The common sow thistle, *Sonchus oleraceus*</note>, about which you also wish to know, it is just like borage, even famous for its use in a poem by **Callimachus** <note>A Greek poet (c. 310–240 BC) whose poem "Hecale" describes the simple life</note>. For it is that very plant which the rustic woman **Hecale** <note>original: "Echate"; a character in Greek myth who hosted Theseus</note> served to **Theseus**, as **Pliny** mentions. 

In truth, it is less celebrated in medical works today: perhaps because the younger doctors do not know by what name it is called among the ancient authors who wrote on medicine, and therefore they do not know its benefits, which we shall now point out. **Dioscorides** names it *sonchus* <note>original: "sonchum"</note>, and testifies that it is called "rough cicerbita" <note>original: "cicerbitam asperam"</note> by the Romans. However, this name—like many other Roman words found in Dioscorides—is corrupted, because in the Greek manuscript it is incorrectly read not as *cicerbita aspera*, but as *circita aspra*. It was named "rough" by the Romans for this reason: because it becomes thorny as it grows old. Indeed, the Greeks still commonly call the herb that we in Latin name *cicerbita* by the name *sonchus*, so that it is a wonder...

### ON THE SOW THISTLE.

It may be <note>meta: completing the phrase from the previous page's catchword</note> that **Simon of Genoa** <note>Simon Genuensis (late 13th century), a physician and chaplain to Pope Nicholas IV, known for his medical dictionary *Synonyma Medicinae*</note>, who learned many plant names from Greek herbalists, was nevertheless ignorant of what the *sonchus* <note>original: "sonchus"; the Greek name for the sow thistle</note> was among the Greeks. He mentions it under the letter **S** and cites the words of **Dioscorides** <note>Pedanius Dioscorides (c. 40–90 AD), the author of *De materia medica*</note> concerning the sow thistle, yet he neglected to say what plant it actually is, or by what name it is known among us. 

It is no less worthy of wonder that **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder (23–79 AD), author of the *Natural History*</note> did not provide a Latin name for this herb, despite its frequent use as food. For in Book XXII, chapter 22, he referred to the plant that we commonly call *cicerbita* <note>original: "cicerbita"; likely the common sow thistle (*Sonchus oleraceus*)</note> by its Greek name, *sonchus*. He described it in such a way that it cannot be doubted that the *sonchus* of the Greeks is the herb the Latins call *cicerbita*. 

Furthermore, Pliny, together with Dioscorides, enumerates so many uses for this herb that I am sometimes ashamed of the physicians of our time. They only approve of those remedies prepared at great expense, while the very poorest people sometimes dine on things that are better than those drugs. What should make us even more ashamed is that they do not seek medicines from India or Arabia—as if from another world—but rather ignore those which Nature, that parent of all things, has placed openly before everyone. 

The **weasel**, when about to fight against serpents, fortifies itself by eating the sow thistle, and refreshes itself during the struggle by frequently returning to it. This has been witnessed by many who have seen such a close-fought battle. We, on the other hand, buy **theriac** <note>original: "theriaca"; a complex "universal" antidote to poison made of dozens of ingredients</note> against poisons from the Egyptians at a high price, even though they are still ignorant of its most important part—which we call the "base"—as well as many other "simples" <note>original: "simplicia medicamenta"; individual medicinal herbs used as ingredients in compound drugs</note> necessary for that same composition. In our age, these ingredients are known neither by the Greeks nor the Latins, much less by the "barbarians" <note>here referring to non-classical or medieval Arabic sources</note>. According to **Galen**, the prince of physicians, the absence of even one of these components can ruin the entire mixture. 

Truly, the works of Nature are more perfect and easier to find, if only they were not undervalued for that very reason. However, regarding the sow thistle—or *cicerbita*—the occasion for these remarks, both Dioscorides and others testify to its great efficacy against poisons, but especially those of scorpions...

### NICOLÒ LEONICENO ON THE SOW THISTLE.

...the Greeks, as well as Pliny among our own writers, and from the more recent ones the **Conciliator** <note>Pietro d'Abano (c. 1257–1316), a famous Italian physician and philosopher known as "The Conciliator" for his effort to reconcile Greek and Arabic medicine</note>, who lists the *lactucella* <note>original: "lactucella"; literally "little lettuce," a name used for several plants</note>—by which I believe he understands the sow thistle—among seven other herbs that possess a power against poisons equal to theriac <note>original: "theriaca"; a legendary ancient herbal compound used as a universal antidote</note>. This is consistent with what Pliny says: that it is similar to lettuce, except for being prickly.

Furthermore, **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the most influential Persian physician-philosopher of the Islamic Golden Age</note> mentions it among the Arabs, provided that the sow thistle is the herb he calls *taraxacon* <note>original: "taraxacon"; while this now refers to the dandelion, in the medieval period it was often confused or grouped with wild chicory and sow thistles</note> in the Second Book of the *Canon*. I know that many of the most celebrated physicians of our age, and especially **Gerard of Verona** <note>Gerardus Veronensis, a 15th-century physician and scholar involved in the translation of medical texts</note>, have held this opinion. 

For I do not wish to decide on that matter now, as I have for some time intended a work for this very purpose: namely, to clarify the Arabic names found written in the Second Book of Avicenna’s *Canon*. I will perhaps complete that same work more promptly now that I understand you desire it no less than those things we have recently explained. However, if we delay your eagerness in this matter a little longer, you will bear it with a calm mind, hoping especially for what happened to you in this letter—if indeed it deserves the name of a letter, having grown almost to the size of a volume. The later it was delivered to you, the greater the interest <note>original: "foenore"; a metaphor suggesting that the long delay is repaid by the greater value and length of the response</note> it brings.

Regarding the *cicercia* <note>original: "cicercia"; likely the chickling vetch or grass pea (*Lathyrus sativus*)</note>, it remains for me to respond so that your inquiries may be satisfied in every part. This type of legume is commonly 
<margin>Cicercia.</margin> called *cicercia*, but it is named *cicercula* by **Pliny** in Book XVIII, chapter 12. It is called *lathyron* <note>original: "lathiron"</note> by **Theophrastus** <note>The Greek "father of botany" (c. 371–287 BC)</note> in Book IX of *On Plants*, and by **Galen** <note>Aelius Galenus (129–216 AD), the prominent Greek physician whose theories dominated Western medicine for centuries</note> (who cites the same Theophrastus) in Book II of *On Foods*. Indeed, **Theodorus** <note>Theodorus Gaza (c. 1398–1475), a major Greek humanist who translated botanical works from Greek into Latin</note>, most learned in both Greek and Latin, translates the Greek *lathyron* as the Latin *cicercula* in his translation of Theophrastus. 

Farewell at Ferrara, on the Kalends of February <note>February 1st</note>, 1504.

# THE WORKS OF NICOLÒ LEONICENO

...[knowledge which is] pleasant <note>original: "cundam"; likely the end of "iucundam" (pleasant) or "fecundam" (fruitful)</note>, and extremely necessary for physicians to know: lest those seeking the viper for the composition of theriac <term>theriaca: a famous "universal antidote" containing dozens of ingredients, including viper flesh</term>, deceived by the similarity, capture a *dipsas* <note>The dipsas was a legendary serpent whose bite was said to cause unquenchable thirst</note> instead. But both this error and many others pertaining to the knowledge of serpents, we shall demonstrate in this same work. We write this against the "barbarian" authors <note>original: "autores barbaros"; Leoniceno uses this term to refer to medieval Arabic and Latin medical authorities, whom he accused of corrupting original Greek medical science</note> who have corrupted this part of medicine—as they have almost all others—with nearly infinite lies. We shall begin with the viper, which has, as we said, a great similarity to the *dipsas*. 

<margin>The Dipsas.</margin> However, the investigation into the *dipsas* will be more difficult than it was or will be for the viper, insofar as the *dipsas* does not possess any unique natural property by which we can distinguish it from all other serpents—as we did with the viper—to arrive at a certain and indubitable knowledge of it. For those who think there is a better way to show which serpent is a viper and by what name it is commonly called, other than the path we have followed, are mistaken. 

For from the things that Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the Persian physician whose "Canon of Medicine" was the standard textbook in Europe until the Renaissance</note> writes in Book V, in the chapter *On vipers to be received for the composition of theriac*, no one could easily judge what a viper is. This is partly due to the obscurity of the language used almost everywhere by Avicenna (or perhaps his translator), and partly because most of the things written there can be considered false if they are compared with what Galen <note>Claudius Galenus (129–c. 210 AD), the Greek physician whose authority Leoniceno sought to restore over medieval interpretations</note> had previously written about the same serpents in his book *On Theriac, to Piso*. 

It seems that Avicenna, when writing about this same antidote, wished to interpret Galen; however, he perverted many things, as we shall immediately show. For Galen, in the aforementioned book *On Theriac, to Piso*, maintains that vipers have a wider head and body, and not a slender and tiny neck as Avicenna writes. Furthermore, Avicenna says that their tails are short (to use his own terms) and make a noise as they move—a description that does not at all [agree] <note>The text cuts off here, but the catchword "gruit" indicates the word "congruat" or "congruit," meaning to agree or match</note> with those words of Galen...

### ON SERPENTS.

[...it] agrees <note>original: "gruit"; likely the conclusion of "congruit" (it agrees)</note> with those who command that vipers be required for the composition of theriac <term>theriaca: a complex ancient medical "universal antidote" made from dozens of ingredients, including prepared viper flesh</term>, provided they do not have coiled tails, nor a noisy gait, but are instead silent and quiet. Furthermore, the sign by which **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian physician whose "Canon of Medicine" was the standard medical text in the Middle Ages, though often criticized by Renaissance humanists like Leoniceno</note> distinguishes the male from the female in the same genus of vipers is not entirely the same as the one provided by **Galen** <note>Claudius Galenus (129–c. 216 AD), the most influential Greek physician of the Roman Empire</note>. For **Galen** says that there are more than two canine teeth <note>original: "caninos dentes"; referring to the fangs</note> in the female, while in the male there are only two. This very distinction was sung in an elegant poem by **Nicander**, the famous prophet of medicine:

->The male is known to spew poison from twin canine<-
->teeth: but the female viper carries more of these.<-

**Avicenna** noted this same difference based on teeth simply, rather than specifically on the canine teeth, with these words: "And their sign is that the males have one tooth on every side, and the females have several." But perhaps it is false that the male has only one tooth on every side and the female several, unless we understand this to refer to the canine teeth. For it is possible that the male also has more than two of the other teeth which are not canine. No less doubt is raised by what **Avicenna** adds afterward: "And the variegated horned ones and the asps <note>original: "aspides"</note> ought to be avoided." These words show that **Avicenna** felt these serpents also belonged to the genus of vipers, which—just like the males of the same genus that live in ponds, on the shores of waters, and in the sea—should be rejected. Then **Avicenna** adds: "And the stony ones <note>original: "petrosae"</note> are to be omitted." He immediately provides the reason for this precept: because among them are the *oak-snakes*, which cause thirst. In these words there are two errors: first, that he makes the *oak-snakes*—that is, that genus of serpents which the Greeks call <gloss>dryines</gloss> <note>original: "δρύινες"</note> because they live in the roots of oaks—to be of the same genus as vipers, when they are actually a different genus; the second is that he does not distinguish the *oak-snakes* from those that cause thirst. Those that cause thirst are called <gloss>dipsades</gloss> <note>original: "διψάδες"</note> in Greek from that very effect. **Avicenna** speaks more clearly on this in Book IV, in the chapter "On the species of serpents"...

[...Avicenna] indicated with these words that the viper is not a species, but rather a genus, containing many species under itself;

> And the second order is concerning vipers, of which there are again various species. For among them are the *alelisati* vipers <note>A transliteration of an Arabic term for a specific viper, likely the *Vipera lebetina* or similar</note>, and among them are the oak vipers, and among them are those that cause thirst <note>The *dipsas* serpent, named for the Greek word for thirst</note>, and the rest which we shall discuss.

But even from those things which **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), whose *Canon of Medicine* was the primary medical textbook in Europe for centuries</note> writes in the same Book IV, in the chapter "On the Bite of Vipers," one would not know any better which serpent is the viper, nor would he be able to indicate by what name it is commonly known. This is because the signs of viper bites written here by Avicenna are partly common to other serpents as well, and partly poorly translated from **Paul** <note>Paul of Aegina (c. 625–690 AD), a Byzantine Greek physician whose medical encyclopedia was a key source for later Islamic and Renaissance doctors</note>. 

For the **amphisbaena** <term>amphisbaena: a mythical serpent with a head at both ends; the name comes from the Greek "to move in two directions"</term> serpent also causes the same effects by its strike as the viper, as not only **Dioscorides** <note>Pedanius Dioscorides (c. 40–90 AD), the author of *De Materia Medica*, the ancient world's foremost authority on herbal and animal medicines</note> and Paul testify, but even Avicenna himself. Except that Avicenna seems ambiguous regarding this serpent: Because he sometimes calls it "leaping in two directions" <note>original: "salientem ad duas partes"</note> in imitation of the Greek name; but other times he calls it *haren* or *carenet*. And he says he thinks it belongs to the genus 

<margin>Scytale.</margin>

of sea dragons. The **scytale** <term>scytale: a serpent of uniform thickness throughout its length, often appearing the same at the head and tail</term> also, which Avicenna calls by the corrupted name *Scyscetalin*, brings the same evils as vipers, as Dioscorides and Paul clearly indicate. However, Avicenna speaks obscurely, saying the color of the *Scyscetalin* is similar to the "one that leaps in directions" <note>referring back to his name for the amphisbaena</note>, and that the symptoms and the cure for it are the same. 

Nevertheless, we do not condemn Avicenna simply because he assigns symptoms to the viper that are common to certain other serpents, since Dioscorides and Paul did the same. But we intend only to prove this: that it is not possible from these signs, as some believe, to clearly show what a viper is. From other things which the same Avicenna incorrectly translated from Paul, we strive to demonstrate both points: that these descriptions contribute nothing to the knowledge of the viper, and that Avicenna frequently interprets the words of the ancients poorly. Among other signs of viper bites, Avicenna first posits this: that sometimes the blood begins as watery, and then becomes foamy. <meta>This page continues Nicolò Leoniceno’s critique of the Greek historian Herodotus and the medical accuracy of ancient naturalists regarding the viper. Leoniceno is specifically refuting Herodotus's claim that vipers would overpopulate and destroy humanity if they did not have a self-destructive reproductive cycle.</meta>

# NICOLÒ LEONICENO

[...if vipers] had the same method of reproduction as other serpents, they would become the destruction of the human race: in this very reasoning, **Herodotus** is immediately proven most false. For if his reasoning were true, then by that same providence of nature, the basilisk, asps, horned vipers <note>original: *cerastes*</note>, the hemorrhous <note>original: *hemoroũ*; a snake whose bite was believed to cause uncontrollable bleeding</note>, the water-snake, the spotted cenchrus, and many other species of serpents—some of which are no less harmful, and some even more deadly to man than the "winged serpents"—should also be required to bear live young instead of eggs, and the male should die during mating while the female dies during birth. Yet both of these traits are reported only of the viper. That the viper alone among serpents bears live young is also confirmed by **Aristotle**.

But even if the other point were true—that in the genus of vipers the male dies in mating and the female dies in birth—**Herodotus** still does not prove what he intends by his reasoning. For even with two parents removed from the population, many offspring survive, since the birth of a viper is extremely prolific. According to **Aristotle** in the sixth book of *The History of Animals*, a viper can bear more than twenty young in a single day. **Pliny**, in the tenth book of his *Natural History*, also testifies to this number, except **Pliny** asserts that they are not all born on one day (as **Aristotle** says), but that the viper gives birth to individual pups on successive days. This opinion was also followed in translation by **Theodore Gaza** <note>A 15th-century Greek scholar and translator of Aristotle</note>, who was at times too much an admirer of **Pliny’s** wording.

From these accounts, it follows that the viper both is and is not the <term>marassus: a regional Italian name, *marasso*, for the common European adder (*Vipera berus*)</term>, or the <term>scorctionem: likely *scorzone*, another regional name for a dark-colored viper or snake</term>. Since only the viper among serpents bears live young, as **Aristotle** says and **Pliny** agrees, it necessarily follows that the viper is the serpent commonly called the *marassus* or *scorctione*, because the *marassus* is a female viper. However, because the viper supposedly bears its young one by one over nearly twenty days (as **Pliny** says), while the *marassus*—as is visible to the eye—brings many into the light in a single day, it can be concluded by reasoning in the "second figure" <note>A term from formal logic referring to a specific structure of a syllogism used to prove a negative</note> that the viper is not the *marassus*. Therefore, from the words of **Pliny**, and even those of **Aristotle** if we believe the translator **Theodore Gaza**,

<meta>This page continues Nicolò Leoniceno’s defense of Aristotle’s natural history against the potential misinterpretations of Pliny the Elder and the "younger" scholastic philosophers. It follows the discussion of whether vipers bear their young all at once or over several days.</meta>

->### ON SERPENTS ###<-

a contradiction follows. But let others see how they might defend **Pliny**. We easily vindicate the greatest philosopher, **Aristotle**, from such a great error, just as we intend to defend certain other passages by the same philosopher that have been poorly understood by younger philosophers—doing so here even while we are primarily occupied with other matters. The words of **Aristotle** regarding the birth of the viper are found written thus in the Greek manuscript: <note>original Greek: "τίκτει δ’ ἐν μιᾷ ἡμέρᾳ καθ’ ἓν, τίκτει δ’ πλείω ἢ εἴκοσιν"</note> "she gives birth to them one by one in a single day, and she bears more than twenty." Which we interpret word-for-word as: <note>original Latin: "Parit autem una die singulos, parit autem plus quam uiginti numero"</note> "She bears them individually in one day, and she bears more than twenty in number." The true meaning of these words is this: not that she bears one pup on each successive day <note>Leoniceno is correcting the idea that the birth process takes twenty days</note>, but rather that on a single day she bears more than twenty in total, yet one at a time—that is, not two, three, or four at once, but one after the other. This is also what the female *marassus* <term>marassus: likely referring to the common European adder or a similar viper</term> does, which is observed to bear several young in one day, yet individually. However, whether she always bears more than twenty in a single day, or sometimes fewer, I do not believe this is a fixed law of nature. For it is possible that, just as in many other animals where the number of offspring is not strictly predetermined, **Aristotle** did not hesitate to write in his *History of Animals* regarding this serpent's birth not what always happens, but rather what frequently occurs. Thus, no contradiction follows from his writings when they are correctly interpreted. 

Furthermore, even if **Herodotus** spoke the truth when he said there are "winged serpents" in Arabia that bear live young, **Aristotle’s** opinion—which asserts that only the viper among serpents bears live young—is not destroyed. This is because, according to the same philosopher, being winged or wingless does not change the species, as he proves in the first book of *On the Parts of Animals* using the example of ants and glow-worms <term>cicindelarum: glow-worms or fireflies, which appear in both winged and wingless forms</term>, which are found as both winged and wingless within the same species. These things are mentioned here in passing, both to defend **Aristotle** and to support our own opinion, which relies heavily on **Aristotle’s** authority regarding the viper. Now let us return to the *dipsas* <term>dipsas: a legendary venomous snake whose bite was said to cause unquenchable thirst</term>, in which the same...

<meta>This page continues Nicolò Leoniceno’s critique of medieval and ancient authorities on natural history. Having previously corrected misunderstandings regarding the birth of vipers, he now turns his attention to the anatomical descriptions provided by the influential Persian physician Avicenna, specifically focusing on the "dipsas" (a thirst-inducing serpent) and the common viper.</meta>

-># NICOLÒ LEONIČENO #<-

The same logic applies to the viper: for if we wish to define it through the words of **Avicenna** in Book IV, in the chapter *On the serpent that causes thirst* <note>original Latin: "De serpente faciente sitim"</note>, and to reveal the common naming to those who wish to know it, the reader’s mind will hesitate no less in this case than it did regarding the viper’s birth. This is all the more true because **Avicenna** seems to contradict himself in his description of the **dipsas** <term>dipsas: a legendary serpent whose bite was said to cause an unquenchable, fatal thirst</term>. In the chapter of Book IV cited just above, he depicts the **dipsas** with a small head and a thick neck, with its curvature beginning from that thick neck and continuing down to a slender tail—these are almost the literal words of **Avicenna**. Later, he adds on the authority of certain others that the form of the **dipsas** is the same as the form of the viper.

And yet, **Avicenna** himself in Book V—in the chapter where he discusses the vipers that are used in the composition of **theriac** <term>theriac: a famous ancient "universal" medicine and antivenom made from dozens of ingredients, including viper flesh</term>—says that vipers are serpents possessing flat heads, which are specifically wide near a very small and slender neck. Therefore, the form or figure of the **dipsas** cannot be the form of the viper. Indeed, <note>Leoniceno is pointing out the logical impossibility here</note> if the **dipsas**, according to **Avicenna**, has a flat and wide head with a very small and slender neck, it contradicts his earlier description. 

Furthermore, the comparison of the **dipsas** and the viper can produce a great deal of ambiguity in **Avicenna’s** work. This is because this author, as we showed above, maintains that "viper" is not the name of a specific species, but rather a genus containing many different species under it. This leaves us in doubt as to which species of viper the **dipsas** is supposed to resemble—unless, perhaps, someone were to say that all species of serpents contained under the genus of vipers (according to **Avicenna**) have the very same form. In that case, one could simply state that the form of the **dipsas** is the form of the viper. However, it is foolish to even imagine such a thing. Even if this were granted, another equally ridiculous point follows: that **Avicenna** meant nothing else than that the **dipsas** resembles itself in form, since, according to **Avicenna**, the **dipsas** is a species of viper, as we have proved before. Therefore, we must seek something that is so unique to the **dipsas** that it is found in no other kind of serpent...

<meta>This page continues Nicolò Leoniceno’s critical examination of the viper and the dipsas. He now investigates whether the "dipsas" is a unique species characterized by the thirst it induces, or simply a type of viper influenced by its environment.</meta>

->### ON SERPENTS ###<-

[...is born], just as bearing live young is a property unique to the viper alone among all the genera of serpents. But someone might say that this thirst is peculiar to the **dipsas** <term>dipsas: from the Greek "dipsa," meaning thirst; a serpent whose bite was believed to cause fatal dehydration</term>. This is easy to find in the words of **Avicenna**, who calls it "the thirst-maker" <note>original Latin: "sitim facientem"</note>, because it causes an intolerable thirst, as the verses of **Lucan** <note>Marcus Annaeus Lucanus (39–65 AD), a Roman poet</note> show, which are written as follows:

> Aulus, a young standard-bearer of Tyrrhenian blood,
> Stepped upon a dipsas, which turned its head back and bit him.
> Scarcely was there pain or the sensation of the tooth,
> And the very face of death was free from horror; the wound threatened nothing.
> But behold, the silent venom enters, and a consuming fire
> Devours the marrow, burning the innards with a hot decay.
> The plague drank up the moisture spread around the vital organs,
> And began to scorch the tongue against the dry palate;
> There was no sweat to flow into his weary limbs,
> And the vein of tears fled from his eyes.

Whoever offers this response to me might have said something of substance, were it not for the fact that the same effect is found in the serpents commonly called vipers. Indeed, vipers and dipsads agree not only in form or figure—as **Avicenna** seems to think—but also in many other respects. Several of them possess this specific natural property: whether by the eating of their flesh or by the bite they inflict with their teeth, they cause an unmeasurable thirst. This was so pronounced that **Galen** <note>Claudius Galenus (129–c. 216 AD), the most influential physician of antiquity</note> doubted whether the genus of vipers and dipsads was the same, or rather different, as many philosophers and physicians before him seem to have believed when they distinguished the viper from the dipsas.

Therefore, **Galen** writes in Book XI of *On Simple Medicine* that, in this state of ambiguity, he questioned the **Marsi** <term>Marsi: an ancient Italian people renowned in antiquity as healers and snake-charmers</term> as to whether they had any sign by which they could discern each genus—namely, to distinguish between dipsads and vipers. They responded that there was no separate genus of dipsas at all; rather, those vipers that lived near the sea and in places full of saltiness possessed salty flesh. For this reason, many such vipers are found in **Libya**...

->### NICCOLÒ LEONICENO ###<-

[...such things:] that Italy lacks them because of the region's humidity. If their opinion is true, we can solve the proposed question in a few words, saying this: the **dipsas** is a Libyan viper, or a Libyan **marassus** <term>marassus: a Renaissance-era term for a type of viper, often associated with specific regional varieties</term>, living in arid and salty places such as the land of Libya. 

To easily lean toward this opinion of the Marsi, this especially helps: the fact that **Aristotle** and **Pliny**—two authors most diligent in handing down the history of both other animals and especially serpents—left behind nothing, as far as I know, written about the nature of the dipsads, as if they were included among vipers of the same genus; except that Pliny, in only one or two places while mentioning certain medicines, remembers the dipsas along with the viper. 

From this, however, it cannot be proven that the dipsas is a species different from the viper, since there are some vipers that cause thirst and others that do not, according to the variety of places in which they live. And those that do cause thirst are nicknamed "**dipsads**"; while those that do not are simply called "**vipers**," just as we are about to demonstrate shortly from the words of **Galen**. Added to this is the fact that Galen did not dare to openly condemn this opinion of the Marsi; he only said he doubted whether what he had received from the Marsi was entirely true, or false in some respect.

<margin>That the dipsas is a *marassus*</margin>
Therefore, just as we defer a more certain opinion on this to another time, so now we constantly affirm that the dipsas is either a *marassus* born in arid and salty places, or so very similar to a *marassus* that it is extremely difficult to tell them apart. Since **Galen**, a man of such great learning and experience, frankly confesses that he did not know how to distinguish one from the other; and for that reason, he consulted the Marsi as those more skilled from their constant hunting of serpents. Who did not know it themselves, although practiced in handling serpents with impunity...

> *The swelling mixes all things together, now larger than the whole body, and having surpassed the human scale, the gore rises far and wide over all the limbs as the poison lifts it.* <note>original: "Miscent cuncta tumor, maior iam corpore toto, / Humanumq; egressa modum super omnia membra / Inflatu sanies late tollente ueneno." How also **Albert the Great** <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a medieval scholar who wrote extensively on animals.</note> makes two chapters, one regarding the **dipsas**, the other regarding the **prester**. And indeed, that the first kind killed **Aulus**, while the second killed **Nasidius**, according to the verses of **Lucan** <note>Aulus and Nasidius are soldiers in Lucan's poem; Aulus dies of unquenchable thirst from a *dipsas* bite, while Nasidius swells up until his armor bursts from a *prester* bite.</note>. Thus might Albert be excused, along with any others who have inserted two chapters—one on the *dipsas* and another on the *prester*—into their treatises. 

But against this excuse stands the fact that **Dioscorides**, **Paulus** [of Aegina], **Nicander**, and **Pliny** among our own writers, make mention of only one species of **dipsas**, which is named from its diverse effects: **dipsas** from the thirst it causes, but **prester** from the "burning" or inflammation. <note>The author is arguing that these are two names for the same animal based on its symptoms.</note> Furthermore, that the **prester** of which **Lucan** speaks is the same one discussed by the aforementioned authors can be proven by an equal argument: because almost the same effects are attributed to the **dipsas** by them as are attributed to the **prester** by **Lucan**. 

Perhaps also **centris** and **ammoatis** are not the names of other serpents distinct from the **dipsas**, but it is one and the same serpent which is called both **prester** and **causon** from the "burning," as we said, and **centris** likewise; because, as the commentator on **Nicander** says, its face tapers to a point, and so it is likened to a **centron** <note>original: "centro"; a sting or sharp point.</note>. It is called **ammoatis**, however, because it has its hiding places in the sands. <note>From the Greek *ammos*, meaning sand.</note> 

Truly, I do not wish to decide on this matter, both because the subject is obscure and because each opinion has great authorities to support it. There are many other examples available to me from which I could show that the philosopher **Albert**, regardless of the authority of the poet **Lucan**, was deceived—as can be seen—by the diversity of names, and in vain multi-

...implied, as if nature—when she chose to act as a stepmother rather than a parent—had not produced enough such pests in the generation of serpents, unless we ourselves needlessly invented other species of these same serpents and just as many types of death in addition. Unless perhaps **Albertus** thought the **armene** was not as malicious as the **basilisk**, because it could, yet perhaps would not wish, to harm as much as the **basilisk**. But whence comes this piety in the **armene**? Whence this mercy? Indeed, I think the **basilisk** cannot be compared to the **armene** in malice unless it is compared to itself; for although it is one serpent, I believe the reason it was considered as two is that various authors wrote of the same serpent—some under the Greek term **basiliscus**, others under the barbarian term **armene**—yet handed down the same effects and the same cure, as we have shown before. ...received, it is indeed cited by **Albertus** regarding the **basilisk**; but regarding the **armene** <note>A serpent mentioned in the previous page, which Leoniceno argues is identical to the basilisk.</note>, not at all. These are the signs of the bite of the **ceristalis** or **sirtalis** from **Semerion** and **Avicenna**, as recorded by **Albertus** himself:

> The **ceristalis** is a serpent of the viper kind, and of the second order; it is ash-colored and two cubits <note>About 3 feet or 90 centimeters.</note> long. Regarding those whom the **cerastes** has bitten, **Dioscorides** and **Paulus** write these signs:

> The site indeed rises up with hardness and pustules. Moreover, a discharge <note>original: "sanies"; a thin, greenish-black fluid from a wound or sore.</note> flows from the bite, sometimes...

...indeed black, and sometimes reddish. Moreover, a paleness appears over the entire body, and the penis suffers from a tension <note>original: "tetanum patitur." In this historical context, this likely refers to a state of painful, persistent erection or rigid contraction caused by the venom.</note>, while the mind becomes deranged. A clouding comes over the eyes, and finally, the victim dies convulsed in the manner of tetanus. For because he had read about the **cerastes** separately in **Pliny** and **Solinus**, or any other Latin or Greek authors, and read separately about the **ceristalis** or **sirtalis** in **Semerio** and **Avicenna**: attending only to this diversity in names, he fell into error, thinking that the difference which existed only in the words was also a difference in the thing itself. It also seems that this confusion of names disturbed **Avicenna** to no small degree, so much so that regarding this very serpent, which he names the **sirtalis**, he doubted to which order it belonged; although **Albertus**, based on the opinion of **Avicenna** as much as **Semerio**, places it in the second order. For these are the words of **Avicenna**, who was in no small doubt concerning the **sirtalis**:

> And I indeed spoke of this serpent in a speculative place <note>original: "in loco extimatiue."</note>, and I do not know it, nor its order, nor its genus with certainty, and I do not know whether this is a repetition <note>original: "in iteratione," referring to whether he is accidentally describing the same snake twice under different names.</note> or not.

<margin>The Arabs drew everything from the Greeks.</margin>
These are the words of **Avicenna**, full, as it appears, of doubts: some of which I hope I can easily resolve by relying on the authority of **Nicander**, **Dioscorides**, as well as **Galen** and **Paulus**, from whom the Arabs received almost everything, though they took some things wrongly.

For regarding the rank in which the **sirtalis** serpent is to be placed, we are prepared to answer using the same authors from whom we proved that the **ceristalis** or **sirtalis** is the serpent called **cerastes** <note>The horned viper (*Cerastes cerastes*), known for the horn-like scales above its eyes.</note> by the Greeks. Since the Greek authors mentioned above place the **basilisk**, the **asp**, and the **cerastes** in that rank of serpents whose bite admits no cure except for the amputation of the limb touched by the poison, it can now be clear that the **sirtalis** belongs to the first rank, following the way **Avicenna** <note>A Persian polymath (c. 980–1037) whose "Canon of Medicine" was a standard textbook in Europe for centuries.</note> speaks of the ranks of serpents. Therefore, **Albertus** does not seem to have placed it correctly in the second rank. 

As for the other doubt concerning **Avicenna’s** **sirtalis** serpent—namely, whether he made a redundant repetition—it is not quite as easy to resolve. This is because the "horned" serpent <note>original: "cornuta"</note>, which **Avicenna** discussed before he spoke of the **sirtalis**, appears to be the species the Greeks call the **cerastes**, if we look at the name and the remedies **Avicenna** applies to the bite. We have already demonstrated above that this same serpent is called by the corrupted name **ceristalis** by **Albertus**, and **sirtalis** by **Avicenna**. Indeed, **Avicenna** writes the following regarding the treatment of the horned serpent: 

> "And what is specifically assigned to it is that radish seed be given in wine as a drink." 

**Dioscorides** <note>An ancient Greek physician and botanist (c. 40–90 AD) who wrote "De Materia Medica."</note> likewise writes that the same radish seed drunk with wine helps against the bite of the **cerastes**. Next, **Avicenna** adds that Indian cumin, sesame with wine, and castor <note>original: "castoreum." This is a secretion from the scent glands of beavers, highly prized in ancient medicine.</note> with wine are beneficial for the same bite. **Dioscorides** similarly writes of sesame that it heals the bite of the **cerastes**. 

Indian cumin, moreover, is that which is called **ammi** <note>Bishop’s weed (*Trachyspermum ammi*), an aromatic plant with seeds similar to cumin.</note> by the Greeks and the Latins. Although **Dioscorides** testifies that it is called "Ethiopian" rather than "Indian" cumin. Regarding **ammi**, however, **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder (23–79 AD), author of the encyclopedic "Natural History."</note> writes in the twentieth volume of his *Natural History* in this manner: 

> "There is also something very similar to cumin, which the Greeks call **ammi**; when two drachms are drunk with wine, it mitigates scorpion stings along with linseed, and specifically those of the **cerastes** when taken in an equal potion..."

Likewise, **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder (23–79 AD), author of the encyclopedic *Natural History*.</note> writes in his 32nd volume about **castoreum** <note>A yellowish secretion from the scent glands of the North American or European beaver, historically used in medicine.</note>: the testicles of the beaver act as a remedy against the **cerastes** <note>The horned viper.</note>. **Avicenna** also orders ground salt mixed with **alkitran** <note>original: "alkitran"; a term for cedar resin or liquid pitch.</note> to be applied to the bite of the "horned" serpent. **Pliny**, however, in the 31st volume of the same *Natural History*, recommends the nature of salt with **oregano** and **cedria**—that is, cedar gum, which the Arabs call **alkitran**, though some wrongly interpret it as liquid pitch—against the **cerastes**. 

But if we consider the description of the **horned** serpent <note>original: "cornuta"</note> in **Avicenna**, it seems that the "horned" one is not of the **cerastes** type, but rather of the **asp** kind. Indeed, **Albertus** <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a medieval scholar who wrote extensively on animals.</note>, alleging both **Avicenna** and **Semerion** <note>Possibly a reference to a source used by Albertus, though the identity is debated among scholars.</note> regarding the **horned asp**, says it is a serpent of the "first rank" <note>The most lethal category of venomous creatures.</note>, whose length is from one cubit to two <note>Approximately 1.5 to 3 feet.</note>, and there are two protrusions above its head like two horns; the color of its body is red, and its belly is like dry, hard scales, which hiss and make a noise against the ground when they walk. Its teeth are even and not curved, and it mostly lives in sandy places. 

**Avicenna** writes nearly all of these things word-for-word regarding the "horned" serpent. Therefore, **Avicenna** cannot avoid one of two things: either he incorrectly applied remedies that were appropriate for the **cerastes** to the bites of **asps**, or, if the serpent he treats as the **horned** one is that which the Greeks call the **cerastes**, he has pointlessly repeated the same serpent in another chapter under the name **sirtalis**. 

Perhaps, however, it should be considered separately and more diligently against **Semerion** and **Albertus** whether there are any horned serpents within the genus of **asps**. 

<margin>Asps lack horns.</margin>

For **Nicander** <note>A Greek physician and poet of the 2nd century BC, famous for his works on venomous animals.</note> denies this, saying that **asps** do not have horns, but rather certain calluses protruding on the forehead around the eyebrows, which make their eyes seem hidden in a kind of cavity. Furthermore, **Albertus** writes that **Solinus** <note>Gaius Julius Solinus, a 3rd-century Latin compiler known for his "Collection of Memorable Matters."</note> says that **asps** attack men with their horns, but this is not probable. <page-num>271</page-num>

this multi-colored serpent is called the ***cenchris*** <note>original: *cenchris*; from the Greek word for "millet."</note> among the Greeks, because its body is clearly distinguished by small spots that are just like grains of millet <note>original: *grana milij*</note>. From the symptoms of its bite and the particular variety of its color, it is demonstrated that the ***arachin*** <note>A name used by medieval authors, likely a corruption of an Arabic term.</note> is one and the same as the ***cenchris***—also known as the millet-serpent—and the ***saliviso*** or ***famiuso*** serpent. Regarding the ***arachin***, **Albertus** <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a German scholar who attempted to categorize all known animals.</note> and **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian physician whose "Canon" was the primary medical textbook of the Middle Ages.</note> equally reported that it is a malignant serpent of the second order, killing on the second day with a corrosion of the liver and a "breaking of the intestines," and that it is varied in color and not of great size. This "breaking of the intestines" is a condition which **Erasistratus** <note>A Greek physician and anatomist (c. 304–250 BC).</note> says occurs along with a similar affliction of the liver in the colon and the **jejunum** <note>The middle section of the small intestine.</note>, although by a translation error, as we have said, "jejunum" was placed in the text instead of "bladder" <note>original: *vesica*</note>.

I will seem to speak beyond belief if I say that **Albertus** and **Avicenna** have diversified this serpent with almost as many names as nature has varied it with spots. For they not only called the same species of serpent ***arachin***, ***centrida***, ***salivifum***, or ***famiusum***, and "millet-serpent" in different places, but one might easily guess that they even named the ***cenchris*** as the ***caharum*** <note>Another medieval name derived from Arabic translations.</note>. This is evident partly from the marks reported on the body, partly from the bite of the ***caharum*** serpent, and furthermore from the remedies which **Avicenna** uses for the bite of that same serpent. For **Albertus** and **Avicenna** both write of the ***caharum*** serpent that its color is the color of sand and that there are "tracks" upon its body—by "tracks," I believe, they mean marks or spots—and that from its bite there occurs an abscess <note>original: *apostema*</note>, or as **Albertus** says, a "very great swelling" <note>original: *inflatura permaxima*</note>.

By this "swelling," I believe they are hinting at the tumor of the flesh which **Dioscorides** <note>A 1st-century Greek physician and botanist.</note> and **Paul** <note>Paul of Aegina, a 7th-century Byzantine physician.</note> wrote arises from the bite of the ***cenchris***, as we mentioned before. Moreover, in the Hebrew codex of **Avicenna**, among other signs of the ***caharum*** serpent's bite, sharp pain in the bladder, the liver, and the **mirach** <note>A medieval anatomical term for the abdominal wall or the epigastric region, derived from Arabic.</note> are numbered; these do not differ much from those symptoms which occur in the bite of the ***cenchris***, as [**Erasistratus**]...

<page-num>272</page-num>

<header>NICOLAUS LEONICENO</header>

**Erasistratus** <note>A famous Greek physician and anatomist (c. 304–250 BC).</note>, whose words we recounted above, bears witness to this. Furthermore, the mention made among other signs of the bite of the ***cahari*** <note>An Arabic-derived name for the millet-serpent.</note> serpent affecting the bladder—which we touched upon under another name for the same serpent, namely the ***famiuiso*** <note>A corruption of a name used in medieval translations of Arabic medical texts.</note>—reveals an error of translation. As we said before, "jejunum" <note>The middle section of the small intestine.</note> was substituted for "bladder" because of the similarity of the names in the Greek language <note>original: "iēiunũ pro uesica propter nominum in lingua Græcorum uicinitatem." The Greek words *nēstis* (jejunum) and *kystis* (bladder) were often confused by translators.</note>. Moreover, that it is the same serpent which has been multiplied under so many names due to the variety of languages is likewise proven by this argument: that **Semerion** <note>Likely referring to Simeon Seth, an 11th-century Byzantine Jewish physician.</note> speaks only of the "miliary" <note>Millet-like.</note> serpent, just as **Nicander**, **Dioscorides**, **Paulus**, and our own **Lucan** <note>A group of classical authorities: Nicander (poet), Dioscorides (pharmacologist), Paul of Aegina (surgeon), and Lucan (Roman poet).</note> do regarding the ***cenchris***. No other names are found among these same authors for the ***cenchris***, the miliary serpent, or any other species of serpent.

But **Avicenna** <note>The Latinized name of Ibn Sina (980–1037), whose *Canon of Medicine* was a standard text.</note> himself seems to have recognized his own error. For although he had spoken previously of the "miliary" and the ***arachi***, he later adds these words when discussing the ***famiuiso***:

> And indeed, I have brought forth the discourse on this serpent according to estimation, just as I did the discourse on the one before it; and perhaps it is not of this order, but of the order of those that cause putrefaction, and its cure is the same as the cure for vipers.

"According to estimation," says **Avicenna**, "I have spoken of this serpent"—that is, led by conjecture alone, and not having certain knowledge of it. Furthermore, the remedies which **Avicenna** adds for the bite of the ***cahari*** are almost all the same ones that **Dioscorides** and **Paulus** noted for the bite of the ***cenchris***: namely, the root of birthwort <note>original: *aristolochiæ*</note> with wine, and the root of asphodel. However, that word is corrupted in **Avicenna's** text, for ***assoasu*** is written instead of ***asphodelo***. Other remedies include centaury, gentian, lettuce seed, flax seed, and wild rue—for which one reads ***alharmel*** <note>The Arabic name for *Peganum harmala*, or Syrian Rue.</note> in **Avicenna**.

From this, the error of those people is made manifest who, in certain medicinal compositions, add hemlock seed <note>original: *semen cicutæ*</note> instead of ***alharmel*** seed. Hemlock is a poison which is, as we have shown elsewhere, ruinous. The only remaining doubt is why **Avicenna** would name both ***alharmel*** and wild rue together in the same treatment for the bite of the ***cahari*** serpent <note>Leoniceno is pointing out that since they are the same plant, naming both suggests Avicenna did not realize they were synonyms, further proving his confusion.</note>.

<summary>Leoniceno argues that many medieval serpent "species" are actually just the Greek cenchris (millet-serpent) misnamed through translation errors. He warns that these linguistic blunders led to dangerous medical practices, such as substituting poisonous hemlock for wild rue.</summary>

...[had] determined. However, I think that "wild rue" <note>original: "rutam syluestrem"</note> was an explanation placed in the margin, which was later inserted among the other medicines due to a flaw in the manuscript. Nor can it be said that *alharmel* <note>The Arabic name for Syrian rue (*Peganum harmala*).</note> in this passage signifies hemlock <note>original: "cicuta"</note> or its seed, since both are poison and have no effectiveness against the bites of serpents. But even among these same medicines named by **Avicenna** <note>The Latinized name of Ibn Sina (980–1037), the influential Persian physician.</note> for the bites of the *chaari* <note>The millet-serpent.</note>, I find two other errors: for I find "cinnamon" in Avicenna in place of "cardamom" written in **Dioscorides** <note>A 1st-century Greek physician and author of *De Materia Medica*.</note>; and "bindweed" <term>uolubilis<gloss>A climbing or "twining" plant, likely *Convolvulus*.</gloss></term> in place of "wild thyme" <note>original: "serpillo"</note>. 

The error regarding cinnamon is minimal and almost non-existent, since it is recommended against poisonous animals just as much as cardamom is. There is a much greater fault regarding the bindweed plant, which by its nature has no efficacy against serpents. <margin>From where wild thyme takes its name.</margin> Wild thyme, however, has such power that some have thought its name was given to it for this very reason: because it opposes serpents <note>Leoniceno is referencing a common folk etymology: *serpillum* (thyme) was thought to be related to *serpens* (serpent) or *serpere* (to creep).</note>. 

**Albert** <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a medieval scholar who wrote extensively on natural history.</note> also seems to have rashly doubled the species of the water-snake <term>hydrus<gloss>From the Greek *hydros*, a water-snake.</gloss></term>: for he speaks of it in its own chapter on the *hydrus*, and in another on the *andrius*. **Avicenna**, however, doubts whether the *andrius* and the *hydra* are the same serpent, although he wrote two chapters about them. But we resolve this doubt of Avicenna’s by using **Nicander**, **Dioscorides**, and **Paul** <note>Paul of Aegina, a 7th-century Byzantine physician.</note>. 

<margin>Water-snake.</margin> What the earlier authors called the *hydrus*, the later ones called the *chersidrus* <note>original: "chersidrum." From the Greek *chersos* (dry land) and *hydros* (water), indicating an amphibious nature.</note> (as the commentator on Nicander says), because it is an inhabitant of both land and water. **Dioscorides** and **Paul**, however, named it "hydrus" by its ancient name; and the signs of the bite of the *hydra* reported by **Avicenna** are found written in Dioscorides and Paul regarding those whom the *hydrus* has bitten. But also those remedies which Avicenna hands down for the treatment of the *andrius* serpent, Dioscorides and Paul likewise prescribed almost the same ones for healing those whom the *hydrus* has bitten: so much so that, both from the signs and from the method of treatment, it cannot be doubted that the *hydrus* and the *andrius* are the same serpent in Avicenna; and therefore it was in vain for Albert, who in these [names] of serpents...

<header>BY NICCOLÒ LEONICENO</header>

It follows that **Albertus Magnus** <note>A 13th-century Dominican friar and polymath who sought to catalog all natural knowledge.</note> followed **Avicenna** in doubling the species. But here also, for the sake of establishing greater credibility, we shall subjoin the opinions of both the Arab and the Greek authors—which differ very little—concerning both the *hydrus* and the *andrio* serpents, or rather, the single serpent, since it is one and the same animal varied only by its names. The signs of the bite of the *hydrus* <note>A water-snake, from the Greek *hydros*.</note> or *hydra* according to Avicenna are these:

> The bite spreads and widens, and its color becomes dark. A black moisture, very abundant and extremely foul-smelling, issues from it. **Dioscorides** and **Paul** <note>Paulus Aegineta, a 7th-century Byzantine Greek physician.</note>, however, wrote the following concerning those whom the *hydrus* has bitten: The wound dilates and becomes large with a livid color. Indeed, a black, abundant, and foul discharge <term>sanies<gloss>A thin, watery, and often bloody discharge from a wound or ulcer.</gloss></term> flows from it, of the kind usually excreted from ulcers that consume a limb.

In the case of the *andrio* <note>Likely a corruption of the Greek *enydros*, another term for a water-snake.</note>, although Avicenna writes of other signs for its bite, he nevertheless employs the same remedies in its treatment as Dioscorides and Paul used for the bite of the *hydrus*. These include a weight of two drachmas of birthwort <term>aristolochia<gloss>A plant used in antiquity to treat snakebites and promote childbirth; its name means "excellent birth."</gloss></term> with wine, or mixed with vinegar, as Avicenna writes. 

But as Dioscorides writes, it should be given with posca <note>original: "pusca" — a drink made of vinegar and water common in the Roman era.</note> and the juice of horehound <note>original: "prassij"</note>. Avicenna writes of a plaster made of lime and oil; whereas Dioscorides prescribes a mixture of ash and oil, the bark of oak roots, barley flour, and mountain calamint, as is also written in Avicenna. In place of the latter, we find "oregano" written in Dioscorides. 

Added to this is the fact that regarding the *hydrus* serpent, "Semerion" is cited by Albertus, which varies little or not at all from the signs of the bite set down by Avicenna or Dioscorides; regarding the *andrio*, however, he is entirely silent. Concerning the *haemorrhoos* <note>The "bleeder-snake," so named because its venom was believed to cause uncontrollable bleeding from every orifice.</note> as well, which is a single species of serpent and is not distinguished among Greek authors except by the difference between the male and the female—of which the former is called *haemorrhoos* and the latter *haemorrhois*—Albertus treats it under three names: first as *halfordio*, then *haemorrhoos*, and afterwards *fabri*. He did not notice that the difference lay only in the names, not in the nature of the serpent...

But neither is Albertus free from the error we attributed to Avicenna; in fact, he errs even more than Avicenna, <margin>The vulture louse.</margin> because he claims that Galen uses the name "vulture louse," even though Avicenna says (and Albertus himself confirms) that the "vulture louse" is called *memucle* in Greek. ...just like its bite, because this is a certain variety of it, although it differs in this: it does not so clearly appear to have two heads; and these are the things **Avicenna** <note>The Latinized name of Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the influential Persian physician.</note> says about this serpent.

These are indeed **Albertus’s** words. However, **Avicenna**, whom **Albertus** cites, writes thus about the same serpents in Book IV, in the chapter *On the Sciscetalis Serpent*:
> Its color is similar to the one moving toward both sides <note>original: "salienti ad duas partes"; a literal translation of the Greek name 'amphisbaena'.</note>, but that one is worse, and its symptoms are those [same] symptoms, and its treatment is that [same] treatment.

Indeed, anyone might rightly doubt, against **Avicenna** and **Albertus**, what sort of bite it is, or what symptoms follow from the bite of the **amphisbaena** <term>amphisbaena</term> <note>From the Greek for "going both ways," a legendary serpent with a head at each end.</note>. One might also wonder what the method of treatment is, lest that which is being sought seems to be explained by something else equally unknown. For this error arises from the fact that the words of **Albertus** and **Avicenna** concerning the <term>sciscetalis</term> <note>A corrupted medieval spelling of the Greek "scytale," a snake of uniform thickness.</note> and the **amphisbaena**—or as he should have said, the "one moving toward both sides"—are actually the words of **Dioscorides** <note>Pedanius Dioscorides, a 1st-century Greek physician and author of *De Materia Medica*.</note> and **Paul of Aegina** <note>A 7th-century Byzantine physician.</note> regarding the *scytale* and *amphisbaena*, but badly interpreted. For, to say nothing of the corruption of the names—which is not of great concern to philosophers and physicians—they have not been reported in their proper place.

For when **Dioscorides** had taught what sort of symptoms arise from the bites of vipers and what the method of treatment is, he afterwards added these points concerning the *scytale* and *amphisbaena* serpents:
> Similar things happen to those bitten by the serpent called the **amphisbaena**, or by the **scytale**: the remedies are the same, and therefore there is no need to write a specific entry for this kind.

It was necessary, therefore, for **Avicenna** or **Albertus** (who seems to have followed **Avicenna** in these matters) to place the *sciscetalis* and the *amphisbaena* (or "the one moving toward both sides") in the same order as **Dioscorides**—namely, after the vipers. This would allow them to teach that they produce the same effects and require the same treatment. Or, at the very least, if they wished to change the order, they should have revealed to their readers what the symptoms of those bites were and what the cure was. Yet they seem to have done this in another chapter, but under different names: namely, <term>harem</term> and <term>carem</term> <note>Likely Latinized versions of Arabic names for specific serpents.</note>, about which they wrote thus...
