...wrote **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the preeminent Persian physician whose "Canon of Medicine" was a standard text in Europe.</note> in the chapter *On the Harem and Carem*:
> Certain wise Arabs have said—and I think they are of the kind of sea dragons or others—that the wise **Semerion** <note>A likely corruption of a Greek or Arabic name cited in medieval manuscripts.</note> named both of them, saying that from their bite happens what happens from the bite of vipers, and it is likely that their treatment is the treatment for vipers. 

**Albertus** <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a Dominican friar and polymath who attempted to catalog all natural knowledge.</note> says almost the same things about the *harem* and *carem* based on the authority of **Semerion** and **Avicenna**. However, this **Semerion** is not cited regarding the <term>scyscetalis</term> <note>A medieval corruption of the Greek *scytale*, a snake of uniform thickness.</note> and <term>amphisbaena</term> <note>A legendary serpent with a head at each end.</note>—or "the one moving toward both sides"—so it becomes likely that **Avicenna** and **Albertus** wrote two chapters about the same serpents as if they were different ones: one titled *On the Scyscetalis*, the other *On the Harem and Carem*.

Yet **Albertus** erred much more; he not only doubled but even tripled the serpent called <term>scytale</term> by the Greeks and even the Latins, [listing it] under the name *siseculus*, under *arem* or *carem*, and under the name <term>situla</term> <note>Literally "a bucket" or "water-jar"; used as a name for a serpent in Lucan's poetry.</note>. At times he suggested it was of its own kind, at other times of another—that is, a species of *situla*.

Moreover, it is clear that the second species of *situla* described by **Albertus** is actually the one that the Greeks and Latins call the *scytale*. **Dioscorides** <note>A Greek physician and botanist of the 1st century AD.</note> makes this serpent equal to the **amphisbaena** in its effects and the treatment of its bite. This is evident from those things which **Albertus** writes about this species of *situla*, what **Solinus** <note>A 3rd-century Roman geographer known for his "Collection of Remarkable Facts."</note> writes about the *scytale*, and what **Lucan** <note>A Roman poet (39–65 AD) who described various Libyan serpents in his epic poem, *Pharsalia*.</note> writes about his *situla*—which, however, is not a *situla*, nor even a species of it. 

**Albertus** writes that it is a serpent wondrously beautiful, so much so that it holds onlookers in admiration; but it is sluggish and small, and the one it strikes is completely burned up, and this serpent sheds its skin in winter. But **Solinus** wrote these same things about the *scytale* in these words:

> The **scytale** shines with such variety on its back that it delays onlookers because of the grace of its markings; and since it is slower at crawling, it captures those it cannot overtake by stunning them with its wonder. Nevertheless, in this brightness of scales, it is the first to shed its winter skin. 

**Lucan** writes the same about the *scytale*: 
> "And the **scytale**, the only one about to shed its skin while the frost is still scattered." 

Therefore, it appears clearer than light <note>original: "luce clarius"</note> that **Albertus** mistook the *situla* for the *scytale*, and no...

<meta>This page continues Nicolai Leoniceno’s critique of Albertus Magnus’s "On Animals." On the previous page, Leoniceno argued that Albertus had confused various serpent names due to poor translations. This page focuses on the distinction between the "tirus" and the "viper," and the significant medical error regarding which snakes are used to create the medicine known as theriac.</meta>

# NICOLAI LEONICENI

<page-num>279</page-num>

->### ON SERPENTS.<-

...deceived by the proximity [of names], he assigned a serpent of its own kind to another. But this error indeed pertains to the <term>dipsas</term> <note>original: "dipsadem"; a serpent whose bite was famously said by the ancients to cause an unquenchable, fatal thirst.</note>, which **Albertus** placed under the same genus as the <term>scytale</term> <note>original: "scytale"; a snake described by classical authors as having a body of uniform thickness from head to tail.</note>; the other [error] pertains to the viper. For just as he derived *sciseculum* from *situla*—or, if we wish to speak correctly, from the *scytale*—so he also estimated that the <term>tirus</term> <note>original: "tirum"; a medieval Latinization of the Arabic term for a viper, which Albertus mistakenly treated as a distinct species.</note> was a different species from the viper. This is indicated by the words of the same **Albertus** in Book II of *On Animals*, which are found written in this manner:

> For all kinds of serpents produce eggs except for the **tirus**, as **Aristotle** says; and his text is corrupted, for that which is truly the **tirus** is well-known among us, and from it **theriac** <note>original: "theriaca"; a complex medical concoction used as a universal antidote, traditionally requiring the flesh of vipers.</note> is made.

In these words of **Albertus** there are two errors. The first is that he was ignorant of the custom of Arabic translation, which very frequently substitutes *tirus* for *vipera* (viper). The second, of much greater importance to life, is that he believed the serpent from which true theriac is prepared to be oviparous <note>egg-laying</note>, rather than viviparous <note>giving birth to live young</note>. This is contrary to the opinion of all the ancients—and especially **Andromachus** <note>Physician to Emperor Nero and the reputed inventor of the "Thieriac of Andromachus."</note>, who first taught the precept that vipers, and no other serpents, should be mixed into theriac. 

Whether **Albertus** received this error, like most others, from **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the influential Persian physician.</note> himself—since in the books of the same **Avicenna** translated from Arabic into the Latin language, it appears that the *tirus* and the *vipera* are frequently named as if they were different serpents—I cannot judge with absolute certainty. For it is possible that **Avicenna's** translator sometimes put *tirus* for *vipera*—that is, the genus for the species—which we consider not so much an error as giving an occasion for error to others who are not paying attention. But if **Avicenna** uses the same word everywhere, namely <term>alphe</term> <note>original: "alphe"; a Latinization of the Arabic *al-af'a*, meaning viper.</note>, which signifies "viper" among the Arabs, then he himself wanders much further than his translator; for he puts the name of a simple species for the name of a genus, as when he writes these words in Book IV, in the chapter *On the Species of Serpents*:

> And the second order is of vipers, of which there are diverse species; for among them are the **alelisati** <note>original: "aleliſati"; a medieval corruption of an Arabic term, likely referring to the "cleansed" or "prepared" vipers used in medicine.</note> vipers, and among them are those that cause thirst, and the rest.

Leoniceno traces this mistake back to linguistic misunderstandings in Arabic-to-Latin translations used by medieval scholars.</summary>

# NICOLAI LEONICENI

<page-num>180</page-num>

the remaining ones of which we shall speak, such as the one that makes the victim thirsty, which the Greeks call the <term>dipsas</term> <note>original: "dipsada"; a serpent whose venom was famously believed by ancient writers to cause an unquenchable, fatal thirst.</note>. He might name this as a species of viper—which could be easily tolerated, since it is the same serpent as the viper according to the opinion of the **Marsi** <note>The Marsi were an ancient Italic people renowned in antiquity as gifted snake-charmers and healers.</note>, or at least very similar to the viper according to the opinion of everyone else, including the opinion of **Avicenna** himself. 

But regarding the oak-dwelling serpents—a kind distinct from vipers, which are named <term>dryini</term> <note>original: "dryini"; derived from the Greek "drys" (oak).</note> by the Greeks, as we said before, because they live in the roots of oaks—**Avicenna** later calls these "ilicine" <note>original: "ilicinium"; pertaining to the holm-oak or ilex tree.</note> in his list of other serpent species. Either he does not make a distinction between the oak and the holm-oak, or perhaps he thinks the oak-serpents are different from the holm-oak serpents, having been deceived by the diversity of names, as we have shown in many other instances. 

That he wishes, I say, for both the oak-serpents and many others of which he promises to speak to be species of the viper, is the mark of a man misusing a specific name in place of a generic name. Indeed, <term>alphe</term> <note>original: "alphe"; a Latinization of the Arabic "al-af'a," the standard word for viper.</note> signifies "viper" among the Arabs; this is a single, simple species according to **Aristotle**, **Nicander**, **Dioscorides**, **Andromachus**, **Galen**, **Paul** [of Aegina], and the rest of the more ancient physicians. 

Furthermore, wherever the translator of **Avicenna** interprets the Arabic word *alphe* as <term>tirus</term>, as if he wished to say *therium* <note>original: "therium"; from the Greek "therion" (wild beast). In medical contexts, this often referred specifically to venomous snakes used in medicine.</note>, he puts the name of the genus in place of the name of the species. **Galen** testifies in his exposition of the second book of *On the Regimen of Acute Diseases* that this is a thing frequently done by all men. And we see this practiced not only by **Galen**, but also by **Aristotle** regarding this same serpent. 

For instance, when **Galen** says in the book *On Theriac to Piso* that **Andromachus** was the first to establish the mixing of *theria*—that is, vipers—into <term>theriac</term> <note>original: "theriaca"; a complex polypharmaceutical "universal antidote" that was one of the most prestigious medicines of the Renaissance.</note>, and when in the same place he also approves of another etymology. We ourselves inserted this into our book titled *On the Errors of Pliny and Other Physicians*, relying on the authority of the same **Galen** (though we did not cite **Galen** by name in that specific passage). There we stated that the theriac of **Andromachus**—for we were speaking of it then—and the theriac <term>troches</term> <note>original: "trociscos"; small medicinal lozenges or cakes. Viper flesh was processed into these "troches" before being added to the final theriac mixture.</note> [derived] from it...

### ON SERPENTS

...[they] held this name because they are prepared from <term>theria</term> <note>From the Greek "therion," meaning a wild beast or creature; in medical contexts, it specifically referred to venomous serpents.</note>, that is, vipers, which are of the genus of wild beasts. But some ask: why are they not called "viperine" rather than "theriacal," or in Latin "feral" <note>Latin: *feralis*. While meaning "of wild beasts," it also carried a connotation of death or funerals, which is why Pliny considered it an "ill-omened" name.</note>, using the specific name of the serpent rather than the more common one?

And what prevents us, I say, from naming these same <term>trochisci</term> <note>Small medicinal lozenges or cakes, a common form for storing ingredients like processed viper meat before they were mixed into the final theriac.</note> "viperine" in Latin, just as they are "theriacal" in Greek? Since Pliny, a most learned man, preferred to call "viperine" the salt—which the Greeks call "theriacal salt" for the same reason as the theriacal lozenges, because it is made from vipers—rather than using the ill-omened name "feral." In Book 30, Chapter 3, he writes: *Likewise, the brain of a rooster taken in food with viperine salt is used for fresh wounds.* <note>original: "Item gallinacei cerebrum recentibus plagis sale uiperino in cibo sumptũ."</note> 

The same reasoning applies to the entire antidote, which, if we wish, we can call "viperine," just as the Greeks sometimes call it an <term>antidote from vipers</term> <note>original: "ἀντίδοτον δι’ ἐχιδνῶν" (antidoton di’ echidnōn)</note>. For what does it matter whether we call it a "viperine antidote" or an "antidote from vipers," since the name is derived from vipers in either case? 

However, there are those who argue that theriac cannot receive its name among the Greeks because it admits "wild beasts" into its composition. They claim that since "wild beast" is such a general term, the word itself would no more imply that a viper should be used in the composition of theriac than it would imply a basilisk should be used. 

They do not notice that this same argument applies to their own position. For if it is called "theriac" in Greek (or "feral" in Latin, as they interpret it) because it works against the bites of wild beasts, it ought also to be effective against the bites of wild boars, lions, and elephants, which no one would doubt belong to the genus of wild beasts. Therefore, neither etymology can be defended as true unless, in both cases, the general name is understood in a more specific sense. 

Just as in the case of the whole antidote, we approve of both etymologies on the authority of **Galen** <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–c. 216 AD), the most influential physician of antiquity, whose writings on theriac remained standard for over a millennium.</note>: both the one assigned from its use, which it provides against venomous wild beasts, and the other from the beasts which [are mixed] in it...

We can demonstrate this same distinction in naming from many other places in Galen’s work, such as the passage we cited at the start of our discussion from Book XI of *On Simple Medicine*, where the conversation concerned choosing vipers for the composition of theriac. Regarding these, Galen wrote:
>> It is safest to avoid vipers hunted in such places—namely, dry and salty areas—whether they are for use as food or for the composition of a drug, such as that most celebrated one which all physicians call **theriac**.

Also, in his book *On Theriac to Piso*, Galen clearly shows that before Andromachus, there was no antidote called "theriac," even though there was that composition which the great King **Antiochus** <note>Likely referring to Antiochus III or VIII, both of whom were known for their interest in toxicology.</note> is said to have used against all venomous animals, and the other called **mithridates** after King **Mithridates**, whose invention it was. For Galen writes as follows concerning King Mithridates and the antidote he invented in the aforementioned book:
>> For they say that even Mithridates, that great warrior, did not take theriac—for it did not yet exist—but rather another antidote of many mixtures, which is itself called by his name.

But if, as Galen says, theriac did not yet exist in the time of Mithridates, then the remedy of Antiochus was not theriac either, as he lived long before him. If anyone truly...

# THE WORKS OF NICCOLÒ LEONICENO #

[Gale]nus <note>The text begins with the end of the name "Galenus" (Galen), the influential 2nd-century Greek physician.</note> implies that only the composition of **Andromachus** <note>Andromachus the Elder, physician to Emperor Nero and creator of the refined "Theriac" formula.</note> should be called "theriac" in the simplest sense. He also shows the reason why this specific remedy is called theriac above all other antidotes: namely, the mixing in of **viper flesh**. For if the name were derived solely from its utility against the bites of serpents, then "theriac" would have existed before its actual invention, since the **mithridate** <note>original: "mithridates"; a famous all-purpose antidote used before the invention of theriac.</note> antidote is no less effective against those same bites—excepting only the bite of the viper—and indeed, as Galen says in the passage cited above, it is even more effective against some of them than theriac itself.

**Alexander** <note>Alexander of Aphrodisias, a 2nd-century commentator on Aristotle.</note> also discusses this in the final problem of his first book, in which he asks why theriac—which is hot and dry by nature—nonetheless settles the thirst of those bitten by a **dipsas** <note>term: dipsas; a legendary snake whose venom was said to cause an unquenchable, fatal thirst.</note> who are suffering from intolerable dryness, rather than increasing it. It is clear from his discourse, where he speaks simply of "theriac," that he believed only one antidote should be called by that name: the one which receives vipers into its composition.

Indeed, near the end of the solution to that problem, he says:

> The flesh of vipers, when mixed with the other medicines placed in theriac, possesses a natural power to resist all venomous animals and deadly drugs.

From these words of Alexander, it can also be established that it is not the viper flesh alone—nor even when seasoned with oil and dill—but rather when combined with more than **sixty other medicines** <note>original: "plus quàm sexaginta numero"; the standard recipe for Theriac of Andromachus eventually included 64 ingredients.</note> blended into a single nature, that it possesses such power. This is the same point made by Galen in his book *On Theriac, to Piso*, which we have frequently cited: that it has great power against all poisons, but especially against the viper.

Therefore, to return to the **theriac troches** <note>term: trociscos (troches); small medicinal lozenges or cakes. In this context, they are the "viper biscuits" made of dried viper flesh and flour used as a base for the final antidote.</note> from which our dispute began: since they themselves have no greater efficacy against poisons than the viper flesh itself (from which they differ only by the addition of **fine flour** <note>original: "similagine"; the finest wheat flour used to bind the viper meat into stable cakes.</note>), and since this flour is added not to increase the power of the meat but rather to allow for the formation of the troches, these same troches are not named for the utility they bring, but rather for that which is **contained** in them...

<meta>This page continues the philological and medical debate regarding the naming of "theriac." The previous page established that the term specifically refers to an antidote containing viper flesh; this page clarifies why the flesh itself isn't called "theriac" and classifies the three distinct types of antidotes recognized by ancient medicine.</meta>

### ON SERPENTS ###

[...in which] the beast is contained, named by the Greek word *theriaci* <note>original: "theriaci"; derived from the Greek *thērion*, meaning a wild or venomous beast.</note>. Otherwise, a question would arise as to why the meat itself is not called "theriac" on its own. This question is impossible to solve for those who claim the name comes only from its utility <note>i.e., its "usefulness" in treating bites.</note>; but for us, it is very easy, as we assign the name not to its use, but rather to what is contained within it. Indeed, viper flesh does not "contain" itself, but rather is contained within other things. For this reason, doctors are not accustomed to calling the meat "theriac flesh," in the same way they refer to **theriac troches** <note>term: troches; small medicated lozenges or cakes (from the Greek *trochos*, wheel) used as a way to preserve ingredients.</note> and **theriac salts**, which are themselves manufactured from viper flesh with certain other ingredients added. 

But if someone, disregarding the common custom of speech, wishes to call the flesh of the viper "theriac," let him know that he will signify nothing more than "viper-like," or at the very least, he will be using a very general term that signifies every medicine which might be beneficial in any way against any poison. 

Lest we labor too much over the ambiguity of the name, it must be understood that there are, as we have said before, three species of antidotes: 

<margin>Three species of antidotes.</margin>
The first is that which is effective against **deadly drugs** <note>original: "pharmaca mortifera"; referring to ingested poisons.</note>, which of course kill a person when taken either through food or through drink. 

The second is that which is beneficial against the bites of certain venomous animals, such as a **rabid dog**, a **scorpion**, **venomous spiders** <note>original: "phalangiorū"; refers to a specific type of venomous spider mentioned by Pliny and Aristotle.</note>, and **vipers**. Such antidotes, as **Galen** says in his book *On Antidotes*, the younger doctors—one of whom was **Asclepiades** <note>Asclepiades of Pharmacion, a 1st-century physician famous for his multi-ingredient recipes.</note>—were accustomed to naming "theriac medicines." 

The third species of antidote is that which helps against diseases contracted from a **corrupt diet**. 

If indeed any antidote, such as the one established by **Andromachus**, helps against all the evils we have mentioned, this is not called a "theriac medicine," but simply **Theriac**. For this reason, although Galen makes mention in that same book *On Antidotes* of many remedies that are wonderfully effective against deadly drugs and the bites of venomous animals—such as **mithridate**, **athanasia** <note>term: athanasia; literally "immortality," a name for several complex ancient cures.</note>, the **ambrosia of Philip of Macedon**, the antidote made from bloods, and another named after the **skink** <note>term: scincus; a type of lizard used in ancient pharmacology, believed to have aphrodisiac and antitoxic properties.</note>—none [of these are called theriac in the same absolute sense].

<summary>Leoniceno distinguishes "Theriac" from other antidotes, arguing the name specifically denotes the inclusion of viper flesh. He categorizes ancient antidotes into three types: those for ingested poisons, those for venomous bites, and those for dietary illnesses.</summary>

# NICOLAUS LEONICENI #

Now, some believe that only the composition of **Andromachus** <note>Andromachus the Elder was the court physician to Emperor Nero and is credited with improving the formula for theriac by adding viper flesh.</note> should be honored with the name "theriac," which they do not call "theriacal medicine," but simply "theriac." However, if the Arabs, and certain Latin authors who sometimes believe the Arabs more than they ought, use this name "theriac" more loosely, we judge that greater faith should be placed in the Greek authors regarding a Greek word. Nevertheless, if those same Arabs would recall what we said above concerning the **theriac of Antiochus**, the **theriac of the Diatesseron** <note>term: Diatesseron; an ancient four-ingredient remedy consisting of gentian, laurel berries, birthwort, and myrrh.</note>, and the other **theriac of the rustics** <note>original: "theriaca rusticorum"; often referring to garlic, which was known as the "poor man's theriac" for its perceived anti-poison properties.</note>, they could easily be brought into one accord with the Greeks.

For even if **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian physician whose "Canon of Medicine" was the standard medical textbook in Europe for centuries.</note> says in the second book of his *Canon*, in the chapter "On Squill," that it is a "theriac for venomous things," and likewise says of **opoponax** <note>term: opoponax; a gum resin used in perfumery and herbal medicine.</note> that it is a "theriac" when drunk with **aristolochia** <note>term: aristolochia; also known as birthwort, a plant used in ancient medicine specifically for snake bites.</note> for stings—and similarly for its juice—nevertheless, this same Avicenna admits in that same book that it is an improper manner of speaking when a **simple medicine** <note>term: simple; a single-ingredient medicinal herb or substance, as opposed to a "compound" made of many parts.</note> is called a "theriac." For, as he says, the name of theriac is more worthily attributed to **artificial medicines**, that is, compound ones, while the name **bezoar** <note>term: bezoar; originally a "stone" found in the stomachs of goats, believed to be a universal antidote.</note> is attributed to individual substances occurring according to nature.

Yet elsewhere this same Avicenna seems to confuse "bezoar" with "theriac," writing in this manner: 
>> **Bezoar** and **theriac** are all those medicines whose property is to preserve health and the power in the vital spirit, so that they may expel the harm of poison from themselves.

To me, however, it seems that the name "bezoar" among the Arabs signifies the same thing as the word **alexipharmic** <note>original: "alexipharmacum"; from the Greek *alexo* (to ward off) and *pharmakon* (poison/drug).</note> among the Greeks. 
<margin>Alexipharmic.</margin>
This is a general term for all remedies, whether against the bites of venomous animals or against deadly poisons such as **aconite** <note>term: aconite; a highly toxic flowering plant, also known as monkshood or wolfsbane.</note>, **quicksilver** <note>mercury.</note>, and similar substances that are introduced into our bodies through food or drink.

<margin>Theriac is suited only for serpent bites.</margin>
However, a **theriacal drug**, or "theriacal medicine" as the younger physicians call it, is suited only for the bites of serpents, as we have said above on the authority of the physician **Asclepiades**. This is also indicated by the name itself, which is derived from *theria* <note>original: "therijs"; from the Greek *thērion*, meaning a wild or venomous beast.</note>, that is, venomous animals. Generally, however,

### ON SERPENTS ###

**Galen**, as we have said, applies the name **theriac** only to the composition of **Andromachus**. Therefore, in my opinion, **Nicolaus Florentinus** <note>Niccolò Falcucci (d. 1412), an influential Italian physician known for his massive medical compilation, the "Sermones medicinales."</note> did not determine these names correctly in Book IV, in the chapter "On Bezoar Medicines," when he wrote these words:

> You can see that these two names, **bezaar** and **theriaca**, can be taken in three ways, as **Serapion** <note>Serapion the Younger, an 11th or 12th-century Arabic medical author whose work on simple medicines was widely used in Europe.</note> suggests in his work on simple medicines, in the chapter "On the Bezoar Stone": first, in the broadest sense for every medicine that primarily or secondarily works to liberate one from poisons; in another way, broadly for the bezoar medicines mentioned above; and in a third way, strictly. For example: **Theriaca** for the theriac itself, which is a specific confection called the "great theriac" or "the deliverer," and it is called **Galen's theriac**; it is the one in which **viper flesh** <note>original: "caro tiri"; "tiri" refers to the *tyrus*, a type of viper. Viper flesh was the signature ingredient of the "Great Theriac."</note> is included. It is not called theriac for that reason, as many assume; rather, it has been granted the name of its class because of the excellence of its theriacal power, and it deserved to be called by its own name. It is this which is understood when the term is used absolutely. Similarly, **bezaar** <note>term: bezaar (bezoar); originally a stone found in the stomachs of goats, believed to be a universal antidote. Here used as a general category of medicine.</note> taken strictly refers to a certain stone which, because of the excellence of its bezoar-like power, has likewise been called by the name of its class.

These are indeed the words of Nicolaus. From these words, it appears that he also confuses these two names, **bezaar** (or **alexipharmacum** <note>term: alexipharmacum; from the Greek 'alexein' (to ward off) and 'pharmakon' (poison). A general term for an antidote.</note>) with **theriac**, although among the Arabs, **bezaar**—like **alexipharmacon** among the Greeks—can be either a simple or a compound medicine. **Theriaca**, however, is only a compound, and not just any compound, but specifically the one **Andromachus** is said to have composed. Therefore, neither the broadest nor the broad interpretation of "theriac" is correct in his view. Even the third and most narrow definition can be rejected on the grounds that theriac understood in this way is not Galen’s theriac, but rather Andromachus’s. It seems that Nicolaus has placed too much trust in **Avicenna**, who falsely accused Galen of having changed Andromachus's antidote by adding some things and removing others for no necessary reason, but only so that he might claim the title of the same antidote for himself—

# NICOLAUS LEONICENUS #

...[names they] would employ, even though **Galen**, in all his treatises and works on **theriac** <term>theriac: a famous ancient poly-pharmaceutical "wonder drug" used as an antidote to all poisons and a cure-all for diseases</term> antidotes, most strongly approves the composition of **Andromachus** <note>Andromachus the Elder (1st century AD), physician to Emperor Nero, who famously added viper's flesh to the earlier recipe of Mithridates.</note>. As we have often said, Galen names that composition alone as "theriac," as if it encompasses the benefits of all other antidotes; for this reason, he strives everywhere to preserve it uncorrupted. 

Indeed, **Nicolaus** <note>Niccolò Falcucci (d. 1412), also known as Nicolaus Florentinus, a prominent physician of the late Middle Ages.</note> criticized those who think Galen’s theriac is named because it is made from **viper flesh** <note>original: "tiri carne"; the term "tirus" or "tyrus" was a medieval Latinization for the venomous snake used in the recipe.</note>. Perhaps he would have better criticized those who did not even recognize the true viper. This man [Nicolaus], though otherwise a devoted student of Galen’s doctrine, did not notice that he was accusing the "Prince of Physicians"—a man no less distinguished in literature than in the medical art—of having poorly interpreted the name of his own antidote and of having been ignorant of its meaning. 

However, so that this error of Nicolaus and others who hold the same view may appear more clearly, I will set down **Galen’s** own words. In his book *On Theriac, to Piso*, he writes the following regarding the etymology of that word:

> Because this man—**Andromachus**, of whom I was speaking just before—thought to mix into the medicine ***theria*** <note>original Greek: "θηρία" (*thēria*), meaning wild beasts or venomous creatures.</note>, that is, **vipers**, which are a type of venomous wild beast: it is called "**theriac**" by us not only because it works well against their bites, but because it also receives those very venomous beasts, namely vipers, into its own mixture; for that reason, it is natural for us to name it "theriac."

Truly, this error of Nicolaus—which, to tell the truth, is not his own error but that of other famous authors of his age, from whose books he received it—could perhaps be tolerated on account of the corrupted and mutilated translation of Galen’s books on theriac that we currently possess. **Gentilis** <note>Gentile da Foligno (d. 1348), a renowned Italian physician and professor known for his commentaries on Avicenna.</note>, however, in his exposition of the fifth book of the *Canon* of **Avicenna**, in the chapter "On the Great Theriacs," admits both meanings of "theriac": namely, that it is so named from its effect against serpents and other poisonous medicines, and from the flesh of the viper <note>original: "tiri"</note>. He does not apply both meanings to one and the same theriac, but rather to different ones. For in the aforementioned chapter on the **the**-

...[he] writes under the name of theriac: Since the name **theriac** <term>theriaca: an ancient compound medicine used as an antidote to poison</term> is taken from its effect, because it is similar to poisons, the name is applied to all medicines that are useful against poisons and against difficult ailments. These are called **theriacal medicines**, whether they are simple or compound. In this way, garlic is called the <term>theriaca rusticorum</term> <note>original: "theriaca rusticorum"; literally "the peasant's theriac," a common historical term for garlic due to its perceived protective properties</note> by **Galen** in the twelfth book of his *Method of Healing*, and pears are called the <term>theriaca fungorum</term> <note>original: "theriaca fungorum"; "the theriac of mushrooms," referring to the belief that eating pears could counteract poisonous fungi</note>, and so it goes for many things. Thus, there is the <term>theriaca diatesseron</term> <note>A famous "four-ingredient" remedy consisting of gentian, birthwort, laurel berries, and myrrh</note>, into which the flesh of the **viper** <note>original: "tiri"; a medieval Latin corruption of the Greek word for a venomous beast, used specifically for the vipers used in medicine</note> does not enter. In this sense, **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the influential Persian physician whose "Canon of Medicine" was a standard text in Europe</note> uses the term "theriacal" in his work *On the Powers of the Heart*, and in the second book of the *Canon*, chapter twenty. However, when this name is taken specifically from the flesh of the **viper**, it applies only to those theriacs that actually contain it.

These are the words of **Gentilis** <note>Gentile da Foligno (d. 1348), a renowned Italian physician and commentator on Avicenna</note>. If he were perhaps asked why pears are rightly called the "theriac of mushrooms," given that mushrooms are not serpents—and the name "theriac" is derived from *theria*, which means "serpents"—he would, I believe, offer no answer other than the one he noted shortly before the words written above. He bases this on the authority of a certain Arab named **Azarangi** <note>Likely a corruption of a name like Al-Zahrawi or another Arabic authority cited in medieval texts</note>, claiming that *theriaca* is so named because it counteracts the venoms of serpents and of other poisonous medicines. 

For this name, as they say, has two parts: one, *tiri*, which signifies "serpents," and the other, *ka*, which signifies "poisonous medicines." Therefore, on account of this second part of the name—the *ka*—it seems to **Azarangi**, and to **Gentilis** who follows him, that pears are rightly called the "theriac" of mushrooms, which are poisonous. 

I am sometimes ashamed when I see men famous in the art of medicine wander so childishly concerning medicinal names. If only their errors were confined to names, and did not also plunge them into matters dangerous to life itself! We have demonstrated that this has happened up to the present day regarding the flesh of the **viper**—for so they call it—which is a medicine so necessary for the composition of **theriac**. As far as pears are concerned, which are called the "theriac of mushrooms," we have also previously declared why garlic is called "theriac" by **Galen**. Moreover, concerning pears...

...it must be established that they are called **theriac of mushrooms** <note>original: "fungorum theriaca"</note> only to the degree that they have the same effect against the poison of mushrooms or fungi as the standard theriac <term>theriaca: the "universal" antidote of the ancient world, often containing dozens of ingredients</term> has against all poisons. Perhaps it would have been more reasonable to phrase it this way: it applies to the **true theriac**, which contains the flesh of the **viper**, since other compositions are not true theriacs, but are named so through a kind of metaphor. 

However, even true theriac itself is not called theriac solely because of the serpent it contains, but also because of the use it provides against the bites of serpents <note>The Greek word "therion" means "wild beast" or "serpent"</note>. Therefore, Gentile’s distinction—that some theriac is named from what it contains and some only from its effect—is not entirely to be approved. This is because no theriac is "true" without the flesh of the serpent, and that which contains it is called theriac for a twofold reason, as we have previously shown by the authority of **Galen** <note>Claudius Galenus (129–c. 216 AD), the most influential physician of antiquity</note>. 

But perhaps such a long investigation into names is more suitable for grammarians than for philosophers or physicians. For, as Galen says in a certain passage on simple medicines and in many other places, the cure of diseases is achieved through the knowledge of things rather than words. However, because we recently noticed that in our book entitled *On the Errors of Pliny and Other Physicians* <note>original: "De Plinii atque aliorum medicorum erroribus"; Leonicenus’s most famous work (1492), which sparked a massive intellectual debate by pointing out botanical mistakes in ancient texts</note>, we were criticized by certain doctors and petty lawyers in long-winded speeches regarding the etymology of the word **theriac**, we ourselves have been forced, now that the opportunity has been given to us, to become more wordy in our own defense.

# ON SERPENTS #

...dealing with their errors, we leave it free to anyone to call that serpent, whose flesh is mixed into the theriac <term>theriaca: a complex ancient "universal antidote" believed to cure all poisons; its most vital ingredient was processed viper flesh</term>, either a *tirus* <note>original: "tirum"; a medieval Latin term for the viper used in medicine, likely corrupted from the Arabic word for the antidote itself</note>, or a viper, or by whatever other name they please. For this reason, we have attacked the younger physicians, not because they sometimes call the viper a *tirus*, but rather because they thought the *tirus* was a different creature from the viper. Furthermore, they sought the *tirus* from as far away as Syria, when a much better variety was to be found right here in Italy. Finally, they seemed until now to have been ignorant of what serpent the *tirus* or the viper actually was; this was not merely an error in naming, but rather an error regarding the thing itself. 

For let us imagine that the translator of **Serapion** <note>Johannes Serapion the Younger, a 12th-century physician whose work was a bridge between Arabic and Latin medicine</note> had provided the correct title "On the Flesh of the Viper," and that all those medicinal properties attributed to the flesh of the *tirus* had been, in that same translation, assigned to the flesh of the viper (with only the name of the serpent changed). Would the younger physicians have known from Serapion what or what kind of serpent the viper was, whose flesh is so greatly commended for medical use? I certainly do not think so. For if they could have known this simply by a correct translation of Serapion’s words, why did they not equally learn it from **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the most influential philosopher-physician of the Islamic Golden Age</note>, who in the second book of his *Canon* also writes of the more remarkable properties of viper flesh? Why did they not likewise learn from **Dioscorides** <note>A 1st-century Greek physician whose "De Materia Medica" was the primary authority on botany and drugs for 1,500 years</note> and **Galen**, who write the same things about the flesh of the *echidna* <note>original: "echidnae"; the Greek word for viper</note> or viper that Serapion writes about the flesh of the *tirus*—especially since Serapion himself cites both authors regarding the powers of that same flesh? 

From this citation, they could have easily perceived that the *tirus*, the *echidna*, and the viper are the same serpent. But since most of them were ignorant of what the name "viper" signified among the Latin speakers, they were also unable to understand what "echidna" meant in the Greek texts, or what "tirus" meant in the Arabic translation. Therefore, regarding that which we boasted in our letter to **Alexander Agathimerus** concerning the *tirus* and the viper, we now also justly boast of this: that we were the first who—ten years before that same letter was published—taught that the *tirus* and the viper are the same serpent which is commonly called the **marasso** or **scortio** <note>These are regional Italian names for the common European adder or viper</note> in the common tongue. <margin>Gentilis was considered the "soul" of Avicenna.</margin>Therefore, wherever we decided that **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the Persian physician whose "Canon of Medicine" was the standard textbook in Europe for centuries</note> should be criticized because he thought the *tirus* was different from the viper, we did this according to the explanation of **Gentilis** <note>Gentilis da Foligno (d. 1348), a famous Italian commentator on Avicenna known for his devotion to the text</note>, who is considered the "soul of Avicenna." For since Avicenna’s meanings are everywhere hidden and almost imperceptible because of the author’s—or at least the translator’s—barbaric obscurity, we cannot judge Avicenna otherwise than as he is presented to us by the one considered the chief among his commentators. But then, we ought not to condemn a bad explanation, but rather the author himself, since the author provided the occasion for that same bad explanation. 

This is clearly what we see Avicenna did regarding vipers, of which he listed many species in both his fourth and fifth books, as we have shown before. Yet, the viper is a single species according to **Aristotle, Nicander, Dioscorides, and Galen** <note>the foundational Greek authorities on biology and medicine</note>. Even Avicenna himself seems to have followed these authors in part, such as when he notes that difference in the teeth of male and female vipers, which Nicander and Galen also noted in the viper as a single species. Unless, perhaps, Avicenna—who took the viper, which is a species, for a genus—mistakenly attributed the specific characteristics of the viper to other snakes as well. 

**Albertus Magnus** <note>13th-century German scholar and theologian</note> seems to have imitated this twofold error of Avicenna in the twenty-fifth book of his work *On Animals*. There, after dividing the genus of vipers into species according to Avicenna—of which he says there are many: some called *alelifati* <note>a Latinization of an Arabic term for a type of viper</note>, others *quercinae* <note>original: "quercinas"; literally "oak-vipers"</note>, others *sitire facientes* <note>original: "sitire facientes"; literally "those that make one thirsty," referring to the Dipsas snake</note>, and the rest which he promises to discuss—he later adds these words:
> "Furthermore, a great diversity occurs in serpents regarding the sharpness..."

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of the viper, specifically addressing the differences between male and female serpents in terms of their teeth and the potency of their venom, contrasting the views of medieval authorities like Albertus Magnus with ancient Greek and Arabic sources.</meta>

# ON SERPENTS.

> » <note>original: "tate"; likely the suffix of a word from the preceding page describing the intensity</note> [intensi]ty and the dullness of the venom, according to the male and female sex, even though they are of the same species. For the males have fewer teeth, but more venom—and a sharper venom—than the females. As for the saying that females are worse than the males, this is understood to refer to the bite, insofar as their bite involves a greater number of teeth. Thus says **Albertus** <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a medieval German Dominican friar and philosopher who wrote extensively on natural history</note>.

Perhaps, however, what Albertus states as a universal truth is not true for all serpents, as he seems to suggest, but only for one species: namely, the **viper**. For regarding this creature, **Nicander**, **Dioscorides**, **Galen**, and **Paulus** <note>These are the primary authorities of Greek medicine: Nicander (toxicology), Dioscorides (pharmacology), Galen (systemic medicine), and Paul of Aegina (surgery and encyclopedic medicine)</note> all testify together that the males are more deadly than the females. They also agree that the females have more teeth while the males have fewer—though they do not mean just any teeth, as we also stated near the beginning of this work, but specifically the **canine teeth** <term>canini dentes: the prominent fangs used for injecting venom</term>.

Among other serpents, however, there is no shortage of **Arabic authors** <note>Referring to the Islamic Golden Age physicians like Avicenna or Rhazes</note> who assert the exact opposite: namely, that the females are worse than the males. As for Albertus’s claim that this "worseness" should be understood by the bite due to the number of teeth—this might be plausible in the bite of **elephants** and other wild beasts that possess large, hooked teeth. However, in serpents, this reasoning is not to be accepted. In their case, we should not look at the "crowd" of wounds—which are sometimes so small that it looks as if a needle had pricked the skin—but rather at the harmful **venom** <note>original: "uirus"</note> itself. This venom can be more destructive even if it is pressed in by fewer teeth, as has been proven by experience in the species of the viper.

In other types of serpents, however, I believe neither point has been sufficiently explored: neither whether the females truly have more teeth than the males, nor whether they are less fatal in their venom. For as we said before, the opinions of physicians regarding venom remain conflicted. Regarding the number of teeth, even **Aristotle** seems to be in doubt. In the second book of his *History of Animals*, while discussing the teeth of various animals, he writes these words:

> » Those called **canines** <note>original: "canini"</note> separate the flat teeth from the sharp ones; they share the nature of both, being somewhat wide at the base and somewhat sharp at the tip. Males have more teeth than females, as is evident in the race of humans, sheep, pigs, and goats. In

# NICCOLÒ LEONICENO

For the rest, nothing has been proven as to which have more teeth. From these words of **Aristotle**, I think it is also clear what we said at the beginning of the work against **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the influential Persian physician whose "Canon of Medicine" Leoniceno frequently corrected</note>: that it is one thing to speak of teeth in general, and another to speak of those called **canines** <term>canini dentes: the long, pointed fangs used by predators and venomous snakes to pierce or grip</term>. Regarding other serpents, however, they determine nothing, just as Aristotle leaves it in doubt for all animals, except for man, the pig, the sheep, and the goat.

To further excuse both ourselves and the translators of **Serapion** <note>likely Serapion the Younger, an Arabic author on medicinal simples</note> and Avicenna—who often translate "tyrus" for "viper," as if they meant "therium" <note>original: "tirum, quasi therium." ### ON SERPENTS

...the one we cited before, he concealed. He seems, however, to have wanted to resolve another point regarding the serpent elsewhere—namely, in the first book, chapter VIII of *On the Diversity of Animals*, regarding those things which pertain to their common genera—where he writes as follows:

> The genera of animals, besides these, are not called "large genera" because they do not contain many species; rather, some among them are simple, receiving no formal division within themselves, and these are ultimate species <term>species ultimae: the lowest level of classification that cannot be divided into further sub-types</term>, such as man. Others, however, through formal differences, have diverse modes but do not have proper names for the species that are known to us. Then, a few verses later, he adds these words: Furthermore, the genus of serpents is one of the simple genera of animals—not because it is not divided into species, but because the names of the subordinate species are not known to us; however, the *tyrus* <note>original: "tirus." Often referring to a specific venomous serpent or a viper used in the medicinal "theriac"</note> and the viper are known to us.

In these words, **Albertus** <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a medieval philosopher and scientist who attempted to catalog all known natural history</note> suggests that the serpent is a simple genus, just like man, but for a different reason: not because it is not divided into species, but because those species into which it is divided lack names, except for the *tyrus* and the viper. To say such things, I do not know to whom it would be less appropriate than Albertus, who—besides the *tyrus* and the viper—names so many subordinate species of serpents in Book XXV (where he treats serpents), such as the **asp**, the **horned viper** <term>cerastes: a desert viper with horn-like scales over its eyes</term>, the **situla**, and whatever others he has multiplied in vain. 

Furthermore, a thing is not called a "simple genus" merely because its subordinate species lack their own names. On the contrary, according to **Aristotle** in the first book of *The History of Animals*—the very chapter from which Albertus seems to have taken this division of the simple genus—the opposite appears to be true. For such a genus that can indeed be divided into species (even if they are not distinct by names) is actually opposed to a "simple genus." In that passage, Aristotle uses "simple genus" to mean a simple species—that is, the "most specific" species <term>species specialissima</term> which cannot be divided into further species, such as man. For these are the words of Aristotle, from the passage where we said Albertus took his division of the simple genus:

### ON SERPENTS.

> ...on bricks, then let it be prepared with an equal quantity of its own vinegar mixed with honey in half-measure.

<margin>Lute of wisdom</margin>
These are indeed the words of **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian physician whose *Canon of Medicine* was the standard medical text in Europe for centuries</note>, who incorrectly substituted "lute of wisdom" <term>lutum sapientiæ: a specialized sealing clay used by early chemists and alchemists to airtight-seal laboratory vessels</term> for gypsum <note>original: "gypso"</note>, since it is not gypsum, as is clear from the exposition of **Dinus** <note>Dino del Garbo (d. 1327), an influential Italian physician and commentator on Avicenna</note> on these words. However, we do not reject this exposition of Dinus, but rather another one, in which he writes that serpents in general—according to the opinion of authors whom he does not name—possess the property of preventing the growth of scrofulas <term>scrofulas: a form of tuberculosis affecting the lymph nodes of the neck, often called "the King's Evil"</term>. I, however, believe that by "serpent" in the works of **Paul** <note>Paulus Aegineta (c. 625–690), a Byzantine Greek physician</note> and also Avicenna (who took the same recipe from Paul), we should understand not just any serpent, but specifically the **viper** <note>original: "uiperam"</note>, which, as **Dioscorides** <note>A Greek physician and botanist whose *De materia medica* was the foundational text on pharmacology</note> testifies, prevents the growth of strumas <term>strumas: another term for scrofulous swellings</term> or scrofulas. Truly, as far as this is concerned, the error may be considered the commentator Dinus's own. 

Another error belongs to Avicenna himself, who says that a serpent roasted in an oven ought to be mixed with an equal portion of its own vinegar; yet in Paul's work, no mention is made of vinegar, but rather of the **ash** <note>original: "cinere"</note> which remains from the roasting of the serpent in the furnace. According to Paul, this ash should be mixed not with vinegar, but with an equal portion of **fenugreek** <note>original: "fœno græco"</note>, and finally prepared with honey. Therefore, since Dinus, the commentator on Avicenna, could not divine what exactly "the vinegar of a serpent" was, he intentionally left this difficulty untouched. Avicenna spoke more clearly about this vinegar of the serpent in the second book of his *Canon*, in the chapter *On the Serpent*, where he writes as follows:

> When its skin—that is, the serpent's, for he is speaking of the serpent—is boiled in wine and distilled into the ear, it settles its pain; and the mouth is rinsed with the vinegar in which its skin is boiled to treat toothache.

But because the medicine belongs to Paul, who instructs that ash rather than vinegar be taken, I believe it is more correct that the same medicine be prepared from ash and honey with fenugreek, as we have said—especially since even in Avicenna, the dead serpent is not boiled in vinegar, but in a brick oven, as appeared from his words, which [describe] the roasting of the serpent rather than...

<margin>II</margin> Although Avicenna ascribes not just one property of the viper, but several others in that same chapter to the "serpent" simply, writing from the very start that a preparation cooked from a serpent with water, salt, and vinegar is administered, sometimes with oil added, and that its salt is administered, which has the same potency as the flesh. 

However, **Dioscorides**, **Galen**, **Paul**, and **Pliny** among our authorities have handed these traditions down not regarding every species of serpent, but only regarding the **viper**. It is from the viper's flesh that they taught how to prepare the salt which we said is called <term>theriacum</term> <note>original: "theriacum": from the Greek *therion* (wild beast/serpent), it refers to a famous ancient "universal" antidote</note> by the Greeks and <term>viperine</term> <note>original: "uiperinum"</note> by the Latins, which possesses—as Avicenna says—equal power with the viper’s flesh. 

But salt of this kind, as well as <term>theriac lozenges</term> <note>original: "trocisci theriaci": medicinal discs or pastilles made from viper flesh</note>, are made from the viper alone. Therefore, Avicenna is incorrect to attribute to all serpents what is peculiar to a single species. That he is speaking of the serpent in general and not a specific species from the start is indicated by Avicenna’s own words, which follow:

,, "But we shall speak of the species of serpents in Book IV."

It is as if he had spoken of the serpent in general up to this point, and of their flesh as it pertains to the use of <term>medicine</term>, intending to distinguish the individual species later in the fourth book. Finally, all the words he subsequently adds in this chapter regarding the serpent's flesh—such as that its drying effect is strong but its heating is not intense—and indeed all the effects and properties reported by Avicenna regarding the serpent in general, are those which **Dioscorides**, **Galen**, **Paul**, and **Pliny** likewise record only for the **viper**. <margin>The dangerous errors of Avicenna.</margin>

There is no error in **Avicenna** that is not dangerous to human health, given the man’s massive authority in this day and age. It is even more perilous when dealing with medicines derived from serpents; these cannot be evaluated without risk, let alone when a mistake is made concerning them. If we wish to defend the man to whom our century has given the leadership in medicine against such a great error, we must say that in the aforementioned second chapter of the <term>Canon</term>, he meant the specific serpent known as the **viper** by the general name "serpent." In this matter, **Pliny** is to be listened to only insofar as he wishes both to be crocodiles of their own specific kind, and not that two species—one terrestrial, the other fluvial <note>River-dwelling</note>—are contained under one and the same closest genus called "crocodile." For just as the "river horse" <note>original: "equus fluviatilis"; referring to the hippopotamus</note> is named a "horse" equivocally, and the "sea dog" <note>original: "canis marinus"; usually referring to a shark or a seal</note> is not a true dog but is called a dog by a certain similarity, so too is the terrestrial crocodile called a "crocodile." 

Although neither that "dog" is simply called a dog, nor this "crocodile" simply a crocodile, but rather by the full names "sea dog" and "terrestrial crocodile"—just as the **skink** <term>scincus: a type of lizard, specifically the medicinal skink, often used in ancient pharmacology</term> is named a "terrestrial crocodile" solely because of the same similarity it holds to the river crocodile. And it is, as **Dioscorides** <note>A Greek physician and the author of "De Materia Medica," a foundational pharmacopeia</note> says, a crocodile of its own specific kind. **Pliny** also testifies in his twenty-eighth book that the same **skink** is called by some the "terrestrial crocodile." Yet he himself in book eight said it was not a crocodile, but only similar to a crocodile. Therefore **Galen** <note>A prominent Greek physician and philosopher whose views dominated Western medical science for centuries</note>, in his eleventh book *On Simple Medicine*, where he speaks of the dung of the land crocodile, began in this manner: 

> Of these terrestrial crocodiles, which are small and creep upon the ground, the dung, and the rest. 

It is as if by this way of speaking **Galen** wished to signify to us that terrestrial crocodiles are not true crocodiles, but only small crocodiles that creep on the ground, just as 
<margin>Pygmies.</margin>

> ” The other is, of course, the terrestrial crocodile, similar to the river-dwelling one but much smaller in size. It lives only on land and among the most fragrant flowers; for this reason, its intestines are diligently sought after, filled as they are with a pleasant scent. They call this substance **crocodilea** <term>crocodilea: a substance derived from the "land crocodile" or skink, highly prized in antiquity as a cosmetic and eye medicine</term>, which is most useful for ailments of the eyes when applied with leek juice, and against cataracts <note>original: "suffusiones"</note> or dimness of vision. Applied with henna oil <note>original: "oleo cyprino"</note>, it also removes irritations arising on the face, and with water, it treats all diseases that spread across the face. It restores luster and removes freckles, pimples, and all spots.

<margin>The excrement of the crocodile.</margin>
However, I believe that one should read "excrement" rather than "intestines," and consequently adjust the rest of the following words—namely, that **crocodilea** is "most useful" <note>Leoniceno is making a grammatical point: in the Latin text, the adjective "utilissimam" (feminine) agrees with "crocodilea" (feminine), whereas "intestina" is neuter. This suggests the substance itself, not the organs, is the focus.</note>—just as the requirements of the Latin language demand. For it is not the intestines that are sought for the powers listed by **Pliny**, but rather the excrement, to which even **Galen** says the luxuries of women have given a high price; for so many other medicines for brightening and polishing the face were not enough for them, unless they also used the dung of animals for the same effect. But if someone wishes to defend the manuscript to the letter and read "intestines" instead of "excrement," then it will nonetheless be necessary to admit that those same intestines are not sought for their own sake, but for the sake of the excrement contained within them; and it will become necessary to understand "scent" <note>original: "nidorem"</note> as referring to the fragrant substance itself, which **Pliny** adds afterward is called **crocodilea**. Nor is it truly very surprising that the dung of this animal is fragrant...

<summary>Leoniceno identifies a corruption in Pliny the Elder's Natural History, arguing that ancient cosmetic "crocodilea" was actually the fragrant dung of the land crocodile (skink), not its intestines. He uses both grammatical analysis and the medical authority of Galen to support this correction of the Latin text.</summary>

...because it lives on the most fragrant flowers: for nature so provides that the excrement reflects the scent of the food consumed. Let these things concerning crocodiles be added by us to this work as a surplus <note>original: "ex superabundanti," meaning an additional or parenthetical discussion</note>, since we wished to prove, against **Albertus** <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), the medieval polymath who often categorized animals into broad families or "genera"</note>, that the crocodile is not a genus, as he believes, but a single species, just as **Aristotle** thinks. This proof was not entirely outside the purpose of the work, in which we intended to treat not only the **dipsas** <term>dipsas: a legendary serpent whose bite was said to cause an unquenchable thirst</term>, but many other serpents with which the crocodile shares a venomous bite—similar to a rabid dog—as witnessed by physicians who record it among other animals whose venom is harmful to humans. Although **Aristotle** in the seventh book of his *History of Animals* appears to hold the opposite view, stating that this poison does not harm humans specifically, while it is fatal to other animals. For in the cited book, as translated by **Theodorus** <note>Theodorus Gaza (c. 1398–1475), whose Latin translations of Aristotle were the humanist standard</note>, he writes: 

> Dogs suffer from three diseases: rabies, quinsy <term>angina: here referring to a throat infection or swelling in animals</term>, and gout. Rabies causes madness, and all things they bite become rabid, except for man. 

<margin>A passage of **Aristotle** is corrected.</margin>
However, this passage has stirred great disputes between me and certain grammarians and physicians who support them. Indeed, I was the first who judged this passage in **Aristotle** to be faulty and in need of complete correction, yet with only a small erasure—changing just one or two letters—by reading *pasin* <note>original Greek: πᾶσιν, meaning "all"</note> instead of *plen* <note>original Greek: πλὴν, meaning "except"</note>. Thus, it should be interpreted as "including man," rather than "excepting man." 

For it is patently false that a human bitten by a rabid dog never goes mad. I have proved through a long dissertation against the aforementioned grammarians and physicians—dedicated to the most eminent Cardinal of the Roman Church, named **Alessandro Farnese** <note>Alessandro Farnese (1468–1549), the future Pope Paul III; Leoniceno was a prominent figure in his intellectual circle</note>—that humans fall into madness from the same bite, though more slowly than other animals. Although this correction of the Greek codex, first devised by me, carries great probability—since both reason and experience agree with it—I do not trust it so much that I judge it a fixed opinion, until it is first published and all learned...

...I have advised those who are exceptionally learned and well-read that if they could think of any better way to defend the credibility of the Greek codex and **Theodore’s** translation <note>Theodorus Gaza (c. 1398–1475), a key humanist translator of Aristotle</note>, they would please me no less than they would the spirit of **Theodore** himself. I too have often labored to achieve this very thing—namely, to preserve both the Greek phrasing and **Theodore's** translation—and I have devised various ways in which this might be possible. One among others seemed more probable: if we were to adapt a specific meaning to **Aristotle's** words, whether in Greek or Latin. This interpretation suggests that man is not excepted because *no* human ever contracts rabies, but because *not every* human does. It is as if the human species possesses this prerogative over others: that some individuals within it are endowed by nature with such a constitution that, even when bitten by a rabid dog, they do not contract the disease—a gift that nature has granted to no other kind of living creature. For if we believe **Aristotle**, everything that a rabid dog bites goes mad, except for man.

Evidence that there are indeed certain men who do not go mad when bitten by a rabid dog can be found in the **Psylli** of Libya and the **Marsi** of Italy <note>Two ancient groups famously reputed to be immune to snake venom and capable of charming serpents</note>, who are as unaffected by the venom of a rabid dog as they are by that of serpents. And what you might find more marvelous is that they promise they can bestow this same security upon other men through a certain incantation, which they call *zurmare* <term>zurmare: a term for snake-charming or chanting, likely derived from a medieval or local Italian vernacular</term>. 

Furthermore, from the writings of **Rufus** <note>Rufus of Ephesus, a major Greek physician of the 1st/2nd century AD</note> and **Posidonius** <note>Posidonius (c. 135–51 BC), a Stoic philosopher who wrote on natural history</note>, we have the story of a certain philosopher who, having been bitten by a rabid dog, remained so constant in mind and so firm in his wisdom that he confirmed his own opinion in this matter: 

<margin>A dog has no business with the bath.</margin> 

that a dog should have no business with a bath <note>original: "nullum posse esse cani cum balneo commertium." This refers to the symptom of hydrophobia, where the patient dreads water</note>. Even though the symptoms manifested in him just as they do in others—who, seized by the fear of water following such a bite, believe they see a dog in the water—this philosopher was saved by his perseverance of mind. But what prevents other men, whether they be philosophers or not, from being saved by a similar use of reason? Since the faculty of reasoning is entirely absent in brute animals, it is no wonder that all beasts bitten by a rabid dog go mad and perish from the disease,

...they die, as **Aristotle** says. But a man who is in control of his own mind <note>original: "suæ mentis compos" — meaning sane or conscious</note> sometimes escapes, though not without great danger. **Julius Pollux** <note>A 2nd-century Greek scholar and rhetorician</note> also suggests that such a meaning should be attributed to the words of **Aristotle**, whose opinion we are debating, in the fifth volume of his book titled the *Onomasticon*. > \>\> Rabies is cured with difficulty; gout is altogether incurable; quinsy leads to death. 
> \>\> Whatever a rabid dog bites, it kills. Only man escapes, though not without danger.

These are the words of **Julius Pollux**. If we want his words to agree with what **Aristotle** writes *On Dogs*, they carry this meaning: that out of every kind of animal, the human species is the only one in which some individuals, after being bitten by a rabid dog, sometimes neither go mad nor die from the madness. Any other animal, however, dies from that same bite. The cause of this could be the greater natural difference between a human and a beast than between one beast and another. 

Our previous correction of the manuscript also relied on this reasoning, in which we judged that the word *prius* <note>meaning "before" (adverb of time)</note> should be read instead of the exceptive word *praeter* <note>meaning "except"</note>. This method, touched upon a little while ago, changes nothing of the Greek text and preserves **Theodore’s** translation <note>Theodorus Gaza's Latin translation of Aristotle</note>. Yet even this is not entirely free from dispute and controversy. For who would dare to affirm that no other animal besides man can be found which, because of the resistance of its own <term>temperament</term> <note>The balance of "humors" or bodily qualities (hot, cold, wet, dry) thought to determine health</note>, might—just like a man—occasionally not suffer from canine rabies, despite having endured the bite of a rabid dog? 

Indeed, **Nicolò of Florence** <note>Niccolò Falcucci (d. 1412), a famous Italian physician known for his massive medical encyclopedia</note>, a physician of the weightiest authority, testifies about a certain rabid dog that bit a youth, leading him to madness and eventually to death. Yet that same dog tore the skin of a goose with its teeth, causing a great flow of blood, but it affected the goose with no other ill besides the wound itself. Now...

Let readers judge for themselves how many difficulties this passage in **Aristotle** contains. Some of our friends, failing to notice these problems, seemed to themselves to have won a great victory over us; they rejected our <term>emendation</term> <note>original: "castigatione" — a scholarly correction of a manuscript text</note> and, as they thought, devised a new reasoning. This was not drawn from **Aristotle’s** own teachings, as they claimed, but was a futile search for grammatical excuses, since they could find no other source. Yet, our initial correction of the manuscript avoids all those contradictions that **Aristotle's** words fall into if he truly wrote them as they are found in almost all the Greek copies. For according to our correction, it is not necessary that every single animal, without exception, goes mad when bitten by a rabid dog; rather, it suggests that if they *do* go mad, man might be the first to suffer <note>The author is debating the sequence or likelihood of infection across species</note> for the reasons mentioned above—the same reasons why they more easily suffer the contagion and die. But enough of these matters; as I have said, we have discussed them at length in a much larger work, dedicated long ago to the most learned and most holy Cardinal of the Roman Church, **Alessandro Farnese** <note>The future Pope Paul III, a significant patron of the arts and sciences</note>. Now the time has come to bring an end to this new work, lest if it progresses any further, it might truly seem to earn the title of *Dipsas*—bringing no less thirst to its readers through its excessive length than the serpent brings to those touched by its venom. Only one thing seems to remain: if it pleases you, **Lucretia Borgia** <note>The famous Duchess of Ferrara, to whom this work is dedicated</note>, you who are so diligent a searcher of the wonders in the contemplation of nature, let us briefly describe the image of the *dipsas* so that its form may be set before your Excellence. The *dipsas* is a serpent smaller than our common viper. Some, however, record that it is a <term>cubit</term> <note>About 18 inches or 45 centimeters</note> long, with a head narrower than a viper's; its tail is thin and, in its furthest parts, a pale yellowish color. ## A LETTER FROM NICOLÒ LEONICENO ON THE TIRO
### or viper, to the distinguished physician Alexander Agathimerus of Venice.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'F' depicting a figure seated in a landscape with a tree and distant buildings, framed by stylized floral scrollwork.</image-desc>

Ferrando, a distinguished surgeon of our age, recently returned from Venice to Ferrara and brought me many greetings in your name. Since I was inquiring with great curiosity about you—as a most dear friend and godfather, as well as a former, most beloved pupil—he reported things that brought me immense pleasure. Specifically, he told me that you practice the art of medicine with the highest praise in your homeland, and are especially approved for the fact that, in the works of this art, you follow not the common opinions of the younger physicians, but the most proven of the ancients, such as **Hippocrates** and **Galen** particularly. Furthermore, you most consistently defend their traditions and teachings against those who think otherwise. 

Most recently, however, a doubt arose among the Venetian physicians—truly excellent men—regarding the composition of theriac <note>A complex medicinal compound used as an universal antidote; its ingredients, especially the specific type of snake flesh required, were a matter of intense academic debate</note>. Ferrando asserted to me that you were the one who strongly opposed the common opinion concerning the "Tiro" serpent <note>original: "tiro"—referring to the Tyrus snake mentioned in ancient medical recipes</note> brought from Syria. You contended in a most sharp dispute that for the foreign "Tiro" serpent, one ought to accept the viper or "marasso" <note>original: "maraſſum"—a local Italian name for the common viper</note> familiar to Italy. 

He added that you often wished I had been present at that same dispute. But since that did not happen, he further requested me in your name that I should write out for you in a fuller discourse the reasons I hold regarding that opinion. You have often heard me approving this view in Ferrara, and you yourself judge it to be most true. Although I touched upon these points briefly and succinctly in my book *On the Errors of Pliny and Other Physicians* <note>Leoniceno’s most famous work, which applied humanist philology to correct long-standing botanical and medical mistakes in Pliny the Elder's Natural History</note>, you asked me to confirm my judgment on this same matter even more strongly than I did there. I shall indeed do what you ask gladly, although I know it to be an arduous and difficult task.

<summary>In this opening letter, Nicolò Leoniceno praises his former student Agathimerus for upholding ancient medical authorities and agrees to provide a detailed argument for using local Italian vipers instead of imported Syrian snakes in the production of theriac.</summary>

<keywords>Nicolò Leoniceno, Alexander Agathimerus, Theriac, Tiro serpent, Viper, medical philology, Galen, Hippocrates, Ferrara, Venice</keywords>

# NICOLÒ LEONICENO
<meta>catchword: Who</meta>

...difficult. Since I am about to write something that seems to greatly oppose the highest authority of men of medicine, and also the opinions of many. But we should not fear to defend the truth against those who have declared in their own books: Whoever contradicts another, if he does so for the sake of protecting the truth, ought to be held free from all blame. Nor should the unrefined crowd be valued so highly that we remain silent about what is extremely necessary for life just because it is less popular with them—especially since we subject our work not to the scales of the common people, but to the judgment of the learned.

Avicenna the Arab <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the influential Persian physician whose "Canon of Medicine" was a standard textbook</note> seems to have believed that the **Tiro** serpent is different from the **viper** in the fifth volume of his book *On Medicine*. Indeed, in various descriptions of theriac <note>A famous ancient "universal antidote" that required snake flesh as a key ingredient</note>, he sometimes ordered the use of **troches** <note>original: "trociscos"—small medicinal cakes or lozenges made from processed meat or herbs</note> of the *tiro*, and at other times troches made from vipers. Because of this, many younger physicians of great name in medicine, following (as I believe) the authority of Avicenna, have come to believe that some troches are made from vipers and others from the *tiro*. 

Gentile <note>Gentile da Foligno (d. 1348), a famous Italian physician and commentator on Avicenna</note>, who was also an expositor of this same Avicenna, interprets the "viper" in this author's work not as the *tiro*, nor as one specific type of serpent, but as a term common to many genera or species. For these are the words of Gentile regarding the book by Avicenna that we mentioned:

> "Viper" is used for common serpents, not for those which bite off the head of the male of their species when he mates with her, wherefore the children, seeking vengeance for their father, tear the mothers apart <note>A widespread ancient myth, recorded by Herodotus and Pliny, used to explain the "live-bearing" nature of vipers compared to other snakes</note>.

<margin>Niccolò of Florence.</margin>
Niccolò of Florence <note>Niccolò Falcucci (d. 1412), author of a massive medical encyclopedia</note> also, in his fourth discourse, eighteenth chapter, writing *On the species of serpents, and the tiro, and the viper*, says now one thing, and then another. He speaks not so much from his own opinion as from the opinions of other authors whose writings he collects. For sometimes he suggests the viper is a species of horned serpent (to use his own words) born in Egypt, and he cites Avicenna saying that the "dragons" which kill are of this kind. Not long after, based on the authority of Aristotle, he gives the name *tiros* to serpents that lay eggs but keep the eggs inside themselves until they hatch <note>A description of ovoviviparity, which is characteristic of vipers</note>.

<summary>Leoniceno argues against the medieval tradition (led by Avicenna) that distinguished the "Tiro" from the "Viper," citing various scholarly contradictions regarding their biological nature.</summary>
