<page-num>311</page-num>
-># ON THE TIRO OR THE VIPER.<-

These *tiri* <note>original: "tiri"—a term derived from the Arabic word for vipers, frequently used in medieval Latin medical translations</note>, as we shall prove by the testimony of the same Aristotle, are vipers, which are found in great numbers not only in Egypt, but also in our own soil. The same Nicolus <note>Likely referring to Nicolaus Rheginus or another medieval translator/commentator</note> adds that there are "third-order" serpents—slender and long—named vipers, and that these are the ones specifically found among us. He notes that some are of lesser malice while others are of greater, to the point that they are nearly the same as the "deaf" serpents <note>original: "proximi surdis"—a reference to the "deaf adder" or "asp," a common folkloric and biblical description for certain venomous snakes</note> and are classified among the asps. The same author writes elsewhere in that same chapter as follows:

> Concerning the bad vipers, they are also found among us; and of these, some are short and thick, called in our local language the *scorzon* <note>original: "scorzon"—likely the Italian *scorzone*, a regional name for the common European viper or the grass snake</note>.

From these words, it appears that he also included several types of serpents under the name of "vipers," to the point that he even called asps "vipers." For he also cites Galen writing in the book *On Theriac, to Caesar* <note>A treatise on the universal antidote theriac, traditionally attributed to Galen</note> in this way:

> It is told of the Queen of Egypt <note>Cleopatra</note> that she killed herself by placing her hand upon a *tiro*, and she died at the very hour of its application.

But Galen, in his book *On Theriac, to Piso*, testifies to such an effect not regarding a *tiro* or a viper, but regarding the asp—a different kind of serpent. Indeed, bad translations—as anyone may see for themselves—have given even the greatest authorities of medicine an occasion for wandering into error. For example, Bartholomæus Montagnana <note>An influential 15th-century professor of medicine at Padua</note>, an illustrious physician of his time, fell into the same error, as I believe, for a similar reason. For in a certain consultation, he cites Galen from the eleventh book of *On Simple Medicine*, claiming that Galen calls the *tiro* an *echidna* <note>The Greek word for viper</note>. This much is correct, for by *echidna*, Galen understood the *tiro* or viper, as we ourselves shall soon declare. However, what he adds afterward is partly true and partly false; and if we consider the citation as a whole—if I may speak with the indulgence of such a great man—it is entirely false. For the same Montagnana writes thus:

<margin>Montagnana's error.</margin>

> ...and when you have well examined his words—namely, those of Galen—you will see that there is a species of *tiro* which Galen calls there the *marassum* <note>original: "marassum"—likely referring to the *marasso*, the common European adder</note>, and in truth, it is a species of asp.

In these words, there are two errors: First...

He specifically critiques the misattribution of Cleopatra's death to a "tiro" rather than an asp in medieval texts.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Nicolò Leoniceno’s philological investigation into the naming of serpents. Having previously discussed the "Tiro," he now addresses the confusion between the names of ancient peoples and the names of snakes, while critiquing the errors of medieval and contemporary medical authorities like Montagnana and Gentile da Foligno regarding the ingredients of the medicine known as theriac.</meta>

<page-num>312</page-num>
<header>NICOLÒ LEONICENO</header>

...because he says that Galen, in the book cited earlier, calls the *echidna* <note>original: "echidnam"—the Greek term for a viper</note> or the *tiro* <note>the Arabic-derived term for a viper</note> by another name, the *marassus*. In truth, Galen did not name any serpents *marassi* or *matrassi*, but spoke only of certain men called the **Marsi** <note>The Marsi were an ancient people of Italy renowned in antiquity for their skills as snake-charmers and healers</note>. Galen says that these men hunted *echidnas* (or vipers) in Rome, and that he asked them several questions about vipers, which he calls by no other name there than *echidnas*. 

Now it occurs to me to laugh at the wit of a certain man of letters who, through slander, charged me with a similar error. He claimed that I was led by no other conjecture to think that vipers were the serpents commonly called *marassi*, except for the fact that Galen, in the eleventh book of *On Simple Medicine*, mentions vipers and the **Marsi** who hunt them at the same time. He suggested that I had ignorantly mistaken the name Galen gave to a people as if it were a name for *marassi* serpents. As if we had not learned those tribal names while sitting in the school for boys! If we had said such a thing while still wailing in our cradles, perhaps we might be seen as overly arrogant.

Another error is that of **Montagnana** <note>Bartolomeo Montagnana (d. 1460), a famous professor of medicine at Padua</note>, who classifies the *echidna*—which is the viper or *tiro*, as he himself admits—as a kind of asp. This is despite the fact that Galen, in his book *On Theriac, to Piso*, clearly distinguishes *echidnas* (or vipers) from asps. In that work, Galen investigates the reason why vipers are preferred over other serpents, such as the basilisk and the various kinds of asps, in the composition of **theriac** <note>original: "theriaces"—a famous ancient "universal antidote" containing dozens of ingredients, including fermented viper flesh</note>. 

In that same passage, Galen also provides the reason why vipers are not used whole for medical purposes; rather, the head in particular must be cut off. This is because the head is especially venomous in a viper, for as they say, when it mates, the female—allured by the sweetness of Venus <note>i.e., sexual pleasure</note>—swallows the male's seed and then bites off his head. These words of Galen also demonstrate that **Gentile** <note>Gentile da Foligno (d. 1348), a highly influential medical commentator</note> was wrong to believe that it was not vipers of this specific nature, but rather certain other common snakes, that were mixed into the antidote called theriac. Furthermore, certain more recent authors—one of whom titled his treatise *The Light of Apothecaries* <note>original: "Lumen apothecariorum"—a work by Quiricus de Augustis</note> and the other *The Greater Light* <note>original: "Luminare maius"—a pharmaceutical manual by Joannes Jacobus de Manliis</note>—have written their own tracts on such matters,

<summary>Leoniceno corrects several medical authorities who confused the Marsi people with snakes called "marassi" and clarifies that vipers are distinct from asps, specifically regarding their use in the medicine theriac.</summary>

<header>->TIRO OR VIPER<-</header>

...they have brought forward, they have not only failed to clarify this doubt concerning the **tiro** <note>original: "tiro" — a term derived from Arabic for the viper</note> and the viper, but have rather enveloped it in a kind of Cimmerian darkness <note>a classical metaphor for total obscurity or ignorance</note>, to the point that from their words we can establish nothing certain about what a *tirus* or a viper is. This is true of **Simon of Genoa** <note>Simon Januensis (13th c.), a famous medical lexicographer</note>, as well as the author of the *Pandects* <note>Matthaeus Silvaticus (14th c.), author of the "Pandectae Medicinae", an encyclopedia of medicines</note>, even though it was the duty of their profession to explain these matters of such vital importance to life, rather than many other things of minor concern. For Simon of Genoa said nothing, as far as I know, about the *tiro* or the viper, while the author of the *Pandects* taught only this: that the *tirus* is a species of serpent. 

The author of the *Luminare Maius* <note>The "Great Lantern," a widely used pharmaceutical manual by Giovanni Giacomo de' Manli (late 15th c.)</note> as well, who by the promise of such a grand title ought to have illuminated the minds of physicians more, seems instead to have spread more confusion. For after bringing forward many things about the *tiro* and viper from various authors, he finally added that there are three species of the *tirus* serpent: one of which is called "viper" in common speech, another "tirus," and the third "hydra"; and that good ones are rarely found in our regions. Indeed, he claims that today a serpent called the **scurcio** <note>a local name for a type of viper or grass snake</note> is found, which is taken for the *tiro*. But I believe there are men today who make **theriac** <note>theriacam — a complex ancient "cure-all" medicine containing dozens of ingredients, including viper flesh</note> without any *tiro* at all. 

Truly, at a time when the said *tiri* were not being found, the **College of Physicians of Venice**—men of such consummate learning that one should never suspect anything escaped them—established a specific recipe for **troches** <note>original: "trociscorum" — medicinal lozenges or tablets used as intermediate ingredients in theriac</note> that could be put into theriac in place of the troches made from *tiro*. This man [the author of the *Luminare Maius*], who was otherwise a good explainer of **simples** <note>original: "simplicium medicamentorum" — medicines made of a single natural ingredient, usually a plant</note> frequently in use, is by no means to be approved in this matter. He has created such a supposed scarcity of *tiri*—both for himself and for the Venetian College—even though there is a great abundance of them in Italy; would that there were not! For even if there is some use for this serpent in medicine, it is nonetheless more harmful for its venom than it is beneficial as a remedy. Therefore, so that we may free our age from this [imagined] shortage of *tiri*, and relieve those who are most eager to prepare theriac from the labor of seeking such serpents all the way from Egypt, we shall explain what at last the *tirus* or the vi-

<meta>This page continues Leoniceno’s argument that modern medical writers are confused about the identity of the "tiro" (viper). <page-num>314</page-num>
<header>NICOLÒ LEONICENO</header>

...works, let us show what we have discovered, in which we may rightly glory; for as appears from what was said before, modern physicians have left behind nothing regarding this animal but obscure, uncertain, inconsistent, and occasionally accidental writings. But to bring some light to this darkness, let us proceed by a certain path and order, and first let us see what **Serapio** <note>Serapion the Younger, a 12th-century Arabic medical author whose work was central to medieval pharmacy</note> writes about the **tiro** <note>original: "tiro" — a medieval term derived from Arabic for the viper used in medicine</note>. These are the words of this author speaking about the flesh of the *tiro*: 

,, **Galen** says: The flesh of the *tiro* heats, dries, and strongly resolves <note>in ancient medicine, "resolving" meant breaking down or dispersing harmful fluids or "humors" in the body</note>, 
,, especially when it has been prepared with oil, salt, dill, leeks, and a 
,, necessary amount of water. As some say, the power of this flesh 
,, is a virtue that miraculously reaches the skin of the body, 
,, expelling the superfluities <note>excess or waste fluids thought to cause disease</note> that are within the body. 

And so on with what follows. Since Galen is cited by Serapio in this passage, we must likewise see where Galen speaks these words concerning the *tiro*. However, Galen never names the *tiro*; he only speaks of the **echidna** <note>original: "echidna" — the Greek word for viper</note>, about which these same words are read in the eleventh book of his work *On Simple Medicine* <note>original: "De simplici medicina"</note>, which are written by Serapio based on Galen’s testimony. These words are found in the Greek manuscript of Galen as follows: 

<note>original Greek: τὰς γοῦν τῶν ἐχιδνῶν σάρκας θερμαινούσας καὶ ξηραινούσας ἐναργῶς ἔστιν ἰδεῖν ἀρτυομένας, ὥσπερ ἐγχέλιας ἐλαίῳ καὶ ἁλσὶν καὶ ἀνήθῳ καὶ πράσῳ καὶ ὕδατι δηλονότι μετὰ τοῦ συμμέτρου, ὅτι δὲ καθαίρουσιν διὰ τοῦ δέρματος ἅπαν σῶμα, γνῶναι σοὶ πάρεστιν.</note>

This is the meaning, if it be necessary to interpret the Greek language for others who are ignorant of it (though not for you): 

*One may see that the flesh of vipers clearly heats and dries, if they are prepared just like eels with oil, salt, dill, and leek, and with water added in the proper measure. Moreover, you may recognize that they purge the entire body through the skin.*

In the same chapter, Serapio also alleges that **Dioscorides** <note>Pedanius Dioscorides (1st century AD), author of "De materia medica," the primary authority on substances used in medicine for 1,500 years</note> wrote about the flesh of the *tiro* the same words that the Greek author produced regarding the *echidna*. I deliberately pass over these quotes for the sake of avoiding wordiness, leaving it free for anyone to look them up in their proper place; once a comparison of both authors has been made, one may judge whether what we have said is true.

<meta>catchword: Rightly, therefore</meta>

He argues that the confusion in modern medicine stems from a failure to recognize these terms as referring to the same animal.</summary>

<page-num>315</page-num>
# ON THE TIRO OR VIPER.

Therefore, as we wrote before, **Montagnana** <note>Bartolomeo Montagnana, a famous 15th-century professor of medicine at Padua</note> correctly perceived that the *tiro* or viper is called the **echidna** <note>original: "echidnam" — the Greek term for viper</note> by **Galen**. However, he was not entirely faithful when he also added the name **marassus** <note>original: "marassum" — a common or regional name for a viper in Italy</note> because of certain other words that Galen adds in that same chapter on the echidna or viper. Those words are as follows:

> >> I asked those who hunt vipers in Rome, whom they call **Marsi** <note>an ancient Italian people famous for their skills as snake-charmers and healers</note>, if they had any sign to show by which vipers might be distinguished.

However, Montagnana seems to have thought that the relative pronoun "whom" referred not to the hunters, but rather to the vipers; and therefore he thought that echidnas or vipers were called *marassi* by Galen. But he arrived at the truth by chance rather than by reason, led even by his own error. For those creatures which are called echidnae or vipers by Galen are indeed true serpents, commonly called *marassi* by us. We prove this not by reckless or light conjecture, but by an unassailable argument. **Aristotle**, in the first book of his <term>History of Animals</term> <note>original: "De historia animalium" — Aristotle's foundational work on zoology</note>, discussed the echidna in this manner: *But while other snakes lay eggs, the viper alone gives birth to live young.* <note>original Greek: "ἀλλ' οἱ μὲν ἄλλοι ᾠοτοκοῦσιν ὄφεις, ἡ δὲ ἔχιδνα μόνον ζῳοτοκεῖ"</note> This means, as **Theodore** <note>Theodore Gaza, a 15th-century Greek scholar who translated Aristotle into Latin</note>—a man most learned in both Greek and Latin—interpreted it: *While other serpents produce eggs, the viper alone brings forth a live animal.* In the third volume of the same book, Aristotle also wrote about the birth of the echidna in this way: *It is clear that the race of snakes differs both from those mentioned above and among themselves; for while other kinds of snakes lay eggs, the viper alone gives birth to live young, having first produced eggs within itself.* <note>original Greek: "ἔχει δὲ καὶ τὸ τῶν ὄφεων γένος πρός τε ταῦτα καὶ πρὸς ἄλληλα διάφορα: τὰ μὲν γὰρ ἄλλα γένη τῶν ὄφεων ᾠοτοκεῖ, ἔχις δὲ ζῳοτοκεῖ μόνον, ᾠοτοκήσασα ἐν αὑτῇ πρῶτα"</note> This means, as the same Theodore translated it: *It is evident that serpents differ from those mentioned before as well as from one another. The viper produces a live animal after it has produced eggs within itself, while all other kinds of serpents produce eggs out into the light.* Even those words of Aristotle cited above by **Nicolò** <note>Leoniceno referring to himself in the third person or perhaps a specific citation in his own previous argument</note> from the Arabic translation—concerning *tiros* holding eggs within themselves (that is, not laying eggs externally like other serpents, but giving birth to live animals)—seem to suggest this same view, albeit in a barbaric and quite obscure way. For wherever Greek authors, whether physicians or philosophers, have the word "echidna," the Arabic translations substitute the word "tiro,"

<summary>Leoniceno identifies the "tiro" of Arabic medicine as the "echidna" of the Greeks (the viper), noting that its defining characteristic according to Aristotle is giving birth to live young rather than laying eggs.</summary>

[They] state this, which I could demonstrate with many examples, were I not avoiding the tediousness of wordiness. That "viper" means the same thing to the Latins as **echidna** <note>original: "echidna" — the Greek term</note> does to the Greeks is equally superfluous to prove with testimonies from many translations, since the very etymology of the Latin word makes it clearer than light: for with us, the **viper** <note>original: "vipera"</note> received its name from the fact that it **gives birth by force** <note>original: "vi parit" — Leoniceno is citing a popular but scientifically incorrect ancient etymology which claimed the young vipers forced their way out of the mother's side</note>. That the birth of the echidna is violent and destructive to that same beast was taught by **Nicander** <note>a Greek poet and physician from the 2nd century BCE</note> in his <term>Theriaca</term> <note>a famous hexameter poem about venomous animals and their cures</note>, among many other highly approved authors. We have inserted verses from that author on this same subject, translated by us into the Latin language, in our book entitled <term>On the Errors of Pliny and Other Physicians</term> <note>Leoniceno's most famous work, which sparked a massive intellectual debate by pointing out mistakes in ancient Roman natural history</note>.

Therefore, nothing else seems to remain but for us to demonstrate, in the final place, that the viper is the serpent commonly called the **marassus** or the **scurcio** <note>local Italian names for the common viper, still reflected in regional dialects today</note>. Although this itself is already largely proven, especially to those who previously had a perfect understanding of the nature of these *marassi*. The females of these *marassi*, as is evident to the senses, do not produce eggs like other serpents, but give birth to a live animal, and indeed by force. For they have very often been seen hanging from a high branch of a tree, bringing little *marassi* into the light through a ruptured womb <note>This reflects a common Renaissance belief that vipers climbed trees to give birth so that the offspring would fall to the ground and not bite the mother during delivery</note>.

Yet, suppose there is someone who obstinately contends that the *marassus* differs from the viper. Would this stubborn adversary not be openly calling **Aristotle**—and so many other most serious physicians and philosophers who stated the same as Aristotle regarding the viper—a liar? These men attributed this property of bearing a live animal to the viper alone among serpents. If [the adversary were right], then not only the viper, but also another species of serpent, namely the *marassus*, would bear a live animal. Therefore, if it is a sacrilege to charge Aristotle with a lie—from whose findings nature itself does not disagree—as well as so many other great men who interpreted nature, we can conclude as follows: if *marassi* are a genus of serpent distinct from vipers, then the viper is not the only one among serpents that bears a live animal; but since the viper alone from every genus of serpent bears a live animal according to the authority of Aristotle, therefore *marassi* are not [a different]

He identifies these creatures with the local Italian "marassus," using Aristotle's zoological observations to settle the debate over terminology.</summary>

### ON THE TIROS OR VIPER.

[...is not a] genus of serpents different from vipers. I think these things indeed suffice for the learned for the demonstration of that matter which we especially intended to prove: namely, that the **tiros** <note>original: "tirus" — a term used in ancient pharmacy derived from the Greek word for viper</note>, the **viper**, the **marassus**, or the **scurcio** <note>local Italian names for the common viper</note> are the same species of serpent called by different names, and that this single species is most highly commended in the composition of that same antidote by **Andromachus** <note>the court physician to Nero who famously refined the recipe for Theriac</note>, **Galen**, and the other most ancient physicians who wrote about **theriac** <note>a complex "universal antidote" that was one of the most famous medicines in history</note>. Therefore, the *tiros* is not to be imported from Egypt as if it were a snake unknown to our world, nor should other **troches** <note>original: "trocisci" — medicinal lozenges; here specifically referring to processed viper meat used as a theriac ingredient</note> be devised to take the place of those made from the *tiros*.

But these things, as we said, are enough for the learned. It remains that we also satisfy the judgment of the common crowd. For I do not expect that crafty men will be lacking—as most are in our time, treating the art of medicine more by cunning than by learning—who will thus mock the ears of the ignorant: "Everyone, beware of this poisonous medicine of Leoniceno! He orders the *marassus*—a horrendous, pestilential, and deadly serpent, to be feared almost by its very name alone—to be mixed into theriac in place of the *tiros* or viper; into theriac, I say, the antidote against serpent bites and all poisons established by the ancients." For what else is this but to fatally cut the throats of men with new remedies that differ from common use, and to voluntarily offer poisons to those fleeing the dangers of poison? See how great a capacity for slandering among the unwise is available to malicious men.

But our Galen anticipated this objection (which, though frivolous, is persuasive enough) with a learned response, teaching in his treatises on theriac that **poison is the remedy for poison.**
<margin>Poison is the remedy for poison.</margin>
Many other distinguished physicians, among whom **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder, the Roman natural historian</note> can be numbered, likewise taught this, recording that the entrails of the same serpents, when applied, provide help against the otherwise incurable bites of all serpents. They note that the liver of the **water-snake** <note>original: "hydrum"</note>—which is inferior to no other serpent in its poison—brings aid to those struck by them when it is preserved; and that the scorpion...

<meta>This page concludes Nicolò Leoniceno’s treatise. Having argued that the exotic "tirus" and the common viper are one and the same, he finishes by citing the ancient medical principle that a creature's poison often contains its own cure. He then offers a humble closing to his colleague, acknowledging that his findings may be controversial.</meta>

<page-num>318</page-num>
<header>NICOLÒ LEONICENO ON THE TIROS OR VIPER</header>

...furthermore, it is said to oppose the poison of **spotted lizards** <note>original: "stellionum" — the *stellio* or starred lizard was traditionally believed in antiquity to be venomous</note>. They even promise that the same scorpion, when placed upon its own wound or even consumed roasted, is a remedy against its own sting. Likewise, the flesh of vipers not only heals those whom the viper itself has bitten, but they even promise that those who have at some time consumed the cooked liver of a viper will never be struck by serpents. 

But I have already written more, my dear friend <note>original: "compater" — literally "godfather," used here as a term of endearment for a close colleague</note>, than you perhaps expected from me, whom you know to be very busy. However, because I knew I was writing **paradoxes** <note>meaning arguments that go against common opinion or established medical tradition</note>, I was forced to spend as much effort destroying the opinions of others through long discourse as I did confirming my own view with a lengthy explanation. 

If my work is perhaps not approved by those who prefer "to have learned" rather than "to learn" <note>a jab at conservative scholars who refuse to update their knowledge with new evidence</note>, you must urge these men—who are otherwise naturally argumentative—to try to refute my writings with reason, not with mere quibbles. Let them give me the opportunity to either clear up my errors or at least correct them. For I am prepared to retract anything that they demonstrate I have misunderstood, just as is proper for **philosophers**.
